concepts/absolutism-after-1848.title: Absolutism after 1848 (Habsburg)
concepts/absolutism-after-1848.content:
Absolutism after 1848 (Habsburg)
Absolutismus (“absolutism”) is the word Friedjung and Springer use for the monarchical course in the Habsburg lands after the defeat of the revolutions of 1848–49: government without a working representative constitution, the March constitution of 1849 abandoned, and authority concentrated in the emperor, the army, the police, and a central ministry. The legal hinge of the open form was the Silvesterpatent of 31 December 1851; the everyday face of rule in the interior was the administration later nicknamed the Bachsche System (“Bach system”).
After the revolution
In 1849–51 the dynasty recovered Vienna, Hungary, and Italy by arms (Windischgrätz, Radetzky, Haynau, Russian intervention in Hungary). A unitary constitution of 4 March 1849 had been issued under Schwarzenberg; it was not the path the court kept. Friedjung’s second volume opens the domestic story of the 1850s with the Reaktion after Schwarzenberg’s death: Kübeck and Bach, a supreme police authority, curtailed communal autonomy, abolition of jury trial in the criminal code of 1852, and press and conspiracy control under police minister Kempen.
Silvesterpatent and open Absolutismus
The Silvesterpatent abolished the March constitution and the remaining representative scaffolding. Friedjung treats it as the young emperor’s choice of clarity after diets and ministries that claimed national mandates. From then until war and debt forced new experiments in 1860–61, public law spoke the language of monarchical Absolutismus rather than of a negotiated constitution.
Administration, church, nationality
Interior administration under Bach pressed German official language and central offices against the old Hungarian county system and against provincial estate claims. The church settlement culminated in the Concordat of 1855 after the fall of Josephinism’s state controls (Friedjung’s ecclesiastical books). National programmes were met as subjects under one administration, not as separate constitutions—until Magenta and Solferino (1859) and financial strain reopened the October Diploma (1860) and February Patent (1861).
Vocabulary in the sources
Friedjung writes Absolutismus, absolutistisch, zentralistischer Absolutismus, patriarchalischer Absolutismus, and Bachsche System. Springer narrates the same post-revolutionary government as reaction and absolute rule restored. The deposited sources name the regime Absolutismus and the Bachsche System; they do not use a “neo-” compound for this course.
Related
silvesterpatent-1851 · bach-system · bach · kubeck · schwarzenberg · francis-joseph · concordat-1855 · october-diploma-1860 · february-patent-1861 · nationality-question-habsburg
Period name, not a later school label
Austrian deposits (Friedjung, Springer) describe the post-1849 order as restored Absolutismus tempered by modern bureaucracy—the Bach years—after revolutionary constitutions fail. The page refuses later textbook brands; it stays with period terms of absolute administration, suspended diets, and police.
Parallel conservative settlements
Prussia’s conservative constitutionalism under Manteuffel is a cousin, not a copy: a constitution exists but is worked in a monarchical-police key. French Bonapartism is plebiscitary Caesarism rather than Habsburg official absolutism—compare without merging.
Exit ramps
War defeats and financial need reopen constitutional paper (October Diploma, February Patent; Prussian New Era; French liberal empire). Prefer bach-system, october-diploma-1860, february-patent-1861.

concepts/bach-system.title: Bach system
concepts/bach-system.content:
Bach system
The Bachsche System (DE Bachsche System (“Bach system”)) is the name, fixed in Friedjung’s history and in common political speech, for the absolutist (after 1848) interior regime associated with Alexander Bach after the defeat of the 1848–49 revolutions: bureaucratic centralisation, German as the language of internal administration, imperial codes in place of historic particular law, destruction of the old Hungarian county constitution, and police certainty under Kempen that the barricades must not return. It is the domestic face of the settlement whose external face was Olmütz and whose legal charter was the Silvesterpatent.
Elements
Unitary state. The Lands of the Crown of St Stephen were treated as provinces of a single empire, not as a partner kingdom under the April Laws. Military victory and Haynau’s transitional dictatorship passed into civilian prefectures and Gendarmerie.
Language and personnel. German officialdom and career Beamte replaced autonomous Magyar county structures. Contemporaries cried Germanisation; defenders spoke of modern administration and equality of subjects under one sovereign.
Law. Extension of Austrian civil and criminal organisation (including the criminal code of 1852), continuation of Grundentlastung, and judicial redesign through the organisation work in which Bach and Kübeck both sat — allies on centralism, enemies on persons and church policy.
Police and press. Independent police power under Kempen watched former democrats (Bach’s own past included) and smothered open party life. The system’s ideal subject was the apolitical taxpayer and conscript.
Church. The Concordat of 1855 tied ultramontane support to the throne, completing a conservative synthesis that Josephinist bureaucrats like Kübeck found dangerous.
Contradictions
Friedjung records praise for energy — roads of authority, tax yield, apparent order — and condemnation for lack of wisdom among nationalities. The old aristocracy (Windisch-Grätz) saw democracy in bureaucratic dress; Magyars under Deák refused recognition; non-German peoples received equality mainly as equal subordination. After Schwarzenberg’s death the system had no minister-president: Francis Joseph reigned through rival ministers, so “Bach system” names a dominant interior style rather than a single cabinet dictatorship.
Crisis and end
The Italian war of 1859 bankrupted the prestige of bureaucratic absolutism. Bach fell; the October Diploma and February Patent opened competing constitutional paths. The name remained a partisan weapon: for liberals and Magyars, shorthand for oppression; for later centralists, memory of a hard but serious state. In this wiki the concept links bach, silvesterpatent-1851, absolutism-after-1848, and the Hungarian passive resistance that prepared dualism.
Administrative absolutism after victory
Friedjung’s Bach chapters define the system: unified bureaucracy, German as administrative medium, suspended constitutional life, police surveillance, and the claim to modernise the empire from above after 1849. It is Absolutismus of officials, not a return to pure pre-March custom.
Tools
Gendarmerie, censorship, district offices, and the concordat with Rome are the practical instruments. Nationality claims are answered by equal subjection to the same administrative grid rather than by federal diet politics.
Crisis
Magenta–Solferino and financial strain force constitutional experiments that end the pure Bach era. Prefer bach, absolutism-after-1848, nationality-question-habsburg.

concepts/bonapartism.title: Bonapartism
concepts/bonapartism.content:
Bonapartism
Bonapartism in these deposits is the political force that treated the Napoleonic name as a popular and military title to rule France after Waterloo—distinct from legitimism, from Orléanist parliamentary culture, and from republican socialism.
Name without a throne
Delord follows the scattered imperial family and the survival of the name among soldiers and rural France. July Monarchy proscription laws keep Louis-Napoléon a problem; Ham becomes a workshop of popularity—material brochures, friendly provincial press, visits by republican writers including Louis Blanc, correspondence that keeps exterior doors open. Persigny appears as the devotee organizer who fuels the pretender’s imagination and walks the road of Strasbourg and later street work.
From elections to empire
1848 converts name into candidacies and a presidential majority; Lamartine’s eloquence fails to raise a popular barrier; Ledru-Rollin and Louis Blanc speak in validation debates without extinguishing the danger; Barrot’s ministry tries liberal cohabitation and fails; Morny’s coup and the Second Empire turn movement into state. Bonapartism thus claims to stand above parties by direct appeal to people and army—Delord’s critical object from conspiracy through plebiscite.
Continuity into the Liberal Empire
Later liberalization (Ollivier’s Empire libéral) does not erase Bonapartism; it is an argument inside it about how much parliamentary life the Napoleonic executive can absorb. Keep liberal-empire for that phase and this page for the broader force.
Instruments
Beyond the name of Napoleon, Delord and Ollivier show Bonapartism as prefects, official candidates, controlled press, and plebiscite—tools that outlast any single speech about order and glory. Liberal Empire reforms renegotiate those tools without discarding the executive core.
Name and army, name and people
The deposits stress the two constituencies Bonapartism addressed. To the army, the Napoleonic name carried the memory of glory and the promise of careers open to talent—the legend of the colonne and the eagles that the Second Empire’s own iconography renewed. To the rural and popular France, the name carried the order-and-land tradition and, after Ham, the material-reform programme that could speak to workers without class war. It is this double address—above parliament, below parties—that Delord’s critical genealogy identifies as the force’s secret: Bonapartism claimed to be neither right nor left but the nation itself choosing one family to embody its will. The prefect and the plebiscite were its instruments precisely because both reached the individual elector past the assemblies.

concepts/burschenschaften.title: Burschenschaften
concepts/burschenschaften.content:
Burschenschaften
Burschenschaften are the German student associations of the post-1815 generation that Treitschke’s Deutsche Geschichte treats as youthful carriers of national and liberal agitation inside the German Confederation—watched, restricted, and partly broken by Bund and Austrian-led police measures.
Wartime generation
Volunteers of the wars of liberation returned to lecture halls with a language of German unity, Christian-German morals, and hostility to particularist cabinets. The Wartburg festival (1817) stages student nationalism as public theatre; officials read conspiracy. Treitschke follows how university corporations cease to be private clubs and become political symptoms in diet debates and diplomatic notes.
Karlsbad climate and Hambach
Kotzebue’s murder supplies the pretext for the Karlsbad framework of press and university control. Dissolution orders, blacklists, and informants run through Treitschke’s Bund chapters. Hambach (1832) shows the later popular-national festival where student and civilian liberalism meet again under surveillance. The Rhine crisis of 1840 and 1848 Frankfurt later recruit from the same generational vocabulary even when formal Burschenschaft structures have been harried.
Backward glance
Sybel’s Empire-founding history still looks back on student liberalism as pre-history that Prussian state power eventually organizes from above—useful continuity, not a claim that Burschenschaften “caused” 1871. Prefer hambach-festival-1832, metternich-system, and frankfurt-national-assembly-1848-49 for linked episodes.
After Karlsbad
Treitschke follows student corporations under Bund police pressure after Kotzebue’s assassination and the Karlsbad decrees. Membership bans, surveillance, and exile paths still leave a generational language of Burschenschaft idealism that reappears in 1832 Hambach and 1848 assembly rhetoric.
Student nationalism after the Wars of Liberation
Treitschke’s early volumes and Beilagen treat the Burschenschaften (“student fraternities”) as the youth politics of German unity and liberal constitution after 1815—Wartburg gestures, colours black-red-gold, and conflict with Metternich’s police federalism. The murder of Kotzebue and the Carlsbad framework criminalise much of the movement’s public life.
Unbedingte and repression
Deposits distinguish moderate and radical (“unconditional”) currents. University persecutions, black lists, and the long police shadow through the Vormärz are part of Treitschke’s Confederation crisis story. By 1848 former Burschenschafter reappear in national assemblies with the same colours now on a wider stage.
Placement
Not a full social history of students; the concept marks the youth-national opposition inside the Bund that Carlsbad tried to freeze. Prefer carlsbad-decrees-1819, german-confederation, metternich.

concepts/carbonari.title: Carbonari (Carboneria)
concepts/carbonari.content:
Carbonari (Carboneria)
The Carboneria (“charcoal-burners’ society”; members Carbonari) was the chief Italian secret society of the Restoration decades before young-italy. In La Farina’s Storia d’Italia it is the daughter of freemasonry and the mother of Mazzini’s association: freemasonry supplied philanthropic language; carbonarism carried the will to national independence into military and provincial Italy; Young Italy later took unity and independence from the carbonari while rejecting much of their ritual politics.
Origin, symbols, and double face
La Farina places the society under the legendary protection of Saint Theobald, a French hermit who lived by making charcoal in a German wood. Symbols were the axe and other tools of charcoal-burners; members called one another not brothers but cugini (“cousins”). Lodges were vendite (“sales”). The society mixed the best and the worst: generous men intolerant of common servitude, brave officers, magistrates indignant at daily injustice, youths burning with patria—and also contumacious soldiers, licentious priests, and men greedy for revenge or tumult. To defy Neapolitan ferocity, La Farina wrote, required the heart of a martyr or of a rascal.
Murat, the Bourbons, and 1820–21
Under Murat the society spread; the king was warned that carbonarism was the enemy of thrones and that he should free his realm of it if he could. Distrust bred hate: Murat proscribed the Carboneria; in Calabria the head of Capobianco, a powerful carbonaro officer, fell after a treacherous arrest at a banquet. Enraged carbonari then turned toward the old Bourbon princes as instruments of revenge. In Sicily Ferdinand and Bentinck received them; the hereditary prince Francis sought initiation. Calabrian and Abruzzese vendite prepared rising; Teramo raised the cry of Ferdinand Bourbon. Persecution strengthened the sect; Bourbons of Sicily showed themselves ever more obsequious to carbonari when it served the restoration game.
In the continental kingdom after 1815 the society passed from speculation to action. La Farina counts some one hundred sixty-three carbonari or supposed carbonari destroyed in various ways in the south alone as the price of liberty’s unfruitful blood; the government thought itself secure just when the association measured its forces and moved from defence to offence. The Neapolitan revolution of 1820 and the Piedmontese movement of 1821 are the public military-political face of that passage. Austrian intervention and the collapse of constitutional experiments drove survivors into exile, prison, or silence.
Papal states, sanfedisti, and Austria
In the Papal States carbonari who showed themselves were excommunicated and condemned while sanfedisti were protected and exalted—a pairing that made peoples hate religious and civil authority together. Fierce secret war of insult, property, and person ran between the two camps. Austrian commissioners hunted affiliates in the Legations; some suffered hard trials, others fled. In Lombardy carbonari conspired in understanding with other Italian provinces; Vienna arrested many. When Pius VII seemed near death in spring 1817, carbonari of the Marches planned to profit by proclaiming liberty and Italian independence at Macerata; the pope recovered and plans shifted.
Relation to freemasonry and to Young Italy
Freemasons and carbonari both aspired to liberty but disagreed on means: the former followed French philosophical doctrines and often French dynastic parties; the latter respected other symbols and local military networks. La Farina judges that if Italian princes, suspicious of every citizen congregation, had not proscribed both vendite and lodges, carbonari might have been their support. Instead proscription pushed the best energy into later forms. young-italy inherited the unitary and independence aims while discarding oligarchic constitutional sketches, anti-Catholic extremes La Farina attributes to some carbonaro pacts, and pure faith in closed rites without popular education.
In Tuscany and the south into the 1840s “reformed” carbonarism could still share with Young Italy the aim of overthrowing governments while keeping initiation solemnity; labels blurred under police pressure. Neapolitan police directors who had once been of the sect became its fiercest persecutors—the renegade pattern La Farina notes in Giampietro after Patrizio.
Place in the corpus
Carbonarism is the Restoration’s Italian conspiracy: half patriotic army of the night, half mixed social revolt, broken in 1821 yet leaving personnel, habits of secrecy, and a national vocabulary that Mazzini reorganized on republican and unitary lines. Without it Young Italy has no mother; with only it, the Risorgimento has no 1859–61 state.

concepts/charte-constitutionnelle.title: Charte constitutionnelle
concepts/charte-constitutionnelle.content:
Charte constitutionnelle
The Charte constitutionnelle is the constitutional text of Restoration and July Monarchy France—1814’s granted charter and 1830’s revision—through which Duvergier’s parliamentary history reads every cabinet fight of the Bourbon and Orléanist decades.
1814 bargain
Louis XVIII’s Charte offers liberties and chambers under monarchical initiative. Ultras want more throne and altar; liberals want the Charte read as contract. The ambiguity is the politics.
1830 revision
After the July Days the Charte is amended for an Orléanist public: popular sovereignty hints without full democracy, pays légal instead of universal suffrage. February 1848 ends the Charte era for the Republic’s constitution-writing. Prefer ultra-royalism, july-monarchy, pays-legal.
Granted charter theory
The 1814 Charte’s self-presentation as royal grant shapes ultra and liberal readings. Ultras emphasize monarchical source; liberals emphasize binding text. Duvergier’s early volumes are largely a war of interpretations inside that frame.
Ordinances of 1830
Charles X’s July ordinances smash the working compromise and hand the Charte’s future to the Orléans branch. The 1830 revision is both continuity and coup against the senior line—Duvergier’s founding paradox of the July Monarchy.
End of the Charte era
February 1848 moves France into republican constitution-making. The Charte becomes historical reference and legitimist nostalgia rather than living public law. Empire constitutions later invent other executive-plebiscitary forms.
Granted charter of 1814
Duvergier opens the parliamentary century with Louis XVIII’s Charte constitutionnelle (“Constitutional Charter”): a monarchical grant, not a national convention’s constitution—bicameralism, hereditary peerage, elected chamber on narrow franchise, public freedoms under law, and Catholicism as religion of the state in the original key. The Charter becomes the sacred text of doctrinaire liberalism and the hated compromise of ultras.
1830 revision
The July Revolution revises rather than abolishes the Charter: Louis-Philippe as king of the French, purged peerage provisions, colour of popular ratification. Duvergier’s narrative treats loyalty to the Charter as the July Monarchy’s official ideology even while electoral law hardens the pays légal.
After 1848
Republic and Empire replace Charter language with constitutions and plebiscites, but parliamentary memory still measures rights and usurpations against the Charter experience. Prefer louis-xviii, charles-x, july-revolution-1830, pays-legal.
See also

Related pages in this wiki’s France / Italy / Germany / Russia / Austria clusters for the same years.

Sources

















SourceTreatmentDuvergier t.11814 presentation; octroi language; early conflictsDuvergier t.10Ordinances judged against constitutional right
1814 and 1830
Duvergier’s early volumes treat the Charte as the Restoration’s bargain—granted liberties under monarchical initiative—then the 1830 revision as Orléanist re-founding after Charles X’s ordinances. Ultra and liberal readings of the same text drive the parliamentary wars of the 1820s.

concepts/concert-of-europe.title: Concert of Europe
concepts/concert-of-europe.content:
Concert of Europe
The Concert of Europe names the post-1815 practice by which the great powers—above all the victors of 1814–15—claimed a shared right to manage crises, congresses, and interventions so that no single revolution or conquest would again overturn the continental order.
After Vienna
The settlement of 1814–15 (territorial map, German Confederation, restored dynasties) did not end wartime coalition habits. Congresses and ministerial meetings—Troppau, Laibach, Verona among them—extended the claim that Europe’s peace was a common responsibility of courts. Austrian deposits (Springer, Helfert) place Metternich’s system inside that claim: intervention against revolution in Italy and the Germanies was justified as European police, not merely Habsburg self-interest. French parliamentary histories register the same structure from the other side—how far Paris would accept or resist interventionist language after 1815 and again after 1830.
Rules and fractures
The Concert presumed monarchical solidarity and suspicion of open national and liberal upheaval. It fractured when interests diverged: Belgian separation after 1830, the Eastern Question, and finally the Crimean War, when Austria’s pressure on Russia broke the old intimacy of the Holy Alliance without creating a stable new alignment. By the 1859 Italian war the deposits show a Europe of competing national cabinets more than a single restorative choir.
Content of the idea
In this wiki the Concert is not a formal constitution; it is the habit of great-power management that links Vienna to the intervention congresses and to Metternich’s police of unrest. It explains why smaller states and revolutionary movements faced not only their own prince but a European opinion of courts.
After Vienna
Springer, Helfert, and Duvergier’s earlier volumes describe the post-1815 practice of great-power consultation—congresses, protocols, and ambassadorial conferences—aimed at containing revolution and managing Ottoman and colonial side-crises without a general war among the victors of Napoleon. The Sainte-Alliance (“Holy Alliance”) language of Alexander I sits beside the more practical Vienna/Aachen/Troppau/Laibach/Verona sequence.
Intervention principle
Troppau and Laibach articulate collective intervention against constitutional revolutions in Naples and Piedmont; Verona and the Spanish expedition of 1823 extend the logic. Britain’s reservations (Canning’s line in Duvergier) mark the concert’s internal fracture: solidarity against Jacobinism versus refusal of unlimited intervention.
Exhaustion
By the Rhine crisis, the Eastern Question, and 1848, the concert’s automatic solidarity is weakened. Crimean war will openly split the old allies. On this wiki the concept names the 1815–1840s habit of managed counter-revolution, not a permanent legal constitution of Europe.

concepts/doctrinaires.title: Doctrinaires
concepts/doctrinaires.content:
Doctrinaires
The doctrinaires (“Doctrinaires”) were the small but influential constitutional group of the French Restoration who sought a middle way between ultra-royalism and pure liberal opposition, grounding the Charte in a theory of representation, capacity, and strong but lawful government.
Name and milieu
Duvergier records that Fiévée called them “the politicians,” that the public began to designate them as doctrinaires, and that the duc de Richelieu sometimes qualified them as niveleurs (“levellers”). The label stuck to the circle around Royer-Collard, with de Serre, Barante, and, in varying proximity, Guizot and Decazes’s parliamentary friends. They were few in number, high in the journals and in committee, and expensive—Richelieu feared they would rate their services too high even while admitting their usefulness.
Politics under Richelieu and Decazes
After the Chambre introuvable, the problem was to govern the Charte without surrendering to ultra majorities or to a Jacobin street. Decazes manoeuvred to separate Richelieu from pure right ministers such as Feltre; Molé’s influence came and went. The doctrinaires supplied speeches and doctrines for a royalist constitutionalism that accepted 1789’s civil settlement while rejecting both White reaction and democratic sovereignty without brakes. Royer-Collard’s interventions on electoral law, magistracy, and budget in 1815–16 already sketched the type: against integral ultra capture of the Chamber, for a monarchy that could dissolve and choose ministers yet not erase representative forms.
Doctrine
In substance they taught government by the capacités (“capacities”)—property, education, social weight—rather than by number or by birth alone; a crown above parties; and a press and tribune free enough to ventilate opinion but not to dissolve authority. Benjamin Constant’s sharper liberal theory of neutral power and inviolable civil liberties ran parallel and sometimes crossed their path; Duvergier sets both against ultra claims that constitutions dispose of all rights at will. Guizot later carried much of the doctrinaire inheritance into the July Monarchy as the theorist of the juste milieu (“just mean”) and resistance to further democratic enlargement.
Historical place
The group never became a mass party. Its importance was definitional: it named the attempt to make the Restoration live as a parliamentary monarchy rather than as a reconquest. When Charles X and Polignac broke that attempt, former doctrinaire language passed into Orléanism. Duvergier’s history is itself written from a parliamentary tradition that still argues with and through them.

concepts/emancipation-of-the-serfs.title: Emancipation of the serfs (Russia)
concepts/emancipation-of-the-serfs.content:
Emancipation of the serfs
Emancipation of the serfs in this knowledge base means the legal destruction of крепостное право (krepostnoe pravo, “serfdom”) in the Russian Empire by the statutes and manifesto of 19 February 1861, as narrated in Kornilov’s course—not a single charitable act but a codified transfer from personal bondage to obligation, allotment, and facultative redemption.
Why the question weighed
Under Nicholas I the peasant question already pressed committees and codification work (Speransky’s legacy, the Committee of 6 December 1826); the emperor felt its importance after the Decembrist shock yet moved hesitantly. Defeat in the Crimean War and Alexander II’s early ministry turned hesitation into legislative machinery: provincial committees, Editing Commissions, Main Committee, State Council.
What emancipation meant
Kornilov separates legal-personal, administrative, and economic meanings. Personally, sale of people, arbitrary transfer into household slavery, and proprietor marriage orders ended. Administratively, peasant communities and peace mediators implemented the statutes—later criticized for bureaucratic tutelage. Economically, land remained proprietors’ property in principle; peasants received permanent use of allotments for dues and might redeem the capitalized obligation by agreement; norms of allotment and dues often worsened the peasant position relative to some provincial hopes; darstvennyi small free grants deepened shortfall in places.
Politics of the concept
Emancipation split nobility, bureaucracy, and press. Herzen’s Kolokol and the Golosa iz Rossii judged whether the commissions had produced true or fictitious freedom; Turgenev could warn against too sharp an attack on the statute because the peasantry would bind the law to its freedom and treat enemies of 19 February as its own enemies. Valuev’s ministry symbolized the post-manifesto attempt to blunt the commissions’ spirit without fully repealing the act. The concept page therefore points to the event emancipation-manifesto-1861 for chronology and keeps here the structural sense of the reform inside the Great Reforms.

concepts/february-patent.title: February Patent
concepts/february-patent.content:
February Patent
The February Patent (Februarpatent, 1861) is the Schmerling-era constitutional charter that reorganizes representation in the Austrian monarchy after the October Diploma—centralist in Hungarian eyes, constitutional in German-liberal ministerial language, and a principal station in Friedjung’s history of Austria after the military reconquests of 1849.
After absolutism and the Diploma
Bach-era bureaucratic rule restored the dynasty without reconciling the kingdoms. Financial pressure and political isolation force experimentation. The October Diploma (1860) elevates historic lands’ rights; the February Patent answers with a stronger imperial parliament and a more unitary reading of the state. Schmerling’s name attaches to the bid to ground Francis Joseph’s monarchy in German-liberal constitutional forms without dissolving executive primacy.
Institutions
Reichsrat structures, relations to land diets, electoral geometries, and ministerial responsibility language define the Patent as a working machine rather than a mere proclamation. The machine only works if the lands send deputies and accept central competence. That condition fails where Hungarian national policy refuses the premise.
Hungarian conflict
Hungarian leadership treats the Patent as incompatible with the laws of 1848 and with the Diploma’s federalizing promise. Non-participation becomes a constitutional weapon. German liberals call it obstruction; the crown faces a half-built parliament.
Unstable constitutional school
The Patent does not settle the monarchy; it schools parties in imperial parliamentary conflict and prepares the failures that make dualism thinkable. Concept and event pages split anatomy versus issuance; together they replace empty labels like ‘neo-absolutism’ with dated instruments—Diploma, Patent, ministries.
German-liberal bet
Schmerling’s camp bets that law, railways, education, and a central parliament can modernize the dynasty and attach German middling classes without repeating 1849’s pure military rule. The bet requires Hungarian attendance it does not receive. Constitutional text without multinational consent becomes a weapon in a war of absences.
Naming without anachronism
This wiki prefers Patent, Diploma, and Absolutismus/military-bureaucratic rule as dated terms from the deposits. It does not rebuild a “neo-absolutism” concept page. The Patent’s job in the corpus is to show the monarchy searching for a post-Bach legal form under Francis Joseph.

concepts/german-confederation.title: German Confederation
concepts/german-confederation.content:
German Confederation
The Deutscher Bund (“German Confederation”), created by the Federal Act of 1815 and seated at the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”) in Frankfurt, was the loose association of German sovereigns that replaced the Holy Roman Empire for the generation of Metternich and the Vormärz. Treitschke and Sybel treat it as an Austrian-led system of order rather than a national state: enough structure to police revolution and mediate princes, not enough to make a single army, customs territory, or citizenry.
Design of 1815
The Bund guaranteed the sovereignty of its members and a federal obligation of mutual defence and internal security. Unanimity or qualified procedures protected small courts; Austria held the presidency. The diet was a congress of envoys, not a parliament. Treitschke’s volumes show how Carlsbad (1819) turned that framework into a working police instrument: press laws, university commissioners, the Mainz investigating commission. The Bund’s legitimacy for conservatives was exactly that capacity to suppress “demagogy” without a unitary empire.
Economy beside the Bund
Political weakness did not stop economic consolidation under Prussia. The Zollverein (“customs union”) grew in the 1830s outside the Bund’s full control and became, in both Treitschke and Sybel, the real preparatory school of kleindeutsch unity. List’s national system and Prussian tariff leadership appear as the productive rival to the diet’s sterility. Middle states bargained between Vienna’s federal politics and Berlin’s commercial pull.
1848–1850
Revolution filled the Bund’s vacuum with the Frankfurt Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”) and provisional central power. When the assembly’s kleindeutsch empire failed and Frederick William refused the crown, Radowitz’s Erfurt Union tried to build a narrower federation beside or instead of the old Bund. Austria under Schwarzenberg fought to restore the diet. Olmütz (1850) and the renewed Bundestag marked the Confederation’s second life—now watched by Bismarck as Prussia’s envoy, who learned that equality inside Austrian presidency was a fiction.
End of the form
Within this wiki’s window the Bund still stands after Olmütz and through the Crimean years. Its destruction in 1866 lies just beyond; Sybel’s whole Begründung is the prehistory of that destruction. For 1815–65 the Confederation is the institutional name of German dualism: Austria’s federal tool, Prussia’s frustration, liberals’ obstacle, and conservatives’ shield.

concepts/great-reforms.title: Great Reforms
concepts/great-reforms.content:
Great Reforms
The Великие реформы (Velikie reformy, “Great Reforms”) are the cluster of structural changes under Александр II (Aleksandr II, “Alexander II”) that opened after the Crimean defeat and whose legal centrepiece was the emancipation legislation of 19 февраля 1861 (19 fevralya 1861, “19 February 1861”). In Kornilov’s course they are not a single statute but a sequence: the shock of the war, the new reign’s first steps, the secret and then public preparation of peasant reform, the manifesto and Положения (Polozheniya, “Statutes”) of 1861, and the related administrative and judicial reconstructions that followed in the 1860s. Within this wiki’s chronological window the emancipation complex is the core; later zemstvo and judicial reforms complete the same historical movement.
Crimean shock and a new reign
Kornilov opens the reform story with the Crimean War’s exposure of the Nicholas system. A million-man army could not master an allied landing of some seventy thousand; supply still ran on 1812 methods; southern provinces were ruined by transport levies; medical services failed; leadership lacked independent skill. Prestige that had seemed colossal after Paskevich’s Hungarian campaign collapsed at the first collision with regular forces of civilized states. The heir who became Alexander II had shared the old confidence; the war changed the political weather around him. Peace, the manifesto of 19 March 1856, the Moscow speech to the nobility, and the first work of Lanskoi and Levshin mark the passage from wartime shock to the decision that serfdom could not remain untouched.
Preparation of emancipation
A secret committee, Rostovtsev’s role, the Lithuanian nobles’ petition, and the rescript of 20 November 1857 to Governor-General Nazimov made the government’s programme public and irreversible in principle. Kornilov stresses the double problem: how to free peasants with enough land, and how to use noble initiative without letting noble appetites destroy the reform’s value for the mass of the people. N. A. Milyutin, in touch with Samarin and Kavelin, and backed at critical moments by Lanskoi, Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna, Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolaevich, and—against court intrigue—by Foreign Minister Горчаков (Gorchakov), became the administrative brain of a radical solution: emancipation with adequate allotments, using the nobility’s committees but not surrendering the drafting to them.
Provincial committees produced projects; Editorial Commissions under Rostovtsev (then under the more hostile Count Panin) worked some twenty months and printed vast materials. Concessions on allotment norms, quit-rent in black-earth provinces, and a twenty-year revaluation of dues were forced on Milyutin’s group; the claim of “perpetual” peasant use of land survived as “permanent” use—legally much the same. In the Main Committee and State Council, factions under Muravyov, Dolgorukov, and others tried to push norms back toward the provincial committees or even toward landless freedom (Gagarin). Grand Duke Konstantin as chairman had to manufacture majorities. The emperor’s will, exercised through that machinery, carried the statutes.
Content and meaning of 19 February 1861
The manifesto and accompanying statutes abolished serfdom as a legal status, regulated allotments and obligations, and created the transitional category of temporarily obligated peasants pending redemption. Kornilov’s lectures analyse the package in legal, administrative, and economic lights for peasants, nobility, and the state. Redemption was designed to capitalize dues; communal and household structures were preserved in ways that shaped rural Russia for decades. The reform was neither the pure radical programme of the Editorial Commissions nor the feudal minimum of the serf-owner party; it was a compromise enforced from above after open bureaucratic war.
Wider reform complex
Emancipation implied further change: local administration, courts, military service, universities, and censorship could not stay exactly as Nicholas left them. Kornilov’s later lectures (beyond the February analysis) treat the 1860s reforms as one historical fabric with 1861. Within this deposit the essential point is causal: Crimea broke the myth of the old order; Alexander’s government chose controlled transformation rather than restoration of the pre-war system; Gorchakov’s diplomacy sought time abroad while the internal reconstruction proceeded.

concepts/holy-alliance.title: Holy Alliance
concepts/holy-alliance.content:
Holy Alliance
The Holy Alliance (Sainte-Alliance, Heilige Allianz, Svyashchennyi soiuz, Священный союз) is the 1815 act and subsequent political language by which Alexander I and fellow sovereigns cloak monarchical solidarity in Christian fraternity—used across Restoration decades as moral cover for intervention against revolution.
Act and Alexandrine intention
In Kornilov’s course the Alliance belongs to Alexander’s late reign: victory mysticism, European arbiter role, and dissatisfaction with purely secular treaties. Sovereigns speak as Christian brothers governing as delegates of Providence. Liberals cry hypocrisy; the courts claim a higher law against Jacobin popular sovereignty.
Blur with conference machinery
The Alliance is not identical to the Quadruple/Quintuple treaty system, yet political speech blurs them. Troppau–Laibach–Verona interventions wear monarchical-Europe language. Metternich deploys religious-moral or legal-federal idioms as needed; Alexander’s piety gives the Alliance its Russian accent.
After Alexander
Nicholas inherits gendarme practice more than mystical texts. The 1849 Hungarian intervention still reads, to friends and enemies, as Holy Alliance habits under a new emperor. German and Austrian narratives keep the phrase as shorthand for conservative partnership even when formal documents differ.
Limits and death of the phrase in practice
Britain never fully inhabits the religious core. Eastern and colonial questions split the ‘brothers.’ Crimean War kills the old solidarity in arms. This concept page holds the ideological-diplomatic label; congress and intervention pages hold deeds.
Language versus ledger
Treaties still need money, men, and ports. The Alliance’s moral vocabulary does not abolish Ottoman questions, colonial rivalry, or Prussian-Austrian jealousy. Deposits that praise or mock the Alliance are usually fighting about whether Christian monarchy is a real European constitution or a veil over force. Kornilov’s Russian classroom leans toward taking Alexander’s sincerity seriously even while tracing political effects.
Pedagogical use in later reigns
Schoolbooks and diplomatic notes after 1825 still reach for the phrase when they want to summon solidarity against revolution. By mid-century the summons works only when interests already align—as in Hungary 1849—and fails when they do not—as in the Crimea. The concept’s historical life is therefore longer than its operational unity.

concepts/july-monarchy.title: July Monarchy
concepts/july-monarchy.content:
July Monarchy
The July Monarchy (1830–1848) is the Orléanist regime Duvergier’s Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire takes as its long middle—the Charter revised after the July Days, Louis-Philippe’s throne born of barricades and settled on notables, and the parliamentary struggles of résistance and mouvement.
Foundations
1830 expels the senior Bourbon branch after Charles X’s ordinances. The Charter of 1830 and the pays légal define a liberal monarchy narrower than democracy: chambers matter, suffrage does not reach the mass. Doctrinaires and opportunistic ministers rotate the meaning of the July Revolution—resistance to further upheaval versus movement toward broader reform.
Cabinets and crises
Duvergier stages foreign and domestic tests: Belgium, the Eastern Question, Rhine weather in 1840, press wars, and the long Guizot ascendancy of immobility. Thiers appears as the man of more adventurous combinations; Guizot as the pedagogue of order. The throne claims 1830’s revolution while fearing another.
End and sequel
Reform banquets, February street fighting, and abdication end the dynasty. Delord’s Empire prelude still needs February to explain the Republic and December. Prefer louis-philippe, guizot, thiers, charte-constitutionnelle, pays-legal, and february-revolution-1848.
Foreign policy style
Orléanist cabinets seek recognition and quiet expansion of influence without Napoleonic risk—Belgium, Mediterranean questions, and the 1840 Eastern crisis as Duvergier stages them. Thiers’s more forward moments frighten the king; Guizot’s peace frightens national pride.
Throne surrounded by republican institutions
Duvergier’s middle volumes narrate the July Monarchy as the attempt to stabilise 1830: a king of the French, not of France by pure divine right; the Charte revised; a chamber politics of doctrinaires, resistance, and dynastic left. The system promises orderly liberty after Charles X’s ordinances and fears both white terror and red republic.
Ministries and immobilism
Cabinets of Casimir Périer, Thiers, Molé, and Guizot mark phases from repression of street republicanism to the Guizot years of prosperity rhetoric and franchise immobility. Foreign policy oscillates among Belgian settlement, Eastern crises, and colonial Algeria—always with an eye to British relations and to not reopening a general war.
End in February
The banquet campaign, Guizot’s fall, and the February days expose the regime’s narrow social base. Delord’s Empire prelude treats the July Monarchy’s end as the door to the republic that will itself yield to Caesar. Prefer louis-philippe, guizot, pays-legal, february-revolution-1848.

concepts/kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch.title: Kleindeutsch and Grossdeutsch
concepts/kleindeutsch-grossdeutsch.content:
Kleindeutsch and Grossdeutsch
Kleindeutsch (“lesser German”) and großdeutsch (“greater German”) name the two rival programmes for national unification debated in 1848–50 and afterward: a German federal state without the Austrian Empire’s non-German lands, under Prussian leadership; or a Germany that included the Austrian hereditary lands and therefore preserved Habsburg primacy or at least dual leadership. Sybel’s Begründung is written from a kleindeutsch national-liberal standpoint; the narrative of Frankfurt, Erfurt, and Olmütz is the story of the first kleindeutsch failure and its causes.
Frankfurt definition
The Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”) at Frankfurt faced an impossible arithmetic. A empire including all Habsburg territories would not be a German national state; a empire excluding them would cut millions of German-speakers from Vienna’s orbit and force Austria to redefine itself as a dual or non-German great power. The kleindeutsch majority solution—hereditary imperial crown for the King of Prussia, Austrian German lands out—was the assembly’s answer. Frederick William IV’s refusal of that crown (“from the gutter”) killed the parliamentary path. Großdeutsch voices, Austrian diplomacy, and middle-state particularism all fought the Prussian hereditary empire for different reasons; Sybel treats the Austrian interest as structural, not accidental.
Erfurt and dualism
After the refusal, Radowitz’s Union tried a kleindeutsch state by princes’ agreement rather than by sovereign assembly. Austria answered with restoration of the old Bund (“Confederation”) and with Schwarzenberg’s pressure. Olmütz (1850) was a großdeutsch—or rather anti-kleindeutsch—victory in the limited sense that it restored a federal form under Austrian presidency and buried the narrower union. It was not a democratic großdeutsch empire; it was the survival of 1815 forms.
Longer meaning
The pair of terms remained the map of German politics until 1866. Economic reality (the Zollverein under Prussian leadership) pulled north and west toward kleindeutsch solutions; dynasty, Catholic Germany, and great-power habit pulled toward Austria. Bismarck’s later wars completed the kleindeutsch programme by force after Sybel’s story has shown why negotiation and Erfurt failed. Within this deposit the concepts are inseparable from Frederick William IV’s monarchical theology, Radowitz’s union project, and Manteuffel’s retreat.
Deposit discipline on the pair
Sybel’s Begründung is the lead voice: Frankfurt’s territorial arithmetic, the hereditary Prussian emperorship draft, and Frederick William IV’s refusal as the death of the parliamentary kleindeutsch fix. Erfurt is the princes’ kleindeutsch second try; Olmütz is its burial under Austrian presidency restored. Treitschke supplies Vormärz economic foreshadowing (Zollverein geography as little-German space). Friedjung and Springer show why Vienna cannot dissolve the empire into a German national state without abandoning Magyar and Slav holdings—the structural veto behind großdeutsch impossibility as democratic programme.
What not to merge
Do not treat großdeutsch as simply “more generous nationalism.” In 1849–50 Austrian policy the anti-Erfurt campaign is great-power dualism, not a liberal greater-German constitution. Conversely kleindeutsch liberals still wanted monarchical federal institutions, not a unitary Jacobin Germany. Keep the pair as rival state architectures, each with its own enemies list.

concepts/liberal-empire.title: Liberal Empire
concepts/liberal-empire.content:
Liberal Empire
The Empire libéral names the late Bonapartist attempt to reconcile hereditary imperial authority with expanded parliamentary life. Ollivier’s multi-volume L’Empire libéral is the deposit’s self-description of that project; Delord’s history supplies the authoritarian foundation against which liberalization is measured.
Why the phrase matters
Without a separate concept, readers collapse 1852–70 into one texture. The deposits refuse that. Early Delord volumes fix coup personnel (Morny, Persigny), army and police, and plebiscitary legitimation. Ollivier’s later volumes narrate programmes, electoral contests, and ministerial self-understanding of a regime trying to live with debate without abandoning the Napoleonic executive. Concessions and opposition growth are historical objects in the same corpus as December 1851.
Ollivier as source and actor
Ollivier is both memorialist and eventual head of government in the liberalizing endgame. Using his volumes therefore requires the wiki’s usual discipline: they are primary-colored narration of intent and quarrel, not neutral statistics. Pair them with Delord’s critical empire history when the page needs the regime’s origin rather than its late apology.
Use in the wiki
Link here from 1860s parliamentary conflicts, Ollivier, and late-Empire elections. Link to second-empire for the regime as a whole and to napoleon-iii / louis-napoleon-bonaparte for the sovereign. Do not treat “liberal empire” as a denial of the coup; the sources present it as a later phase and argument inside Bonapartism.
Ollivier’s wager
The liberal Empire deposit is a wager that the dynasty can widen debate without surrendering the executive. Whether that wager was honest is Ollivier’s own question to his readers; the wiki records the programme as he and Delord stage it.
From authoritarian peak to concessions
Ollivier’s L’Empire libéral is the deposit spine: Napoleon III’s regime after the authoritarian 1850s yields step by step on press, debate, and ministerial responsibility while keeping the imperial executive and the plebiscitary crown. Delord’s darker narrative of the Empire’s origins remains the backdrop; Ollivier narrates the attempt to reconcile Caesar with parliamentary life.
Corps législatif and Émile Ollivier’s ministry
Widened discussion rights, opposition growth (Thiers, republicans), and finally the Ollivier cabinet mark the liberalisation that tries to meet 1869–70 opinion. Italian and German questions constantly disturb domestic relaxation: Rome, Prussia, and public opinion on glory versus liberty.
Limit
The liberal empire is still an empire—plebiscite and dynasty first. Its failure in war lies outside many of this wiki’s 1865 cutoffs but the concept’s deposits already show the internal experiment.

concepts/metternich-system.title: Metternich system
concepts/metternich-system.content:
Metternich system
The Metternich system is the label deposits use for Austrian-led practice of post-1815 order in Germany and Italy: congress diplomacy, federal and peninsular police against revolution, and monarchical solidarity over national or constitutional agitation—personified by Metternich until the March days of 1848 break his ministry.
Congress habit as working method
After Vienna, cabinets meet when revolution threatens recognized thrones. Troppau, Laibach, and Verona codify interventionist habits. The ‘system’ is a repertoire—notes, conferences, diet pressure, armies—more than a single statute. Treitschke and Springer describe Restoration decades as lived method.
German instruments
Carlsbad frameworks, press and university surveillance, and Bundestag politics serve to prevent revolutionary nationalism’s return. Austria claims to guard the federal treaty against Prussian ambition and popular sovereignty alike. Zollverein economics later undercut pure Austrian leadership; political police remains a Metternichian file until 1848.
Italian instruments
Garrisons, treaties with smaller courts, and readiness to march when Carbonari or constitutions threaten the 1815 map make the peninsula a security glacis. Tivaroni’s dominion history is the long Italian indictment; Springer supplies Vienna’s necessity.
Limits and collapse
The system assumes cabinet Europe can outlast newspaper Europe. 1830 forces uneven adaptation; 1848 smashes the ministry in Vienna. The dynasty survives by Windischgrätz, Radetzky, Schwarzenberg—not by conference routine alone. Friedjung begins where the personal chief falls. What continues is the problem of a dynastic great power policing nations in its own house.
Phrase discipline
Here the phrase tracks period diplomatic-police practice in the deposits. It is not a licence for later sociological theory. Pair with Holy Alliance, Vienna congress, Troppau–Laibach–Verona, and 1848 Austrian pages.
Personnel and paper
The system runs through police presidents, ambassadors, diet envoys, and intercepted letters as much as through congress protocols. Metternich’s fame personalizes a machine that includes lesser officials who never enter popular memory. When the man falls in March 1848, parts of the machine still exist—but the aura of inevitability does not.
Why 1848 is the system’s verdict
Economic crisis, confessional and national tensions, and the example of Paris overwhelm conference routine. The speed of Metternich’s fall becomes itself evidence that the system had ruled more by habit and fear than by deep consent. Schwarzenberg’s later toughness is a different style answering the same imperial problem.

concepts/napoleonic-italy.title: Napoleonic Italy
concepts/napoleonic-italy.content:
Napoleonic Italy
Napoleonic Italy names the republics, kingdoms, and departments through which French power reorganized the peninsula before 1814. Tivaroni’s Storia critica del dominio francese is the deposit base—critical of French dominion even while recording modern administrative change.
North
Tomo 1 follows northern Italy: sister republics, the Kingdom of Italy, conscription, codes, prefectures, and the breaking of old municipal and corporate jurisdictions. A generation learned modern state forms under foreign sovereignty. Tivaroni’s critical stance refuses to rewrite Napoleon as Italian liberator; the double legacy remains—administrative modernity plus foreign rule—the inheritance Risorgimento pages must carry without anachronistic gratitude.
Center and south
Tomo 2 treats central Italy and the south, including Murat’s Naples. Joachim Murat’s kingship and 1815 enterprise reconnect Napoleonic memory to Restoration crisis: Tuscan withdrawal, Austrian-led war, Metternich’s refusal of neutrality for an “Austrian state” (Tivaroni’s Tuscan chapters). Southern codes and military habits outlasted the throne.
After 1814
Restoration princes returned under Austrian supervision. Institutions and veterans of the French period reappear in 1831 and 1848 vocabularies; the political problem becomes national independence under new forms (Carbonari, Young Italy, Piedmontese monarchy), not restoration of a French satellite map. Use murat for the person and leopold-ii-tuscany for a court navigating the Austrian aftermath; this concept holds the peninsula system.
Conscription and cadres
French rule leaves military and bureaucratic cadres Italians later reuse. Tivaroni’s memory of the dominion is not only oppression; it is also a school of modern state forms imposed from Paris and Milan.

concepts/national-system-list.title: National System of Political Economy (List)
concepts/national-system-list.content:
National System of Political Economy (List)
Friedrich List’s nationales System der politischen Ökonomie (“national system of political economy”) is the doctrine of his 1841 work of that name — in the deposited Waentig text, first volume on internationaler Handel, Handelspolitik, and the deutsche Zollunion. It is national as against kosmopolitische Ökonomie: not how the whole human race prospers if merchants form one commercial republic, but how a given nation, under given world conditions, reaches prosperity, civilisation, and power through agriculture, industry, and trade.
Theory against practice — and against the school
The book’s Einleitung opens on a half-century of dispute over commercial policy. England’s contemporary Manufaktur- und Handelssuprematie is presented as a consistent system that seeks to monopolise manufactures, great commerce, shipping, colonies, and the seas, and to make other nations manufacture- and trade-subject “wie die Hindus.” Against the school’s free-trade prescriptions List sets recent experience: Russia’s Prohibitivsystem and national prosperity; North America’s freer opening to English goods and “Konvulsion und Ruin.” A science that does not light the path of practice is worthless. Political economy for international trade must learn from experience and fit measures to each nation’s present needs and peculiar state.
Cosmopolitan economy and national economy
Chapter 11 draws the central line. Quesnay first pushed inquiry past the single nation’s administration to the human race and asked one to imagine the merchants of all nations as one Handelsrepublik — that is cosmopolitan economy. Adam Smith, on List’s reading, likewise set out to justify absolute freedom of world trade; his work treats the wealth of all nations of the human race and aims to replace political or national economy with world economy; perpetual peace underlies the argument. J. B. Say requires imagining a Universalrepublik if general free trade is to seem clear. List’s politische Ökonomie refuses that erasure of the nation. Nations are unequal in stage, power, and manufacturing force; a doctrine written for an imaginary world republic does not teach a lagging nation how to rise.
Productive powers before exchange values
Chapter 12 opposes the Theorie der produktiven Kräfte (“theory of productive powers”) to the Theorie der Werte (“theory of values”). Causes of wealth are not wealth. Stock of Tauschwerte (“exchange values”) without the power to create more than one consumes means impoverishment; poverty of stock with strong creating power means enrichment. Die Kraft, Reichtümer zu schaffen is infinitely more important than wealth itself: it secures what is held, multiplies it, and replaces what is lost. Whole nations cannot live on rents as some private persons can. Germany, stripped by plague, famine, and war, repeatedly recovered because it saved productive powers; Spain kept peace, soil, and mines yet sank as productive power drained away. The American war of independence cost enormous sums yet, by securing national independence, so strengthened productive power that peacetime wealth soon surpassed the past. Smith named labour and the productive power of labour in his introduction, yet — dominated by cosmopolitan free trade and by Teilung der Arbeit — did not build the science of productive power that List demands.
National division of work and confederation of forces
Chapter 13 extends division of labour beyond the workshop to the nationale Teilung der Geschäftsoperationen and the Konföderation der Nationalproduktivkräfte — the joining of a nation’s productive forces across lands, branches, and institutions. Political and commercial splintering taxes that confederation; national commercial unity multiplies it. Later theory chapters (14–16) separate private economy from national economy and treat Nationalität as an economic fact: the rational act of the merchant is not always the rational act of the nation.
Stages of development and the narrow case for protection
List’s stage scheme runs: original wildness; pastoral condition; agricultural condition; agricultural-manufacturing condition; agricultural-manufacturing-commercial condition (Agrikulturmanufakturhandelsstand). Free trade with more advanced places best speeds the early climb from barbarism through pastoral and agricultural life into the first manufactures and shipping. A complete Manufakturkraft (“manufacturing power”), large shipping, and great foreign trade require Einschreitung der Staatsgewalt — intervention of state power.
Schutzzoll / Schutzsystem (“protective tariff” / “protective system”) is not a universal maxim. Restriction aimed at planting and protecting one’s own manufacturing power is justified only for nations that already possess the spiritual and material means to plant that power and to seek the highest civilisation and political power, yet are held back by a more advanced foreign manufacturing power — and only until domestic manufacturing no longer need fear foreign competition, thereafter only so far as needed to protect manufacturing “in its roots.” A system that shut out foreign competition entirely and at once would violate both cosmopolitan economy and the nation’s own well-understood interest. Early duties must be moderate and rise only with capital, skill, and enterprise; equal protection of every branch is unnecessary — the great branches (heavy capital, machinery, technical knowledge, many workers, articles of general consumption) claim special care. Temporary loss of exchange-value is the price of building productive power.
Manufakturkraft and the customs house
Chapters on Manufakturkraft bind manufacturing power to personal, social, and political forces, to natural and instrumental powers, to agriculture, trade, shipping, sea power, colonisation, and the stimuli of production and consumption. A pure Agrikulturstaat that only swaps raw produce for foreign manufactures remains dependent. Die Douane als Hauptmittel zu Pflanzung und Beschützung der inneren Manufakturkraft names the tariff administration as the chief instrument for planting and protecting internal manufacturing power; a following chapter answers the school’s objections to the customs house.
Systems List rejects and reclaims
Book III surveys Italian national economists; the Industriesystem (falsely called mercantile by the school); the physiocratic or agricultural system; Smith’s Tauschwertsystem (falsely called the industrial system); and Say’s school. List reads the older industrial/statecraft practice as historically rational and the dominant school as an exchange-value theory that dissolves the nation into individuals and the world market.
Insular supremacy, German commercial union, Zollverein
Book IV turns the theory into German and continental policy. England’s Insularsuprematie structures the choices of continental powers and of North America. Germany, in the recent twenty years, shows what a great nation is without a capable commercial policy and what it becomes with one: a barrel tapped by neighbours (Franklin’s image of New Jersey). England ruined much German manufacturing and poured woollens, cottons, and colonial goods into Germany while shutting out German grain and timber; France sold wine, oil, silk, and fashion goods while cramping German cattle, grain, and linen. Against that pressure List sets the deutsche Handelsunion — German commercial union.
Chapter 36 on the Handelspolitik des deutschen Zollvereins states the German vocation for national manufacturing power: rank in sciences and arts, education and administration; morality, thrift, persistence, invention; population and territory; advanced agriculture and resources. A protective system fitted to those conditions is to bear fruit in internal manufactures, foreign trade and shipping, internal transport, agriculture, and independence. The practical form is the Zollverein: freer exchange inside the German commercial area, external protection as the school of national manufacturing power, with extension of the union (coasts, neighbours, relation to Austria) treated as unfinished commercial-political work.
What the name holds together
In the deposited book the “national system” is one argument chain: nation against world-republic economics; productive powers against mere exchange values; manufacturing power as the lever of agriculture, skill, and political strength; stages that make free trade rational early and temporary protection rational only for a prepared nation blocked by a superior manufacturing foreigner; the customs house as chief planting instrument; the German Zollverein / Handelsunion as the living case against English island supremacy and against commercial dissection of Germany.

concepts/national-workshops.title: National workshops
concepts/national-workshops.content:
National workshops
The ateliers nationaux (“national workshops”) were the state labour organisation created in Paris after the February Revolution of 1848 to absorb unemployment. Their expansion, cost, and dissolution precipitated the June Days.
Creation (February–March 1848)
The provisional government, to give work to the workers, created earthwork shops on the Champ-de-Mars on 27 February. The moderate fraction of that government transformed them into national workshops, organised militarily by the minister of public works, forming a sort of army intended to neutralise the popular forces placed under the Luxembourg delegates and obeying Louis Blanc’s word of order. The droit au travail (“right to work”) promised in February thus took a bureaucratic and drill-ground shape rather than the social workshops Blanc preferred.
Growth and critique
Numbers rose with catastrophic speed. An approximate state drawn at the Hôtel de Ville counted no more than 17,000 unemployed workers in Paris on 2 March; by 15 March the figure was 49,000; by 20 June it passed 107,000. Delord preserves the hostile judgment that the state received no work for the immense sums thrown into this gulf, and that if the organisers of the national workshops had meant to create an army for riot they could not have succeeded better. Parallel chantiers départementaux (“departmental yards”) were invoked as outlets to empty Paris.
Dissolution and June
Government, National Assembly, and public opinion soon agreed to suppress the workshops without a violent shock—which was not an easy task. The government tried to force workers to leave Paris; Falloux reported; dissolution was pronounced. The answer from the eastern quarters was the June insurrection. Cavaignac received executive power to crush it. Thereafter the ateliers nationaux stood in conservative memory as the proof that February’s social promises led to praetorian idleness and civil war, and in democratic memory as a right revoked by a bourgeois assembly.
Later echo
Laws of general security under the Republic and Empire still listed men compromised in June 1848 among those branded dangerous. Bonapartist agents had been accused of fishing in the workshop world before the presidential campaign. The institution itself did not survive the summer of 1848; its political shadow covered the whole Second Republic.

concepts/nationality-question-habsburg.title: Nationality Question in the Habsburg Monarchy
concepts/nationality-question-habsburg.content:
Nationality Question in the Habsburg Monarchy
The Nationalitätenfrage—how Germans, Magyars, Czechs, Poles, South Slavs, Romanians, and Italians were to share one emperor’s state—is for Springer and Friedjung the axis of Austrian politics after 1848, not a side issue.
Springer’s premise
Springer insists that even those who treat “Austria’s true constitutional charter is its language map” as a party slogan cannot refuse exact research into national relations, because the whole political struggle turned essentially on the relation of the several nationalities to one another and on the greater or lesser measure of their state rights and privileges. That the old monarchy had risen to power without resting on the nationalities must not license contempt for them; old Austrian statesmen might feel that political recognition of nationalities stood reason on its head, yet the peoples were facts.
Friedjung: March constitution and after
Friedjung’s ninth book links the constitution of 4 March 1849 and the nationalities: repeated promises of execution; Bach’s circular of 15 August 1849; the ministry’s 29 December 1849 lecture on creating Land representations. He treats government nationality policy, German as state language before 1848, the principle of equality (Gleichberechtigung), the Reichsgesetzblatt, language of instruction, Count Thun and the Czechs, the fatigue of nationalism, and the imperial idea (Reichsidee). Slavic critics who said non-German peoples’ activity was under-mentioned are answered: he did not mean to belittle Poles, Czechs, or South Slavs, but his plan stressed other tasks—reforms of 1849–50 and the following reaction.
Structure of the problem
The deposits refuse a single “solution” page: they show competing national programmes inside one army and one debt, from Magyar April laws to Czech federal hopes to German centralism to South Slav border regiments. Bach’s administrative unity, the Concordat, and later the February Patent are successive state answers. The concept page holds the problem as the sources pose it—not twentieth-century federal theory.
Empire of many peoples
Friedjung and Springer’s Austrian histories make nationality the monarchy’s standing problem after Josephinism and the French wars: Germans, Magyars, Slavs, Italians, Romanians inside one dynastic security system. 1848 turns the problem into open conflict—Vienna, Prague, Pest, Lombardy–Venetia, Croatia—each with diets, national guards, and newspapers.
1848–49 laboratory
Magyar liberal revolution, Jelačić’s Croatian war, Czech federalist hopes, and Italian war against Austria show incompatible programmes under one crown. Windischgrätz, the Constituent at Kremsier, and finally Russian intervention and neo-absolutism answer with arms and bureaucracy rather than a finished federal constitution.
Bach years and beyond
Administrative German-centralism, concordat politics, and later October Diploma / February Patent experiments are successive state answers to the same unsolved nationality map. Prefer bach-system, hungarian-war-independence-1848-49, october-diploma-1860, february-patent-1861.

concepts/neo-guelphism.title: Neo-Guelphism
concepts/neo-guelphism.content:
Neo-Guelphism
Neo-Guelphism is the 1840s Italian programme—most famously associated with Vincenzo Gioberti—of a federation of Italian states under a reforming papacy, which La Farina’s national history and Tivaroni’s post-1849 volumes treat as the great moderate-catholic hope that 1846–49 raises and then breaks.
Programme
A moral primacy of Rome plus a league of princes would give Italy unity without Mazzinian unitarism from below or pure Piedmontese conquest. Early acts of Pius IX make the programme feel near: amnesties, reform talk, and the aura of a national pope. Books and pamphlets spread the federal-papal idiom among elites who fear both Austria and the red republic.
1848 test
War with Austria forces the question neo-Guelphism could not answer: can the temporal pope lead a national war against a Catholic great power? When Pius IX recoils, the keystone drops out. Provisional governments and Piedmont’s army become the real centres; federal-papal paper federations do not.
Aftermath in moderate politics
La Farina and Tivaroni read the disappointment as structural. National leadership migrates to Turin under the Statuto; Cavour’s state will unite by diplomacy and annexation more than by Gioberti’s moral primacy. Prefer gioberti, pius-ix, d-azeglio, and cavour for persons; this concept holds the federal-papal idea and its collapse inside the deposits.
Gioberti’s Primato climate
Gioberti’s Primato and related writings educate a generation of moderate Catholics in a language of Italian civil primacy under papal moral leadership. La Farina’s national-liberal eye is often cool toward the programme’s practicality, yet he cannot deny its 1840s fashion. The concept is broader than one book: it is a political theology of federation.
Why moderates move to Turin
After 1849, the men who still want unity without red republic need an army, a diplomacy, and a constitution that Europe will recognize. Piedmont under the Statuto supplies those; a reforming curia does not. Neo-Guelphism’s failure is therefore also a map of where power actually sits in the deposits’ 1850s.
Gioberti’s programme
La Farina and Tivaroni discuss neoguelfismo (“neo-Guelphism”) as the moderate Catholic-national current associated with Vincenzo Gioberti’s vision of an Italian federation under papal moral presidency—an answer to both pure Mazzinian unitarian republicanism and pure Piedmontese annexationism in the 1840s.
1846–1848 hope and crash
Pius IX’s early reform reputation feeds neo-Guelph enthusiasm; 1848’s war and the papal allocution against national war destroy the illusion that the pope can lead a liberal Italian federation against Austria. La Farina’s unitarian polemic treats the crash as proof that temporal papal power and national war leadership cannot combine.
Afterlife
After 1849 the current fades into liberal Catholicism or into Piedmontese moderate paths; the Societè Nazionale and Cavour’s diplomacy replace federal-papal dreams. Prefer gioberti, pius-ix, charles-albert.

concepts/official-nationality.title: Official Nationality
concepts/official-nationality.content:
Official Nationality
Официальная народность (ofitsial’naya narodnost’, “official nationality”) is Kornilov’s name for the conservative cultural and political programme of Nicholas I after the French and Polish crises of 1830–31, summed in the triad coined by the minister of public instruction С. С. Уваров (S. S. Uvarov): Православие, самодержавие, народность (Pravoslavie, samoderzhavie, narodnost’, “Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality”). It was not a party platform and not a free intellectual school. It was the state’s answer to how Russia might absorb technical and classical knowledge without absorbing the revolutionary West.
Origins
Kornilov roots the doctrine in Karamzin’s earlier defence of autocracy and national peculiarity, and in Nicholas’s own military-service conception of the state: the emperor as first servant, entitled to demand the same hierarchical discipline from all others. The Decembrist revolt of 1825 had already closed the reign of open secret societies; the July Revolution in France, the Belgian crisis, and above all the Polish rising of 1830–31 ended what Kornilov calls the first, still partly reformist period of the reign (1825–31). Thereafter Nicholas “found himself”: the motto of internal policy became the defence of a self-standing Russian order against political temptation and ideological rapprochement with the revolutionary West.
Uvarov, recommended from the old Arzamas circle and installed as minister in 1833, gave that motto its school form. He was to raise useful and loyal servants of the throne and to multiply “mental dikes” against immature minds’ attraction to European notions. Orthodoxy named the established church as moral foundation; Autocracy named undivided monarchical power; Nationality (narodnost’) named a claimed Russian historical individuality against constitutional imitation.
Institutions
The doctrine worked through the ministry of public instruction more than through a written code. The gymnasium and district-school statutes of 1828, the university statute of 1835, the transfer of school supervision from universities to district curators, classical bias in secondary education, and the gradual stripping of “unnecessary” subjects (statistics, logic, part of mathematics) were its machinery. University life was watched; the press and the capital journals were policed; in the western borderlands after 1831 the same triad justified firmer treatment of Polish landowning elites and measures (inventories, later peasant tables in the Kingdom of Poland) that claimed to protect Orthodox or “Russian” peasantry against a foreign nobility.
Official nationality did not monopolize Russian thought. Kornilov’s parallel lectures on the 1830s–40s describe Schellingian circles, Belinsky’s evolution, Westerners and Slavophiles, Otechestvennye Zapiski, Sovremennik, and the official Moskvityanin. The doctrine’s force was that it defined the limits of what the state would teach and tolerate, not that it silenced every salon.
Limits and crisis
Even under the slogan, Nicholas’s government continued limited repairs—Speransky’s code, Cancrin’s finance, Kiselev’s organization of state peasants, the law on obligated peasants of 1842—without admitting a representative constitution. Peasant reform stopped short of compulsory transformation of seigneurial estates in the Great Russian core; the emperor told the State Council he would not force landlords as he forced western inventories. The European revolutions of 1848 opened the third period of the reign: emergency reaction, Uvarov’s exit, and a climate in which the earlier balance of “enlightenment without revolution” collapsed into suspicion of the educated class as such.
The Crimean War then broke the prestige of the whole Nicholas system. Official nationality as a confident doctrine of European police mastery (Aksakov’s later phrase of Russia’s “chief-of-police” role in Europe belongs to that self-image) did not survive Sevastopol. Alexander II’s Великие реформы (Velikie reformy, “Great Reforms”) worked in a different key—emancipation, courts, zemstvos—while still preserving autocracy. The triad remained a conservative memory and a school slogan; it ceased to be the working map of a reign.
