entities/charles-x.title: Charles X
entities/charles-x.content:
Charles X
Charles X (1757–1836), formerly comte d’Artois, was the last Bourbon king of the senior line to reign in France (1824–1830). Brother of Louis XVI and Louis XVIII, he personified the ultra-royalist pole of the Restoration and fell in the July Revolution after the ordinances of the Polignac ministry.
Before the throne
As comte d’Artois under the old regime and in emigration, then as heir after 1814–15, he stood to the right of Louis XVIII’s more flexible practice of the Charte. The assassination of his son the duc de Berry in 1820 hardened court and ultra opinion against the Decazes system. Villèle’s ministry already governed much of the late reign of Louis XVIII when Charles succeeded in 1824.
Accession (1824)
On Louis XVIII’s death Charles left at once for Saint-Cloud; by noon the ministers were taking orders from the new king. Duvergier notes that for two years Louis’s reputation for wisdom had declined, yet the public still did not fear coups from him and lacked the same confidence in the brother. Villèle and Corbière acted in 1824 as they had under the late king; Charles could not dismiss Villèle at the very opening of the reign, though it was not doubted that an occasion would soon appear to place power in hands more skilled and sure—perhaps over the suppression of the press censorship. Official eloquence mixed the grandeurs of old France and the glories of new France, hereditary monarchy and representative institutions, the virtues of both brothers. Chateaubriand, easy to catch with pamphlets, gained little beyond the pleasure of writing that his new brochure had done for Charles what the old had done for Louis XVIII. Louis’s two memorable acts, in Duvergier’s judgment, remained the grant of the Charte and the resistance he had opposed to counter-revolutionary passions—a standard against which Charles would be measured.
Reign
The middle years combined clerical legislation, indemnities to émigrés, and foreign memory of the Spanish expedition of 1823. Villèle’s long ministry gave administrative strength to the Right until parliamentary wear and the election of 1827 forced a more conciliatory Martignac cabinet. Charles’s personal preference ran toward Polignac. Liberal papers in 1829 treated the coming of Polignac as the end of “weak and stupid transactions”; royalist papers spoke of the necessity of salvation.
Fall (1830)
The July ordinances—Chamber dissolved, press struck, electoral law rewritten—were the decisive act of the reign. Paris rose; the senior line abdicated in form and left France. Charles X died in exile in 1836. His reign closed the Restoration experiment: the Charte had been retained in words and broken, in liberal eyes, in the ordinances; the Orléans branch took the crown under a revised charter and the title king of the French.

entities/cialdini.title: Enrico Cialdini
entities/cialdini.content:
Enrico Cialdini
Enrico Cialdini is, in Tivaroni’s L’Italia degli Italiani, a principal regular-army general of Piedmont and then Italy: Crimean brigade commander, organizer of Alpine volunteers, divisional chief in 1859, instrument of southern fortresses after 1860, and—fatally for Italian command unity—one of two men considered fit for supreme command in 1866.
Crimea and the making of a name
Tivaroni’s Crimean chapters place Cialdini’s brigade in the Sardinian contingent that, on 8 September, was to assault the bastion of the tree in support of the French attack on the Malakoff tower. The judgment is cool: the Sardinian corps did not truly join the action and lost only about forty killed and wounded; afterward the Sardinian camp became “picturesque” with huts, roads, and gardens. The prestige of the tricolor nonetheless rose; Cialdini’s name entered the small set of Piedmontese generals known abroad.
1859: volunteers and the fourth division
Before open war Tivaroni records Piedmont opening rolls for volunteers as Cacciatori delle Alpi, organized in six battalions by Enrico Cialdini at Cuneo and Savigliano—at first barely 3,500 men, later toward 13,000 by war’s end (figures he weighs against Carrano). In the regular order of battle Cialdini commands the fourth division: Regina and Savona brigades, Monferrato light horse, bersaglieri battalions, three batteries—about 11,148 men. When Canrobert shifts the line behind the Po between Casale and Alessandria, Cialdini’s division holds Casale, covering whether the enemy marches Novara–Vercelli toward Turin or tries to prevent junction with French columns from the Scrivia.
Dual command, 1866
Tivaroni’s 1866 volumes make Cialdini structural, not ornamental. Italy had two generals thought capable of great command; La Marmora would not take the whole command alone out of regard for Cialdini, nor force Cialdini to accept chief-of-staff functions by withdrawing. Cialdini, knowing many senior officers were “Lamarmoran,” refused outright and would not have the princes with him. After Custoza the plan Usedom urged—observe the Quadrilateral and march with volunteers on Vienna—is the plan Tivaroni says Cialdini adopted in July with La Marmora’s assent. The dualism is presented as a political-military misfortune of the young kingdom.

entities/ciro-menotti.title: Ciro Menotti
entities/ciro-menotti.content:
Ciro Menotti
Ciro Menotti was the leading Modenese liberal of the conspiracy that opened the Italian risings of 1831—La Farina’s chapter on that year begins in his house on the evening of 3 February.
Confidence and betrayal
Menotti was “the most authoritative of the Modenese liberals and the one most in the grace and domesticity of the prince.” Duke Francis IV, tangled in intrigues that reached toward Louis-Philippe and drew Austrian reproaches, had even signed with Menotti an act of reciprocal security for life. La Farina’s judgment is that the duke either trusted that nothing would be done without his knowledge or meant to crush his companions before revealing himself as their enemy.
Night of 3 February 1831
That evening Menotti gathered fifteen chief conspirators at his house to order the rising for the morrow; bands in the duchy and countryside had promised support. The duke, fully informed, went out himself with blunderbuss and pistols, took a battalion, surrounded the house, and called Menotti and his companions by name to surrender. The boldest fired from the windows; a pillar shielding the duke was struck. Soldiers were well disposed to the conspirators but saw no citizen help, knew the gates closed, and would not rise against the prince. After five hours the duke himself aimed a cannon brought up; Menotti tried to escape by the roof, was wounded, and with the others became the duke’s prisoner.
“Send me the hangman”
The same night Francis wrote to the governor of Reggio a letter La Farina calls almost unique for brevity and ferocity: a terrible conspiracy had broken out; the conspirators were in his hands; send me the hangman. Next day the city mourned; the duke stayed covered, showing neither mercy nor rage. Hearing that Bologna had risen and neighboring towns were in tumult, he told Modenese nobles who begged grace that he had spared Menotti’s life and would show more clemency if persons devoted to the prince were respected. As agitation grew he fled Modena, taking the wounded prisoner in chains toward Mantua under Austrian custody. Political prisoners left in Modena were freed; a provisional government declared Francis IV fallen and the state restored to liberty—while Menotti’s fate was sealed away from the city he had tried to raise.

entities/crispi.title: Francesco Crispi (1818–1901)
entities/crispi.content:
Francesco Crispi
Francesco Crispi (1818–1901) appears in Tivaroni’s L’Italia degli Italiani as the principal organizer of the Sicilian insurrection of 1860 that opened the way for Garibaldi—the Mazzinian-turned-realist who, working with the island’s secret committees, prepared the ground in which the Mille would land. Within this wiki’s 1800–1865 frame he is not yet the later minister; he is the Sicilian revolutionary who helped convert Mazzinian conspiracy into a practical island rising at the decisive moment.
The island before the landing
Tivaroni records that a vast plot, in Guerzoni’s phrase, enveloped Sicily and that secret committees held its threads and governed it. Mazzini had taken care to keep himself… in relation to these committees, and the revolutionary element in Sicily, even after the earlier disappointments, remained organized and expectant. Crispi moved in this world of committees, contacts, and projected landings. On the mainland side, the committee at Genoa directed by Antonio Mosto, the group Bette at Messina with Agresta Jonata, and figures such as La Masa planning a landing on the shore of Termini, and Maurizio Quadrio, a faithful friend of Mazzini, all formed the network through which the rising was concerted.
Arrests and the testing of wills
The climate was one of police repression and postponed hopes. After the accession of Francis II, a single phrase of his proclamation of 22 May 1859 had struck the island—that in which he called his father a “great and pious monarch.” The following day many distinguished persons were arrested and made to walk on foot a good part of the Via Toledo and Maqueda. The outcome of the war, the constitution of a Kingdom of Upper Italy, and the revolution of Central Italy could not fail to have repercussions in Sicily and to sharpen its hopes.
Tivaroni records a telling image of the intended technique: the cappellotti (bombs/capsules) that Mazzini had had made in small size so they could be transported far. Thrown on the paving stones, whichever way they fell the striker was struck and the spark of the fulminate communicated to the powder, and the bomb exploded into fragments wounding all who stood near. The detail belongs to the same stubborn geometry of local sparks that fills the 1850s.
A rising that missed its date
The plan proved fragile in execution. When it was resolved to put off the movement indefinitely, and Messina and Catania were warned of the indefinite postponement, Cappello was arrested, and only Giuseppe Campo rose in arms with a few on 10 October in Bagheria, Misilmeri, Fivizzale, Villabate, and Castel San Giovanni with Francesco Andolfo and the Mastricchi brothers. Though the attempt was not seconded, it lasted three… days. Many of the committee figures hid or were arrested. Yet the ground once prepared did not dissolve: the revolutionary element survived the failed October date and awaited Garibaldi’s landing the following year.
Place in the corpus
In Tivaroni, Crispi is part of the Sicilian preparation that makes 1860 intelligible: a Mazzinian network, hardened by failed dates and arrests, that Garibaldi’s expedition could seize on because the committees still held the island’s threads. For this knowledge base he is the Sicilian organizer of the transition from Mazzinian conspiracy to the Thousand—the man whose island work bridged the republican movement and the expedition that would ultimately crown the Savoyard monarchy.

entities/d-azeglio.title: Massimo d'Azeglio
entities/d-azeglio.content:
Massimo d’Azeglio
Massimo Taparelli d’Azeglio is the Piedmontese moderate premier and publicist whom Tivaroni’s first post-1849 volume and La Farina’s national history place between Novara’s defeat and Cavour’s ascendancy—the guardian of the Statuto under pressure and a voice of the formula that Italians must be “made” in civic character as well as on the map.
After Novara
Charles Albert’s war ends at Novara; Victor Emmanuel II keeps the Statuto while Austria watches. D’Azeglio’s ministry defends constitutional continuity, disciplines extreme left agitation, and seeks European respectability for a defeated but un-absolutist Piedmont. Ecclesiastical conflict and legislation on Church privileges already appear as tests of the lay state—ground Cavour will deepen with Rattazzi in the connubio years. Tivaroni’s cabinet crises of the early 1850s still move in a landscape d’Azeglio stabilized.
Publicist of the moderate party
Painter and novelist as well as minister, d’Azeglio’s political prose argues for honest administration, anti-conspiracy legality, and national education of elites. La Farina’s circle reads him as respectable national liberalism against clerical reaction and Mazzinian underground methods. He is not the great diplomatic gambler; he is the moral and parliamentary preparer of a state Cavour can later risk in war.
Yielding the centre
Parliamentary combinations shift; Cavour takes the premiership and the connubio realigns Left and Center. D’Azeglio remains a reference of the moderate Right as war and unity approach. Prefer cavour, victor-emmanuel-ii, novara-1849, rattazzi, and statuto-albertino for the structural arc.
Siccardi climate
Even before Cavour’s full ecclesiastical programme, d’Azeglio’s years already fight Church courts and privilege in Piedmont—Tivaroni’s continuous thread of the lay state under the Statuto.
Moderate Piedmont after Novara
Tivaroni and La Farina place Massimo d’Azeglio among the moderate constitutional leaders who must govern the Statuto (“statute/constitution”) after Charles Albert’s defeat and abdication. The task is double: keep faith with Italian aspirations without another reckless war, and convince Europe that Sardinia is a reliable liberal monarchy rather than a revolutionary export bureau.
Connubio climate and the National Society’s world
d’Azeglio’s premiership years sit just before Cavour’s full dominance; the deposits treat him as the respectable writer-statesman who can speak European liberal language, manage clerical conflict cautiously, and prepare the personnel ground on which Cavour later builds the Società Nazionale and French alliance. His famous formula of “making Italians” belongs to the moderate pedagogy of the 1850s in Tivaroni’s critical story.
Limits
He is not the architect of 1859’s war diplomacy; that passes to Cavour and Napoleon III. This page holds the moderate bridge from 1849 humiliation to the decade of preparation.

entities/deak.title: Deák
entities/deak.content:
Deák
Deák Ferenc (HU Deák Ferenc (“Ferenc Deák”); 1803–1876), the Haza bölcse (HU a Haza bölcse (“Sage of the Fatherland”)), was the jurist-politician who embodied lawful Magyar constitutionalism from the Reform diets through the 1848 ministry and the passive resistance of the Bach years toward the settlement later crowned by the 1867 Compromise. In the Rest of Europe corpus he appears less as battlefield hero than as the enduring alternative to both Kossuth’s exile radicalism and Vienna’s absolutist (after 1848) centralism.
Reform diet and 1848
Deák made his name in the county and diet politics of the Vormärz as a master of statute, precedent, and measured opposition. Grünwald’s Széchenyi world and Springer’s Hungarian chapters place him among those who wanted civil equality, responsible government, and national dignity without Jacobin rupture. In 1848 he entered Batthyány’s ministry (justice), helping to translate the March demands into the April Laws — the statutory core of modern Hungary’s claim to a separate responsible government under the Habsburg king.
Unlike Kossuth, Deák did not become the voice of revolutionary mobilisation once war came. His temperament and doctrine pointed toward legal continuity: royal sanction, diet competence, and the Pragmatic Sanction interpreted as dualist partnership. When the court criminalised the April regime and the war radicalised into deposition of the dynasty (April 1849), Deák’s line was already distinct from Debrecen republican energy even where patriotism was shared.
After Világos: silence as policy
The Bach system tried to absorb Hungary into a unitary empire: German official language, imperial codes, abolition of the old megyék (HU megye (“county”)) autonomy, and police supervision. Friedjung’s second volume treats Magyar society’s answer under Deák’s moral leadership as passzív ellenállás (HU passzív ellenállás (“passive resistance”)): refusal of office, refusal to legitimise the new counties and courts, preservation of the April Laws as the only lawful constitution in abeyance. This was not Kossuth’s diplomacy of European war revision; it was domestic non-recognition that kept a political nation alive without another Világos.
Deák’s authority grew because he had clean hands in the eyes of many moderates: ministry service without the April 1849 dethronement’s full ownership, legal learning, and refusal of both collaborationist careers and sterile conspiracy. Friedjung notes how the failures of the Italian war of 1859 and the financial-military strain of the absolutist state reopened Vienna’s willingness to bargain — and that any bargain would have to address the Deák party’s constitutional minimum.
Toward dualism (to 1865 horizon)
Within this wiki’s chronological frame Deák’s climax is prepared rather than completed. The Októberi Diploma (1860) and Februári Pátens (1861) experiments forced Magyar politics to choose: accept a federalising or centralising imperial charter, or stand on 1848. Deák’s addresses and diet leadership crystallised the claim that only the April Laws, adapted through negotiation on common affairs, could restore legality. Friedjung’s story of the early 1860s is the story of that insistence meeting Schmerling’s February constitution and eventually outlasting it. The later Ausgleich of 1867 lies past the volume edge, but the corpus already names Deák as the domestic architect of the dualist exit from Bach.
Assessment
Where Görgei is military tragedy and Batthyány martyrdom, Deák is duration. Springer’s institutional eye values his legalism; Friedjung’s national-liberal eye values his refusal to trade historic rights for administrative modernisation imposed in German. Against Széchenyi’s despair and Kossuth’s intransigent emigration, Deák offered a politics of waiting that assumed the empire must one day need Magyar consent. The Bach years proved the cost of ruling without it; the October and February experiments proved that half-constitutions would not buy it.

entities/decazes.title: Élie Decazes (1780–1860)
entities/decazes.content:
Élie Decazes
Élie Decazes (1780–1860) is the favourite minister of Louis XVIII’s moderate Restoration phase in Duvergier’s early parliamentary volumes—the man of the centre against ultras, broken by the climate after the Duc de Berry’s assassination. He was also, fittingly, the principal private source for Duvergier’s own history: the Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire acknowledges that of all its communications the most precious were those owed to the duc Decazes, who without reserve opened his portfolios and authorized the author to search there himself for whatever might enlighten him.
From the Hundred Days to the prefecture of police
Decazes, a young man who had refused the oath during the Hundred Days and had been sent into exile at Libourne for his loyalty, returned to Paris after Waterloo. In 1815 he appears as prefect of police, standing with Fouché (minister of police) and General Dessolles (commander of the national guard) against the royalist reaction: none of the three was favourable to it, and Duvergier shows them striving to contain the ultraroyalist passion that produced the famous and sad ordonnance of 24 July. Duvergier’s portrait of his courage against the White Terror and his refusal of the “legitimacy” of the race is the biographical root of his later reputation.
Favourite and programme
Rising as Louis XVIII’s trusted minister, Decazes sought a Restoration that could live with the Charte and with a portion of revolutionary legality. His policy was a royalist liberalism: press openings, electoral management, and ministerial combinations designed to absorb parts of revolutionary France into a Charte monarchy, against émigré maximalism. Ultras hated him as too soft and too close to the king; the moderate experiment rested on the favourite system Duvergier treats as a test of whether the crown would govern through majorities or through court factions.
Duvergier’s parliamentary narrative of the Richelieu–Decazes years shows the fragility of the centre. A strong majority in the Chamber of Peers and a majority of four votes in the Chamber of Deputies had pronounced against the liberal opinion; to secure the ministry Decazes and his allies tried to win Royer-Collard without losing Laîné, gathering the marine minister Portal and even Marshal Gouvion-Saint-Cyr against the royalist right’s constant attack on the latter. The right, deprived of two arguments it had counted on, nonetheless fought the ministry’s projects with rare bitterness; a life pension of 50,000 francs was granted grudgingly and by a very small majority, leaving the duke of Richelieu—travelling in the south of France—with a bitter disappointment. Two tendencies had soon divided the new ministry into two fractions; the public, unable to explain the ministers’ inaction, suspected a want of accord, and the suspicion was founded.
Fall after Berry
The Duc de Berry’s assassination (1820) destroyed the political weather that made Decazes possible. Ultra pressure and the king’s shift ended the favourite’s centrality; the moderate experiment gave way to the ultra recovery that Villèle would dominate. The failure under ultra assault educated the next generation of doctrinaires and Orléanists in how fragile the Charter middle was.
Place in the corpus
For this knowledge base Decazes is the liberal-royal middle of the early Restoration: prefect of police against the White Terror, the king’s favourite trying to reconcile Charte monarchy with revolutionary legality, and the man whose papers became a principal source for Duvergier’s parliamentary history. He personifies the attempt to run a constitution through majorities rather than court factions—an attempt broken by the assassin’s knife in 1820.

entities/eugene-beauharnais.title: Eugène de Beauharnais
entities/eugene-beauharnais.content:
Eugène de Beauharnais
Eugène Rose de Beauharnais (1781–1824), stepson of Napoleon I and son of Josephine, was viceroy of the Kingdom of Italy and a principal instrument of French rule in Lombardy and the Italian peninsula under the Empire.
Youth
Born in Paris in 1781 to the vicomte Alexandre de Beauharnais, deputy of the nobility to the Constituent Assembly and victim of the Terror in 1794, Eugène spent part of the parental imprisonment as an apprentice carpenter. At fifteen he was attached to Hoche’s staff and met Bonaparte, then commanding in Paris—according to Vaudoncourt, when the boy came to ask for his father’s sword held in an arms depot. That request, the Italian narrative records, helped bring Bonaparte near Josephine, Eugène’s mother.
Viceroy of Italy
By decree of 7 June he was named viceré d’Italia (“viceroy of Italy”) and swore to lay down his functions the moment the king (Napoleon as king of Italy) should order it. Napoleon wanted a wholly devoted viceroy: Melzi might be loyal, but not as a son. He needed a blind, obedient, passive instrument; Beauharnais at twenty-four, owing him everything, fitted the need. Melzi, whether from this slight or from Aldini’s appointment, had the official sheet announce his departure from Milan for gout; Napoleon wrote on 28 June that he could not conceive how a man of Melzi’s prudence could show so little in his most important relations.
Role and afterlife
As viceroy Eugène administered the satellite kingdom, commanded Italian and French forces in the later campaigns, and remained, in Italian and French memory, the polished face of dynastic incorporation rather than of pure military occupation. After 1814 he lost the Italian throne, received compensation in the Bavarian sphere through his marriage into the Wittelsbach house, and died in 1824. For Duvergier’s France he belongs to the imperial family network that the Restoration had to exclude and that Bonapartists later partially reclaimed; for the Lombard narrative he is the young French prince set over Milan as Napoleon’s second self.

entities/falloux.title: Alfred de Falloux (1811–1886)
entities/falloux.content:
Frédéric de Falloux
Frédéric de Falloux is the legitimist-leaning minister of education under the Second Republic whose Falloux law Delord and Duvergier place at the centre of the Party of Order’s cultural settlement—Church and state sharing secondary education against socialist and pure republican school ideals.
Law and coalition
The Falloux law expands clerical influence in schooling while binding Catholic notables to the conservative republic that still fears June. It is bargain politics: monarchists and moderate republicans share an enemy on the left.
Empire afterlife
Educational clericalism remains a reference in Empire debates Ollivier’s world inherits. Prefer second-republic-france, cavaignac, coup-of-1851 if present, and louis-napoleon-bonaparte.
Minister of the Party of Order
Falloux enters Duvergier’s and Delord’s Second Republic as a Catholic-legitimist-leaning minister useful to conservatives who still govern a republic. Education is the chosen battlefield.
Falloux law
The law expands Church room in secondary education and binds Catholic notables to the anti-socialist coalition. Republicans of the pure school tradition read it as clerical reconquest; conservatives read it as social defence.
After 1851
Empire politics inherit clerical-education questions without identical party names. Ollivier’s liberal Empire debates still move in a landscape Falloux helped institutionalize. Prefer second-republic-france and cavaignac for the assembly climate.
Legitimist-catholic minister of the Republic
Alfred de Falloux appears in Delord and Ollivier as the Catholic-legitimist notable who can still sit inside the Second Republic’s Party of Order. His ministry is associated with the education settlement that bears his name in contemporary polemic—the Falloux law climate in which the Church regains ground in secondary instruction after the February scare. Delord treats such men as proof that 1848’s republic quickly housed monarchical Catholics once universal suffrage returned the provinces.
Against revolutionary Italy and for moral order
Tivaroni preserves Falloux’s later exchanges with Napoleon III over Italy: the emperor’s claim of “difficultés morales” toward the Italian cause and refusal to turn guns wholly against Piedmont, set against legitimist-catholic pressure. Falloux thus links French domestic clerical politics to the Roman Question and to non-intervention rhetoric after Magenta–Solferino. Ollivier’s liberal-empire volumes keep the same Catholic opposition as a standing difficulty for imperial Italian policy.
Narrative use
On this wiki Falloux is not a full biography of legitimism; he marks the Catholic-order current inside and after 1848 that Delord and Ollivier need when explaining education, the Rome file, and Orleanist-legitimist notables under the Empire.

entities/farini.title: Luigi Carlo Farini (1812–1866)
entities/farini.content:
Luigi Carlo Farini (1812–1866)
Luigi Carlo Farini appears in Tivaroni’s L’Italia degli Italiani as organizer of central Italy’s path after Villafranca and as one of the three intimates who held Cavour to the field on 19 April 1859.
Villafranca and the central duchies
After Villafranca, Napoleon III, coldly received at Milan, told Farini’s envoys that the restoration of the princes depended on the Italians themselves, because Austria could not use arms for them. Tivaroni marks the passage from desperate delusion to a hope that Italian skill must seize. Farini’s dictatorships over Modena, Parma, and the Emilia–Romagna line were the administrative means of preventing the return of the old dynasties while Piedmont negotiated with France and Europe. The free votes and annexation to Victor Emmanuel that followed sit in the same Tivaroni volumes as the political counterpart to Magenta and Solferino.
Cavour’s circle, April 1859
On the terrible day of 19 April 1859, when Cavour feared the collapse of his hopes, Minghetti, Audinot, and Farini ran to Castelli warning that Cavour might abandon himself to extreme thoughts. Castelli found Cavour burning papers; the scene of tears and embrace is told with Farini among those who refused to let the minister desert the field before battle. That night places Farini inside the smallest circle of trust around the architect of Plombières.
After annexation
Tivaroni’s finance chapters treat the assumption of Lombard-Venetian Monte quotas and irritation at delayed union—background to the governments Farini had helped stabilize in the center. La Farina’s fourth volume supplies the earlier papal-state moderate atmosphere in which names like Minghetti already moved; Farini’s own later premiership of the Italian kingdom falls at the edge of the 1865 bound. The deposits keep him tied to central Italy against restoration and to Cavour’s personal trust.
Emilian dictator of annexation
Tivaroni’s 1859–1866 narrative and La Farina’s unitarian line give Luigi Carlo Farini a precise job: after Austrian defeat and the collapse of ducal authority, to organise Emilia and related territories toward annexation to Sardinia under plebiscitary and monarchical forms. “Dictator” in the Roman republican sense of temporary extraordinary power appears in period language for these provisional executives.
From doctor-conspirator to lieutenant of unity
Earlier carbonaro and moderate experiences feed a practical unitarianism that distrusts both pure Mazzinian republican timing and pure legitimist restoration. Farini’s reports and acts in the annexation season are administrative history in Tivaroni: leagues, assemblies, and the road to the 1860 plebiscites.
Kingdom personnel
In the new kingdom he remains among the Right’s governing set—Minghetti, Ricasoli, and the Piedmontese core—until the ordinary parliamentary wear of the 1860s. Prefer italian-war-1859, kingdom-of-italy-1861, and cavour.

entities/ferdinand-ii-naples.title: Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies (1810–1859)
entities/ferdinand-ii-naples.content:
Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies
Ferdinand II is the Bourbon king of the Two Sicilies whom Tivaroni’s southern volumes place from the 1830s through 1848 constitutions and revocations to the reputation liberal Europe fixes as “Bomba”—the monarch Garibaldi’s Thousand and Piedmontese regulars will unseat’s successor in 1860–61.
1848
Constitution under pressure, Sicilian separatism, and repression after the revolutionary year destroy moderate trust. Bombardment memories become European press facts. The kingdom modernizes unevenly while police politics dominate the deposits’ judgment.
Toward 1860
Francis II inherits a state hollowed by that reputation. Prefer expedition-of-the-thousand-1860, gaeta-siege-1860-61, cialdini, and garibaldi for the fall; this page holds the king of the 1848–50s Two Sicilies as Tivaroni casts him.
Kingdom structure
The Two Sicilies under Ferdinand II combine a large southern monarchy, naval tradition, and police politics Tivaroni never confuses with Piedmontese parliamentary development. Modernization projects coexist with distrust of liberal elites. Sicily’s distinct revolutionary calendar complicates any single ‘Naples’ story.
Reputation in liberal Europe
Bombardment and prison stories travel. By the late 1850s the dynasty’s name is a moral argument for interventionists and a problem for those who want only great-power diplomacy. Garibaldi’s 1860 lands in a political climate Ferdinand II helped create even if he dies before the final collapse.
Succession
Francis II inherits the structure and the reputation. Prefer pages on 1860–61 campaigns for the fall; this entity keeps Ferdinand as the long mid-century king of the deposits’ Two Sicilies.
Bourbon king of the Two Sicilies
Tivaroni’s southern volumes and La Farina’s narrative fix Ferdinand II as the long-reigning Bourbon who grants and revokes constitutions under pressure, bombards rebellious cities (the “bomb-king” of liberal polemic), and becomes Europe’s symbol of southern absolutism after 1848–49. The 1848 Sicilian and Neapolitan constitutional moments end in restored police monarchy.
1848–1849 and the reaction
Deposits follow the grant of a constitution, conflict with Sicily’s separate revolution, and the reconquest that leaves political prisoners—Poerio among the famous names—filling European liberal newspapers. Austrian and papal neighbours prefer a stable Bourbon to a revolutionary south; French and British liberal opinion uses Naples as moral contrast to Piedmont’s Statuto path.
Death and the 1860 collapse
Ferdinand dies in 1859 on the eve of the war that remakes the north-centre; Francis II inherits a state Tivaroni already describes as brittle. Garibaldi’s 1860 expedition and collapse of Bourbon arms close the dynasty’s Italian story. Prefer poerio, garibaldi, and expedition-of-the-thousand-1860 for the endgame.

entities/francis-joseph.title: Francis Joseph
entities/francis-joseph.content:
Francis Joseph
Franz Joseph (Francis Joseph, 1830–1916) became Emperor of Austria on 2 December 1848 when his uncle Ferdinand abdicated and his father Franz Karl renounced the succession. The young ruler’s accession, prepared in the circle of Archduchess Sophie and executed under the military recovery of Windischgrätz and the political direction of Schwarzenberg, closed the revolutionary autumn in Vienna and opened the long reign that would carry the monarchy through absolutism after 1848, the Italian and German wars of the 1850s–60s, and after 1865. In Friedjung’s volumes he is less a finished statesman than the crown around which generals, ministers, and national programmes contested the shape of the empire.
Education and elevation
Francis Joseph’s education under Count Bombelles and the plans of Archduchess Sophie for his elevation belong to Friedjung’s book on the throne change. While Ferdinand still reigned and Metternich’s system staggered, Sophie’s circle looked to a prince who could embody military monarchy without the incapacities of the reigning emperor. The October rising in Vienna, the murder of Latour, and Windischgrätz’s reconquest of the capital made a change of person seem a change of regime. Schwarzenberg’s ministry provided the political formula: a young emperor, a strong army, and a refusal to let the Kremsier assembly or the Hungarian diet dictate the empire’s constitution.
Revolution and war, 1848–1849
From December 1848 the emperor’s name stood over the winter campaign in Hungary, the dissolution of the Kremsier Reichstag (“imperial diet / constituent assembly”), and the oktroyierte Verfassung (“imposed constitution”) of 4 March 1849. That constitution promised unity of the customs territory and a monarchical executive while only partially recognizing Hungarian historic rights; it was the cabinet’s answer to both German-Austrian liberalism and Magyar separatism. The summer war in Hungary, Russian intervention, Görgei’s surrender at Világos, and the executions of Batthyány and the Arad generals fixed the reign’s opening image among Magyars as one of severity. Bach’s rise at the interior, military dictatorship in the reconquered lands, and the long quarrel over whether the March constitution would ever be fully executed filled the years to 1851.
Absolutism after 1848
On 31 December 1851 the constitution was revoked. The Silvesterpatent (“New Year’s Eve Patent”) and the Bach system that followed organized the empire as a unitary bureaucratic state: German as the language of higher administration, district offices in place of much noble jurisdiction, gendarmerie, judicial reform, and the completion of Grundentlastung (“redemption of feudal land burdens”) as a social foundation for the new order. Friedjung’s second volume and the later books of the first treat the 1850s as the testing of this experiment — financial strain after the wars, the Crimean alignment that isolated Austria, the Italian war of 1859, and the gradual unravelling that led toward the October Diploma and February Patent just outside or at the edge of dense coverage in some volumes. Francis Joseph remained the personal center: ministers rose and fell; the crown did not become a parliamentary executive.
Germany and Italy
In the German question the young emperor inherited Schwarzenberg’s bid to restore Austrian primacy in the Bund (“Confederation”) and to block Prussian Union projects. Sybel’s narrative of 1849–50 places Vienna’s recovery and the pressure that produced the Olmützer Punktation (“Punctation of Olmütz”) in this reign’s first years. In Italy the loss of Lombardy in 1859 and the further crisis of the early 1860s (Venetia still Austrian in 1865) marked the failure of a purely military-dynastic defense of the 1815 settlement. By 1864–65 the Schleswig-Holstein entanglement with Prussia was already preparing the dualist war that falls after 1865.

entities/frederick-william-iv.title: Frederick William IV
entities/frederick-william-iv.content:
Frederick William IV
Friedrich Wilhelm IV. (1795–1861), King of Prussia from 1840, is the central Prussian figure in Sybel’s narrative of the German national crisis of 1848–50. Gifted, devout, artistically sensitive, and stubborn in doctrine, he combined enthusiasm for German greatness with a monarchical theology that refused a crown offered by a revolutionary assembly and preferred a federal order still reconcilable with Austria and the princes.
Person and accession
Sybel’s portrait at the accession stresses overflowing talent and weak active will. The king was rich in knowledge and taste, pure in morals, easily moved, firm once a conviction had settled—yet apt to shrink from breaking obstacles in practice, only to resume the same design later. Military sense was relatively weak in this Hohenzollern; generals complained of superficial reviews. Drawing, romantic architecture, and old church music engaged him more than the parade ground. Cornelius, Rauch, Ranke, and Humboldt felt the charm of his conversation; the political intimates Gerlach, Bunsen, and Radowitz remained under the spell of his personality for life. He could drop from high pathos into Berlin street wit in a moment. That flexibility made him the hope of many parties in 1840 and the despair of consistent politicians in 1848–50.
March 1848 and the German question
The February revolution and German unrest struck him first in the loss of Neuchâtel to a democratic putsch—an insult he could only protest. Radowitz’s memorandum of November 1847, approved by the king, had already proposed strengthening the old Bundestag (“Federal Diet”) with majority voting on military, judicial, and commercial matters—a plan Sybel judges would have been political suicide for Prussia and the Zollverein (“customs union”) without a thorough remodel of the Bund. Sent to Vienna on 1 March 1848, Radowitz found momentary favour before the revolution overtook every cabinet project.
In Berlin, mass meetings, street fights, and barricades in mid-March forced the king to choose between citizen blood and concession. He chose national concession: promises of German leadership, the black-red-gold colours, and a course that briefly looked like Prussian partnership with the revolution. Yet his deeper monarchical doctrine never accepted a German empire created against the princes. In talks with Dahlmann he refused a Prussian hereditary imperial title that would exclude the Austrian lands; he would rather be hereditary imperial field-commander under an Austrian emperor, with middle-state “imperial defence duchies.” An offer of the imperial dignity from the people without or against the princes, he said, must be answered with cannon. A letter to Metternich of 18 April bound him morally to push the hereditary Roman imperial dignity toward Austria. Ministers who would not sacrifice the Prussian state to the House of Lorraine blocked official pursuit of that plan on the eve of the Prussian national assembly.
Frankfurt crown and Union policy
When the Frankfurt Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”) later voted him the hereditary imperial crown of a kleindeutsch Germany, he refused the “crown from the gutter.” Sybel’s volumes treat that refusal as the death of the parliamentary national solution and the opening of the cabinet dualism that ended at Olmütz. The king still wanted German reform—through princes, through a Prussian-led union of states willing to join, through Radowitz’s Erfurt project—not through a sovereign constituent assembly. His will was tenacious and passive: he would not fight Austria for the Union when his ministers’ majority and his own dread of a princes’ war counselled retreat.
After Olmütz
The collapse of the Erfurt Union and the punctation of Olmütz (November 1850) restored the Bund under Austrian presidency. Frederick William kept the imposed Prussian constitution of 1848–50 in revised form while leaning on conservative ministries (Manteuffel). Illness and the regency of the Prince of Prussia (later William I) closed his effective reign. Sybel’s judgment is severe on the political outcome and admiring of the personal culture: a king who could have led Germany if doctrine and nerve had matched imagination.

entities/gagern.title: Heinrich von Gagern (1799–1880)
entities/gagern.content:
Heinrich von Gagern
Heinrich von Gagern is, in Sybel’s Begründung des Deutschen Reiches and Treitschke’s Deutsche Geschichte, the leading moderate of the Frankfurt National Assembly: advocate of a German hereditary emperor, opponent of the immediate republic, and author of the parliamentary drive that elected Archduke John as Reichsverweser (Imperial Regent).
Before and at the Paulskirche
Sybel lists him among the notables who met yearly across party shades—radicals Itzstein and Hecker and moderates Welcker, Soiron, Bassermann from Baden; the resolute Gagern from Darmstadt; liberals and radicals from Hesse and Saxony—trying to unite federal states against the existing federal constitution. At Offenburg (12 September 1847) Hecker led hundreds of free-minded Badenese to Struve’s programme; the split between republic and emperor would soon open.
In the National Assembly Sybel’s chapter on majority sentiment places Heinrich von Gagern centrally: motion for a directorium; Gagern for a Reichsverweser; growing prospect of that office; motion to abolish the Bundestag; law of 28 June; election of Archduke John; recognition by the governments. Against Hecker and Struve’s noisy demand for immediate proclamation of the German republic, Gagern—as fiery as Hecker and as weighty as Struve—answered that not the republic but a German Kaisertum must be the watchword. No understanding between those two desires existed; decision was deferred to the future national representation.
Ministerial conflicts and kleindeutsch programme
Sybel follows the contrast between Gagern and Ludolf Camphausen, Peucker’s circular, Prussia’s motion and its rejection, fundamental rights, the Poland debate, rising party hatred, and republican arming. Later chapters mark Gagern in Berlin, the question of the imperial head, Gagern’s programme amid desolate splits in the Assembly, Prussian cabinet deliberations, and the delay of the second reading of the imperial constitution. Friedjung’s Austrian volumes register the same name as Frankfurt’s kleindeutsch motor watched from Vienna.
The imperial crown offered to Frederick William IV and refused lies at the end of Gagern’s parliamentary road in this corpus: the moderate national programme without republican rupture and without Austrian hegemony. Treitschke’s earlier volumes supply the pre-March liberal biography that Sybel assumes.

entities/garibaldi.title: Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882)
entities/garibaldi.content:
Giuseppe Garibaldi
Giuseppe Garibaldi (Nice/Nizza, 1807–1882) is, in the Italian and French deposits of this corpus, the popular soldier of national unification: sailor and conspirator of the early 1830s, commander of an Italian legion in the Rio Grande and Montevideo wars, irregular chief in Lombardy and Rome in 1848–49, leader of the Cacciatori delle Alpi (“Hunters of the Alps”) in 1859, and captain of the Mille (“Thousand”) in Sicily and Naples in 1860. La Farina, Tivaroni, and Ollivier converge on a double image—revolutionary initiative that cabinets could neither fully own nor safely do without, and repeated surrender of dictatorship or glory to the Savoyard monarchy that alone held a regular army and European recognition.
Origins and South America
La Farina pauses the 1848 narrative to give origin and habits. Born at Nice, Garibaldi was as an adolescent an intrepid sailor; compromised in the conspiracies of 1833–34, he left for the Americas. In the Rio Grande rising against Rio de Janeiro he raised the republican flag on a small craft, was gravely wounded and imprisoned, escaped, was retaken and shamefully tormented. In Uruguay the Italian legion under his name won honour at battles such as Sant’Antonio; the republic ordered the day and Garibaldi’s name written in gold on the legion’s flag and gave the legion the place of honour in public reviews. News of these feats ran through Italy; 1848 called home the man who had suffered for another country’s liberty.
1848–49: Lombardy, Rome, retreat
Returned, he fought in the north; surrounded by Austrians he fought again at Morazzone and withdrew into Switzerland. La Farina records enemy awe: rough soldiers fabled that demons aided him and that the red shirts marked a pact with hell; General d’Aspre, who had felt his blows at Morazzone, later told a high Piedmontese personage that the man who would have powerfully helped their war was Garibaldi, and they had not known him.
In the Roman Republic he sat among representatives and cut short ceremonial delay with the cry Viva la repubblica! His legion—little more than a thousand men of mixed provinces—stood in the order of battle with Swiss, Union, bersaglieri, and other volunteer bodies. As French forces neared, the first brigade under General Garibaldi held the line from Porta Portese to Porta San Pancrazio. Actions toward Velletri and the long defence fixed a European reputation for irregular war and personal courage. After the fall he led the retreat; prisoners taken toward San Marino received bastinado under papal-Austrian reaction at Bologna. In Piedmont the Chiavari arrest of Garibaldi, fresh from the Roman retreat, provoked tearful Chamber scenes that turned a question of national honour into legal cavils over civil and military codes—Tivaroni’s witness to how far his person already stood for Italy in parliamentary rhetoric.
1850s: legend, exclusion, and the southern imagination
Tivaroni notes Mazzini’s 1854 proposal that Garibaldi raise Sicily; small attempts (Bentivegna) failed. For the Neapolitan people, talk of constitutions meant little until Italy appeared “in the flash of Garibaldi’s sword” and the red shirt. Electoral politics could still defeat his name (Bixio beating Garibaldi at Genoa in one contest Tivaroni records). Mantuan and Venetian patriots who later became Garibaldian officers thread the police histories of the 1850s. The legend was already a political force before any ministry commissioned it.
1859: instrument of Cavour and the Hunters of the Alps
Tivaroni’s 1859 narrative is explicit about cabinet use of the revolutionary. If Austria did not attack, Cavour had considered sending Garibaldi into the Duchies to force intervention; lawyers and agents were placed in Parma and elsewhere; a Sardinian squadron showing troops off Livorno was expected to put the Grand Duke to flight. In December Garibaldi came from Caprera to Turin and conferred with La Farina and Cavour. Facing the usefulness of an alliance with the revolution he had always cursed in Chamber speeches, the old conservative dropped scruples: the sovereign princes were enemies to strike down, and this revolutionary was a friend who would help willingly.
Victor Emmanuel gave Garibaldi special powers; Cavour claimed to have induced La Marmora to accept volunteers against the letter of the French military convention. The Cacciatori delle Alpi took the flower of Italian youth not enrolled in the regular army, under Piedmontese organization and discipline (chief of staff Francesco Carrano). Garibaldi later complained to the Chamber that he was given hunchbacks and cripples while the fit went to the line—colours loaded by resentment, Tivaroni notes. In the field the corps stood in line with the Piedmontese army; the king’s letter of 8 May 1859 from San Salvatore ordered Garibaldi to hinder an enemy march on Turin and to move by Biella and Ivrea against the Austrian right toward Lago Maggiore. At Varese (Urban’s attack, numbers disputed in Guerzoni as cited by Tivaroni) Garibaldi struck the enemy flank toward San Salvatore beyond Malnate and pushed them back; the same evening he entered Como as sudden victor while Urban fell back on Monza. The failed surprise at Laveno and three days facing Urban’s reinforced brigades (on the order of twelve thousand men in Tivaroni’s figures) showed the limits of volunteer war beside the regular campaign of Magenta and Solferino.
1860: Sicily, Naples, hand-over
Ollivier’s liberal-empire history, writing from the French side, treats Garibaldi’s epic and Cavour’s unitarian progress as parallel facts that did not slow Paris politics. He records the argument that it was not Piedmont that sent Garibaldi—and that even if it had, a handful could not have overthrown a government that still had a right to live—yet also the charge that ministers stepped back before Garibaldi while calling themselves his greatest enemies, sending rifled guns to Piedmont and lint to the king of Naples. Cobden’s travel note, cited by Tivaroni, feared that the degraded condition of the Sicilian populations would put Garibaldi in grave difficulty among the least civil peoples of the Mediterranean islands.
In the peninsula’s own narrative the Thousand sailed, overthrew Bourbon authority in Sicily and on the mainland, and entered Naples. Calabria and Basilicata, which had risen for the Bourbons with Ruffo in 1799, could rise in 1860 at Garibaldi’s voice for Italian unity and liberty. Piedmontese troops crossed the papal Marches; Garibaldi met Victor Emmanuel and surrendered the southern dictatorship; plebiscites incorporated the Two Sicilies. The pattern of 1849–59 repeated at larger scale: popular war when cabinets hesitated; monarchical consolidation when the European game required it.
After the kingdom (edge of the corpus)
Ollivier continues into the early 1860s: Ricasoli versus Rattazzi; garibaldian leanings that made ministers suspect to the Florentine Consorteria; the king’s secret feelers toward Garibaldi and Hungary; Cialdini’s threat to shoot bands that cried “To Rome with Garibaldi!”; projects to send Garibaldi abroad so that revolutionary initiative would not steal from the crown the merit of taking the capital. Aspromonte and Mentana lie at or beyond the 1865 horizon of many deposits; within the window he remains the indispensable popular arm of a unification sealed in law by diplomacy and by wars cabinets directed.
Place in the corpus
La Farina supplies the biographical romance and the 1848–49 military portrait. Tivaroni supplies the ministerial calculus of 1859, the Alpine campaign detail, and the southern social premise of 1860. Ollivier supplies the French parliamentary and court reading of the same man as revolutionary embarrassment and irresistible fact. Moderate nationalists distrusted pure Mazzinianism yet could not govern the national imagination without Garibaldi’s name.

entities/gioberti.title: Vincenzo Gioberti (1801–1852)
entities/gioberti.content:
Vincenzo Gioberti
Vincenzo Gioberti (1801–1852) is the philosopher-priest of neo-Guelph Italy whose Primato morale e civile degli Italiani La Farina places at the centre of the 1840s federal-papal hopes—and whose programme collapses when Pius IX recoils from national war. A member of Giovine Italia in his youth, he published in the association’s journal under the name Demofilo, was condemned, and fled into exile, before his Primato made him the intellectual standard-bearer of a Catholic federal Italy under papal presidency.
From Giovine Italia to the Primato
La Farina records the shift within the man and the generation. The abhorrence of the papacy was ancient in Italy, and the evil works of the Roman court supplied new documents daily to the sublime and angry words of Dante, the wise and cold words of Machiavelli, and the impetuous and free words of Alfieri. Five centuries after Dante’s Monarchia, the Primato of Gioberti appeared, proclaiming the contrary principle: it strove to prove that nothing useful was possible in Italy against the pope or without the pope, nothing to be attempted except with him and for him. The book, La Farina notes, would have been fit to be promulgated and recommended by pope and princes; instead it was severely proscribed by them—which increased its value—and was eagerly sought and read while the mere licence to hold it was a danger, and later forgotten.
Gioberti’s argument belonged to a wider neo-Guelph historical school. La Farina groups with it the poet who gave Alexander III poetic praise as founder of the Lombard League, Troya straining his great erudition to absolve the popes (even praising them for having hindered Lombard unification), and Balbo labouring to transform Dante into a Guelph poet—all beside the lesser crowd of novelists, journalists, and poets. The Primato thus stood at the head of a whole historiographic and political programme that read Italian greatness as inseparable from the papacy.
The Prolegomeni and the Jesuits
When applause and attack divided opinion over the Primato, Gioberti grew angry and published his Prolegomeni al Primato, in which, with robust eloquence, he attacked the Jesuit fathers and hurled upon them all the faults of clergy and papacy. Father Francesco Pellico, of the Society of Jesus, brother of Silvio, to whom the Primato had been dedicated, accused Gioberti’s orthodoxy. The quarrel fixed Gioberti in the historical record as both the champion of a reformed papacy and the scourge of the Jesuits—the double edge of the neo-Guelph programme that sought to restore Rome’s moral primacy while attacking the clerical machinery that protected the papal temporal power.
1848–49 and the collapse of the programme
When the revolutionary year came and Pius IX recoiled from national war, the neo-Guelph federal synthesis lost its living centre. Gioberti’s brief political role in the Piedmontese crisis—including the office and ministry that the moderate drift of 1848–49 allowed him—could not convert papal refusal into federal victory. National histories keep Gioberti as the intellect of the missed path: the man who had offered Catholic Italy a federation under a reforming pope was overtaken by the monarchical Piedmontese solution that in the following decade annexed the peninsula from Turin. The books remained as monuments of an option 1848 disappointed.
Place in the corpus
In La Farina, Gioberti is the pivot of the neo-Guelph school and its most powerful single voice; in Tivaroni’s later moderate-state narrative, his federal-papal programme is already history, the name surviving as the example of a constitutional-Catholic alternative to both Mazzinian unitarism and pure Piedmontese dynastic ambition. For this knowledge base he is the intellectual author of the neo-Guelph moment and the necessary complement to the papacy’s 1848 decision, which his whole system assumed and which therefore destroyed him.

entities/gorchakov.title: Alexander Gorchakov
entities/gorchakov.content:
Alexander Gorchakov
Александр Михайлович Горчаков (Aleksandr Mikhailovich Gorchakov, 1798–1883) was the principal foreign minister of Russia in the age of the Великие реформы (Velikie reformy, “Great Reforms”). Kornilov’s course shows him less as a theorist of doctrine than as a cabinet weight who, at decisive moments of the peasant reform, tipped the balance toward the emancipating party, and as the diplomat charged with recovering freedom of action after the Crimean isolation.
After Crimea
The Peace of Paris (1856) left Russia with neutralized Black Sea clauses and a damaged European position. Gorchakov’s long tenure at the ministry of foreign affairs belonged to the programme of собирание сил (sobiranie sil, “gathering of strength”) while internal reconstruction proceeded. The contrast with Nicholas’s “chief-of-police” role in Europe, as later characterized by Ivan Aksakov, is the frame of Kornilov’s narrative: the new reign needed peace and room, not a permanent crusade against Western revolution.
Emancipation politics
Kornilov’s detailed account of 1857–61 places Gorchakov inside the ministerial struggle over serf reform. When court serf-owners tried to destroy N. A. Milyutin’s credit with the emperor by charging him with radical and even revolutionary designs, Lanskoi’s defence in the council of ministers was seconded by Gorchakov; outside the council Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna added her protection. That combination kept Milyutin in play long enough for him to become, from early 1859, the working deputy minister who carried the Editorial Commissions’ work through to the statutes of 19 February 1861. Gorchakov thus appears in the internal story as a great-power minister who understood that the empire’s recovery abroad required a serious settlement of the peasant question at home.
European line
In the German and Italian crises of the later 1850s and early 1860s, Russian policy under Gorchakov was no longer the automatic Austrian alignment of Münchengrätz and the intervention in Hungary. Gratitude and debt after 1849 had been spent in the Crimea; the new line mixed reserve, occasional pressure on Austria, and attention to the Eastern Question once the reforms had begun. Within this wiki’s deposits the essential Gorchakov is the minister of the reform years: foreign office support for the emancipators, and diplomacy of recuperation after Sevastopol.

entities/gorgei.title: Görgei
entities/gorgei.content:
Görgei
Görgei Artúr (HU Görgei Artúr (“Artúr Görgei”); often printed Görgey; 1818–1916) was the principal field commander of the Magyar Honvéd (“national defence”) army in 1848–49 and the general who ended the war by unconditional surrender to the Russian field army at Világos (HU Világos (“Világos/Şiria”), 13 August 1849). In Friedjung’s narrative he is both the officer who restored operational coherence after the winter disasters and the man whose quarrel with Kossuth’s political leadership and choice of Russian rather than Austrian captivity shaped the bitter memory of defeat. Austrian pride, the same corpus stresses, was deeply wounded that the main Magyar army laid down its arms before Paskevich and not before Haynau.
Formation and rise
Görgei entered the revolutionary war from the old imperial officer corps and rose with the improvised national army. Springer and Helfert place him among the few professional soldiers who could organise march, supply, and battle against imperial regulars. His early reputation rested on cold discipline and on refusal to let politics dictate every movement of columns — a trait that already separated him from the radical oratory of the Debrecen government. By the winter of 1848–49, after Windisch-Grätz’s advance on Pest-Buda and the flight of the Magyar authorities east of the Tisza, the field army’s survival depended on such professionalism.
Spring 1849: recovery and Buda
In the spring campaign of 1849 Görgei became the embodiment of Magyar recovery. Friedjung’s account of the war after the Russian decision to intervene treats his offensive as the reason Vienna could no longer pretend that the Hungarian theatre was a mere provincial revolt: the Honvéd retook the initiative, recovered the plain, and forced the reconquest of Buda. The recovery raised popular hope and deepened Kossuth’s political investment in total victory; it also convinced Francis Joseph’s government, already hardened by the March constitution of 1849 and by Schwarzenberg’s centralism, that only a great-power coalition could finish the war. The same spring offensive is therefore both Görgei’s military high point and a strategic provocation that accelerated the invitation to Nicholas I.
Dual power: general and governor
The political crisis of the summer of 1849 made Görgei more than a corps commander. After the Debrecen deposition of the House of Habsburg (14 April 1849) and the elevation of Kossuth as kormányzó (HU kormányzó (“governor/regent”)), the field army and the civilian dictatorship pulled apart. Friedjung records the charge, common among Kossuth’s circle, that Görgei aimed at a military dictatorship or at a separate negotiation with the dynasty; Görgei’s own lifelong defence cast Kossuth as the politician who had made compromise impossible and then fled responsibility. What the sources agree on is the fact of dual power: decrees from the governor and orders from the general no longer formed one chain of command. When the Russian masses and Haynau’s reconstituted imperial army closed in, that dualism became fatal.
Világos, 13 August 1849
Outnumbered and cut off from any European ally, Görgei chose to offer unconditional submission to the Russian commander Paskevich rather than to the Austrian Feldzeugmeister Haynau. On 13 August at Világos the main army laid down its arms. Paskevich’s triumphant report to the Tsar — that Hungary lay at His Majesty’s feet — is quoted by Friedjung as the seal of the episode; Austrian pride, he adds, was wounded to the quick that the surrender had not been made to the emperor’s own general.
The choice of Russian captivity had immediate legal and moral consequences. Friedjung states expressly that the fate of the captured Magyar officers would have been milder had Görgei’s army surrendered to the Austrians; bitterness in Vienna and in Haynau’s headquarters therefore outweighed impulses of clemency. Haynau’s decree of 18 August defined who might hope for pardon: common soldiers and NCOs, and officers who had never worn the emperor’s coat, were in principle free; officers who had broken an imperial oath went before courts-martial. A further decree of 22 August undercut the appearance of amnesty by incorporating Honvéd rank and file into the imperial army — some 40,000 officers and men at once — under the fiction that this was ordinary recruitment rather than punishment. About 490 former imperial officers faced the court at Arad; many more escaped or were tried elsewhere. The executions at Arad and the hanging of Batthyány in Pest became the public face of the settlement; Görgei himself was spared execution, a fact that emigration propaganda never forgave.
Memory and judgment
In the Kossuth emigration Görgei remained the scapegoat of national disaster: the general who had broken faith with the April independence and handed the nation to the Tsar. Military writers in the later Habsburg and Dualist periods reopened the file, stressing the hopeless correlation of forces after Russian intervention and the absence of any realistic western rescue. Friedjung’s synthesis keeps both registers: he will not whitewash the political rupture with Kossuth, and he will not deny the operational skill of the spring, nor the structural cruelty that followed a surrender made to Russia rather than to Austria. Görgei lived on into the age of the Compromise and beyond, a living monument to the unresolved civil war inside the Magyar elite of 1849.

entities/guizot.title: François Guizot
entities/guizot.content:
François Guizot
François Guizot enters Duvergier’s parliamentary history as a young Protestant chosen secretary-general under the abbé de Montesquiou in 1814—an appointment that displeased Monsieur and the ultras, yet marked him as a man of talent. He defended, in pamphlets reprinted almost entire by the Moniteur, a middle path between full press liberty and permanent censorship: liberty in principle, temporary restraint in fact, because France had thrice failed to sustain unlimited freedom of the press when it was taken too suddenly.
Doctrinaire path under the Restoration
As a disciple of Royer-Collard he belonged to the doctrinaire strand that sought to reconcile the Charte with strong government. Under later Restoration cabinets he appears as director of communal and departmental administration while Villemain handled arts and letters—administrative posts that trained him in the machine of prefects and elections. With Odilon Barrot, Barthe and others he helped found the electoral society Aide-toi, le ciel t’aidera (Help yourself, heaven will help you), meant to keep liberal agitation strictly legal and to influence the departments. Guizot served as president of its elected committee; carbonari-leaning younger republicans (Bastide, Godefroy Cavaignac, Joubert) formed a loud minority that had to be co-opted by adjunct seats.
In the Revue française he celebrated the 1827 elections as passionate yet free of passion—an assembly in which every shade had taken its place—and he tied the liberal victory partly to Aide-toi, drawing fire from rivals who thought other societies undervalued.
July 1830 and the Orléanist settlement
When Charles X and Polignac published the July ordinances, deputies and journalists organized resistance. Duvergier’s chapter on the Révolution de Juillet records a protest prepared by Guizot among the successive meetings at Dupin’s, the National, Casimir Périer’s and Laffitte’s, while combat spread and the tricolour rose at the Hôtel de Ville. The Orléans solution that followed opened the July Monarchy in which Guizot would later dominate the centre-right.
Minister of the July Monarchy
Under Louis-Philippe, Guizot became the emblem of résistance: enlargement of material prosperity and primary instruction coupled with refusal of further electoral reform. Duvergier’s volumes track him as theorist of the pays légal (legal country of censitary electors) against the pays réel. Foreign policy associated with his name stressed peace and the English entente; domestic politics stiffened against banquet campaigns for reform. When the monarchy fell in February 1848, his fall symbolized the exhaustion of that settlement. Delord later recalls Louis-Philippe’s confidence—voiced in Guizot’s circle—that certain dangers “would never arrive.”
After 1848
The Second Republic and Empire leave him on the margins of Delord’s narrative of conspirators and prefects; his durable imprint in these deposits is Restoration–July: doctrinaire pamphlets, Aide-toi, and the censitary defence of the Charte of 1830.
Resistance and the pays légal
François Guizot embodies the July Monarchy’s late immobilism in Duvergier: enlarge middle-class capacity by peace and enrichment, refuse to dissolve the pays légal by franchise extension, govern through chamber majorities managed with prefectural art. “Enrichissez-vous” belongs to the polemical memory of that programme even when the exact phrase’s currency varies in later retellings; the deposits agree on the substance—capacity over numbers.
Fall with February
The banquet campaign targets Guizot personally as much as the dynasty. His dismissal comes too late to save Louis-Philippe. Delord treats the fall as the end of the doctrinaire claim to have ended revolution by notable government.
Protestant notable
European liberal Protestant connections and ambassadorial intervals appear as secondary colour; the core is domestic parliamentary hegemony until the street breaks the Charter world.

entities/haynau.title: Haynau
entities/haynau.content:
Haynau
Julius Jacob Freiherr von Haynau (DE Freiherr von Haynau (“Baron Haynau”); 1786–1853) was the imperial general who finished the Hungarian war in the field after Windisch-Grätz’s recall and who organised the exemplary terror of Arad and Pest in the autumn of 1849. European liberal opinion made his name a byword for cruelty; Friedjung’s narrative ties that cruelty to structural facts — Russian surrender at Világos, broken officers’ oaths, and a court that wanted Hungary incapable of a second 1848.
Command in 1849
Haynau took the principal Austrian command when the winter campaign under Windisch-Grätz failed to destroy the Honvéd. Brescia had already given him a reputation for ruthless repression in Italy; Hungary became the larger stage. Operating beside and sometimes awkwardly with Paskevich’s Russians, he pressed the reconstituted imperial armies as Görgei’s forces lost room to manoeuvre. The war’s end, however, denied him the full theatre of surrender: Görgei capitulated to the Russians at Világos on 13 August 1849. Friedjung underlines the wound to Austrian pride and the harsher spirit that followed in Haynau’s headquarters because the enemy’s main body had not stacked arms before the black-and-yellow standards.
Decrees of August 1849
As de facto military governor Haynau issued the decrees that framed the White Terror’s legality. The order of 18 August distinguished groups: ordinary Honvéd soldiers and NCOs, and officers who had never held imperial commissions, might hope for freer treatment; former imperial officers who had fought against their oath went to courts-martial. About 490 such officers were collected for the Arad proceedings; others fled or faced other tribunals. A further decree of 22 August undercut amnesty appearances by folding tens of thousands of Honvéd men into the imperial army as if by recruitment. Political leaders — Batthyány foremost — fell under separate lethal categories. The executions of 6 October (Arad generals; Batthyány at Pest) fixed the calendar of Magyar national mourning.
Reputation and removal
Haynau’s regime of flogging, hanging, and confiscation served Schwarzenberg’s short-term need for paralysis of resistance and became a long-term political liability. Foreign protests, including later famous street attacks on Haynau in Western Europe, advertised Austrian shame. Vienna eventually removed him from the Hungarian pinnacle as civilian Bach administration replaced military dictatorship. In the corpus he is the necessary brutal instrument between Windisch-Grätz’s aristocratic war and Bach’s bureaucratic peace — not the designer of the unitary state, but the man who cleared its ground with scaffolds.

entities/hecker.title: Friedrich Hecker (1811–1881)
entities/hecker.content:
Friedrich Hecker
Friedrich Hecker (1811–1881) is the Baden radical of April 1848 whose republican volunteer rising fails early—the signal that German 1848 will not be a clean popular-war unification from the southwest. In Helfert’s Austrian revolutionary panorama and Sybel’s German foundation narrative he appears as the radical pole against which the Frankfurt parliamentary path defined itself.
Baden before the rising
The deposits show Hecker at the centre of the radical preparation in the southwest. In the districts of the Odenwald and Kraichgau and into Hesse, plans were laid for a provisional democratic organization: in every village a Volksverein (people’s association) was to be founded, the associations of an administrative district bound into district associations, those into Kreisvereine (circle associations), and the whole run up into a Landesverein (state association). This was the tissue of democratic Germany that the republicans meant to raise before the Frankfurt parliament could give the nation a constitution.
At the Frankfurt Vorparlament (pre-parliament) the radicals pressed their moment. Joseph Fickler of Constance, editor of the Seeblätter, long an overthrow-man and very popular in the Baden lake district, wanted the republic proclaimed at once, and was with difficulty held back by Itzstein, Soiron, Brentano, and even the arch-radical Gustav von Struve—while Hecker, said to have held a pistol to Fickler’s breast, dissuaded him. Yet it was promised that recourse would be had to force if the government refused the demands. At Heidelberg, Welcker’s eloquence had already managed to restrain the passionate efforts of a court—the same spectrum of pressure and counter-pressure that the revolutionary spring produced everywhere in the south.
Column and defeat
Hecker’s armed band and the push from Constance met regular and militia forces; the rising collapsed. Exile followed. Frankfurt’s later parliamentary path looked moderate beside this premature republic of the gun. The contrast is institutional: the National Assembly’s speeches cannot use Hecker’s failed column as a victorious founding myth, while democrats cannot accept that only professors will make Germany. The rising thus marks a permanent split in 1848’s toolkit—petition and parliament versus volunteer war.
Memory
National-liberal historiography uses Hecker as type of radical impatience; democratic memory uses him as martyr of the unfinished republic. Exile froze Hecker as symbol more than as minister; later memory wars over 1848 reuse him. Within this wiki he stays inside the 1848 operational story that Sybel and Helfert supply: the premature republican war of the southwest against which both the Frankfurt parliament and the eventual monarchical restoration defined themselves.

entities/jelacic.title: Josip Jelačić (Ban Jellačić)
entities/jelacic.content:
Josip Jelačić (Ban Jellačić)
Ban Josip Jelačić (Jellačić in Friedjung’s German spelling) is the Croatian ban whose conflict with the Hungarian government of 1848 became, in Friedjung’s Österreich von 1848 bis 1860, a principal instrument of the court’s recovery against Batthyány and Kossuth.
Against the Hungarian ministry
Friedjung’s contents and narrative place the ban against the Hungarian government after Windischgrätz had crushed the Whitsun rising in Prague. Serbs rose against Hungary; Batthyány carried complaints about Jellačić to Innsbruck; the ban himself appeared at Innsbruck; he was dismissed from office yet continued resistance. The Hungarian diet’s resolutions of 11 July, the Wessenberg ministry’s bearing in the Croatian question, and Bach’s proposals for settling the disorders form the ministerial counterpoint. Friedjung stresses the camarilla: Archduchess Sophie in connection with Windischgrätz and Jellačić; her passionate speech at Innsbruck; Windischgrätz’s instruction for the emperor’s adjutant-general; the ban’s restoration to his offices while the Wessenberg ministry remained ignorant of the court’s measures. Then followed Jellačić’s entry into Hungary, the Hungarian diet’s readiness for war and arming orders, and Batthyány’s resignation.
Southern Slav programme and after
In the later administrative chapters Friedjung notes Jellačić’s wish to unite all South Slavs; boundary disputes between Croatia and the Banat; strife between Serbs and Croats; Swabians in southern Hungary; General Mayerhofer as governor of the Banat; Serb discontent. The ban who had served the dynasty against Pest did not obtain a simple South-Slav state; the neo-absolutist decade reorganized the south under military and bureaucratic lines.
Springer and Helfert corroborate the same 1848 geometry: Croatian military border energy turned against Magyar revolutionary government in the name of the crown. For this KB Jelačić is the South-Slav military lever of Habsburg counter-revolution—not a liberal Croatian national partner of Kossuth.
Ban of Croatia and the Habsburg sword
Friedjung and Springer place Josip Jelačić (Ban Jellačić) at the hinge of 1848–49 when Vienna needs a South Slav military-political instrument against revolutionary Hungary. The Ban (“ban / viceroy”) of Croatia is not a liberal national hero in these deposits; he is the imperial general-politician who can raise Croatian forces, cut Magyar communications, and embody the dynasty’s claim to reassemble the monarchy against Pest.
1848–49 campaigns
Narrative blocks follow his moves in the autumn of 1848 toward the Hungarian theatre, coordination and tension with Windischgrätz and the Vienna military party, and the symbolic value of a non-Magyar army inside the St Stephen lands. Helfert’s revolutionary history likewise keeps the Ban among the names that turn the Habsburg civil war into a war of nationalities under dynastic supreme command.
After the Russian intervention
Once Nicholas I’s armies and Haynau’s repression close the Hungarian war, Jelačić’s wartime role fades into the neo-absolutist settlement’s military memory rather than into constitutional Croatian autonomy of a liberal type. Prefer hungarian-war-independence-1848-49, russian-intervention-hungary-1849, and nationality-question-habsburg for the system.
