entities/kossuth.title: Kossuth
entities/kossuth.content:
Kossuth
Kossuth Lajos (Louis Kossuth, 1802–1894) was the leading orator and political organizer of the Magyar reform opposition in the 1840s and the dominant civilian figure of revolutionary Hungary in 1848–1849. Friedjung, Springer, and Helfert place him beside Count Széchenyi, Ferenc Deák, and Count Lajos Batthyány as the men who turned the old Hungarian constitution into a modern national programme — and who then drove that programme into war with the dynasty, Croatia, and the non-Magyar nationalities of the crown of St Stephen.
Reform opposition
In the diets of the Vormärz Kossuth’s journalism and speeches radicalized the language of Hungarian state right. Where Széchenyi had preached economic improvement, credit, and cautious reform within loyalty to the dynasty, Kossuth pressed for responsible government, the conversion of noble privilege into a parliamentary nation, and the primacy of the Magyar language in administration and diet. His newspaper work and county politics made him the voice of the gentry opposition. The famous speech of 3 March 1848, demanding a constitution for Hungary in the hour of European revolution, is treated across the Austrian narratives as the spark that linked Pest to the March days in Vienna.
April laws and responsible ministry
After Metternich’s fall the Palatine Archduke Stephen and the court conceded a responsible Hungarian ministry. Batthyány became minister-president; Kossuth took finance and, through war credits and oratory, effective leadership of the national cause. The áprilisi törvények (“April Laws”) of 1848 transformed the medieval diet constitution into a modern parliamentary kingdom: personal union with the Austrian lands through the monarch, but separate ministry, budget, and national force. The laws did not settle Croatia’s relation to Pest, the Military Frontier, or the political rights of Serbs, Romanians, and Slovaks. Jellačić’s appointment as Ban of Croatia and the Serb rising against Magyar centralization turned the spring of liberty into a war of nationalities inside the crown.
War leader
As conflict with Jellačić and then with the imperial armies deepened, Kossuth’s finance speeches against Austria and his organization of the Honvéd (“national defense force”) made him the civilian face of resistance. After the October crisis in Vienna and the winter campaign, the diet’s refusal to accept Ferdinand’s abdication as binding on Hungary, Görgei’s generalship, and the Debrecen declaration dethroning the Habsburgs (April 1849) marked the high point of the independent revolutionary state — with Kossuth as governor-president. Russian intervention in 1849 destroyed that state. Görgei’s surrender at Világos, the execution of Batthyány, and the hanging of the Arad generals closed the war; Kossuth escaped into exile and long remained the voice of the defeated cause abroad.
After Világos
Inside Hungary the 1850s belonged to Bach’s administration and to the silent legality of Deák’s circle, not to Kossuth’s émigré republic. Friedjung notes Deák’s reserve and the old-conservative addresses that sought arrangement with the dynasty without Kossuth’s programme. Later Compromise politics (1867) are thinner in these sources.
Assessment in the corpus
Austrian liberal-national historians treat Kossuth as both the necessary awakener of Magyar political life and the author of a unitary Magyar state idea that could not contain the kingdom’s peoples and could not coexist with a unified Austrian empire. Springer’s maxim that Austria’s true charter was its language map is the structural rebuttal to Kossuth’s historic-right kingdom. Narrative pages should present his programme as contemporaries named it — responsible ministry, April constitution, national defense, dethronement — without modern party labels.
Magyar tribune of 1848–49
Friedjung and Springer place Lajos Kossuth at the centre of Hungary’s revolutionary executive: journalist-orator, finance and defence organiser, and the name Europe attaches to Magyar independence. The April Laws and Batthyány ministry are the liberal opening; Kossuth’s leadership marks the radicalisation toward total war with the dynasty and toward the Debrecen independence declaration.
War leadership and exile
Relationship with Görgei and the generals, conflict with conservative magnates, and the final catastrophe after Russian intervention define the arc. Exile afterward turns him into the touring symbol of defeated liberal nationalism for Western publics—more pamphlet than power.
Nationality tension
Slav and Romanian movements inside the Crown of St Stephen experience Magyar liberal centralism as oppression; the deposits do not hide that the war of independence was also a war among nationalities. Prefer hungarian-war-independence-1848-49, jelacic, russian-intervention-hungary-1849.

entities/kubeck.title: Kübeck
entities/kubeck.content:
Kübeck
Karl Friedrich Freiherr von Kübeck zu Kübau (DE Freiherr von Kübeck (“Baron Kübeck”); 1780–1855) was the elder statesman of Habsburg bureaucracy who shaped the Silvesterpatent and fought Alexander Bach for the soul of absolutism after 1848. Friedjung’s second volume makes him the anti-advocate: absolutist and centralist, yet hostile to the March-liberal past and to the clerical bargain Bach struck with Rauscher.
Elder of the Beamtenstaat
Kübeck’s career ran through finance and administration in the Vormärz; 1848–49 recalled him as a man who understood accounts, organisation commissions, and the distrust of parliamentary rhetoric. Schwarzenberg used technical talent wherever found; after the Hungarian war Kübeck chaired critical organisation work on political administration and justice, sharing the centralising task with Bach while despising Bach’s person and origins.
Author of Silvester
As president of the advisory Reichsrat rebuilt for the post-constitutional order, Kübeck supplied the juristic and political arguments for killing the March 1849 constitution. The Silvesterpatent of 31 December 1851 was his monument: open monarchical government without the Reichstag machinery of 1849, preservation of unitary administration, and a council of notables instead of national representation. Friedjung treats Silvester as Kübeck’s victory over residual constitutionalism inside the court.
War with Bach
Victory bred a new war. Kübeck wanted absolutism without the “cunning of the advocate” and without surrender to the Concordat’s clerical immunities. He kept Metternich’s table talk that mocked Bach, Bruck, Stadion, and Schwarzenberg as improbable saviours. When Tsar Nicholas visited Vienna in 1852, the emperor of Russia conspicuously favoured Kübeck and snubbed Bach — a scene Friedjung uses to show how personal and ideological the split had become. Kempen’s police independence complicated both men. Kübeck died in 1855 as the Concordat he disliked was being sealed; Bach outlasted him but not the system’s crash in 1859.
Significance
Kübeck personifies the Josephinist-bureaucratic strand of absolutism after 1848 — central, secularising in instinct, hostile to both popular politics and ultramontane privilege. Beside him Bach personifies the converted 1848 talent that would buy church support and modernise through codes. Their duel explains why “the Bach system” never meant a seamless ministry: Silvester was Kübeck’s; daily interior power was Bach’s; the crown refused to unify them under a new Schwarzenberg.

entities/la-marmora.title: Alfonso La Marmora (1804–1878)
entities/la-marmora.content:
Alfonso La Marmora
Alfonso La Marmora (also written Lamarmora) is, in Tivaroni’s third Italia degli Italiani tome and in Sybel’s German foundation narrative, the Piedmontese general and minister who carried Cavour’s Prussian policy and later headed the Italian side of the 1866 war. The deposits stress diplomacy and military reputation more than battlefield anecdote alone.
Mission to Berlin
When Cavour sent La Marmora on special mission to Berlin to congratulate the king on his accession, he gave instructions (La Marmora’s own later pamphlet on the political-military events of 1866 recalls a letter of 16 January 1861) to make clear that united Italy had a true and permanent interest in intimate relations with Prussia, to which a principal part in Germany’s constitution was reserved. A copy of the Turin foreign minister’s despatch of 29 October 1860 said that, given the remarkable analogies between Prussia’s and Sardinia’s historical tendencies, Italians were accustomed to regard Prussia as their natural ally whose approval they especially desired.
La Marmora, long a student of foreign armies and convinced of the serious consistency of the Prussian, argued with foreign minister Schleinitz against the opinion then common in Germany that the Quadrilateral was necessary to German defence, holding that the natural frontier between Italy and Germany is marked by the Alps. Schleinitz replied that many in Prussia did hold the Quadrilateral necessary to German interests, yet did not seem, La Marmora thought, to share that view himself. The mission concluded little formally, but La Marmora saw the Prussian parliament vote a Vincke motion favourable to Italy and found Prussians ready to push their state onto the path Italy had taken.
Place in the wars
La Farina already knows the family name in the 1848–49 officer lists; Tivaroni’s 1859–66 volume keeps La Marmora among the regular army chiefs of the unitary wars. Sybel’s fourth volume tracks him densely in the 1866 alignment. Ollivier’s liberal empire volumes register the French view of the same Italian-Prussian pairing. For this KB he is the professional soldier-diplomat of the Cavour succession—not Garibaldi’s volunteer pole, not Mazzini’s republican—linking Turin to Berlin before Custozza (1866) stained his later premiership in Italian memory outside these deposits’ full detail.

entities/lamartine.title: Alphonse de Lamartine
entities/lamartine.content:
Alphonse de Lamartine
Alphonse de Lamartine is the poet-politician of February 1848 whom Duvergier’s parliamentary history and Delord’s Empire prelude place at the Provisional Government’s foreign ministry—the moderate republican face that refused the red flag and then lost the street and the election to harder forces.
February and the Provisional Government
After the July Monarchy’s fall Lamartine’s speeches and the famous rejection of the red flag for the tricolour define the Provisional Government’s self-image: a republic without Jacobin terror, addressing Europe as peaceful while Polish and Italian sympathies complicate the message. As foreign minister he is the voice Europe hears from Hôtel de Ville politics. Duvergier’s chronology keeps him central through the spring of clubs, National Workshops, and the election of a Constituent Assembly.
Loss of the initiative
April elections return a conservative countryside against Paris radicalism. May’s invasion of the Assembly and June’s workers’ rising push executive power toward Cavaignac. Lamartine’s own presidential candidacy in December is buried under Louis-Napoleon’s name and legend. Delord reads the poet-minister as the Republic’s lyrical opening that could not become a durable executive—necessary to February, insufficient to hold France.
After power
He remains a literary and moral reference of moderate republicanism in the early Empire climate Delord sketches, without recovering ministerial weight. Prefer february-revolution-1848, second-republic-france, cavaignac, and louis-napoleon-bonaparte for the system arc.
Foreign circulars
Duvergier preserves the Provisional Government’s diplomatic language under Lamartine—reassurance to monarchies, sympathy for nationalities—as the tightrope of a republic that feared a coalition war while feeding European revolution by example.
Hôtel de Ville and the tricolour
In Delord’s February cast, Lamartine’s authority is oratorical before it is administrative. The Provisional Government’s first days require a language that can hold both the National Guard of the quarters and the radical clubs without surrendering the Republic to a pure committee of public safety. His refusal of the red flag in favour of the tricolore (“tricolour”) is not a decorative anecdote in the deposits: it is the moment when moderate republicanism claims the street’s symbolism against socialist and club pressure. Duvergier’s parliamentary volumes treat the same weeks as the hinge from dynastic opposition banquets to a republic that must invent ministries, foreign circulars, and electoral law in a few weeks.
Foreign ministry under scrutiny
As foreign minister Lamartine issues the circulars that try to tell Europe the French Republic will not export Jacobin war while still speaking the language of nationalities. Duvergier preserves the tension: Polish and Italian sympathies in Paris versus the need to avoid a coalition like 1792–93. Chamber and press debates later in 1848 still quote that spring diplomacy when accusing the Provisional Government of either weakness abroad or dangerous encouragement of foreign revolution. The poet’s European reputation is an asset Delord notes when explaining why the early Republic could sound grand and still lose domestic control.
From spring clubs to December ballot
After the April elections return a conservative majority, Lamartine’s personal popularity no longer organises the Assembly. The May invasion of the chamber and the June Days shift executive gravity to military republicanism under Cavaignac. Lamartine’s presidential candidacy in December is a residual moderate name on a field dominated by Louis-Napoleon’s plebiscitary legend. Delord reads the arc as February’s lyrical opening that could not become a durable executive—necessary to the week of the barricades, insufficient against rural suffrage and Bonapartist memory.

entities/ledru-rollin.title: Alexandre Ledru-Rollin
entities/ledru-rollin.content:
Alexandre Ledru-Rollin
Alexandre Auguste Ledru-Rollin appears in Delord’s first volume of the Second Empire as the radical republican orator who, from the July Monarchy chamber through the Provisional Government of 1848, spoke a democratic language the right found hardest to bear—and who, when Louis-Napoléon’s multiple election came before the Assembly, mounted the tribune for “the language of politics.”
Under the July Monarchy
Delord introduces him as an advocate like Odilon Barrot and Crémieux, elected for the Sarthe in place of Garnier-Pagès. Two memoirs—one on the state of siege in 1832, another on the events of the rue Transnonain—had marked him for democratic electors. At the death of the duc d’Orléans he affirmed that sovereignty passed not to a legislature incapable of constituent power but to the nation entire—radicalism that already defined the deputy of the Sarthe against dynastic continuity.
1848 and Louis-Napoléon
In the validation debates over Louis-Napoléon’s elections, Delord lists speakers including Cavaignac, Jules Favre, Lamartine, Buchez, Viellard, and Ledru-Rollin. After Favre’s report favorable to admission and after republicans such as Louis Blanc spoke of confidence and magnanimity—Blanc even suggesting suppression of the presidency as the simple way to block Bonaparte—Delord says it was time for political language: Ledru-Rollin climbed the tribune, “certainly, of all the members of the government, the least agreeable to the right.” The Assembly validated; Louis-Napoléon later resigned the seat; Delord judges that Bonapartism left the incident strengthened.
Character in Delord’s plot
Ledru-Rollin stands for the mountain-democratic wing that could neither absorb the Napoleonic name nor control the rural vote that elected the prince-president. His presence in the Executive Commission’s mixed personnel is part of Delord’s larger story: republican divisions opened the road that Persigny, Morny, and the Élysée would take in December 1851.
Interior and the radical republic
Ledru-Rollin’s weight in Duvergier and Delord is the ministère de l’Intérieur (“Ministry of the Interior”) of the Provisional Government: commissioners sent into the departments, pressure on local notables, and the claim that the Republic must be made in the provinces, not only proclaimed in Paris. Against Lamartine’s European reassurance he represents the democratic left that fears the countryside will elect a monarchical or clerical assembly if left to old influences. Delord’s personnel lists keep him among the names that make Orleanist and moderate Europe nervous in March–April 1848.
Suffrage, workshops, and rupture
Universal male suffrage is the institutional earthquake relative to the July Monarchy’s pays légal (“legal country” of restricted voters). Ledru-Rollin’s current of the party treats the National Workshops and the right to work as tests of whether February was social as well as political. When April returns rural conservatism and June ends in Cavaignac’s repression, the Mountain’s later opposition—including Ledru-Rollin’s line—defines itself against both the general’s sword and Louis-Napoleon’s name. Delord uses that left opposition as part of the Second Republic’s fragmentation before 1851.
Exile and the Empire’s negative cast
After the failure of the radical line he becomes, in Delord’s Empire prelude, a reference point of the defeated democratic republic—more useful to the narrative as contrast to imperial order than as a returning minister. Prefer february-revolution-1848, june-days-1848, and second-republic-france for the system arc; this page holds the interior radical of spring 1848.

entities/leopold-ii-tuscany.title: Leopold II of Tuscany
entities/leopold-ii-tuscany.content:
Leopold II of Tuscany
Leopold II (Leopoldo II), Habsburg grand duke of Tuscany, rules in the deposits as the long sovereign of the “mild” central Italian state—heir to Ferdinand III’s restoration settlement that Tivaroni narrates for Florence, and later the prince who faced 1847–49 constitution and Austrian return.
Restoration inheritance
Tivaroni’s Austrian-dominion central Italy opens the Tuscan restoration under Ferdinand III’s return (Florence, 17 September 1814) with Fossombroni and a legislative commission of Tuscan jurists—signal that the grand duke was not irreconcilable toward those who had served the French period. Rospigliosi’s reaction (civil status suppressed, divorce abolished, tithes restored, French codes replaced) sits beside Ferdinand’s easy temperament in Tabarrini and Poggi. In 1815, for Murat’s enterprise, the court withdrew toward Liguria leaving ministers; soon 4,000 grand-ducal soldiers followed the Austrians on the Naples expedition after Metternich, via Corsini at Vienna, would not tolerate an “Austrian state” remaining neutral. That is the house Leopold II inherited: Habsburg cadet throne, administrative mildness, and limits set in Vienna.
Reform and 1848 in La Farina
La Farina’s later books place Tuscan opinion inside the peninsula’s reform wave: petitions and civic courage in the Legations still measure desires against the 1831 memorandum; Tuscany under Leopold appears among the states where moderate reform and national feeling pressed princes before full war. The grand duke’s constitutional experiment and flight/return in 1848–49 belong to the same narrative arc as Charles Albert and Pius IX—central Italian princes caught between subjects and Austrian power (detailed on linked event pages where present).
Character in the wiki
Leopold II is not a Piedmontese nation-builder; he is the Habsburg grand duke of a cultivated buffer, whose police and finance Tivaroni can call tempered or retrograde by turn, and whose fate shows that even the “mildest” Italian court remained inside the Austrian system when war came.

entities/list-friedrich.title: Friedrich List
entities/list-friedrich.content:
Friedrich List
Friedrich List is the economist of Das nationale System der politischen Oekonomie whose restored full OCR in this wiki underpins both this entity page and the concept national-system-list—productive powers, infant industry, and national economy set against the free-trade cosmopolitanism List attributes to the already-dominant English school.
Life hinge in the deposit
The book, not a decorative biography, is the deposit core. List writes from German and American experience toward a single claim: free trade suits the manufacturing power that already holds the machines and ships; rising nations need temporary protection of productive powers—skills, plant, transport, credit, and a unified internal market—before they can open without becoming agricultural clients. Railway and customs-union politics in the German states are the practical theatre the text keeps pointing toward.
System of productive powers
List’s stages argument treats pure agricultural specialization as dependence. National association (including customs unity) is an economic weapon as well as a political hope. The wiki’s concept page carries doctrine structure chapter by chapter; this entity holds the author-position: the German economist who made protection a national-developmental language rather than a mere fiscal expedient.
Reception without school labels
German historical-political volumes in the wider corpus meet List as a name inside tariff and Zollverein-era argument. This page refuses later textbook school tags not present in the deposits. Prefer national-system-list and zollverein for doctrine and institutional reception; return here for the man as the book’s voice.
National economy and the English school
List’s polemic targets what he casts as cosmopolitan free-trade doctrine suited to English manufacturing supremacy. German and other continental readers are invited to treat customs policy as educational and temporary, not as permanent isolation. The book’s historical examples—Spain, Italy’s commercial past, the United States, Germany’s fragmentation—are pedagogies of power, not antiquarian digressions. Productive power (skills, machines, organization) outranks exchange value counted only in the moment of trade.
Zollverein horizon
Even when List is not writing a year-by-year Zollverein chronicle, the logic points toward larger internal markets and coordinated tariffs among German states. Later German political histories in the corpus meet that horizon when they discuss customs unity as national preparation. This entity page does not invent List’s parliamentary career details absent from the restored book deposit; it keeps the author-function of the Nationale System.

entities/louis-blanc.title: Louis Blanc
entities/louis-blanc.content:
Louis Blanc
Louis Blanc (1811–1882) is the socialist of the Provisional Government of 1848 whom Duvergier’s parliamentary volumes and Delord’s Empire prelude place beside the Luxembourg Commission—the man of the organisation du travail whose programme becomes both symbol of February’s social promise and scapegoat of the conservative order that follows June.
Organisation of labour
Blanc’s pre-1848 writings on the organization of labour and social workshops feed workers’ expectation that the Republic means the right to work, not only a change of dynasty. In the Provisional Government he is associated with the Luxembourg labour commission rather than with a full ministry of labour armed with budget and coercion. That half-power is structural: socialists can be blamed for National Workshops and street pressure they do not fully command, while moderate republicans delay structural property change and fear “the reds.”
The phalanstère question and the French attitude
Delord preserves the texture of the social debate around Blanc and his circle. In the language of the hour, France was “generous” and “paid willingly the glory and the folly of her children”; the Republic would not reproach itself for spending millions in pure loss to clarify a problem on which the fate of the workers depended—so it was said of the phalanstère of M. Considerant. The quarrel among republicans themselves ran across the electoral question: some wanted to name deputies who would swear the oath and sit in the Chamber; others would designate candidates only on condition that the elected refused the constitutional oath; a third fraction, the least numerous, stood for complete abstention. The famous warning that France would pass from the numbness of habit into the sleep of shame, and from the sleep of shame into that of death, belonged to this same radical-critique literature. Blanc’s socialism thus lived inside a divided republican camp, unable to command even the electoral strategy of its own left.
June, proscription, and exile
When the workshops become fiscal and political crisis, the June Days smash the social republic’s street base under Cavaignac. Blanc flees into exile. Delord records the proscription’s own history: it begins the day after the February revolution; the principal actors of 15 May took the first road into exile, passing into Belgium, whose government did not welcome them. The rapprochement between the English and the French of the last thirty years delivered the accused of 15 May, of 24 June 1848, and of 13 June 1849 from the scruples of patriotic hatred, and they found in England the asylum Belgium refused them. Blanc’s name remained shorthand for “1848 socialism” in Party of Order rhetoric and in Delord’s reading of the Republic as prelude to Bonapartist order.
Reputation after 1848
In the deposits of the Empire’s historians Blanc is less a returning minister than a type: the intellectual of workshops versus the peasant and notable majority that elected Louis-Napoleon. Duvergier’s institutional pages separate Blanc’s Luxembourg talk from the Finance ministry’s National Workshops administration—a split that lets opponents blame “socialism” for a hybrid policy no single minister owned. The Second Republic’s failure is narrated partly as the failure of his social programme to command France outside Paris.

entities/louis-napoleon-bonaparte.title: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte
entities/louis-napoleon-bonaparte.content:
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte—nephew of Napoleon I, prisoner of Ham, prince-president, then Napoleon III—is the central French actor of Delord’s first volume: a pretender who learned to speak the language of the people while republican elites divided over how to treat his name.
Ham and the manufacture of popularity
Delord dwells on the prison years. Brochures on material questions (including sugar) drew friendly notices; the Progrès du Pas-de-Calais urged the prince to remain the man of the people. Visits by republican writers—Louis Blanc, Degeorges, Peauger—and correspondence with Béranger, Chateaubriand, Thiers, George Sand kept exterior doors open. Louis-Napoléon’s own letters, as Delord quotes them, claim that the Napoleonic cause moves hearts where Blanc or Sand move only cold reason. Persigny appears as the devotee who fueled the pretender’s imagination, carried the artillery manual, and walked the road to Strasbourg.
1848: elections, validation, presidency
After February the name returned with force. Multiple departmental elections, agitation at the barriers, and a chamber debate with Cavaignac, Favre, Lamartine, Buchez, Viellard, and Ledru-Rollin ended in validation; resignation of the seat still left Bonapartism stronger. Lamartine could not raise a workers’ manifestation against the pretender’s re-entry. The December 1848 presidential election made Louis-Napoléon head of the Republic; Barrot’s first ministry tried liberal cohabitation; the Élysée’s own men prepared the rupture consummated on 2 December 1851 with Morny’s organization of the coup.
Toward the Empire
The same person becomes napoleon-iii; the regime becomes the second-empire / second-empire-france. Italian policy after 1858 (Plombières, 1859 war) shows the imperial executive acting as a European great power—pages linked from the Italian cluster.
Pretender under the July Monarchy
Before 1848 the deposits (Delord, Duvergier’s late volumes) treat Louis-Napoleon as the Bonaparte heir of Strasbourg and Boulogne failures—prisoner, pamphleteer of Idées napoléoniennes, living on the legend of the uncle more than on a party machine. Orleanist police and chamber incidents keep the name alive without yet making him inevitable.
1848: from validation debates to the Élysée
Delord narrates the 1848 elections, chamber debates on validating a Bonaparte, and the resignation incident that still strengthens the name. December’s presidential victory under universal suffrage is the decisive plebiscitary fact: rural France and the Napoleonic legend defeat Cavaignac’s republican sword and Ledru-Rollin’s democratic left. The presidency then becomes the platform for conflict with the Legislative Assembly and for the coup of 2 December 1851.
Toward Napoleon III
This entity page stops at the man who becomes emperor; institutional Empire, Crimean and Italian wars, and liberalisation sit on napoleon-iii, second-empire-france, and Ollivier’s liberal volumes. Keep the distinction: Louis-Napoleon is the pretender-president; Napoleon III is the crowned executive of Delord’s title.

entities/louis-philippe.title: Louis-Philippe
entities/louis-philippe.content:
Louis-Philippe
Louis-Philippe (Louis-Philippe Ier, roi des Français) is the Orléanist sovereign Duvergier’s Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire installs after the July Days of 1830 and follows through mouvement and résistance until the collapse of 1848. He is a parliamentary king by profession of faith and a barricade king by origin—an unstable double that the eighteen-year reign never fully resolves.
Installation of a kingdom of the French
Duvergier’s tenth volume narrates the ceremonial and legal transfer. Attributes of royalty—crown, sceptre, sword, hand of justice—are offered by marshals (Tarente, Reggio, Trévise, Molitor). Crowds are not uniform: some cry Philippe VII, others Philippe I, the better instructed Louis-Philippe Ier. The name quarrel is settled by joining the Orléans names as Louis-Philippe Ier. More serious is the oath. The majority would keep ordinary forms; Dupont (de l’Eure) demands a formula more exclusive of the fallen dynasty, warning that men will otherwise swear mental fidelity to Charles X. Pasquier, backed by Guizot and Broglie, answers that one cannot destroy arrangements and consciences by a phrase. The king signs the deputies’ declaration, the peers’ adhesion, and the oath formula; acclamations close the scene. The public title is king of the French, not king of France—the charter’s revolutionary-monarchical compromise.
The departing Bourbons
Commissaries manage Charles X’s exit. Money is advanced from the new king’s own funds when the fallen court lacks cash; Barrot’s memoirs, as Duvergier uses them, record Charles’s dignified thanks and the duchess of Berry’s sharper line—that Louis-Philippe minds their baggage while taking their crown. The contrast between the old king’s grave resignation and the dauphin’s bearing strikes observers. Legitimist Europe and legitimist France never accept the substitution; the July throne must live with that permanent negation.
Parliamentary kingship and the pays légal
The reign’s working theory is government through chambers, ministries, addresses, and electoral colleges of the pays légal. Duvergier’s volumes track doctrinaires, centre-left, and conservative resistance as they define how far the charter may bend. Guizot’s earlier disgrace under the Restoration (removal from the Council with Royer-Collard and Camille Jordan) already marks him as a man of parliamentary combat; under the July Monarchy he becomes the symbol of capacity, resistance, and refusal to enlarge the suffrage. Banquet campaigns for reform eventually meet a ministry that will not yield—and a Paris that still knows how to unmake dynasties.
Foreign posture and domestic fear
Orléanist foreign policy, in the parliamentary histories, prefers recognition and peace to revolutionary propaganda, disappointing those who wanted 1830 exported. Domestically the regime fears both legitimist rising and republican-secret-society conspiracy. The National Guard, the press regime, and electoral geometry are instruments of a monarchy that claims to be middle-class and national while narrowing the active citizenry.
From July glory to February fall
1830 made the dynasty; 1848 unmakes it when Paris decides the parliamentary machine no longer represents the city. Abdication and flight close the experiment. Detailed sequences live on july-revolution-1830, guizot, pays-legal, and february-revolution-1848; this page holds the person who wore the charter crown between two Parisian verdicts.

entities/louis-xviii.title: Louis XVIII (1755–1824)
entities/louis-xviii.content:
Louis XVIII (1755–1824)
Louis XVIII (1755–1824), brother of Louis XVI, is in Duvergier’s Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire the restored Bourbon who had to reconstitute a royalist party almost from nothing and rule through the Charte (\“Charter\”) after the Empire’s collapse. He is not painted as a pure reactionary twin of Charles X: he is the king who granted and worked the Charte, balanced ultras and doctrinaires, and whose death opened the harder ultra course.
Exile, Hartwell, and the death of the royalist party
Duvergier recalls that after 18 Fructidor 1797 a royal agency in Paris had been in habitual relation with Louis XVIII—Royer-Collard, Becquey, the abbé de Montesquiou, Clermont-Gallerande, Quatremère de Quincy—constituted through Camille Jordan in Germany. When the princes shifted direction and the count of Artois, then in England, was given the leadership of a single merged committee, the agency resolved to dissolve; Royer-Collard’s collective note explained that they had accepted their mission in independence of foreign powers, only to observe events, cultivate opinion, and manifest the king’s beneficent intentions.
By 1813, Duvergier writes, outside a very narrow circle the royalist party no longer existed—if Louis XVII (as the pretender was still styled by some) counted on such servants to recover his crown, he would remain his whole life at Hartwell. Nothing less than the Emperor’s faults and the misfortunes of war could restore the party to life. Louis XVIII at Hartwell received various counsels; Duvergier preserves the indecision around him, the voyage of the count of Bruges to Hartwell, and his own movements to London and Compiègne as the allies prepared the fall of the Empire.
Restoration and the bargain with the imperial state
On 1 January 1814, after years of silence, Louis XVIII published a declaration promising to maintain administrative and judicial bodies in the fullness of their attributions, to keep office-holders in their places, and to forbid investigations that would reopen revolutionary wounds—the programme of a restoration that accepted much of the imperial state machine. In 1814 the count of Artois entered France by Pontarlier and the duke of Angoulême by Saint-Jean (as Duvergier’s summary records the dispositions), while the question whether the king would accept the Senate’s constitution divided the camp. Fouché’s intervention between Artois and the Senate, the intervention of Emperor Alexander, the declaration of 15 April, and the distinction Duvergier draws between an ostensible and an occult ministry all belong to the delicate founding of the new reign. Louis XVIII’s entry into Paris, the granting of the Charte constitutionnelle, and the balancing of the ultras in the Chambre introuvable of 1815 fill the parliamentary volumes as the working out of that bargain.
The king of the Charte
The Chambre elected in August 1815, Duvergier notes, resembled none of those that had preceded it: it contained thirty-three members of the old Chamber of Deputies, seventeen of the Chamber of Peers, and a large bloc of men who had proved their devotion to the royal cause during the Hundred Days either as office-holders or as national-guard officers. Four months earlier no one would have believed the electoral colleges of the Empire could produce such a Chamber. Louis XVIII, who was to owe so much to it, also had to restrain it. His speech on the Charte stressed that it was a constitution carefully drawn before being granted, to which reflection attached him daily, which he had sworn to maintain, and to which all, beginning with his own family, would swear obedience—human and therefore perfectible, but no one was to be exempt from it.
In this reading Louis XVIII is the author of the 1814 promises and the head of the parliamentary restoration Duvergier chronicles: the king who managed the first experiments of government parlementaire under the Charte, balanced the ultraroyalist reaction of the Chambre introuvable against the moderate ministries (including Decazes), and kept the crown a parliamentary actor rather than a purely despotic one. His death in 1824 handed the throne to Charles X and the harder ultra course that would end at 1830.

entities/manin.title: Daniele Manin (1804–1857)
entities/manin.content:
Daniele Manin
Daniele Manin (1804–1857) was the Venetian lawyer who, in the March 1848 rising, placed himself at the head of the restored Republic of San Marco and became the chief civilian of its long siege against Austria. In La Farina’s unitary narrative and Tivaroni’s critical history of Austrian dominion, he appears not as an improviser but as the representative of a specifically Venetian, moderate-legal liberalism that the revolution swept toward a republic it had not originally demanded—and which in 1849 the monarchy of Charles Albert and the ministries of Paris could not save.
Venetian moderate liberalism
Before the bombs and barricades, the Venetian moderates did not ask for revolution. La Farina records their programme as the demand for honest observance of existing laws and of promises already given, and their hope for a Lombardo-Veneto kingdom with Austria that would enjoy the same relations the Kingdom of Italy had once had with France—autonomy, not rupture. It was in this spirit that Niccolò Tommaseo wrote, joining Manin as captain of that tendency, that they should form not a moderate party but a legal opinion, animated by affection: “formiamoci non in partito moderato, ma in opinione legale, e questa opinione animiamo d’affetti” (“let us form ourselves not as a moderate party but as a legal opinion, and let us animate this opinion with affections”). Nothing less could be asked, La Farina adds, nor in more respectful and tranquil ways.
The Five Days of Venice
News of the Vienna rising reached Venice on 16 March 1848 and produced intense agitation; the next day the people rose in tumult, demanding liberty. The first eruption had a precise target: the workers fell on Colonel Marinovich, their chief, a fierce and hated man. He scorned their clamour and the following day returned to his office as usual; but no sooner had he entered, threatening and proud, than the workmen set upon him and killed him. At that noise the civic guards ran to the arsenal, met no resistance, and occupied the most important posts.
The Austrian authorities chose not to fight for a city that had escaped their hold. Under the capitulation, the commandant Count Zichy agreed that the military would leave Venice by sea, leaving in the city the Italian soldiers, the war material, and the military chests; the new government would provide for the transport of the troops and give them three months’ pay; as security for the observance of the pact, Count Zichy would leave Venice last. The deputies announced the obtained capitulation to the people, shouting viva Venezia e l’Italia. More than twenty naval officers deserted their ships and came to offer their services to the republic.
Power passed into the hands of the commander of the civic guard, Angelo Mengaldo, that a provisional government might be constituted. Assembling in the piazza the civic militias and the people, and after the patriarch had blessed the Italian and Venetian flags, Mengaldo proposed the names of the government members, who were accepted by acclamation and universal applause. Manin stood at the centre of this restored republic—the government that, in the words of the moment, had no thought of war or political league among the Italian provinces, its letters of 28 March 1848 containing no word of war and no plan for political alliance.
Between republic and the Alpine–Lilybaeum question
The republic quickly revealed the tension latent in its own geography. La Farina records the reproach that for Manin the Alps and Lilybaeum (the far south) might as well have been Marghera and Chioggia—that Venice, as in the days of her ancient doges, seemed to be not sister but lady and dominatrix of the Venetian cities. The deputies of Treviso were the first to demand a deliberative vote in the councils in the name of their fellow-citizens. The disasters as mainland towns fell again into Austrian hands stimulated the partisans of union with Piedmont: they raised a menacing voice inside Venice, accused the government of having caused the loss of the provinces, and pointed to the Piedmontese army as the sole palladium of safety. Manin, who had suspended the convocation of the assembly, reconvened it on 21 June for 3 July—a further temporizing that stirred his adversaries, weakened his authority, and seemed born of a desire to spin out time.
The Venetian government under Manin pursued a stubborn diplomatic course. Tivaroni preserves the clear and unambiguous demand Manin addressed for the relief of Friuli against the invading corps of Nugent, and the mission of Minister Paleocapa from Venice to the king’s camp to hasten aid for the Friuli and to press the plan that would prevent the junction of the Austrian corps of Verona and the Isonzo. When asked how the republic would answer if its government were disliked by the king, Venice’s answer was that neither its acts nor its opinions would exercise any influence on the political destinies of the nation, which alone must remain arbiter and judge.
Why a republic could not be saved
Tivaroni’s judgment is precise about the structural limits. Had Charles Albert sent a strong reinforcement against Nugent, the republican Venice would have become monarchical unanimously. Instead the king believed Durando and the pontifical and Venetian volunteers enough against Nugent and turned himself to the siege of Peschiera. And France refused the republic: Lamartine, who wanted to impose peace and dictate its conditions but not to wage war to the end, would not recognize Venice. French silence told Milan to Charles Albert, Venice to Austria, Sicily to England, Savoy to France—the diplomatic partition that left a city-state, however heroic, without a great-power patron. The question whether a kingdom of Upper Italy in 1848 would have led more easily to unity Tivaroni declines to answer as a hypothesis that bears no fruit; what is certain is that no French or Piedmontese army arrived in time, and the republic’s envoys discovered what other 1848 governments learned: sympathy is not shipping, and non-intervention can be a sentence of slow defeat.
Capitulation and after
Austrian pressure on the terraferma and at sea turned the republic into a besieged city-state; hunger, bombardment, and disappointed hopes of rescue closed the final phase. The outcome was capitulation in 1849, not negotiated autonomy inside the empire. For Tivaroni, Venice’s fall is another demonstration that 1848 could seize famous cities without permanently breaking Habsburg military power; for Austrian administrative memory the episode justified tighter control of the Adriatic shore. Manin lived in exile, the name carried into unitary politics as proof that municipal Italy could govern itself under fire; the person outlived the republic as argument—about what kind of Italy 1848 almost made and what kind of empire suppressed it.
Place in the corpus
In La Farina, Manin is the legal-moderate face of a municipal revolution that outgrew its programme; in Tivaroni, he is the diplomatic and military co-ordinator of a besieged state whose requests to Turin were precise and whose hopes of Paris were refused. For this knowledge base he stands between the Savoyard dynastic path and Mazzinian conspiracy: a liberal republican who wanted autonomy first and discovered that the war for Italy’s independence could not be fought city by city.

entities/manteuffel.title: Otto Theodor von Manteuffel
entities/manteuffel.content:
Otto Theodor von Manteuffel
Otto Theodor von Manteuffel (1805–1882) was the Prussian conservative statesman who, in Sybel’s narrative, took the helm as the Erfurt Union collapsed and signed the retreat before Austria at Olmütz. He personifies the ministerial majority that chose peace and restoration of the old Bund (“Confederation”) over Radowitz’s risk of war.
From interior to Olmütz
Manteuffel appears in Sybel’s first volume among the conservative names (with Bismarck-Schönhausen) who contested liberal and national currents after 1848. In November 1850, when Count Brandenburg fell mortally ill after the cabinet decision against Radowitz’s war course, Manteuffel took the chair of the ministry and, during Brandenburg’s illness, the interim direction of foreign affairs. Sybel describes his anxiety amid mobilizations in Hesse, Austrian armaments reported from Bohemia, and a threatening note from the Austrian envoy Prokesch. Telegrams of Russian armaments stiffened the peace party. The negotiations that produced the Olmützer Punktation (“Punctation of Olmütz”) were Manteuffel’s work opposite Schwarzenberg: demobilization, abandonment of the Union’s pretensions, and return of German questions to the restored federal diet.
Ministry after 1850
As minister-president he managed the revised Prussian constitutional system in a conservative sense, bargained with Austria over the Bund and the Zollverein (“customs union”), and handled federal interventions such as the Hessian constitutional conflict, where Sybel shows him mediating between radical federal intrusion and Prussian interest. He was not a romantic like the king and not a national-liberal like Sybel’s heroes; he was the administrator of retreat and order after a policy the crown would not fight for.
Place in the story
For Sybel, Olmütz under Manteuffel is humiliation necessary only because Frederick William would not sustain Radowitz. For the longer Prussian story, Manteuffel’s years are the bridge between the failed Union and the New Era and Bismarck’s later conflict ministry. Within this deposit he is the signature of 1850: peace without honour in the national-liberal reading, survival of the Prussian state in the conservative one.
Prussian reaction ministry
Sybel’s Begründung volumes treat Otto Theodor von Manteuffel as a central civilian of the post-1848 Prussian settlement: interior and then leading ministerial responsibility in the years when the constitution is applied in a conservative key, the press and associations are disciplined, and Prussia prepares the diplomacy of the 1850s toward Austria and the mid-sized states.
Olmütz climate and the Bund
Manteuffel’s name attaches to the policy climate of retreat from Radowitz’s union plans and accommodation with Austria at Olmütz (Olomouc)—in Sybel’s nationalist reading a humiliation that later Bismarckian politics must reverse. Administrative continuity, police reliability, and monarchical prerogative matter more in this portrait than parliamentary charisma.
Bridge toward the New Era
When the regency and “New Era” language arrive, Manteuffel’s system is the foil: solid, unpopular with liberals, useful to Sybel as the bureaucratic Prussia that still held the state together after March 1848. Prefer olmutz-punctuation-1850, frederick-william-iv, and german-confederation.

entities/mazzini.title: Giuseppe Mazzini (1805–1872)
entities/mazzini.content:
Giuseppe Mazzini
Giuseppe Mazzini (born Genoa, 1805 in La Farina’s dating; died 1872) was the principal theorist and organizer of unitary Italian republican nationalism after the failure of the older Carboneria (“Carbonari”). Across La Farina’s Storia d’Italia and Tivaroni’s volumes on Austrian dominion and on L’Italia degli Italiani, he appears not as a single episode but as a continuous presence: founder of Giovine Italia (“Young Italy”), correspondent of failed expeditions, triumvir of the Roman Republic, issuer of national loans and secret committees after 1849, and critic of the monarchical settlement that Cavour and Victor Emmanuel completed without a republic.
Formation and Giovine Italia
La Farina opens a dedicated chapter on Young Italy by placing it in succession to freemasonry and carbonarism: it inherited humanitarian doctrines from the free masons and the desire for unità (“unity”) and independence from the carbonari. Mazzini founded the association; he had already, around 1828, directed the literary paper Indicatore Genovese. The programme aimed at reducing Italy to a single democratic and independent state. La Farina insists that national unity was not a mere “dream of Young Italy”: earlier Italian writers and even princes had hoped for it; Young Italy continued that line while differing from carbonaro constitutional schemes on representation, religion, and the form of government. Where carbonaro pacts could point toward oligarchic assemblies or toward displacing Catholicism itself, Young Italy, in La Farina’s contrast, would strip the pope of temporal power only and sought results through popular education and insurrection rather than through the closed rites of the older sects.
Tivaroni’s central-Italian volume places Mazzini among the names that structure the national thought of 1815–1849—beside Manin, Gioberti, Pius IX, and Charles Albert—and shows him already “radicalizing” while Tuscan men of letters abhorred priestly dominion. In Livorno and Pisa the young Mazzini appears with Guerrazzi and Bini around the Indicatore Livornese; Guerrazzi later turned antagonist (1834), censuring Mazzini’s ardent and overbearing character. Police notes mark abbot Atto Vannucci and others as heads of Young Italy branches; reformed carbonarism at Pisa could still agree with Young Italy on overthrowing constituted governments even while keeping initiation rites. Tivaroni stresses how thin the unitary republican minority remained in Tuscany against local autonomy; yet the Mazzinian programme kept a public face through advanced journals that pushed toward unitarian goals.
In the south the same name met different soil. Tivaroni’s Neapolitan volume records that true Mazzinians seemed few outside Abruzzo and long unknown to those of Naples; Neapolitan liberals laughed at Mazzini’s unitary programme and only unwisely took it as auxiliary. Musolino and Settembrini founded affiliations of Young Italy and suffered arrest at Catanzaro; a “reformed” Young Italy could take on a carbonaro flavour. Carlo Poerio could treat unity as a utopia for grandchildren. Regional jealousies—each province wanting another to rise first—hampered general plans, as in the lonely Muratori band at Bologna before the Bandiera attempt.
Letter to Charles Albert, trials, and the Savoy expedition
A long printed letter of Mazzini to King Charles Albert circulated: all Italy waited for a single word to make itself the king’s. The Savoyard courts answered with trials. La Farina lists Mazzini among those condemned to ignominious death, exposed to public vengeance, declared enemy of the country, while others went to the galleys or fled. The 1834 expedition toward Savoy, intended under Ramorino with Polish veterans and the cry of republic, independence, and unity, collapsed in delay, leaked designs, spies, and want of money. Mazzini, exhausted and fevered, still tried to hold the band together; on a false alarm he seized a musket, took a few steps, and fell in a faint. The failure fixed the pattern of his career: exile, correspondence, and repeated attempts rather than a single victorious campaign.
Bandiera brothers, Ricciardi, and the 1840s
Tivaroni follows the Bandiera brothers through letters to Mazzini that state their faith: independent, free, united Italy, democratically constituted as a republic with Rome as capital. Mazzini and Ricciardi tried to restrain premature moves; projects swung between Romagna and the south. Ricciardi travelled Paris–Marseille–Livorno–Corsica for a Mazzinian general rising; the Bandiera landing and disaster still stained the cause. Mazzini’s own Ricordi on the brothers, as cited by Tivaroni, show him receiving eager recruits while measuring what their rank and character might give the cause. After defeats he published Fede e Avvenire, approaching the democratic mysticism of Lamennais: the fallen would yet instruct the living.
1848–49: Rome
In the Roman constituent world La Farina places Mazzini beside Cernuschi, Saliceti, Garibaldi, and Dall’Ongaro as deputies given seats when Rome conferred citizenship on Italians of other provinces. Mazzini entered the assembly on 6 March to high applause. He became the moral centre of the Roman Republic after the pope’s flight—the high point of democratic-republican power in the peninsula before the French expedition restored Pius IX. Garibaldi’s legion and the street cry of the republic mark the same months; the defence and fall of Rome closed the open revolutionary phase without reconciling Mazzini to monarchy.
After 1849: loans, committees, Sapri, and rivalry with Piedmont
Tivaroni’s 1849–59 volume shows the Italian National Committee and Mazzinian subscriptions for rifles destined to whichever province rose first against the common enemy, while a competing subscription for Piedmontese cannon collected large sums. Practical republicans after 6 February looked toward Piedmont and a regular army; impartial history, Tivaroni adds, must still register Mazzini’s declining prestige without erasing his networks. In Austrian Venetia and Lombardy, trials list possession of Giovane Italia fascicles, Mazzinian loan certificates (one silver pencil-case hid a twenty-five-lire Prestito nazionale Italiano ticket), and affiliation to secret committees. Mazzini hid in Genoa; after Panizzi’s failure to free Settembrini and the Santo Stefano prisoners, Carlo Pisacane proposed the Sapri expedition. Mazzini accepted it as he had always accepted like projects, raised money in England, returned to Genoa in May 1857; Saffi’s preface to Mazzini’s works, as quoted by Tivaroni, tallies little more than fifty thousand lire (twenty-two thousand from Adriano Lemmi) among good and bad means. Already in 1854 Mazzini had proposed to Garibaldi a Sicilian rising; Bentivegna’s small attempt followed. Cadore schemes with Calvi and Orsini’s Modenese entry belong to the same stubborn geometry of local sparks.
Amnesties in Piedmont could expressly exclude Mazzini. During 1859 he wrote on the Savoy question; Tivaroni notes him sufficiently informed of Plombières terms that remained verbal until Cavour’s letters were published. He estimated volunteer numbers fantastically high. At Villafranca, Cavour’s fury included the cry that he would take Solaro della Margherita by one hand and Mazzini by the other and become conspirator and revolutionary rather than execute the treaty—testimony, in Tivaroni’s narrative, to how far the monarchical minister still measured himself against the republican name. Saffi could even argue that Villafranca saved Italy from becoming Napoleon’s absolute dependency. In the Romagna and central duchies, Mazzinian names (Dolfi, Cironi) worked for unity while moderate programmes looked more “practical” to many Tuscans; papal and Austrian agents still threatened that if Rome answered petitioners with Nescio vos, Mazzini and “his assassins” would reign within a month.
Place in the corpus
La Farina—himself later a servant of the monarchical National Society—treats Mazzini as midwife of national consciousness and as rival. Tivaroni embeds him in police history, southern reluctance, Tuscan minorities, volunteer war, and the diplomatic revolution of 1858–61. For this knowledge base Mazzini is the republican pole of the Risorgimento: unitary map and moral conspiracy against which Statuto Piedmont, the National Society, and Cavour’s diplomacy defined themselves. The republic he wanted did not become the state of 1861; the national idea he organized did not disappear with his institutional defeat.

entities/metternich.title: Metternich
entities/metternich.content:
Metternich
Klemens Wenzel Lothar von Metternich (1773–1859) was the principal architect of Austria’s European and internal policy from the last Napoleonic wars through the March crisis of 1848. As foreign minister and later state chancellor he stood for the monarchical principle, the European concert of great powers, and the practical defense of a polyglot Habsburg state against liberal and national dissolution. In the language of the Viennese system he was the guardian of Legitimität (“legitimacy”) and of the Bund (“German Confederation”) as instruments of order after 1815; in the language of his enemies he was the embodiment of Stillstand (“standstill”) and police surveillance. His fall on 13 March 1848 opened the revolutionary year in the Habsburg lands and, through the shock to federal Germany, the crisis that Sybel later treated as the first act of German national reorganization.
Career and system
Metternich’s formative years lay in the Rhineland and in the diplomacy of the Coalition wars. After the Congress of Vienna he directed Austrian foreign policy through the congress system and the interventions of the 1820s, then through the quieter decades in which Austria’s European prestige rested less on reform at home than on the reputation of the chancellor and the army. Friedjung’s reading of the Metternichsches System (“Metternich system”) insists that it was not mere abstract doctrine: it was the working answer of a multi-national empire to the double threat of French-style constitutionalism and of national movements that would carve the monarchy into language-states. The system combined diplomatic leadership among the great powers, federal primacy in Germany through the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”) at Frankfurt, and internal administration that preferred bureaucratic caution, censorship, and the cooperation of the provincial estates to a single imperial representative body.
Under Emperor Francis the succession and the education of heirs remained unsettled; under the weak Emperor Ferdinand a Staatskonferenz (“State Conference”) of archdukes and ministers governed in the emperor’s name. Metternich’s weight in that conference was great but not absolute. Archdukes Karl and Johann, Archduchess Sophie’s circle around the young Archduke Francis Joseph, and Hungarian magnates all contested pieces of policy. Hungary, with its historic constitution and diet, was the standing exception to administrative uniformity; Metternich’s notes and conversations on the Magyar kingdom show both awareness of danger and reluctance to force a settlement that might shatter the dual structure of the empire. Reforms that Joseph II had attempted in language and administration were not resumed as a systematic programme. The result, in Springer’s and Helfert’s narratives of the Vormärz, was a surface of order over Mißbehagen (“discontent”) — economic hardship, national awakenings among Czechs, Magyars, Italians, and South Slavs, and a liberal opposition that used provincial diets, above all in Lower Austria, as legal platforms.
European position
In Germany Metternich’s Austria claimed the presidency of the Confederation and the right to treat national and liberal agitation as federal crimes. The Karlsbad decrees and the later federal measures against universities and the press belonged to this federal-police dimension of the system. In Italy Austrian garrisons and treaties with the Italian courts made Vienna the guarantor of the Restoration settlement; Italian national conspiracy and the states of the peninsula therefore appear in Austrian sources as both diplomatic and internal security problems. In the wider concert Metternich sought to keep Russia and Prussia aligned against revolution while avoiding wars that would overstrain Austrian finance. The system’s strength was its reputation and its network of cabinets; its weakness was the absence of a reformed army, treasury, and representative life that could outlast the chancellor’s person.
March 1848 and after
The February revolution in Paris and the Italian and German disturbances of early 1848 reached Vienna through petitions, student agitation, and the Lower Austrian estates. On 13 March the capital rose; Metternich resigned and left the city. Friedjung and Springer treat the resignation as the collapse of a personal and institutional order rather than a mere change of ministry: the Vormärz (“pre-March”) ended with the man who had defined it. A constitution was promised; ministries changed; the empire entered the open revolutionary year.
Schwarzenberg and Bach rebuilt authority after 1848–49 on different principles — military decision, administrative centralization, and, after 1851, open absolutism after 1848 — but they still faced the nationality map Metternich had managed by delay. Sybel’s German narrative uses the fall of Metternich as the European precondition for the Frankfurt Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”): once Vienna’s federal policeman was gone, the national question in Germany could be posed in a constituent assembly until Austria recovered and forced the dualist contest back into cabinet channels at Olmütz.
Assessment in the corpus
Friedjung’s Liberal-national history grants Metternich seriousness as a defender of the imperial idea against national dissolution while condemning the sterility of reform. Springer’s Austrian volumes make the language map and the Hungarian parties the true constitutional problem the system never solved. Helfert opens his revolutionary history with Metternich’s own motto on how little wisdom governs the world — an ironic frame for a chancellor who believed wisdom consisted precisely in preventing the peoples from governing.

entities/minghetti.title: Marco Minghetti
entities/minghetti.content:
Marco Minghetti
Marco Minghetti, Bolognese moderate, appears in the Italian deposits as confidant of Cavour on the Plombières design, witness of the April 1859 crisis, and earlier as a name Pius IX turned toward when the Quirinal emptied in 1848.
Plombières through the Memorie
Tivaroni quotes Cavour repeating to Minghetti in autumn 1858 what Napoleon had finally allowed at Plombières: the Kingdom of Upper Italy might include the Legations as far as Ancona under a veiled “vicariate” formula. Population arithmetic and the map of a French-protected settlement run through that conversation. Minghetti is not the negotiator of Plombières; he is the domestic confidant through whom the deposit lets readers hear Cavour’s post-meeting gloss—moderates of the Romagna learning the price and shape of French alliance.
1859 crisis and annexations
In the war crisis Minghetti’s memoirs again supply Tivaroni with cabinet and diplomatic texture: how Turin read Paris, how annexations in central Italy strained the original Plombières sketch, how Bolognese and Romagnol moderates fitted or resisted Piedmontese timing. The Bolognese origin matters: Legations politics is not abstract geography for Minghetti. Farini, Ricasoli, and other central Italian managers appear as peers in the same moderate world.
Earlier Roman opening
La Farina’s volumes place Minghetti among the moderate names available when papal government collapsed into flight and provisional arrangements in 1848–49. The later Cavourian confidant is continuous with the earlier Roman-moderate generation that preferred reform and Piedmontese leadership to Mazzinian rupture—without erasing the difference between 1848 confusion and 1859 statecraft. Pair with roman-question and pius-ix for the ecclesiastical-state problem that outlasted Minghetti’s confidences.
Regional and fiscal state
Tivaroni’s unitary-administration debates place Minghetti among those who must turn annexation into prefectures, taxes, and schools—the unglamorous half of making Italy after the battles.
Moderate of the Right
Marco Minghetti appears in Tivaroni and La Farina as Bolognese moderate, economist-administrator, and later prime minister material of the Historic Right. Before 1861 he is part of the central-Italian transition from papal/Austrian shadow to Piedmontese annexation politics; after, he is budgets, regions, and the problem of administering a south and a church question the war did not dissolve.
Finance and administration
Deposits stress competence over charismatic war leadership. Minghetti’s cabinets and programmes belong to the attempt to make the Statuto kingdom solvent and centralised enough to hold Venice and Rome still outside the borders. Clerical conflict and regionalism are standing limits.
Placement
Pair with farini, ricasoli, cavour, and kingdom-of-italy-1861; this page is the administrative moderate of unity’s second phase.

entities/morny.title: Charles de Morny (1811–1865)
entities/morny.content:
Charles de Morny (1811–1865)
Charles Auguste Louis Joseph de Morny is, in Taxile Delord’s Histoire du second Empire, half-brother of Louis-Napoleon by the same mother (Queen Hortense’s circle in the public genealogy Delord discusses), organizer of approaches to the prince, and a civilian pilot of the 2 December system.
Kinship and resemblance
Delord pauses on the “prodigious and striking resemblance” everyone remarked between Morny in his last years and Napoleon III. Morny liked to wear hair, moustaches, and beard in the Emperor’s fashion, which made the likeness more perfect. Delord uses the point in a cautious digression on Louis-Napoleon’s paternity: children of the same mother but not the same father—would Morny have so strongly resembled his brother if the brother so strongly resembled the king of Holland? He then leaves resemblance questions as always doubtful and turns to the correspondence of Louis Bonaparte.
1848 approaches
In the propaganda of 1848–49 Delord notes that important names such as the prince de la Moskowa and the comte de Morny were persons to whom openings might later be associated; for the moment Louis Bonaparte kept coldness toward many great imperial names. Walewski, Delord adds elsewhere, brought Morny closer to Louis Bonaparte—the bridge between Orléanist-society talent and the prince-president’s circle.
Coup planning
In September 1851 the President summoned to the Élysée MM. de Morny, Rouher, and de Persigny to study the coup plan prepared by the prefect of police Carlier; after deliberation execution was adjourned. When the coup finally ran on 2 December, Morny’s place in Delord’s cast is the civilian executive of the operation and of the early Empire’s parliamentary management—not a doctrinaire theorist but the flexible operator who made the new regime socially and legislatively workable. His death in 1865 falls at the edge of this wiki’s chronological close.
Half-brother politics and the December machine
Delord’s Second Empire volumes give Charles de Morny a structural role: half-brother connection to Louis-Napoleon, worldly Orleanist manners, and organisation of the coup’s civilian-political side beside the generals. The deposits treat him as the man who translates conspiracy into prefectures, press management, and parliamentary management of the new authoritarian constitution’s first bodies.
Corps législatif and ralliement
As president of the Corps législatif (“Legislative Body”) Morny becomes the Empire’s manager of a muted chamber—elections managed, debate bounded, budget and address politics as safety valves. Delord’s tone mixes admiration for tactical skill with the moral ambiguity of a regime born in December. Economic and railway interests appear in the same portrait as tools of ralliement for notables who will not love the emperor but will sit and enrich themselves.
Death and the liberal turn’s shadow
Morny’s death mid-decade removes a flexible intermediary just as pressures for a more liberal empire accumulate in Ollivier’s later story. Prefer coup-2-december-1851, napoleon-iii, and liberal-empire for the arc; this page holds Delord’s political manager of the authoritarian peak.

entities/murat.title: Joachim Murat
entities/murat.content:
Joachim Murat
Joachim Murat, Napoleonic king of Naples, is in Tivaroni’s critical histories of French and Austrian dominion the southern hinge between Empire and Restoration: a French marshal on an Italian throne whose 1815 enterprise forced every central Italian court to choose between neutrality and Vienna. He is not rewritten as an Italian national founder; he is the most Italianized face of the Napoleonic satellite system in the south.
King of Naples under French dominion
Tivaroni’s French-dominion tomes treat Murat’s Naples inside the reorganization of the peninsula—codes, conscription, administrative modernization under a foreign dynasty. The judgment remains critical of French dominion even while recording institutional change. The same volumes trace the overlapping French and Austrian occupations of central Italy around the fall of the Empire, when Murat’s pressure on Tuscany was felt through mobilization and counter-mobilization: the attempt to keep French troops off the Livorno road, the posting of couriers, and the military moves around Siena and Florence belong to the same tense winter of 1814–15.
Tivaroni preserves the retrospective judgments that Italian memory attached to the Napoleonic and Murat years. To one who enumerated the improvements of the French period, a figure replied that he had served the usurper too—“you did badly, I served him, you could have served him”—and, perhaps without meaning to speak a truth, added that it would have been well had he delayed another ten years. Another recalled that a “prince of good mind,” as Guerrazzi puts it, was dislodged for the enterprise of Murat in 1815 and had to withdraw to Liguria. The passage captures the ambivalent inheritance: administrative progress remembered beside dynastic illegitimacy.
1815 and the refusal of neutrality
When Murat moved in 1815, Tivaroni’s Austrian-dominion central Italy shows Metternich’s line: Tuscan and other “Austrian states” were denied the right to stand neutral. War against Murat was obligatory alignment. The Austrian-led campaign closed the episode, forcing the Tuscan grand duke to leave his state and disrupting the fragile restored order. The lesson for later decades is structural: independence maneuvers that ignore Austrian primacy end in military settlement, a pattern 1831 and 1848 would repeat under different flags.
Afterlife in Risorgimento memory
Carbonaro and moderate generations inherited veterans, place-names, and administrative habits from the Murat years without restoring his throne. The Rimini proclamation and the last campaign enter Italian narrative deposits as a national-language gesture by a French-made king—too late for Napoleon, too early for a durable southern national state. Bourbon restoration closed the episode with Murat’s death. Pages on napoleonic-italy, leopold-ii-tuscany, and italian-revolutions-1831 carry the sequel; this page holds Murat as the person through whom Tivaroni links French dominion to Austrian restoration.

entities/napoleon-iii.title: Napoleon III
entities/napoleon-iii.content:
Napoleon III
Napoleon III is the imperial title and regime identity of Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte after the 1852 re-establishment of the Empire—the end-state Delord prepares through Ham, 1848, the presidency, and the men of the Élysée, and the sovereign Ollivier later tries to liberalize from inside. Delord insists that character study matters because this man played a considerable role; origin, education, and legend are not gossip but political causes.
Blood, name, and apprenticeship
Delord opens the biographical problem that contemporaries never dropped: is Charles-Louis Bonaparte truly the son of King Louis, or a man who believed early in the Bonaparte star without the blood? The historian treats the question seriously because the public’s curiosity and malice shaped the legend the prince later used. Birth in Paris (1808), absence from Holland, the incompatibilities of the royal couple, and the first Emperor’s system of family placement form the childhood frame. Captivity at Ham produces brochures and Rêveries politiques that Delord says the later emperor never stopped mining for laws and speeches. Conspiracy, Strasbourg, Boulogne, prison, and escape are the apprenticeship of a pretender who learns to wait for universal suffrage and army memory.
From prince-president to emperor
The man is the same as louis-napoleon-bonaparte: multiple elect of 1848, president by rural vote, organizer of 2 December 1851 with Morny, Persigny, and the army. The title Napoléon III marks plebiscitary empire once the Republic is closed. Prefer the Louis-Napoléon page for pre-1852 narrative detail; this page for the sovereign identity of the Empire and its working habits.
Machines of popularity and power
Delord stresses machines of popularity: provincial press, workers’ and soldiers’ memory of the first Empire, material pamphlets, and a circle—Persigny the devotee, Morny the organizer, later Rouher in administration—that turns name into state. Official journeys are painted and celebrated; flatterers salute “visible providence.” Delord’s edge is classical and harsh: a people that has sacrificed liberty may lose even the faculty of feeling its ills and grow angry at those who point the suffering out. Roman games under Caesars are his comparison for bread-and-spectacle politics. The Empire claims to stand above parties by direct appeal to people and army.
Police, Marianne, and the attentat climate
Volume two’s chapters on Pianori and other attempts, Corsican brigade guards, cabaret “faits divers,” and departmental arrests under the Marianne pretext show a regime living under December’s memory and under dagger and pistol. Ordinary justice and police sometimes trade places. The cent-gardes scandal rumour of 1855 and the emperor’s reply about corps spirit belong to the same texture. Orsini (1858) has its own event page; here the structure is continuous insecurity paired with continuous surveillance.
Liberal Empire
Ollivier’s L’Empire libéral narrates the attempt to reconcile hereditary imperial authority with expanded parliamentary life. Programmes, electoral contests, and ministerial self-understanding fill those volumes. Liberalization does not erase the founding coup; it is an argument inside Bonapartism about how much debate the executive can absorb. See liberal-empire and bonapartism.
Italian and European policy
Italian deposits place Napoleon III as Piedmont’s partner in 1859 and as the power that both enables and constrains unification—victories in Lombardy, armistice at Villafranca, garrison and temporal logic around Rome. Foreign policy detail lives on italian-war-1859, plombières-agreement-1858, and roman-question; this entity keeps the person-title who authorized alliance, war, and limitation.

entities/nicholas-i.title: Nicholas I
entities/nicholas-i.content:
Nicholas I
Nicholas I (Nikolai I, Николай I) is the emperor Kornilov’s Kurs istorii Rossii places from the Decembrist crisis of 1825 to the Crimean War’s exposure—autocracy reconstituted after Alexander I, police and ideology tightened, peasant emancipation deferred until the next reign. The portrait is institutional as much as personal: a ruler who learns politics from a military conspiracy and then builds a state that treats independent opinion as a security problem.
Accession under the shadow of December
Alexander’s death and Constantine’s renunciation hand Nicholas the crown under Senate Square. The failed rising is not decorative prologue but founding trauma: investigation commissions, five executions, Siberian columns, and a court that reads constitutional speech as treason. Kornilov’s chapters assemble Decembrist programmes, memoirs, and the official inquiry so that 1825 explains Nikolaevan psychology—why the emperor distrusts the guards’ political clubs, why he prefers chancery and corps to public argument, why mercy and severity intertwine in exemplary punishments. The young officers’ European wars had taught them constitutions; the new reign answers with the rope and the march to Siberia.
Machinery of order at home
Administration, the Third Section, and the ideological formula often summarized as Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality structure the reign’s self-presentation. Serfdom remains the social base; serious agrarian reform waits for Alexander II. Universities and the press are policed; education is a loyalty problem as much as a cultural one. Kornilov stresses parade-ground habits at court: the military review as model of the state, personal inspection as substitute for deliberative government. Projects that touch land and status are delayed, narrowed, or buried under committees. Baltic emancipations under Alexander—personal freedom with land left to landlords—are not generalized across the interior. Landlord philanthropy and private experiments appear in the lectures as exceptions that prove the structural freeze.
Official nationality as administrative religion
Kornilov’s chapters on ideology and school policy show autocracy teaching itself a doctrine. Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality functions less as philosophy than as a loyalty test for gymnasium, university, and office. Censorship and the Third Section do not merely punish; they define the perimeter of permissible Russianness. The emperor’s personal religiosity and military piety fuse with this teaching state. Opposition is coded as foreignness or conspiracy even when it speaks patriotic language.
Gendarme of Europe
Abroad, policy defends the 1815 settlement and intervenes against revolution. Holy Alliance language still suits a reign that presents itself as Europe’s policeman. The decisive Central European act inside this corpus is the 1849 intervention in Hungary—Russian arms restoring Habsburg authority after the spring and summer of Magyar war. That success hardens the image of Nikolaevan strength and binds Petersburg to Vienna’s counter-revolution. Western liberal and radical opinion reads the intervention as proof that Russian autocracy is an international system; Kornilov keeps the military-diplomatic fact inside the Russian narrative of order exported.
Crimea and the broken pose
The Crimean War breaks the pose of unreformable strength. Administrative-military failure before the allied siege and the coalition against Russia open the path Alexander II will take toward the emancipation manifesto and the reform statutes. Kornilov’s architecture is deliberate: Nikolaevan order explains both the long freeze and the shock that makes thaw politically thinkable. Victory in Hungary did not predict victory in the Black Sea; the same military monarchy fails a different European test.
Person, succession, and legacy inside the course
The emperor’s suspicion of independent opinion sticks to every institution he trusts. Succession to Alexander II does not erase the police state overnight; it inherits a society the previous reign refused to unbind and a fiscal-military apparatus exposed as obsolete. Entity pages for Alexander I, the Decembrists, the Hungarian intervention, and the emancipation manifesto carry linked sequences; this page holds the reign as system—December to Sevastopol.
