events/central-italy-revolutions-1831.title: Central Italian revolutions (1831)
events/central-italy-revolutions-1831.content:
Central Italian revolutions (1831)
Central Italy’s 1831 risings are the Austrian-belt frame for the crisis told in close narrative under italian-revolutions-1831 and ciro-menotti. La Farina supplies the day sequence; Tivaroni supplies the dominion structure that made Vienna the ultimate arbiter.
Modena: Menotti and the duke’s flight
On 3 February 1831 Duke Francis IV of Modena stormed Ciro Menotti’s house, took the conspiracy chiefs after five hours of resistance, and wrote toward Reggio for the hangman. News that Bologna had risen forced the duke’s flight with the wounded Menotti toward Mantua; a provisional government declared Francis fallen. Menotti’s later execution after Austrian restoration made him the martyr name of the year.
Papal Legations
In the Papal State, wider discontent met a government short of arms and money. Bologna’s provisional government proclaimed on 5 February 1831; columns such as Sercognani’s were received with festival; papal edicts under Bernetti marked the counter-stroke. Reformists later still measured petitions against the powers’ memorandum of 1831—proof that even diplomatic advice for administrative reform could not substitute for force once conspiracy left the salon.
The expectation of French support
Tivaroni preserves the exact calculation on which the conspirators staked the year. Gualterio affirms that Zucchi held in his hands a letter from Marshal Gérard declaring that if a single Austrian soldier set foot in the duchy of Modena or in the Legations, France would have prevented it by force of arms. With such assurances the plotters, in agreement with the Italian committee at Paris, resolved with Ciro Menotti to rise in Modena and Bologna: they would easily triumph over the weak pontifical government; they would receive every kind of aid from the exiles; France would prevent Austria from smothering the movement, which might spread into Tuscany (where Guglielmo Libri was active), into the Neapolitan provinces, and beyond. The military committee took concrete shape under the count Carlo Pepoli by decree of 6 February, with General Giuseppe Grabinsky established at Bologna, commander Luigi Barbieri, and inspector of reviews Emilio Gandolfi; Barbieri was named commander of the civic guard, and the advocate Canuti, who had taken the largest part in the affair, was its soul. The rising’s fate turned precisely on whether the Gérard assurance was real—and it was not, so the Austrian columns that Metternich sent found the Legations without the promised French shield.
Austrian dominion as structure
Tivaroni’s central Italy under Austrian dominion places 1831 inside a system already demonstrated in 1815, when Metternich refused neutrality to Tuscan and other Austrian states against Murat. Intervention restored princes. Survivors of Carbonaro daylight failure moved toward new organizing forms—toward Mazzini’s generation and Young Italy. Leopold II’s Tuscany navigated the same Austrian field without becoming the main battlefield of February 1831.
Austrian police war
La Farina’s 1831 narrative stresses how quickly provisional governments in the duchies and Legations face Austrian columns. French non-intervention (or limited signalling) leaves the field to Metternich’s system. The year becomes a lesson moderates and Mazzinians interpret differently—organization versus conspiracy timing.

events/chambre-introuvable-1815-16.title: Chambre introuvable (1815–1816)
events/chambre-introuvable-1815-16.content:
Chambre introuvable (1815–1816)
The Chambre introuvable (“Chamber beyond finding,” or “incomparable Chamber”) was the Chamber of Deputies elected in France in August 1815, after the second return of the Bourbons and the close of the Hundred Days. Louis XVIII, in the first joy of the result, gave it the name that stuck: a chamber so royalist that, months earlier, no one would have believed the old imperial electoral colleges capable of producing it. Duvergier de Hauranne’s parliamentary history treats it as unlike any French assembly that had preceded it, and as the parliamentary face of the ultra-royaliste (“ultra-royalist”) reaction that followed Waterloo and the second Restoration.
Composition and spirit
Among the new deputies Duvergier notes only thirty-three members of the former Chamber of Deputies and seventeen of the short-lived Chamber of Representatives of the Hundred Days, together with men such as Prosper de Barante and others drawn from provincial notables. The majority was ultra-royalist in temper: hostile to the imperial personnel, eager for exceptional justice, clerical endowment, and electoral laws that would fix the royalist victory. The court and the ministry of the duc de Richelieu stood in a more cautious relation to Europe and to the Charte of 1814; the Chamber pressed harder than the cabinet toward réaction (“reaction”).
Legislative programme
The session opened with the king’s speech and the addresses of the two chambers. The majority then drove through measures of exceptional security: a law of sûreté générale (“general security”), a law on cris séditieux (“seditious cries”), and the law of the cours prévôtales (“provost courts”) for rapid repression. A proposal against the irremovability of the magistracy brought Royer-Collard into the debate. The trial of Marshal Ney and the escape of Lavalette inflamed ultra anger against what they saw as ministerial softness. The amnesty law, reported by Corbière, produced speeches by La Bourdonnaye, Royer-Collard, and de Serre; the Chamber rejected the commission’s categories and confiscation scheme but still imposed the banishment of the régicides (“regicides”) and other hard terms. Individual motions sought clerical endowment, control of civil-status registers, and pressure on the University.
Elections, budget, and rupture with the ministry
On the electoral law Villèle reported for the majority. The question of renouvellement intégral (“integral renewal”) of the Chamber—whether the whole body should sit for a long term instead of partial renewal—became a trial of the parliamentary principle. Royer-Collard, de Serre, and Decazes opposed the ultra construction; La Bourdonnaye, Villèle, and Corbière defended it. The ministry was defeated on the point that defined whether France would live under a cabinet responsible to a fixed ultra majority. Budget debates, the arrears of the public debt, and the question of clerical woods forced further ministerial concessions. Foreign diplomacy watched with unease; Duvergier records Wellington’s letter to the king as a symptom of allied anxiety. The Chamber of Peers rejected the electoral law. Between ministry and majority the rupture became open. After Garnier’s budget report and Kergorlay’s report on clerical endowment, and after a speech by de Serre, the session was abruptly closed.
Dissolution
Louis XVIII dissolved the Chamber about ten months after its election. The name introuvable thus marks both the king’s initial delight and the later decision that such a majority could not be the permanent partner of a Charter monarchy under European observation. The episode fixed Villèle, Corbière, and La Bourdonnaye as leaders of the parliamentary Right, and Royer-Collard’s circle as the counter-weight that Duvergier and contemporaries already linked to the emerging doctrinaires (“Doctrinaires”). The next chambers of the Restoration were elected under different conditions, but the memory of 1815–16 remained the standard of ultra ambition and of royal dissolution as a check upon it.

events/concordat-1855.title: Concordat of 1855
events/concordat-1855.content:
Concordat of 1855
The Konkordat of 18 August 1855 between the Austrian Empire and the Holy See was the ecclesiastical pillar of Francis Joseph’s absolutist (after 1848) decade. Friedjung presents it as Bach’s bargain with Cardinal Rauscher: Rome’s blessing on the unitary throne in exchange for a rollback of Josephinist state control over the Church.
Bargaining context
After Silvester, the young emperor needed moral legitimacy that neither a parliament nor Magyar consent supplied. Archduchess Sophie’s circle and the episcopate offered a Catholic consolidation. Bach, fighting Kübeck and Kempen inside the administrative summit, sought allies; Rauscher delivered clerical support for centralisation if the state loosened its grip on doctrine, marriage, schooling, and discipline. Pius IX’s curia, restored in Rome by French arms and aligned against revolutionary nationalism, welcomed a model treaty with the senior German Catholic power.
Friedjung’s counterfactual is sharp: Schwarzenberg, apostle of Staatsallmacht, would not have signed a Concordat on these terms. The treaty is therefore dated to the post-1852 personal regime — emperor without minister-president, Bach without Schwarzenberg’s cover.
Provisions and sting
The Concordat enlarged church jurisdiction, strengthened ecclesiastical influence over education and matrimonial barriers, and weakened the old placet and bureaucratic supervision associated with Joseph II’s tradition. Critics in the Reichsrat milieu and police warned that clerical immunity and Catholic associations would escape the state that claimed to be absolute. Liberals in German-Austria and passive resisters in Hungary read the Concordat as double reaction: ultramontane and bureaucratic at once. Bach’s elevation to the baronage (1854) and his motto In cruce spes mea became wits’ shorthand for the alliance.
Unravelling
Military defeat in 1859 and the constitutional turn of 1860–61 stripped the Concordat of its political sponsors. Later liberal ministries would dismantle pieces of the 1855 regime; within this corpus the Concordat stands as the high-water mark of throne-and-altar absolutism after 1848, paired with the Bach system and the Silvesterpatent as the domestic settlement of the 1850s.

events/congress-of-vienna-1814-15.title: Congress of Vienna (1814–1815)
events/congress-of-vienna-1814-15.content:
Congress of Vienna (1814–1815)
The Congress of Vienna resettled Europe after the Napoleonic wars: dynastic restorations, a German Confederation in place of the Holy Roman Empire, Austrian primacy in Italy’s north and centre, Prussian gains in the west and in Saxony’s partition, Russian hold on the bulk of the former Duchy of Warsaw as Congress Poland, and a concert among the victorious courts. In this corpus the congress is the starting gate for Metternich’s system, Alexander I’s Holy Alliance language, and the constitutional map that 1830 and 1848 would assault.
In the deposits
Kornilov treats Alexander’s European role and the Polish settlement as premises of Nicholas’s reign and of Russian western policy. Springer’s Austrian history and Treitschke’s German history take the federal act and the restoration settlement as the legal and territorial baseline of the Bund era. Duvergier’s parliamentary France opens with the restored Bourbons under a European order fixed at Vienna—Charte politics inside a continent that had already decided borders and dynasties.
What was settled (as the sources use it)
Exact protocol lists are less important in these narratives than consequences: Austria returns as Italian and German arbiter; Prussia becomes a Rhine power; Russia’s Polish kingdom links domestic autocracy to European guarantee; France is restored but watched. The Hundred Days and Waterloo forced a second peace, but the congress system of later Troppau–Laibach–Verona congresses treats Vienna as the normative map.
Sequel pages
metternich-system, concert-of-europe, troppau-laibach-verona, alexander-i, and Italian dominion pages carry enforcement and challenge. Do not invent Iberian or Balkan settlements the deposits do not narrate for this KB’s geographic honesty.
Settlement of Europe
Kornilov, Springer, Treitschke, and Duvergier all open their post-Napoleonic stories with Vienna: territorial bargains, legitimacy rhetoric, and the new/restored map. Poland’s fate under Russian primacy, Prussia’s Rhine gains, Austria’s Italian and German positions, and the Bourbon restorations structure later national histories.
Institutions
The German Confederation, the concert practice of the great powers, and the Holy Alliance language of Alexander I are Vienna’s institutional legacy in the deposits. La Farina’s Italian proem treats the same congress as the locking of foreign hegemony on the peninsula.
Not a peace of nations
Period authors already note that peoples and nationalities were objects, not authors, of the settlement—an observation 1848 will explode. Prefer holy-alliance, german-confederation, alexander-i, metternich.

events/coup-2-december-1851.title: Coup of 2 December 1851
events/coup-2-december-1851.content:
Coup of 2 December 1851
The coup d’État of 2 December 1851 destroyed the Second Republic’s constitutional balance and opened the path to the Second Empire. Delord narrates it across successive chapters: the night at the Élysée, the proclamations of the 2nd, legal resistance, Baudin’s death, the fusillades of the 4th, and proscription.
Night of 1–2 December
Conspirators gathered at the Élysée. Vieyra arrived; Morny was at the Opéra-Comique then took the interior. The national printing works prepared decrees; police commissioners received Maupas’s last instructions. Arrests struck generals Cavaignac, Changarnier, Lamoricière, Bedeau, colonel Charras, Thiers, Greppo, Roger (du Nord), Le Flô, Baze. Persigny went to the École militaire; Espinasse marched on the Palais-Bourbon despite lieutenant-colonel Niol’s protest. Maupas telegraphed Louis-Napoléon.
2 December
Paris woke to proclamations and decrees, a proclamation to the army, and a press silence that left the people without independent papers. Catholic associations, Delord notes, aided the coup’s atmosphere. Representatives met at Yvan’s and Odilon Barrot’s; the President was declared déchu (forfeit) and the High Court summoned; Dupin’s weakness and Daru’s meeting framed legal opposition. Arrests continued on the place de Bourgogne and at Crémieux’s. Louis Bonaparte showed himself to the population.
Legal resistance and street blood
At the mairie of the tenth arrondissement deputies proclaimed forfeiture, exhorted soldiers to defend the Constitution, and met only passive obedience to military chiefs. Berryer addressed the crowd; police and Magnan’s troops emptied the mairie; deputies rode in prison vans to the quai d’Orsay barracks. The High Court tried to sit; Victor Hugo and Michel (de Bourges) called the people. On 3 December barricades rose; representative Baudin was killed on a barricade. Saint-Arnaud’s proclamations, charges of lancers, and on 4 December heavy fusillades on the boulevards (Poissonnière, Bonne-Nouvelle, porte Saint-Denis) completed the military decision. A decree of 5 December opened proscription.
Forfeiture text
Deputies including Odilon Barrot, Tocqueville, Gustave de Beaumont, Dufaure, Duvergier de Hauranne, Broglie and many others signed the 2 December act invoking article 68 of the Constitution, declaring the President forfeit, convening the High Court, and warning public cashiers not to pay on the fallen power’s order.
Operation of the night and morning
Delord’s narrative of 2 December: army deployments, occupation of printing presses, arrest lists of deputies and generals, placards dissolving the Assembly, and street resistance crushed in the following days. Morny, Persigny, Saint-Arnaud organise civilian and military sides under Louis-Napoleon’s presidency-turning-dictatorship.
Legal mask and plebiscite
Decrees and a swift plebiscite claim popular sovereignty against a quarrelsome Assembly. Proscriptions and the new constitution institutionalise the authoritarian republic that becomes Empire within a year.
Why it closes 1848
For Delord the coup is the last act of the tragedy that began in February—not a sudden accident but the exit from a republic that could not stabilise either social or parliamentary order. Prefer louis-napoleon-bonaparte, morny, second-empire-france.

events/coup-of-1851.title: Coup of 2 December 1851
events/coup-of-1851.content:
Coup of 2 December 1851
On the night of 1–2 December 1851 President Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte broke the constitution of the Second Republic. The longest day-by-day personnel treatment lives on coup-2-december-1851; this slug keeps alternate titles and older links resolving to a full narrative rather than a stub.
Political road
Delord’s arc runs from Ham and 1848 elections through the presidency, Barrot’s failed liberal ministry, and the rise of an Élysée circle that no longer trusted cohabitation with a hostile Assembly. Bonapartism had majority roots in the countryside; parliamentary republicans and Orléanists could not agree on a barrier short of civil war. September 1851 conversations—Morny, Walewski, Palmerston’s English attitude in Delord’s telling—show diplomacy and conspiracy braided before the blow. The coup is presented as consummation of a party that had learned to use legality (elections, presidency) and then discard it.
Cast of the seizure
Morny organizes the civilian and administrative side; Persigny supplies long Bonapartist devotion; the army occupies Paris; legal resistance by deputies is broken. Rouher and other Empire names later solidify the machinery the night made possible. Linked entity pages carry biography without repeating the whole sequence here.
Aftermath
Plebiscitary appeals and the 1852 imperial transformation complete the passage from Republic to second-empire. Liberalization years later (Ollivier’s Empire libéral) do not reverse the founding fact of December. Prefer coup-2-december-1851 when both pages exist and the reader wants maximum narrative density.
From presidency to Empire
Delord’s day-by-day of 2 December and the following plebiscitary Empire make the coup the hinge of Bonapartist legality: force first, universal suffrage afterward. Prefer coup-2-december-1851 as the detailed twin page if both exist; this slug holds the same crisis in the thinner alias band.

events/crimean-war-1853-56.title: Crimean War (1853–1856)
events/crimean-war-1853-56.content:
Crimean War (1853–1856)
The Крымская война (Krymskaya voina, “Crimean War”) of 1853–56 was the military catastrophe that, in Kornilov’s lectures, destroyed the prestige of Nicholas I’s system and opened the reign of Alexander II to the Великие реформы (Velikie reformy, “Great Reforms”). Fought against the Ottoman Empire and then against Britain, France, and Sardinia, it exposed the gap between Russia’s reputation as Europe’s policeman and its real capacity for modern war.
From Eastern Question to coalition
Nicholas’s Eastern policy had long mixed protection of Orthodox interests with the management of a weak Ottoman neighbour—most famously in the Unkiar Skelessi era after the Egyptian crisis. By 1853 disputes over the Holy Places and Russian demands at Constantinople led to occupation of the Danubian Principalities and war with the Porte. Kornilov notes that even against Turkey alone Russia failed to win a quick decision. When France and Britain, then Sardinia, joined the Ottoman side, the war became a test of the whole Nicholas order.
Sevastopol and the home front
Allied landings in the Crimea were limited by sea transport—on the order of some seventy thousand men in Kornilov’s figure—yet the imperial army of roughly a million could not master them. Causes he lists: chaotic military economy, obsolete armament, absence of usable roads and railways to the theatre, and a striking want of generals trained for independent command. Supply of the Sevastopol army still used the methods of 1812; the mass of carts, oxen, and horses ruined the southern provinces while the troops went short. Theft and abuse multiplied expense. Medical and sanitary services failed against southern disease. Strategic plans did not withstand scrutiny. The fall of Sevastopol and the emperor’s death in 1855 sealed the moral verdict before the formal peace.
Peace and political meaning
The Peace of Paris (1856) and Alexander’s manifesto of 19 March 1856 closed the war under a new reign. Neutralization of the Black Sea and the diplomatic isolation of Russia replaced the Münchengrätz alignment and the post-1849 aura of military invincibility. Kornilov stresses that even the heir had believed in the old system’s solidity; after Hungary in 1849 Europe had thought Russian power immense—yet it crumbled at the first serious collision with regular forces of the civilized West. Nicholas Turgenev, he notes, had foreseen something of this already in 1847.
The war’s historical function in the course is causal: it made continuation of pure официальная народность (ofitsial’naya narodnost’, “official nationality”) and unreformed serfdom politically untenable at the top. The Moscow speech to the nobility, the secret committee on the peasant question, and the road to 19 February 1861 follow directly from the Crimean exposure. Горчаков (Gorchakov)’s diplomacy of recuperation is the external counterpart of the internal reforms.

events/decembrist-revolt-1825.title: Decembrist revolt (1825)
events/decembrist-revolt-1825.content:
Decembrist revolt (1825)
The Decembrist rising of December 1825 is, in Kornilov’s Kurs istorii Rossii, the opening crisis of Nicholas I’s reign: guards officers and members of the secret societies attempt to force a constitutional settlement at the succession after Alexander I’s death, and fail in the capital and in the south.
After Alexander and Speransky
Kornilov places Decembrism after the unfinished reform climate of Alexander’s early years and Speransky’s administrative projects, and after the Napoleonic wars that sent Russian officers across Europe. European exposure without a legal channel to limit autocracy feeds society talk of constitution, emancipation, and in some programmes republic. The northern society in Petersburg and the southern society (Pestel’s sharper programme in Kornilov’s architecture) differ in means and end-state, but share refusal of a quiet dynastic transfer when Alexander dies.
Succession moment
Constantine’s renunciation and Nicholas’s accession create the ceremonial pause conspirators use. Senate Square becomes the stage: confused soldiers, conflicting oaths, loyal units, and collapse of the capital rising. Southern failure follows. Kornilov’s narrative is not a romance of almost-liberal Russia; it is a failed officers’ intervention that defines the new reign.
Aftermath
Trials, five executions, and Siberian exile become foundational memory of the Nikolaevan order. Police and ideological hardening follow. Later reform under Alexander II—emancipation included—still moves in a landscape shaped by 1825’s defeat: autocracy warned, society scarred, the word constitution marked. Link nicholas-i, alexander-i, speransky, and emancipation-manifesto-1861 for the longer arc.
Investigation and memory
Kornilov dwells on the investigative commission, the five executions, and Siberia as the pedagogical theatre of the new reign. Later reform generations read the Decembrists as martyrs of a constitution Russia still lacked; Nicholas reads them as proof that mercy is dangerous.

events/duc-de-berry-assassination-1820.title: Assassination of the duc de Berry (1820)
events/duc-de-berry-assassination-1820.content:
Assassination of the duc de Berry (1820)
The assassinat du duc de Berry (“assassination of the Duke of Berry”) on the night of 13 February 1820 struck the younger son of the future Charles X as he left the Opera, and became the turning crisis of the middle Restoration. Duvergier de Hauranne devotes a full chapter sequence to the deed, the session that surrounded it, and the fall of the Decazes system that ultras had already denounced as a surrender to Jacobinism and the press.
Political climate before the blow
The session of 1820 opened under what the king himself called a vague but real unease: each asked of the present pledges of duration. Liberal and independent journals—the Constitutionnel, the Renommée, the Censeur, the Indépendant, the Minerve, the Bibliothèque historique—converged in accusing a faction and an ambitious minister of a plot against institutions. Ultras answered that Decazes threatened to ally with Jacobins if royalists refused to touch the Charte, and that the true choice was the Charte against Decazes. Villèle and the Right used petition debates and electoral theory to rally confidence in the royal word against opposition petitions. The ministry’s position was already eroding when the knife fell.
The crime and the name Louvel
Louvel’s attack on the duke, heir-presumptive in the direct Bourbon line after his father, converted parliamentary bitterness into dynastic panic. Royalist papers treated the murder as the fruit of liberal licence and ministerial weakness; liberals denied collective guilt and feared a White Terror in reverse. The personal tragedy—the duke dying after the Opera—supplied the ultras with a martyr and the court with an argument that conciliation had failed.
Fall of Decazes and ultra advance
In the weeks that followed, Decazes could not hold. The political capital of the assassination passed to the Right. Villèle’s cool, tight argumentation in the Chamber, already visible in petition fights, gained weight as the man of order. Measures of exception and a turn toward a more clerical and aristocratic policy prepared the ground for Villèle’s later predominance and for the Spanish expedition of 1823. The birth of the posthumous duc de Bordeaux (“Duke of Bordeaux,” later comte de Chambord) partially repaired the dynastic wound without repairing the parliamentary truce.
Place in Restoration history
Duvergier’s narrative links 13 February 1820 to the earlier logic of the Chambre introuvable and to the later logic of Charles X: each time the dynasty felt existentially threatened, the parliamentary centre of gravity slid from Decazes-style management toward ultra remedy. The assassination did not create ultra royalism; it removed the last credit of the experiment that had tried to govern against it without dissolving the Charte.

events/emancipation-manifesto-1861.title: Emancipation Manifesto and Statutes (19 February 1861)
events/emancipation-manifesto-1861.content:
Emancipation Manifesto (19 February 1861)
On 19 February 1861 (Old Style) Alexander II signed the statutes worked out by the Editing Commissions and passed, with comparatively small changes, through the Main Committee and the State Council, together with a manifesto in solemn language composed by Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow. Kornilov’s course (Kurs istorii Rossii XIX veka) makes this legislation the hinge of the reign’s first reform period.
Drafting and struggle
The Editing Commissions closed in October 1860; work passed at once to the Main Committee for two full months. Disagreements among members were hard to reconcile; Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolaevich, chair after Orlov’s illness, faced prolonged inability to form majorities on some questions. A noble “feudal” group pinned hopes on P. A. Valuev, then rising from the governorate into the Ministry of State Domains (soon minister of internal affairs after the statutes). That group could not collect a majority; four voices still stood for the commissions’ projects, yet absolute majority failed while Prince P. P. Gagarin held out for landless emancipation and Count Panin disputed many commission decisions. Only by difficult combination was a passable majority formed.
N. A. Milyutin, sharing Samarin’s preference for a radical solution as argued in Sel’skoe blagoustroistvo, had been named deputy minister (at first only “temporarily fulfilling” the office) early in 1859 after Levshin’s retirement, and held the post until the statutes of 19 February. Rescripts and orders on the peasant reform from 1858 to the manifesto were printed in the official collections; the nobility was told that land would remain proprietors’ property but peasants must receive the right to redeem homestead plots in a fixed term and, independently, allotments of field land under obligations.
Content and legal meaning
Kornilov stresses the sheer bulk of the legislation—each statute running over a hundred articles—and its composition across Great Russian, Little Russian, western, and other regional positions (with distinct situations in western Siberia; eastern Siberia had no serfdom). Whatever the material consequences, enormous was the fact that people could no longer sell other people, transfer them from the land into household bondage, or dictate marriage by proprietor’s order. Peasants escaped that unlimited interference in domestic and family life.
Economically the commissions departed from provincial committee norms especially on allotment size and on dues owed for allotments; redemption of obligations (not of the land as such in the legal construction Kornilov explains) was facultative, by voluntary agreement of both sides—Alexander II and Rostovtsev having refused obligatory redemption for proprietors. Allotments went to peasants in “indefinite” or, as Panin insisted, “permanent” use. A small free grant option (darstvennyi nadel) spread dwarf holdings in some steppe provinces where land was still plentiful in 1861. In black-earth provinces proprietors often remained masters of most land with abundant free hands; elsewhere outcomes differed.
Reception and reaction
Peasants expected that proprietors’ power would fall at once and that they would receive in ownership without redemption not only the land they had used but even proprietors’ land, the tsar paying proprietors a “salary.” When the statute showed dues—barshchina or obrok—continuing for an undefined time, possible cut-offs of land, and redemption only by mutual consent, many concluded this was not the true volia (freedom) the tsar could have given, and that proprietors had substituted a false one. Refusal of labour dues and disorders followed; in some places persuasion sufficed; in others bloody pacifications occurred—Kornilov names the catastrophe at Bezdna in Penza province. Impression on society was sharp. In government a turn toward reaction placed Valuev in internal affairs: opponent of the 19 February direction, he had aided Murav’ev and Dolgorukov against the commissions’ project. Lanskoi was removed upward to a count’s dignity; Milyutin became senator with leave to go abroad. Yet thanks largely to the steadfastness of the peace mediators (mirovye posredniki), the statute was in most localities put into life as issued.

events/erfurt-union-1849-50.title: Erfurt Union (1849–1850)
events/erfurt-union-1849-50.content:
Erfurt Union (1849–1850)
The Erfurter Union (“Erfurt Union”) was Prussia’s attempt, after Frederick William IV refused the Frankfurt imperial crown, to build a narrower German federal state under Prussian leadership by agreement of princes—an interim and union constitution, a parliament at Erfurt, and a trial of strength with Austria that ended in the Olmützer Punktation (“Punctation of Olmütz”) of November 1850.
After the Frankfurt crown
When the Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”) offered the hereditary imperial dignity of a Germany without the Austrian hereditary lands, the king rejected a crown from popular revolution. Kleindeutsch hopes did not vanish; they moved from Paul’s Church to cabinet diplomacy. Radowitz, the king’s confidant, became the manager of a union of states willing to accept a Prussian executive and a union constitution short of the full Frankfurt work. The Three Kings’ Alliance (Prussia, Hanover, Saxony) and subsequent accessions gave the project a princely basis. Austria, recovering under Schwarzenberg, refused to be displaced from German primacy and worked to restore the old Bundestag (“Federal Diet”).
Erfurt and dualism
The Erfurt Parliament of 1850 was a union diet, not a sovereign constituent assembly. Sybel treats its constitutional debates and the growing split between a Prussian-led “union” Germany and an Austrian-led return to the federal act of 1815. The middle states wavered; Hanover and Saxony drifted back toward Vienna. Crises in Schleswig-Holstein and especially in Electoral Hesse, where federal execution and Prussian support for the constitution collided, brought armies into motion. Radowitz pressed for firmness amounting to readiness for war; the ministerial majority feared that Prussia’s force was insufficient.
Collapse at Olmütz
In early November 1850 the Berlin ministry, after a scene in which the king privately agreed with Radowitz’s minority yet gave the peace majority free hand, accepted retreat. Radowitz resigned; Brandenburg died within days; Manteuffel took the negotiations. Austrian armaments, Russian pressure, and Prussian isolation produced the punctation of Olmütz: demobilization, abandonment of the Union’s political pretensions, and the road back to a renewed Bundestag under Austrian presidency. Sybel’s national-liberal history calls the outcome a humiliation; it was also the burial of the first kleindeutsch state-building attempt before Bismarck.
Significance
The Erfurt episode fixed the lesson of 1848–50 for Prussian conservatives and national liberals alike: German unity under Prussia would not be granted by Austria or by a princes’ club without a decision of power. The Bund revived; the Zollverein (“customs union”) remained Prussia’s quieter instrument; the constitutional conflict of the 1860s and the wars of unification lay along the line Olmütz had drawn.

events/expedition-of-the-thousand-1860.title: Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
events/expedition-of-the-thousand-1860.content:
Expedition of the Thousand (1860)
The spedizione dei Mille (“Expedition of the Thousand”) was Garibaldi’s May–October 1860 campaign that overthrew Bourbon rule in Sicily and Naples and delivered the south to Victor Emmanuel’s emerging Italian kingdom. Tivaroni’s dedicated book in L’Italia degli Italiani tomo II insists it did not spring fully formed from one brain: Sicilian precursors, long preparation, Garibaldi’s conditions, contested claims of paternity, and Piedmontese half-denials structure the story as much as Calatafimi and Palermo.
Sicilian precursors
Even readers who know the Risorgimento from published books, Tivaroni opens, have learned it imperfectly if they miss the island’s own network. After the rising signals of 4 April 1860, plans at Palermo ran through linked committees (Marinuzzi, Corteggiani, Bruno, Piediscalzi in Oddo’s I Mille di Marsala). The lieutenant’s government under Paolo Ruffo, prince of Castelcicala, still disposed of large forces—Crispi’s diary figures include on the order of twenty-seven thousand men and two thousand Swiss, with some fifteen thousand in Palermo. The rising plan of early April called for detachments in the city’s four sections and squads from the countryside. Trapani and Marsala sought a civic guard; Letizia occupied them with a brigade; Girgenti and Noto saw scuffles. By late April the island could look outwardly quiet while liberals hid or fled. Crispi knew the preparatory net from outside Sicily; few others on the mainland did. The precursors, Tivaroni judges, had done their duty—now the “Redeemer” had to come.
Preparation, hesitation, Quarto
Villa Spinola at Quarto became a headquarters; youths flocked at the word of an expedition. Garibaldi still hesitated. Good rifles existed at Milan; government help through Farini was sought by Crispi and Finzi without solid fruit; La Farina was in Genoa mid-April. Bad news from Fabrizi made Garibaldi call the enterprise impossible and cancel preparations; Türr and Jessie White Mario’s Bertani narrative describe a better telegram—true or invented—that shook him again. After success everyone claimed the decision: Mazzinians because Mazzini and Pilo had prepared the ground (forgetting that without Garibaldi’s choice Mazzini’s initiative would have ended like earlier failures); Bertani denied empty posthumous boasts that the whole concept was one man’s alone. Money stories multiplied (royal two millions after Marsala and Calatafimi for Medici’s follow-on, not before; undocumented tales of tens of thousands from savings banks). What the accounts do show for the eve of sailing is extreme need of cash and the 1,019 rifles from La Farina lowered from the villa.
On the night of 5 May 1860 volunteers left by Porta Pila; toward two in the morning the steamers Lombardo and Piemonte left port, Bixio on one, Garibaldi on the other—Piemonte in the lead. At dawn the adventurous expedition moved to aid Sicily’s insurrection. Garibaldi left a frank letter to the king: the cry of suffering from Sicily had reached his ears.
Marsala, 11 May
A merchantman met on the morning of the 11th reported no Neapolitan warships at Marsala—the two that had been there had gone hunting the enemy. Garibaldi had wavered among Porto Palo, Sciacca, and Marsala; he chose Marsala as nearer and better covered by islands. The steamers touched toward midday. Bourbon ships opened fire late and harmlessly while the Thousand ran from mole to walls; by late afternoon the Piemonte companies were ashore. Garibaldi denied that the English had directly favoured the landing with their means; the tale that Bourbon fire paused on British order was a fable. The town received them coldly at first—“not badly,” he wrote diplomatically; the people cheered, the magnates grimaced. Principal liberals were hidden or fled after April’s failed local move; Neapolitan ships still fired on the city. Overnight some Marsala youths joined. Crispi later summed the island’s role: from Marsala to Palermo the Thousand had Garibaldi and the Sicilian people—arms, money, men. Without Sicilians Garibaldi would not have won; the moral revolution, in that reading, was already done when the ships touched.
The Bourbon army opposite the whole war was still enormous—Cuniberti’s military history of the expedition gives Francis II on the order of 120–130,000 men in line and light units—so the political collapse, not raw numbers alone, decides the narrative.
Calatafimi (15 May) and Palermo (27 May)
From Marsala Garibaldi could have plunged inland to raise the island methodically; he moved toward Salemi and Palermo. Landi’s Bourbon column marched to brush off the “adventurers.” Garibaldi disposed of the Thousand, two added Sicilian companies, rural squads, and a few Marsalesi—little more than two thousand men and six small guns. On the steep height called the Pianto dei Romani the fight fixed the red shirt’s prestige. When Bixio feared retreat, Garibaldi’s cry—placed by Guerzoni at this field though some put the anecdote at Milazzo—was that here Italy would be made or they would die. Calatafimi was a modest combat of a few thousands with light losses, Tivaroni stresses, yet it “stove in the door of Unity”: it encouraged populations and demoralized the regulars. Defeat would have annihilated the revolution among mobile southern crowds; victory fixed the legend. Landi abandoned Calatafimi next morning; Pantaleo offered a crucifix; Garibaldi kissed it bareheaded. The wave spread—Girgenti, Noto, Aidone, and other communes stirred.
Palermo’s taking after the Gibilrossa council (assault versus retreat into the interior) and days of street fighting, bombardment, fired quarters, and opened prisons belongs to the same chapter’s “marvellous” seizure. Bourbon forces many times the improvisers’ number eventually withdrew under armistice terms; the plebeian sequel and the question whether Victor Emmanuel was “male or female” to Marsala mouths show how thin doctrinal unitarism still was among the mass—and how far the name announced by the new “Baptist” nonetheless carried the island.
Milazzo, the mainland, and Piedmont
Milazzo (20 July) opened the strait. The crossing to Calabria and the march on Naples repeated the pattern of small disciplined audacity against a dissolving monarchy. Piedmontese policy, in Tivaroni’s diplomatic notes, denied northern courts any share in the enterprise while Cavour wrote southward in the tone of a partner who could not disavow success. Ollivier records the French argument that Piedmont had not sent Garibaldi—and that a handful could not have toppled a government still fit to live—beside the opposite charge of ministers retreating step by step before him. Annexation by plebiscite and the hand-over to Victor Emmanuel closed the revolutionary dictatorship inside the monarchical constitution.
Place in the corpus
The Thousand is the popular-war climax of the Risorgimento deposits: prepared in Sicily and Genoa, decided in Garibaldi’s will, fought in red shirts, completed in Savoyard law. It is not separable from cavour’s earlier French alliance or from mazzini’s long southern propaganda; it is not reducible to either.

events/february-patent-1861.title: February Patent 1861
events/february-patent-1861.content:
February Patent 1861
The February Patent of 1861 is the imperial act that issues Schmerling’s constitutional framework for the Austrian monarchy—the dated political event behind the longer institutional story of the february-patent concept. Friedjung’s post-1848 Austrian history treats it as a central bid to ground the dynasty in controlled representation after bureaucratic absolutism and after the unsettled year of the October Diploma.
From Bach absolutism to constitutional experiment
Military-bureaucratic rule after 1849 restored dynastic power at the price of political isolation and fiscal strain. The October Diploma of 1860 gestured toward the historic rights of the lands; it did not produce a working imperial settlement. Schmerling’s ministry answers with a clearer parliamentary architecture and a stronger central reading of the state. The Patent is therefore not a first liberal dawn but a second design after the army had already won the civil wars of 1848–49.
What the act does
The Patent organizes Reichsrat representation, defines how the central parliament relates to land diets, and announces a constitutional monarchy still headed by a strong executive. German-liberal ministerial language presents law, budget consent, and public debate as the monarchy’s new supports. Hungarian political leadership reads the same text as a centralist overwrite of March 1848 and of the Diploma’s federalizing promises.
Reception and deadlock
Western-land German liberals prepare to sit and bargain. Hungary largely withholds the cooperation that would make the Patent a shared fundamental law. Other nationalities measure electoral geometry and language practice against their own claims. The monarchy therefore governs with partial houses, boycotts, and recurring crises rather than with a consented constitution.
Place in the arc toward dualism
As a final settlement the Patent fails; as a school of imperial parliamentary conflict it leaves statutes, enmities, and habits. Friedjung’s volumes follow the ministries and deadlocks that flow from 1861. The later Compromise with Hungary lies on the road this failure opens. Use the concept page for institutional anatomy; this event page for issuance and immediate political storm.

events/february-revolution-1848-france.title: February Revolution (1848, France)
events/february-revolution-1848-france.content:
February Revolution (1848, France)
The révolution de Février (“February Revolution”) of 1848 ended the July Monarchy, forced the abdication of Louis-Philippe, and proclaimed the Second Republic under a gouvernement provisoire (“provisional government”). Delord’s history of the Second Empire opens its republican prehistory with the readiness of the National party and the democratic left to form such a government weeks before the final banquet crisis.
Collapse of the July Monarchy
Opposition campaigns for parliamentary reform, the banquet movement, and the rigidity associated with Guizot’s ministry brought Paris to a clash in late February. Barricades rose; the National Guard wavered; the palace lost control of the capital. Louis-Philippe abdicated. The duchess of Orléans’s attempt to present the comte de Paris failed; Delord later recalls her leaving the Chamber on 24 February, taking refuge at the Invalides, then fleeing on foot with her children under the care of friends. On the king’s desk after the flight, papers awaiting signature included, Delord notes, ordinances that would have pensioned Jérôme Bonaparte and raised him to the peerage—symbols of a regime negotiating even with the imperial family until the last hours.
Provisional government
At the Hôtel de Ville a provisional government took shape from the lists prepared by the National circle and the more radical democrats. Lamartine’s presence gave the ministry a national literary name and a voice against the pure red flag. The Republic was proclaimed. Work and order immediately divided the victors: the promise of the droit au travail (“right to work”) produced the national workshops; the Luxembourg workers’ commission under Louis Blanc stood for a more socialist organisation of labour. Sarrans’s Histoire de la révolution de Février, cited by Delord, is among the contemporary narratives the imperial historian still uses.
Bonapartists at the edge
Prince Louis-Napoleon reached Paris only on 25 February and lodged in the rue du Sentier with his old tutor. He wrote to the provisional government placing himself under the republican flag without other ambition than to serve the country; the government packed him back toward England by special train at four in the morning—the surest way, Delord remarks, to give the pretender importance and keep him from wearing himself out in faults. Napoléon-Jérôme had shown himself on the 23rd and 24th hoping to exploit a resemblance to the emperor, without decisive effect. The February days thus opened both the republican experiment and the Bonapartist opportunity that the December 1848 presidential election would crown.
European signal
The fall of the July Monarchy detonated the wider revolutionary year. Austrian and German narratives of March 1848 treat Paris February as the shock that unseated Metternich’s credit. Within France the February victory remained incomplete until the June days tested the social republic and the presidential election tested the imperial name.

events/february-revolution-1848.title: February Revolution (1848)
events/february-revolution-1848.content:
February Revolution (1848)
The February Revolution of 1848 ends the July Monarchy and opens the Second Republic—the French hinge Duvergier’s later parliamentary volumes and Delord’s Empire history treat as the gateway to June, December 1848, and the coup of 1851.
Banquets and collapse
Opposition banquet campaigns against Guizot’s immobilism meet prohibition and street fighting in Paris. Louis-Philippe abdicates; the Provisional Government proclaims the Republic at the Hôtel de Ville. Lamartine’s foreign ministry and tricolour symbolism, Ledru-Rollin’s interior, Blanc’s labour association, and the promise of National Workshops define the spring programme. Universal male suffrage is the institutional earthquake relative to the pays légal of the Charter.
From February to June and December
April elections return rural conservatism. May’s Assembly invasion and June’s workers’ rising hand the sword to Cavaignac. December’s presidential election hands the name of Bonaparte to Louis-Napoleon. February’s lyrical republic becomes, in Delord’s reading, the first act of a tragedy whose last act is 2 December 1851. Prefer second-republic-france, june-days-1848, and person pages for each actor; this event holds the dynasty’s fall and the Republic’s birth week.
European weather
February’s signal feeds Italian, German, and Habsburg revolutions the same year—outside pure Paris chronology but inside the corpus’s 1848 cluster. French deposits remain Paris-centred for the event itself.
Week of the barricades
Duvergier’s detail runs from the banned banquet through Guizot’s resignation, boulevard shootings, and the king’s abdication to the Hôtel de Ville proclamation. The National Guard’s defection and the dynastic left’s loss of control to republican names (Lamartine, Ledru-Rollin, Blanc, Marie, Crémieux, Arago, Garnier-Pagès) are the political content of the street victory.
Social programme of the spring
Ateliers nationaux (“National Workshops”), Luxembourg commission labour talk, and universal male suffrage are February’s social-political dowry. Delord stresses how quickly the programme outruns moderate republican capacity once food, wages, and club pressure meet a conservative elected assembly.
Why the event page stays Paris-centred
Italian and German 1848s are separate event pages; French deposits narrate February as a Paris institutional collapse that becomes a European signal. Cross-link rather than dilute.

events/frankfurt-national-assembly-1848-.title: Frankfurt National Assembly (1848–49)
events/frankfurt-national-assembly-1848-.content:
Frankfurt National Assembly (1848–49)
The Frankfurt National Assembly (Nationalversammlung, Paulskirche) is the German national parliament of 1848–49. Sybel’s Begründung des Deutschen Reiches follows its internal leadership, the Danish war’s feedback into assembly prestige, and the failure to place a crown on a Prussian head—material later Empire-founding narrative needs in order to explain why 1871 was not 1849.
Leadership and the Reichsverweser
Sybel’s table of contents for the National Assembly chapter names the majority’s disposition, Heinrich von Gagern, the motion for a directorium, Gagern’s preference for a Reichsverweser, the growing prospect of that office, the motion to abolish the old Bundestag, the law of 28 June, the election of Archduke John, and recognition of John by the governments. The Assembly thus tried to invent a provisional central executive above the Confederation diet it was replacing.
Danish war and Malmö
The Schleswig-Holstein war repeatedly decides the Assembly’s fate in Sybel’s telling. Wrangel’s Prussian operations, the armistice politics of Malmö, and foreign pressure from Russia, France, and Austria against a pure German course turn military events into parliamentary crises. Passionate debate, republican street attempts and their suppression, and sinking prestige mark the sequence. Sybel later recalls how the sad course of a war begun with joy acted decisively on the destinies of the Frankfurt parliament and of the Prussian Union.
Constitution and the imperial offer
The constitutional work—fundamental rights, the question of Austria’s place, the hereditary emperorship offered to the king of Prussia—belongs to the same arc. Rejection in Berlin and the collapse of the Assembly end the attempt to found the Empire from below by national representation. Later chapters on Erfurt, Olmütz, and the restored Bund are sequels: governments reclaimed German public law after Frankfurt failed.
Afterlife in Sybel’s later volumes
Frankfurt does not vanish in 1849. Sybel’s 1860s narrative still measures Prussian refusal to treat a revived Frankfurt majority diet as the old Bundestag, and still tracks middle-state Abgeordnetentage and Fürstentag politics that invoke the city as German capital of opinion. The Assembly is therefore both a failed founding and a permanent reference point.

events/gaeta-siege-1860-61.title: Gaeta — papal refuge (1848–49) and Bourbon last stand (1860–61)
events/gaeta-siege-1860-61.content:
Gaeta
Gaeta enters this corpus twice as a fortress of last resort: first as the refuge of Pius IX after his flight from Rome (November 1848), under the hospitality of Ferdinand II of Naples; later as the final Bourbon stronghold of Francis II against Piedmontese arms in 1860–61. La Farina’s fourth volume opens its Roman book with the path to Gaeta; Tivaroni’s central and southern volumes and the Italia degli Italiani tomes carry both papal and Bourbon sieges.
Pius IX’s flight (1848)
After Pellegrino Rossi’s ministry concentrated authority and drew hatred from enemies and friends of liberty alike, the pope’s position collapsed. La Farina narrates the secret departure: outside Rome’s walls, joined to Count and Countess Spaur, the pontiff rode the Terracina road to Molo di Gaeta and paused in a public inn. Spaur went swiftly to Naples with a papal letter; Ferdinand hurried with extreme reverence and prayed him to accept hospitality in the castle of Gaeta, which the pope granted. La Farina stresses the Neapolitan king’s joy: in the presence of the Vicar of God he could break oaths sworn in God’s name, knowing the benefit and the shared interest that bound them. Brothers, Rosmini, and Montanari learned of the flight only the next day though promised a place in the escort; they left Rome at hazard not knowing which road to take.
From Gaeta issued acts the Roman deputies refused to treat as authentic. On the evening of 3 December the council of deputies resolved that the act said to be signed by the pontiff at Gaeta on 27 November lacked for them any character of authenticity or regular publicity—and that even if it did not, it would not present under any form the basis they required. Gaeta thus became the external capital of restored papal temporal claims while Rome moved toward the Republic of 1849.
Bourbon endgame (1860–61)
Tivaroni’s southern and 1859–66 volumes place the second Gaeta after Garibaldi’s southern campaign and the Piedmontese intervention: Francis II shut himself in the fortress; Cialdini’s operations and the long siege closed the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. The name that had sheltered Pius now sheltered the last Bourbon king until surrender opened the road to the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy. The double use of the fortress in twelve years—papal reaction and dynastic end—makes Gaeta a hinge between 1849 and 1861 in the Italian deposits.

events/gastein-convention-1865.title: Gastein Convention (1865)
events/gastein-convention-1865.content:
Gastein Convention (1865)
In Sybel’s narrative the name Gastein marks the royal sojourn and telegraph hub while Bismarck settled peace preliminaries and borders with Denmark’s aftermath—and, in the wider German dualism story, the 1865 convention that divided administration of the conquered duchies between Austria and Prussia.
King at Gastein, minister at Vienna
After preliminary peace terms, Bismarck left Vienna for the king at Gastein; preparations for the definitive Vienna peace treaty went forward in Berlin (schemata by Balan and Werther; commercial claims). Border bargaining over Schleswig enclaves historically under Jutland administration produced agreement—Ripen for Denmark; Arrö and a strip south of Kolding as compensation—settled with telegraphic correspondence to Gastein and Copenhagen. Gastein thus functions as the monarch’s seat of sanction while detail is cut in Vienna.
Dual possession after Denmark
The duchies stripped from Denmark had to be held somehow under two German great powers. The convention associated with Gastein (August 1865 in the political calendar Sybel’s war sequel implies) assigned administrative spheres—commonly Schleswig to Prussia and Holstein to Austria in the public settlement—buying time inside the Confederation while deepening the dualism Sybel’s earlier books already map at the Bundestag. Rechberg’s fall after the Vienna peace work belongs to the same Austrian ministerial instability.
Sybel’s fourth volume records the terms as joint possession under German sovereignty: the two duchies were ceded to Prussia and Austria in common ownership, the two powers pledging to decide the future of that ownership only in agreement with each other—a Condominium whose very wording invited the clash over whether the partners would agree on the duchies’ final destiny. The same volume ties the Gastein weather to the wider European map: the Vienna treaty of 12 June, Prussia’s refusal of any German land cessions to France, Napoleon’s silence on that refusal, and his attempt to detach Italy from Prussia by Napoleon’s manifesto of 11 June. Gastein thus marks the August pause before the open rupture of 1866: the partition that postponed, but could not settle, the question the Condominium left unanswered.
Limit of the deposit for this page
Sybel’s third volume as mined here is richest on the war-to-peace hinge and the king’s Gastein presence; the formal articles of the August 1865 convention are the political completion of that dual possession. The page therefore anchors Gastein as peace-management seat and symbol of Austro-Prussian partition of the duchies, not as a liberal national assembly.

events/hambach-festival-1832.title: Hambach Festival (1832)
events/hambach-festival-1832.content:
Hambach Festival (1832)
The Hambach Festival (Hambacher Fest) of May 1832 was the great open-air demonstration of south-west German liberalism and national aspiration under the Restoration Bund—black-red-gold colors, toasts to popular sovereignty, and a shock to the diet’s police system already shaped by Carlsbad.
Place in Treitschke’s sequence
Treitschke’s middle volumes move from Burschenschaft and Wartburg through the 1830s press and festival culture. Hambach gathers burghers, students, and political writers of the Palatinate and neighboring states in a mass meeting that spoke the language of German unity and freedom more loudly than academic conspiracy. It belongs with the post-1830 vibration after the French July Revolution, when German governments feared imported unrest and when the Confederation’s machinery of press and university control, forged in 1819, faced a new public.
Programme and reaction
Speeches attacked the particularism of the Bund and the censorship regime; foreign liberal sympathies (Polish, French) appeared beside German national rhetoric. The Confederation’s answer was tighter press and association controls—continuation of the Carlsbad logic rather than its repeal. Volume 3’s beilagen on Bavaria and the Carlsbad decrees and on Metternich and the Prussian constitution frame the official mind that read Hambach as sedition. For the deposits, Hambach is evidence that national-liberal opinion had a public stage a decade and a half before 1848, even while sovereignty remained with the princes and the diet—and that the Rhine crisis of 1840 would later show how quickly national feeling could also turn against France.
Police aftermath
Treitschke notes the Bund and state reactions: press restraints, surveillance of speakers, and the reading of Hambach as proof that Karlsbad had not ended the movement. The festival’s memory feeds later national historiography more than it yields an immediate constitution.
Mass festival of the Vormärz
Treitschke’s volumes treat the Hambach gathering as the great open-air demonstration of south-west German liberalism and nationalism after the July Revolution’s echo: black-red-gold, speeches against the Bund’s police order, and alarm in Munich, Berlin, and Vienna.
Repression sequel
Federal and state measures tighten press and association law; the festival becomes exhibit A for Metternich’s claim that public politics must be throttled. It stands between Carlsbad’s generation and 1848’s assemblies as proof that national-liberal opinion could already mass outside courts and chanceries.
Placement
Pair with burschenschaften, carlsbad-decrees-1819, july-revolution-1830 as European stimulus.

events/hundred-days-1815.title: Hundred Days (1815)
events/hundred-days-1815.content:
Hundred Days (1815)
The Cent-Jours (“Hundred Days”) were the interval between Napoleon’s landing from Elba in March 1815 and the second Restoration of Louis XVIII after Waterloo. Duvergier de Hauranne’s history of parliamentary government treats the episode less as a military monograph than as a crisis of allegiance: army, peasantry, notables, and the fragile Charter settlement of 1814 all had to choose again within weeks.
Return and allegiances
Napoleon addressed soldiers and country people in proclamations that denied definitive defeat and denounced those who, having fought France for twenty-five years in foreign armies, now claimed to command French eagles. Duvergier stresses a distinction the Restoration undervalued: if many generals and superior officers hesitated to leave peacetime leisure for a new war, the soldats (“soldiers”) and much of the rural poor remained open to the imperial name. The rich and educated classes leaned the other way. Officers who, like La Bédoyère, deliberately helped Napoleon master France were, in this reading, guilty toward both the king and the country that had just accepted the first Restoration.
Conspiracy theories flourished at court and in the ministries: only a plot, some argued, could explain the emperor’s progress. Duvergier answers that the government did not know well enough that Napoleon held the ranks and the villages even when he lacked the marshals. Imperial placemen who had filled cartons with petitions begging the legitimate king to pardon services rendered to the “usurper” now feared that the returned emperor would not pardon services rendered to the king.
Paris, chambers, and the second abdication
The political improvisation of the spring—the Additional Act, the Chamber of Representatives, the appeal to national defence after Ligny and Waterloo—belongs to the same parliamentary story. After the defeat in Belgium, Paris again became a field of rival authorities. The second abdication and the return of Louis XVIII closed the Hundred Days in calendar terms; in political memory they reopened the question of who might sit in a Bourbon chamber and who must be purged. Delord later notes figures such as the glove-maker Dumoulin of Grenoble, who had offered Napoleon a large sum on the return from Elba on condition of attachment to the imperial person, and who after Waterloo passed into conspiracy and Bonapartist demonstration—an example of how the Hundred Days stocked the underground of the Restoration.
Aftermath
The second Restoration brought occupation, indemnity, and the ultra Chamber of 1815. Trials and exceptions—Ney above all—folded the military crisis into civil reaction. The name Cent-Jours remained a measure of imperial vitality and of Bourbon fragility: a few weeks had sufficed to dissolve the first Restoration’s appearance of permanence. For Duvergier the lasting lesson was parliamentary and social rather than purely strategic: any French regime after 1815 had to reckon with an army and a peasantry that could still answer the imperial call, and with a liberal public that would judge the Bourbons by the Charte as much as by victory.

events/hungarian-april-laws-1848.title: Hungarian April Laws 1848
events/hungarian-april-laws-1848.content:
Hungarian April Laws 1848
The áprilisi törvények (“April Laws”) of 1848 converted the historic Hungarian constitution into a modern parliamentary kingdom under the Habsburg king. Sanctioned in the wake of the Vienna March and of Kossuth’s 3 March demands, they created a responsible ministry at Pest, annual diet, national budget, and the legal basis for a Hungarian fighting force, while leaving the monarch as the personal link to the other Austrian lands. They are the legal charter of revolutionary Hungary and the text against which later imperial constitutions and military reconquest were measured.
Framing
Count Lajos Batthyány headed the first responsible ministry; Kossuth at finance and the reform diet majority drove the legislative package. The laws abolished many feudal burdens, extended political rights within a still restricted suffrage, and made Magyar the language of the reformed state. They assumed the unity of the lands of the crown of St Stephen under Pest’s ministry — including Croatia-Slavonia and, in Magyar reading, Transylvania’s union. That assumption collided at once with Croatian state right under Jellačić, with Serb movements in the south, and with Vienna’s claim that common affairs of the dynasty could not be unilaterally nationalized.
Contents in outline
Responsible government replaced the old palatine-council dualism in practice; the diet became a regular legislature; personal union rather than a merged empire defined Hungary’s tie to Austria. Military and financial clauses gave the ministry means to arm. Agrarian provisions paralleled the end of robot in the western lands. What the laws did not contain was a federal settlement among the kingdom’s peoples or a clear list of “common” matters acceptable to both Buda-Pest and Vienna.
Path to war
Through summer 1848 the April constitution was the Magyar programme. Jellačić’s Croatia, the Serb rising, and imperial appointments that treated Hungary as a rebellious province turned legal dualism into civil war. After October in Vienna and Francis Joseph’s accession, the diet’s refusal to accept the new emperor on Vienna’s terms and the later dethronement at Debrecen carried the April state beyond personal union into open separation — until Russian and Austrian arms destroyed it in 1849. Absolutism after 1848 then governed Hungary without the April Laws; Deák’s later legalism would treat them as the valid continuity of Hungarian public law.

events/hungarian-war-independence-1848-4.title: Hungarian War of Independence 1848–1849
events/hungarian-war-independence-1848-4.content:
Hungarian War of Independence (1848–49)
The Hungarian War of Independence is the long military-political struggle Springer’s Austrian volumes and related deposits place between Pest’s April laws and the Russian intervention that ends the field war—the Magyar revolution’s armed phase inside the Habsburg crisis.
From laws to war
April laws and responsible ministry in Buda-Pest collide with court reaction, Croatian and other national forces, and imperial armies. What begins as legal revolution becomes open war under Kossuth’s leadership climate.
End
Russian intervention and Világos crush the field army; Bach’s administrative era follows in Friedjung’s post-revolutionary Austria. Prefer russian-intervention-hungary-1849, kossuth, bach, nicholas-i.
April laws to open war
Springer’s Austrian frame starts from legal revolution in Hungary—April laws, responsible ministry—then tracks the slide into war as court reaction, nationalities’ conflicts, and imperial armies answer Pest.
Military-political leadership
Kossuth’s political leadership climate and the field commands (including figures the corpus names in passing) turn the kingdom into a war state. This page is the war arc; person pages hold biographies.
Russian end and Bach aftermath
russian-intervention-hungary-1849 ends the field war; Friedjung’s Bach-era Austria administers the victory. The war’s memory structures Magyar politics for the next constitutional round (October Diploma, February Patent) in Springer’s later chapters.
From April Laws to open war
Friedjung and Springer follow Hungary from the March–April 1848 constitutional breakthrough (Batthyány ministry, April Laws) into conflict with Croatia, the dynasty, and finally full-scale war. Jelačić’s intervention, the Vienna October crisis, and Windischgrätz’s campaigns mark the militarisation of what began as a personal-union constitutional reform.
Independence and Debrecen
Kossuth’s line and the Debrecen declaration of independence rupture the legal fiction of fighting merely against a bad ministry. The war becomes European: Polish generals in Hungarian service, Austrian need for Russian arms, and British/French diplomatic distance.
Világos and repression
Russian intervention under Paskevich and the surrender at Világos end field resistance; Haynau’s reprisals and the Bach system settle accounts. Prefer russian-intervention-hungary-1849, kossuth, jelacic, nicholas-i.

events/italian-revolutions-1831.title: Italian Revolutions of 1831
events/italian-revolutions-1831.content:
Italian Revolutions of 1831
The Italian revolutions of 1831 were the central-Italian answer to the July Revolution—La Farina’s Storia d’Italia gives them a full chapter that opens in Modena with Ciro Menotti and spreads at once into the Papal Legations.
Modena
On the evening of 3 February Menotti and fifteen chiefs met to launch the rising; Duke Francis IV surrounded the house, took the conspirators after a five-hour fight, and wrote for the hangman. News that Bologna had risen and nearby cities were in tumult changed his face: he fled, dragging the wounded Menotti toward Mantua. A provisional government in Modena declared the duke fallen and liberty restored. The pattern—conspiracy intertwined with a prince who had toyed with liberalism, then Austrian shadow—sets La Farina’s tone for the year.
Papal State
“At the same time,” La Farina continues, wider conspiracies worked in the States of the Church, where the people were more discontented and torn, and the government lacked arms and money, disordered and unready. A provisional government at Bologna issued a proclamation dated 5 February 1831. Columns such as Sercognani’s poorly armed youths were received with festival in town after town; only places like Rieti, by local counsel, refused gates. Cardinal Bernetti’s edicts and episcopal notices mark the papal counter-stroke as the movement ran through the Legations and Marches. Reformist petitions later in La Farina’s volumes still measure themselves against the memorandum of 1831—the moderate ceiling reformers claimed even when asking Austria-backed changes of Gregory XVI.
Outcome in the narrative
Austrian intervention restored princes; Menotti’s captivity and death sealed Modena’s failure; the Legations returned to papal and Habsburg force. The year taught a generation that July 1830 would not automatically free Italy and pushed conspirators toward new forms—Mazzini’s Young Italy among them—after Carbonaro methods failed in open daylight.
Carbonari aftermath and central Italy
The 1831 movements in Modena, Parma, and the Romagna erupt in the after-echo of July 1830. Provisional governments and tricolour hopes meet Austrian intervention and French hesitation. La Farina and related Italian narratives treat the year as proof that without a strong Italian military core, local revolutions remain exposed.
Failure as education
Defeat scatters exiles into the generation that will build Young Italy and later moderate Piedmontese policy. 1831 is thus both a crushed spring and a school. Central Italy learns the cost of rising without a guarantor; cabinets learn that Metternich’s police still functions after 1830’s scare.

events/italian-war-1859.title: Italian War of 1859
events/italian-war-1859.content:
Italian War of 1859
The Italian War of 1859 is the Franco-Piedmontese campaign against Austria that breaks the post-1849 freeze in Lombardy–Venetia—prepared in the Plombières understanding, fought along the Magenta–Solferino line, and halted at Villafranca before Venetian liberation is complete. It is at once a national war and a Bonapartist European intervention.
Diplomatic preparation
Cavour seeks a great-power partner; Napoleon III’s bargain ties French arms to Piedmontese ambition and to a redesigned Italian map that still protects French interests, including around Rome. Austrian ultimatum and Piedmontese mobilization supply the formal opening; the deeper cause is the failure of the 1850s settlement to answer the Lombard and Italian national question after Radetzky’s restoration. French domestic politics after Orsini also press the emperor toward an Italian gesture that is not pure revolution.
Campaign geography and contemporary narrative
La Farina’s military prose—truce expiry, orders toward Magenta and the Buffalora bridge, bersaglieri, the king’s claim to first touch Lombard soil, customs-house fire, entry into Magenta amid acclamations—shows how contemporaries lived the advance as liberation geography. Austrian withdrawal toward Pavia, open roads to Milan, and the joy in other cities that hear Magenta is taken, all belong to the campaign’s popular political meaning. Franco-Piedmontese victory at Magenta opens the Lombard capital; Solferino confirms Austrian defeat in the decisive battle mass. Older 1848 echoes make 1859 read as a second, better-armed crossing of the same political river.
Villafranca and the incomplete victory
Napoleon III’s armistice at Villafranca stops short of Venice and short of the maximum nationalist programme. Motives recorded across French and Italian narratives include the carnage of Solferino, fear of wider German involvement, and the emperor’s need to control the Italian outcome rather than ride an uncontrolled revolutionary wave. Cavour’s resignation crisis marks the collision between Piedmontese aims and French limitation. Lombardy passes toward the Sardinian crown; Venetia remains Habsburg; central Italy’s annexations continue by plebiscite and diplomacy rather than by this war alone.
Austrian dominion frame
Tivaroni’s critical history of Austrian dominion supplies the structural other side: 1859 as the moment the post-1849 system cracks in the north without yet clearing Austria from the peninsula. Military defeat does not instantly dissolve the political apparatus of the Regno Lombardo-Veneto everywhere; it opens the diplomatic auction in which France remains a broker.
Aftermath
Garibaldi’s southern expedition and the 1860–61 unitary completion stand on ground this campaign opened and left unfinished. For Delord’s Empire, the war is a glory that deepens Roman and European entanglements. For Italian unitary writers, it is breakthrough and frustration in one season. Linked pages carry Plombières, Cavour, Napoleon III, and the Roman question; this event page holds the war’s arc from bargain to armistice.

events/july-revolution-1830.title: July Revolution 1830
events/july-revolution-1830.content:
July Revolution 1830
The July Revolution (Trois Glorieuses, July 1830) is the Parisian and parliamentary crisis that topples Charles X after the ordinances and installs Louis-Philippe as king of the French under a revised charter—the hinge of Duvergier’s Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire between Restoration and Orléanist rule.
Ordinances as rupture
Polignac’s ministry and the July ordinances strike press and electoral arrangements the charter-reading public treats as fundamental. What the court calls monarchical self-defence the capital calls coup. Journalists, deputies, and barricades move on different clocks toward the same result: collapse of Bourbon authority in Paris.
Three days and dynastic bargain
Combat produces provisional politics of city hall, hotels, and chamber fragments. Republican voices exist; the brokered outcome is Orléanist. Duvergier records the name quarrel (Philippe VII / Philippe I / Louis-Philippe Ier), the oath quarrel with Dupont de l’Eure against mental fidelity to Charles X, and the marshals’ presentation of crown and hand of justice—theatre meant to fuse nation and monarchy.
Exit of Charles X
Commissaries manage the fallen court’s departure. Advances from the new king’s funds, Charles’s grave thanks, and the duchess of Berry’s sarcasm—that Louis-Philippe minds their baggage while taking their crown—belong to Duvergier’s closing tableaux. Legitimist Europe never accepts the substitution.
European signal and domestic limit
Abroad, 1830 cracks pure Restoration readings of 1815 without general war; Belgium, Italy, and Poland take signals. At home the pays légal monarchy must disappoint legitimists and social republicans alike. The National Guard and the Charter of 1830 become twin props of a regime born on barricades and afraid of them.
Charter politics after the barricades
The revised charter and the title “king of the French” try to write street victory into monarchical law. Duvergier’s interest is how parliamentary government then actually works: ministries that must live by addresses and elections, yet fear the people who made the throne. 1830’s opening glory becomes 1840s’ stalemate over reform banquets.
International aftershocks without general war
Belgium’s secession crisis, Italian and Polish movements, and conservative alarms in German courts all take French July as signal. The Orléanist cabinet’s preference for recognition and peace over exported revolution disappoints those who wanted a new 1792. The revolution is thus both European event and carefully nationalized French settlement.

events/june-days-1848.title: June Days 1848
events/june-days-1848.content:
June Days 1848
The June Days (journées de Juin) are the June 1848 Paris workers’ insurrection after the assault on the National Workshops—crushed by Cavaignac for the party of order and treated in French deposits as the social civil war inside the Second Republic that prepares fear’s road to Bonapartist presidency and empire.
February coalition under strain
February joined bourgeois reformers and Paris workers against the July Monarchy. Workshops and social decrees tried to hold the coalition. By spring the Constituent’s moderate majority fears permanent socialist pressure; workshop policy becomes the test of whether the Republic is social or merely political.
Closure and barricades
Closing or draining the ateliers detonates the working-class east. Barricades rise against a republican executive and assembly rather than against a king. The fighting is remembered as fratricide inside the revolutionary capital—hence its later use by conservatives and Bonapartists as proof that street sovereignty destroys society.
Cavaignac’s victory
General Cavaignac receives executive force to crush the rising. Artillery and line troops clear the streets at high cost. Victory makes him the order candidate of the frightened pays légal—and still fails to stop Louis-Napoléon’s presidential mass election. Delord’s path to the Empire runs through the provincial and bourgeois fear June planted.
Meanings in the corpus
Republicans read tragedy: the Republic kills its popular wing. Order politicians read necessity: workshops and clubs threatened property. Bonapartists read opportunity: assemblies cannot hold France without a name and an army. Link Cavaignac, workshops, Second Republic, and the prince-president.
Social geography of the fighting
The June map of Paris—eastern faubourgs against western and orderly battalions—becomes a political legend as much as a military report. Witness literature and assembly debates fix images of workers’ despair and of bourgeois dread. Delord later harvests that dread for the story of why a Bonaparte name could seem a refuge.
Workshops as constitutional flashpoint
The ateliers nationaux were emergency employment and political symbol at once. Closing them was read as class verdict dressed as budget necessity. June therefore sits at the join of fiscal panic, socialist expectation, and republican legality—an unstable join the Second Republic never repairs.
