events/kingdom-of-italy-1861.title: Kingdom of Italy (1861)
events/kingdom-of-italy-1861.content:
Kingdom of Italy (1861)
In March 1861 the Turin parliament proclaims Victor Emmanuel II King of Italy—the legal consummation of the 1859–60 wars and annexations, still missing Rome and Venetia. Tivaroni’s second Italia degli Italiani volume treats the title as crown on a map already remade by French alliance, plebiscite, and the Thousand; La Farina’s national-liberal history writes the same fusion as fulfilled programme of the moderate party.
How the map was made
Lombardy comes through the French war and cession diplomacy after Magenta and Solferino; central duchies and much of the Legations through provisional governments and annexation votes under Farini, Ricasoli, and allied moderates; Sicily and Naples through Garibaldi’s expedition and Piedmontese regular intervention ending at Gaeta under Cialdini. The Statuto Albertino extends rather than a new constituent assembly rewriting sovereignty from below. Tivaroni’s narrative roots the claim in what he calls the configuration indicated by geography, by the unity of race, language, and customs—the natural title the national movement invoked against the map of 1815. Across Italy the hopes sharpened; central Italy, risen during the war, prepared its defences, expecting one last battle that would drive Austria definitively out of Italy. Mazzinian unitarists and federalists contest the meaning; the deposits used here are consolidator voices.
The Upper-Italy counterfactual
Tivaroni records the argument, advanced as the annexations pressed forward, that had a kingdom of Upper Italy been constituted instead, even the acquisition of the Quadrilateral would not finally have prevented further annexations—to which France resigned itself at the last instant and out of absolute necessity. At most, so the reasoning ran, another sacrifice of territory might have been exacted; but once the Upper-Italian kingdom existed, what human force could have blocked the further drawing-together of the peninsula? The passage captures how the title of 1861, in the deposits, is presented less as a finished legal act than as the working assumption of an Italy that would keep moving toward its natural and national limits.
What the title does not finish
The roman-question and Venetia remain open. Administrative unification, southern brigandage, debt, and foreign recognition fill the years after the proclamation. French garrison in Rome and papal temporal claims block the capital Italians already name. The kingdom is a programme still at war with geography. Prefer architect pages for persons; this event holds the 1861 legal birth inside the corpus window.
Parliament and succession of cabinets
After Cavour’s death the title outlives its greatest minister. Rattazzi, Ricasoli, Minghetti, and La Marmora rotate the problem of governing a half-finished state under great-power eyes. Prefer their entity pages for cabinet detail.
Missing pieces
Tivaroni ends many 1861 pages by naming what the proclamation does not take: Rome under French protection, Venetia under Austria. The kingdom is therefore a programme of further wars and negotiations, not a finished map.

events/kremsier-reichstag-1848-49.title: Kremsier Reichstag 1848–1849
events/kremsier-reichstag-1848-49.content:
Kremsier Reichstag 1848–1849
The Kremsierer Reichstag (“Kremsier / Kroměříž constituent assembly”) was the Austrian empire’s elected constituent body after it was moved from Vienna to the Moravian episcopal town of Kremsier in the winter of 1848–49. There deputies drafted a federalizing constitution based on popular sovereignty and equality of nationalities — a draft dissolved by force when Schwarzenberg’s ministry imposed the constitution of 4 March 1849. Friedjung makes Kremsier the high point of Austrian liberal-constitutional labor and the measure of what absolutism after 1848 rejected.
From Vienna to Kremsier
After the October rising the court would not leave a constituent assembly in a reconquered but unreliable capital. Kremsier offered distance and military security. The assembly continued work on fundamental rights, the relation of central state to provinces and districts, and the language and nationality clauses that set Palacký and Rieger’s Czech federalism against German-centralist liberals. Bach, still moving from revolutionary advocate toward ministerial power, appeared in the debates; Stadion brought ministerial constitutional drafts stressing imperial unity.
The draft
Committee work produced a constitution that located sovereignty in the people, organized autonomous communes and lands, and tried to make the empire a constitutional whole without simply restoring historic diets as noble corporations. It was the most elaborate attempt in the corpus to write a single Austrian state that was neither pure German centralism nor a mere personal union of historic crowns. Opponents in the army and among aristocrats saw popular sovereignty and federal complexity as the road to dissolution.
Dissolution and the imposed constitution
Stadion’s arrival and the ministry’s decision ended the experiment. The Reichstag was dissolved; on 4 March 1849 the emperor octroyed a unitary constitution: strong monarchical executive, unified customs territory, limited liberties, partial and tactical recognition of Hungarian arrangements, and Grundentlastung (“redemption of feudal burdens”) as social ballast. Kremsier’s draft remained a monument for later federalists; for 1849–60 it was a dead letter, and after 31 December 1851 even the imposed constitution was revoked.
German parallel
Sybel’s account of the Austrian question at Frankfurt runs in parallel: while Kremsier tried to refound the empire internally, Frankfurt tried to place Austria’s German lands inside a national German state. Schwarzenberg’s answer to both was the same in spirit — military-monarchical unity of the whole monarchy and refusal of a kleindeutsch emperor in Germany. Kremsier and the Paulskirche failed within weeks of each other as instruments of popular constitution-making.

events/magenta-solferino-1859.title: Magenta and Solferino (1859)
events/magenta-solferino-1859.content:
Magenta and Solferino (1859)
Magenta (4 June) and Solferino (24 June) 1859 are the decisive Franco-Piedmontese victories over Austria in the Lombard campaign—the military core of Tivaroni’s 1859 narrative between Plombières preparation and the political brake at Villafranca.
Opening the plain
After the Austrian ultimatum and Piedmontese refusal, French armies under Napoleon III join Victor Emmanuel. Magenta opens the road to Milan and breaks the first Austrian defensive crust in the plain. Public opinion in Italy treats the battle as proof that the national war is real—not a cabinet feint. Volunteers, municipal proclamations, and the flight of Austrian administration in Lombard towns form the political weather Tivaroni braids with operations.
Solferino
Solferino, the larger and bloodier general action, shatters the Austrian main army’s hold and makes continued defense of Lombardy untenable. Casualty shock on the French side matters as much as the tactical win: imperial second thoughts begin here. The battle’s horror later feeds humanitarian memory outside this corpus; inside Tivaroni it is the climax that should have opened Venetia and a wider settlement—and did not.
Political sequel
Villafranca stops the war short of Venetian liberation and of the maximal Plombières map. Cavour’s resignation crisis follows a peace he rejected. Prefer italian-war-1859 for the full war page, plombières-agreement-1858 and villafranca-1859 for diplomacy, cialdini and la-marmora for Piedmontese arms; this page holds the two battle names as the military hinge of 1859.
Armistice politics
Villafranca follows the blood of Solferino in Tivaroni’s sequence: Napoleon III’s halt reshapes what Piedmont can claim. Military victory becomes diplomatic half-victory; central Italy’s annexation path must then do work the French alliance will not finish in Venetia.
Allied war in Lombardy
Tivaroni’s 1859 narrative gives Magenta and Solferino as the twin pitched battles of the Franco-Sardinian campaign against Austria after the war’s opening on the Ticino. French imperial arms and Piedmontese contingents force Austrian withdrawal from much of Lombardy; the butchery of Solferino enters contemporary memoir as shock even in victory.
Diplomacy beside the battlefield
Villafranca’s preliminary peace—Napoleon III’s sudden stop short of Venetia—dominates Tivaroni’s political reading: glory enough for the emperor, unfinished national business for Italians, cession of Lombardy via French mediation toward Sardinia, and central-Italian revolutions still to settle by annexation politics.
Memory
The battles justify the Italian war’s military seriousness in unitarian narrative while explaining why 1866 and 1870 remain necessary in later volumes outside this page’s core.

events/mexican-expedition-1861-67.title: Mexican expedition (1861–1867)
events/mexican-expedition-1861-67.content:
Mexican expedition (1861–1867)
The French expédition du Mexique (“Mexican expedition”) was the Second Empire’s overseas war that began as a tripartite debt intervention and became the attempt to plant the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor of Mexico. Delord’s third volume gives the diplomatic origin, the military sequence from Vera Cruz to Puebla and Mexico City, and the Miramar negotiation; Ollivier’s liberal-empire memoirs touch the parliamentary cost at home.
London convention and rupture of the allies
Obscure intrigues about a Spanish candidature for a future Mexican throne had already been woven in London in July. Spain, Britain, and France signed the convention that covered claims against Juárez’s Mexico. Spaniards preceded English and French forces and occupied Vera Cruz. Allied commissioners issued a manifesto; the preliminaries of La Soledad followed, then broke. At the Orizaba conference the allies parted abruptly. Britain and Spain withdrew from the interior adventure; France remained. Delord’s chapter “Les Français au Mexique” opens on that isolation.
Lorencez, Forey, Bazaine
General Lorencez attacked toward Orizaba; the town pronounced for Almonte. The march on Puebla brought the French check that forced a change of command. General Forey replaced Lorencez. Puebla, first city of Mexico by strategic position and second by commerce, stood on the high plateaux almost equidistant from Mexico City and Orizaba, knot of the great roads from the Pacific to the Gulf. After a siege and the combat of San Lorenzo, Forey took the place. On 12 June Napoleon III, learning of the capture, wrote to thank the general, consoling himself for the loss of so many brave men with the thought that their death had not been useless to the interests and honour of France or to civilisation. The victor had at once to give Mexico City an administration and the country a government. A triumvirate summoned an assembly of 215 notables to choose a definitive form; the monarchical solution and the call to Maximilian followed.
Maximilian
Maximilian had been living sadly at Miramar in forced idleness, unable to console himself for the loss of his brilliant position at Milan. A Mexican deputation carried the offer of the crown to Miramar. Napoleon brought Maximilian and Charlotte to Paris; hesitations delayed acceptance; a convention between Maximilian and Napoleon III fixed the terms of French support. The new emperor and empress sailed; their entry into Mexico opened the second phase of the war—guerrilla resistance under Juárez, mounting cost, and eventual French evacuation under pressure of United States recovery and European complications. Delord’s headings follow Maximilian from acceptance through departure and entry to the later isolation that French withdrawal sealed.
Parliamentary France
In the Corps législatif the Mexican question fed address debates. Jules Favre attacked the expedition; Jérôme Napoleon and others divided imperial ranks; credits and the Palikao endowment became symbols of a policy critics called a sink of men and money. Ollivier’s circle treated the affair among the errors that a liberal empire would have to liquidate. By 1866–67 the flag came home; Maximilian’s fall closed the adventure that had begun as a creditors’ landing at Vera Cruz.

events/milan-five-days-1848.title: Milan Five Days (1848)
events/milan-five-days-1848.content:
Milan Five Days (1848)
The Five Days of Milan (18–22 March 1848) are the municipal rising that forces Radetzky’s Austrians from the city and opens Lombardy’s war year—Tivaroni’s and La Farina’s hinge between urban revolution and Charles Albert’s intervention.
Barricades and withdrawal
Popular and bourgeois Milan fights street by street; the garrison withdraws toward the Quadrilateral. Provisional authorities face the choice of pure municipal revolution or fusion with Piedmont’s national war. The deposits stress speed and civic energy without pretending the Austrian army has been destroyed.
From city to theatre
Charles Albert’s army enters the Lombard theatre; the Five Days become the political justification of a wider Italian war. Later reverses and Radetzky’s professional reconquest close the cycle Tivaroni narrates without romantic erasure of Austrian recovery. Cattaneo’s federal-municipal strand (where the corpus carries it) contests pure Piedmontese absorption; the moderate national histories still read Milan as proof Italy can rise.
Linked pages
Prefer radetzky, charles-albert, novara-1849, and wider 1848 Italy pages for campaign sequel; this event holds the Milanese urban spark and the week that made Lombardy a war question.
Provisional authorities
Once Radetzky withdraws, Milan must govern: food, order, envoys to Turin, and the question of fusion with Piedmont. Tivaroni’s narrative treats these days as politics under arms, not only street epic. The municipal revolution becomes a diplomatic object for Charles Albert and for other Italian courts watching Lombardy.
Austrian return path
The Five Days do not destroy the Quadrilateral system. Radetzky’s later reconquest is already latent in the professional army’s withdrawal to strong places. National histories that celebrate March must still explain Custozza and the return of black-yellow authority—Milan’s week is the opening act, not the whole war.
Street warfare and municipal power
The Five Days (Cinque giornate) show a great Austrian garrison forced out by urban combat and civic organization before regular Piedmontese cover is secure. Barricades, parish networks, and provisional authorities turn municipal patriotism into military fact. La Farina-type narratives linger on popular initiative; Tivaroni’s dominion frame stresses how hard the empire must work to return.
After the joy, the war of armies
Expelling the garrison is not the same as winning the war. Radetzky regroups; Charles Albert’s campaign becomes the decisive regular war; Novara will close the first independence war. Milan’s five days remain the purest symbol of urban Italy’s 1848 capacity—and of its dependence on a wider military outcome it cannot alone guarantee.
Political meanings
Moderates read disciplined civic virtue; democrats read popular sovereignty; Austrians read treachery in a crown land. The event therefore feeds three incompatible lessons that later years keep quoting.

events/novara-1849.title: Battle of Novara (23 March 1849)
events/novara-1849.content:
Battle of Novara (1849)
Novara (23 March 1849 in the Italian national chronology of La Farina and Tivaroni) closed Charles Albert’s second war against Austria. Defeat of the Piedmontese army under Radetzky’s command forced the king’s abdication in favour of Victor Emmanuel II and reopened Lombardy to Austrian reconquest after the hopes of 1848.
Strategic setting
La Farina’s dedicated chapter on the day of Novara and the abdication first measures the two armies and their spirit. The Piedmontese ministry, seeking to surprise Radetzky, took no extraordinary provision for the public treasury; no entrenched camp was prepared at Novara; no fortification covered the Cava, which dominates the Ticino passage near Pavia and the Po toward Mezzana. Democratic authority was already decaying across Italy—a “sad omen and great discouragement” as a new war approached.
Dispositions on the eve of battle, in La Farina’s account, scattered Piedmontese strength: first division at Vespolate between Mortara and Novara; second at Cerano and Casalnovo; third at Romentino and Galliate toward the Buffalora bridge; fourth before Trecate; fifth behind the Gravellone opposite Pavia. The Austrian army concentrated between Pavia and Cortolona. Divided for simultaneous defence and offence, Piedmontese forces were scarcely enough for defence alone against an invader not inferior in numbers, force, and discipline.
The day
La Farina narrates Piedmontese positions reinforced—Guards brigade on the right, Cuneo on the left, twenty-four guns at the centre and wing extremities, cavalry behind the Guards, further horse and eight guns in reserve near the city on the Novara road. Late hour and gunfire heard from the Vigevano side made the Italian line believe it would not be attacked that day, until half-past four explorers announced the enemy’s approach. General D’Aspre came with some fifteen thousand men and forty-eight guns. The Austrian blow fell on a force not concentrated for a decisive defensive battle; the result was Piedmontese defeat.
Political sequel
News of Novara travelled beyond Italy: Monti, after long journeys, reached Debreczen only to learn that the Italian army had not only resumed hostilities but been beaten at Novara—closing any hope of coordinated pressure with Hungary. Charles Albert abdicated. Victor Emmanuel II inherited the Statuto, the army’s remnant, and the diplomatic problem of living beside a victorious Radetzky. Tivaroni’s later volumes treat Novara as the military end of the democratic-national biennium in the north; the Roman and Venetian republics fell in the same season of reaction. The monarchical Risorgimento after 1852 would restart from Turin under Cavour, not from the field of 1849.
Second campaign’s end
Tivaroni and La Farina date the military close of Charles Albert’s second war against Austria to the defeat at Novara. Radetzky’s victory forces armistice, abdication, and the bitter peace that leaves Lombardy–Venetia under Austria and Piedmont under the Statuto and Victor Emmanuel II.
Political consequences
Moderate Piedmontese politics reorganise around keeping the constitution, paying the costs of war, and postponing revenge until diplomacy (Crimea, Plombières) reopens the file. Republicans read Novara as proof kings cannot free Italy; moderates read it as proof preparation and alliances are required.
Memory
Novara pairs with Custozza as the military school of 1848–49 failures before 1859’s French alliance reverses the balance in Lombardy.

events/october-diploma-1860.title: October Diploma (1860)
events/october-diploma-1860.content:
October Diploma (1860)
The Októberi Diploma / Oktoberdiplom (HU Októberi Diploma; DE Oktoberdiplom (“October Diploma”); 20 October 1860) was Francis Joseph’s first major retreat from Silvester absolutism: an octroyed federalising charter that restored historic Landtage and a narrow Reichsrat while trying to keep sovereignty in the crown. Friedjung reads it as the monarchy’s admission, after the Italian war, that Bach’s unitary machine could no longer extract loyalty or credit; Magyar politics under Deák read it as an insufficient half-step beside the April Laws of 1848.
Why October became possible
Defeat in 1859, the loss of Lombardy, financial exhaustion, and the discredit of the Concordat-era bureaucracy forced a change of system. Bach left the interior; conservative aristocrats (the old federalist and stilständisch currents that had hated Bach) regained the emperor’s ear. The Diploma spoke their language: the historic kingdoms and lands as building blocks; provincial diets; a central council for common affairs that was not a democratic parliament. It was reform from above to pre-empt revolution and to woo Hungary without accepting 1848 in full.
Terms and architecture
The Diploma restored diets in the lands and sketched a Reichsrat fed from those diets for imperial matters — diplomacy, army, finance of common needs — while promising Hungary special regard for its historic rights. It was not the March 1849 unitary constitution revived, nor a return to Vormärz estate life pure and simple; it was a conservative federalism under an still-absolute monarch who granted statutes rather than recognising popular constituent power. German centralists and many bureaucrats disliked the concession to historic crowns; Magyar lawyers measured every clause against the April Laws and found the responsible Budapest ministry and the full diet sovereignty missing.
Reception and failure
In Hungary the Diploma did not end passive resistance. Deák’s line demanded lawful continuity with 1848, not a new imperial octroi. In the German-Austrian lands liberals wanted a stronger central parliament; conservatives wanted the Diploma as a ceiling. Within months the court veered toward Anton von Schmerling and the Februarpatent (1861), which recentralised representation and alienated Magyar and federalist opinion in the opposite direction. The Diploma thus marks a brief aristocratic-federal moment between Bach and Schmerling — important as proof that Silvester was reversible, inadequate as a settlement of the nationality and Hungarian questions.
Horizon toward dualism
Friedjung’s narrative uses the Diploma to open the 1860s constitutional struggle that ends, beyond his densest pages, in the 1867 Compromise. For this wiki the page’s job is to fix the Diploma as the first post-absolutist offer: historic lands against Bach’s Einheitsstaat, still short of Deák’s legal dualism.

events/olmutz-punctuation-1850.title: Olmütz Punctation (1850)
events/olmutz-punctuation-1850.content:
Olmütz Punctation (1850)
The Olmützer Punktation (“Olmütz Punctation”) of 29 November 1850 was the agreement signed at Olmütz between Manteuffel for Prussia and Schwarzenberg for Austria that ended the autumn war crisis over Hesse and Holstein, buried the Prussian Union constitution of 26 May, and restored the path to the old Confederation’s forms under Austrian presidency. Sybel’s second volume of the Begründung des Deutschen Reiches gives the chapter-length narrative used here.
Autumn crisis
After the Erfurt Union experiment and the Hesse constitutional conflict, Prussian troops held stage-roads and positions toward Fulda while Bavarian and federal execution forces pressed north. Austria mobilized heavily in Bohemia; Russian solidarity with the restored Bundestag was advertised; Nicholas treated refusal of Austrian demands on Hesse as a casus belli in the diplomatic traffic Sybel records. Brandenburg fell mortally ill; Radowitz left the foreign office; Manteuffel took the working lead of a peace policy while Frederick William IV ordered mobilization (5–6 November) amid popular jubilation—Landwehr streaming to the colours—yet still sought to avoid war with Austria.
Skirmishing at Bronzell (shots, a few wounded jägers, one Prussian horse) excited Frankfurt’s great-German envoys toward talk of federal breach and war; Schwarzenberg stayed coldly calm and used each Prussian concession to raise the next demand: clear Hesse, do not hinder Holstein execution, positively abolish the Union constitution before free conferences on federal reform.
Concessions and the meeting
Prussia abandoned mediation for the Kiel stadtholdership, withdrew opposition to Holstein execution, and on 15 November asked the Union princes’ college to annul the 26 May constitution—news that stunned allies who had just been told to ready troops under Prussian command. Baden, Nassau, Mecklenburg-Schwerin treated the Union as extinct. The king had reached the limit of the concessions he inwardly wanted (restoration of princely authority in Hesse and Holstein, riddance of the liberal Union text) but still clung to Prussian occupation of the stage-roads so that federal execution could not finish without him.
On the evening of 28 November 1850 Manteuffel and Schwarzenberg met at the inn “zur Krone” in Olmütz and negotiated from six o’clock; on the 29th they concluded and signed the Punctation. Sybel notes that wonderfully no original of the Punctation is found in the Prussian state papers. Manteuffel also accepted an article Schwarzenberg tabled. Ladenberg moved rejection in Berlin; the king treated Austria’s yield on conferences and joint commissions for Hesse and Holstein as a great victory of his own policy. Opponents drew the lesson that Prussia feared war on any terms and could be managed by alternating conservative pressure and threats.
Meaning in the corpus
Olmütz is the diplomatic defeat of the Prussian Union road and the interim victory of Schwarzenberg’s Austria in Germany—paired in Sybel with the military humiliation feared by the war party and with the later Prussian recovery under different ministers. It belongs with erfurt-union-1849-50, german-confederation, and the careers of manteuffel, schwarzenberg, and frederick-william-iv.
Terms and sequence
After the Union’s military and diplomatic isolation, Manteuffel negotiates the punctation at Olmütz (Olomouc): Prussian climb-down, demobilisation pathways, and return toward a Bundestag Austria can again chair. Sybel’s national-liberal bitterness and Austrian relief narratives should both be representable without modern score-settling.
Consequences inside the wiki
Radowitz exits; the Union’s assembly track dies; German politics enter the 1850s reaction climate in which Bismarck later learns Bund obstruction from the Prussian seat. Link forward to Manteuffel’s system and backward to Erfurt and the imperial crown refusal.

events/orsini-attentat-1858.title: Orsini attentat 1858
events/orsini-attentat-1858.content:
Orsini attentat 1858
The Orsini attentat is the 14 January 1858 bomb attack on Napoleon III and the empress by Felice Orsini and accomplices—an Italian revolutionary strike in the heart of the Second Empire that Delord narrates in police and trial detail and that European politics links to the season opening toward Plombières and the war of 1859.
Antecedents: Orsini in England
Delord’s summary places the attack after the reception of the diplomatic corps at the Tuileries on 1 January 1858, amid what he calls the general tranquillity of spirits. The narrative turns to the antécédents de l’auteur de l’attentat (“antecedents of the author of the attack”): Orsini in England, seeking accomplices; the fabrication of the bombs (bombes); and Orsini and Pieri in Paris. The attack was thus prepared abroad and imported to the capital—part of the international revolutionary traffic that the Empire’s police tracked from London refuges.
The evening of 14 January
Orsini fixed the day of the attack for 14 January. Pieri was arrested on the pavement of the rue Le Peletier; that arrest, Delord notes, changed nothing in the ordinary dispositions of the police. Then came the triple explosion. The emperor, the empress, and General Roguet were in the cortège; the emperor went on to the Opera. Delord records the attitude morale de la foule sur les boulevards (“the moral attitude of the crowd on the boulevards”) and the emperor and empress returning to the Tuileries. Bombs thrown at the imperial cortège killed and wounded bystanders in the street; the sovereigns survived. Arrests of the authors of the attack followed quickly.
Trial, letters, and the question of pardon
The procès d’Orsini et de ses complices became continental news. Delord explicitly asks whether there was ever serious question of granting a pardon to Orsini, and preserves the testament of Orsini and his last letter to the Emperor. Orsini’s address—condemning the emperor against the duty of Italian liberation—struck Napoleon III’s self-image as national arbiter and as heir of a revolutionary name. The trial, the scaffold, and the letters fed a European melodrama: bombs, blood on Paris stones, an Italian patriot instructing a French emperor. The government’s refusal to commute the sentence answered the shock, while the letters themselves kept the Italian cause alive in the sovereign’s conscience.
Repression and ministerial consequence
Legislation and ministerial shifts answered the shock. Order and Catholic opinion demanded severity; the Empire had to prove it could protect the person it offered as guarantor of property and faith. Delord’s chapters on earlier attempts (Pianori and others) already show a regime living with dagger and pistol; Corsican guards, cabaret rumours, and the trade between ordinary justice and political police form the atmosphere into which Orsini stepped. The attentat was extreme, not unique—it intensified a permanent insecurity around the man who claimed to be France’s necessary master.
Catalyst toward the Italian war
Diplomatic and secret paths toward the Cavour meeting at Plombières and the Austrian war ran through the political season the bombs opened. Deposits do not reduce 1859 to a single blast; they treat the attentat as catalyst inside a longer Italian file already pressing the Tuileries. The double movement—repression at home, national war abroad—is core Bonapartist timing in the French deposits: fear produced laws, calculation produced interviews with Cavour, and the same sovereign who tightened domestic surveillance reopened the Italian map.

events/plombières-agreement-1858.title: Plombières agreement (1858)
events/plombières-agreement-1858.content:
Plombières agreement (1858)
The Plombières conversations of 20–21 July 1858 between Napoleon III and Cavour fixed the secret political bargain behind the Franco-Sardinian war of 1859: French military support to drive Austria from Italy, a reorganized peninsula, dynastic marriage, and territorial payment to France. Tivaroni’s narrative, built on Cavour’s letter of 24 July 1858 from Baden to Victor Emmanuel (published by Chiala) and on Bianchi’s report of a sealed holograph, is the densest deposit account in this corpus.
Path to the waters
Orsini’s bomb against the emperor might have been expected to end French patronage of Italian nationalism. Instead Cavour received from a familiar of Prince Napoleon at the Palais Royal a letter sketching alliance terms, mutual advantages, and the marriage of Prince Napoleon to Princess Clotilde. Nigra’s mission to Paris confirmed that something real moved in the emperor’s mind. In June the physician Conneau came to Turin to invite Cavour to Plombières, where Napoleon was taking the waters. Only the king and La Marmora knew the journey’s reason; Cavour wrote that despite habitual self-confidence he was not without unease.
The two days
He arrived 20 July and saw the emperor on the 20th and 21st. Napoleon opened at once: he was resolved to support Sardinia with all his forces in a war against Austria, provided a non-revolutionary casus could be justified before diplomacy and before French and European opinion. Cavour’s suggested grounds—commercial-treaty complaints, the 1847 Austrian treaties with Parma and Modena—were set aside as too slight or already spent at the 1856 Paris congress. The emperor pointed to discontent in Massa and Carrara: an address to the king of Sardinia might provoke the Duke of Modena and thereby Austria. The cause was found.
War aim, admitted without difficulty: expel the Austrians entirely from Italy, leaving them not an inch of ground. The pope and the king of Naples required special regard; Cavour agreed. On future sovereigns, the emperor would gladly see a Murat again at Naples; Cavour named the Duchess of Parma for Florence. Then the French price: would Victor Emmanuel cede Savoy and the county of Nice? Cavour answered affirmatively for Savoy (Nice the more delicate point in the letter’s balance). The Clotilde marriage tied the houses.
After-status of the secret
Much remained verbal until later publication of the letters; Tivaroni notes Mazzini writing on Savoy as one already sufficiently informed of terms. The public war of 1859, Magenta and Solferino, Villafranca’s check, and the 1860 cession of Savoy and Nice are the agreement’s unfolding and partial frustration. Sybel’s German volumes place the same bargain inside the European system that also shaped the German question; Ollivier reads the Italian war’s aftermath from inside the liberal empire’s parliamentary struggles.
Place in the corpus
Plombières is the diplomatic keystone between Crimean Piedmont and the battlefield of 1859: not a published treaty but a recorded imperial–ministerial pact whose casus, map, marriage, and territorial coin organize the monarchical Risorgimento’s French phase.

events/polish-november-uprising-1830-31.title: Polish November Uprising (1830–1831)
events/polish-november-uprising-1830-31.content:
Polish November Uprising (1830–1831)
The польское восстание 1830–1831 (pol’skoe vosstanie 1830–1831, “Polish uprising of 1830–1831”), also called the November Uprising, was the armed revolt of the Kingdom of Poland (Congress Poland) against the Russian emperor that, in Kornilov’s periodization of Nicholas I, closed the reign’s first, still partly reformist phase and opened the era of официальная народность (ofitsial’naya narodnost’, “official nationality”).
Setting
The Congress Kingdom, created in 1815 with Alexander I as king, had a constitution, a separate army, and a large Polish landowning elite that remembered the Duchy of Warsaw and the Napoleonic years. After 1825 Nicholas ruled the Kingdom as a personal union under the empire’s military and dynastic supremacy. Secret societies, cadet discontent, and the shock of the French July Revolution of 1830 prepared a rising that began in Warsaw in November 1830. Kornilov treats the war as one of the European aftershocks of 1830, parallel to Belgian separation and French constitutional monarchy—except that in Poland the opponent was the full power of the Russian state.
Course and defeat
The rising expelled the grand-ducal regime, formed a national government, and fielded the Polish army against Russian columns under Diebitsch and later Paskevich. After campaigns of 1831 Warsaw fell; the constitutional Kingdom as Alexander had designed it ceased to exist in practice. Emigration of officers and politicians to the West (the Great Emigration) carried the Polish question into French and British public life for a generation.
Consequences for Russian internal policy
Kornilov’s structural point is not only military. Defeat of the rising, coming after the July Revolution, convinced Nicholas that limited constitutional experiments and ideological “rapprochement” with the West were dangerous. The second period of the reign (roughly 1831–48) made defence of a self-standing Russian order the motto of policy. Уваров (Uvarov)’s triad Orthodoxy–Autocracy–Nationality belongs to that turn. In the western provinces and the former Kingdom, the government tightened control over schools, the church settlement, and the landowning elite; later inventory regulations in the western guberniyas and peasant measures in the Kingdom claimed to protect peasants against a Polish nobility branded as foreign and rebellious. Paskevich’s long viceroyalty symbolized military government over a disarmed society.
European resonance
For Metternich’s Europe the rising was another proof that national-liberal forces threatened the 1815 settlement; for liberals it was a martyrology. Russia’s victory reinforced the image—later broken in the Crimea—of Nicholas as Europe’s conservative sword. Inside Russia the war fed the educational and censorship machine that Kornilov describes under Uvarov and the Third Section.

events/rhine-crisis-1840.title: Rhine Crisis (1840)
events/rhine-crisis-1840.content:
Rhine Crisis (1840)
The Rhine crisis of 1840 was the moment when French talk of the Rhine frontier after the Eastern Question settlement met a German public answer—Treitschke’s fourth volume frames 1830–1840 as “the penetration of French liberalism” and closes that decade with a national mood that could turn against France as readily as it had admired July 1830.
After July and before 1848
Treitschke’s book on 1830–1840 treats the July Revolution and the European settlement, the vibration of liberalism in the Bund states, and the material modernization that already bound the Zollverein world (he notes, among other figures, that by 1840 the Customs Union already counted 145 beet-sugar factories). Political culture, not only tariffs, is his subject: the press, Young Germany, and the readiness of burgher opinion to speak in national terms.
Frontier rhetoric and German answer
When French parliamentary and journalistic voices in 1840 raised the left bank of the Rhine in the heat of Near Eastern diplomacy, German songs and pamphlets answered with the Rhine as a German river. The crisis did not produce a war; it produced a demonstration of national feeling inside a still-particularist Confederation—evidence Treitschke places on the road from Burschenschaft and Hambach toward 1848. Governments that had feared French contagion in 1830 now watched a German public define itself against French claims without yet possessing a German state.
Place in the sequence
Together with Hambach (1832) and the later March days, 1840 shows that national language had a mass audience years before the Frankfurt National Assembly. It also shows the double edge of that language: hostility to French ambition could strengthen Prussian and federal military readiness without dissolving dynastic sovereignty. Treitschke’s narrative keeps the episode inside the Restoration Bund, not as a premature unification war.
Eastern Question meets German song
Treitschke’s fourth–fifth parts narrate the 1840 war scare when French revisionist noise under Thiers meets a German patriotic reaction on the Rhine—armaments, verses, and fortification talk. The peaceful settlement and Straits framework cool the immediate danger but leave a memory of Franco-German hostility inside the Confederation public.
Prussian and confederal dimensions
Friedrich Wilhelm IV’s early reign atmosphere mixes romantic national gesture with inconclusive politics; the crisis is a stress test for Bund military arrangements and for Prussia’s claim to guard Germany’s west. Prefer frederick-william-iv, thiers, german-confederation.

events/roman-republic-1849.title: Roman Republic (1849)
events/roman-republic-1849.content:
Roman Republic (1849)
The Repubblica romana (“Roman Republic”) of 1849 was the democratic regime proclaimed at Rome after Pius IX’s flight to Gaeta, defended against a French expedition, and extinguished with the restoration of papal temporal sovereignty under Oudinot. La Farina’s books on the Roman government and the proclamation of the republic, and Tivaroni’s aftermath chapters, are the main deposits.
Proclamation
While negotiations ran at Gaeta, the Roman government, exercising a near dictatorship, published acts leading to a constituent assembly. Debates turned on whether the state should be a democracy under the name of Roman Republic and how it should relate to other Italian provinces through an Italian constituent. Voices such as Cesare Agostini spoke in that constitutional struggle. Moderates elsewhere could write “God keep us from a Roman republic” and prefer constitutional paths; La Cecilia worked to dissuade proclamation; Montanelli stood far from the concept. Inside Rome the cry prevailed. Garibaldi, among the people’s representatives, cut short ceremony: to delay a moment was crime—Viva la repubblica! The assembly and street repeated it.
Personnel and arms
Rome gave citizenship and seats to Italians of other provinces: Mazzini entered the assembly on 6 March to high applause; Cernuschi of Milan, Saliceti of Naples, Garibaldi of Nice, Dall’Ongaro of the Veneto sat with Romans. Forces included old line regiments, new light infantry, Swiss, a Union regiment, bersaglieri, Upper Rhine chasseurs, Roman and Bolognese legions, and the Garibaldi legion—little more than a thousand men of mixed provinces, ardent and held in hard discipline. Planned strengths La Farina records for the republic’s army (artillery, horse, and foot on the order of tens of thousands on paper) outran what the short war fully realized.
French intervention and fall
France’s expedition under Oudinot became the decisive external fact. Garibaldi’s first brigade held the line from Porta Portese to Porta San Pancrazio; fighting toward Velletri and the defence of the walls fixed the military legend. On 14 July 1849 Oudinot declared the temporal sovereignty of the Head of the Church restored; on the 15th he attended the religious-political restoration. A tricolour waved in a general’s face with the cry Viva la Repubblica Romana belongs to the last gestures Tivaroni preserves. Garibaldi’s retreat and the bastinado of prisoners taken toward San Marino mark the papal-Austrian reaction in the provinces. Orsini’s later hatred of Napoleon III still counted the expedition against the Roman Republic among the emperor’s Italian sins.
Aftermath
Students and republicans filled papal and Austrian prisons with twenty-year sentences for conspiracy. Piedmont’s politics digested the shock differently: the Statuto held under Victor Emmanuel while Rome returned to cardinals and French protection—the seed of the long questione romana (“Roman question”) that outlived Cavour.

events/russian-intervention-hungary-1849.title: Russian intervention in Hungary (1849)
events/russian-intervention-hungary-1849.content:
Russian intervention in Hungary (1849)
Nicholas I’s intervention in Hungary in 1849 is the military-political decision Kornilov’s Kurs istorii Rossii and the Austrian narrative volumes (Springer; Friedjung’s post-revolutionary Austria) treat as the end of the Hungarian revolutionary field war: Russian corps enter after Habsburg setbacks, Magyar resistance collapses toward Világos, and imperial military control is restored in the eastern half of the monarchy.
Request and entry
Austrian deposits record the dynasty’s need for external force once the Hungarian war outruns imperial resources and the court must choose between prolonged civil war and a Russian hammer. Nicholas answers as gendarme of the 1815 order. Intervention is framed as monarchical solidarity and police against revolution, not as a conquest for Petersburg’s permanent annexation. Russian columns change the force ratio within a campaign season; the political meaning is a dual sword for one emergency.
Operations and end-state
The deposits do not turn this page into a full order-of-battle monograph; they fix the sequence: entry, joint pressure with Habsburg forces, collapse of organized Hungarian field resistance, Világos, and the reprisal climate that follows. Springer and Friedjung treat the restored order as military first—administration and Bach-era centralism come after the guns. Kornilov treats the episode as the peak of Nikolaevan European prestige, the moment Official Russia looks indispensable to dynastic Europe.
Persons and linked wars
Prefer nicholas-i for the emperor’s system, hungarian-war-independence-1848-49 for the Magyar war arc, and Austrian post-1849 pages for Bach and the neo-absolutist administrative vocabulary Friedjung actually uses. Hungarian political leadership (Kossuth’s climate) belongs on those person and event pages; this event holds the intervention decision and its end-state.
Crimean shadow
The gratitude Austria does not fully repay becomes part of the diplomatic loneliness Friedjung assigns to the 1850s. Success as gendarme in 1849 is not automatic alliance capital in 1854–56. That irony is already a deposit theme, not later editorializing.
Coordination with Austria
Deposits stress that Russian entry answers an Austrian strategic emergency, not a unilateral Russian war of annexation. Joint pressure produces the end-state; political credit and blame are then fought out in diplomacy for a decade.
Nicholas answers Franz Joseph
Friedjung and Kornilov’s era frame: the young Austrian emperor requests, and Nicholas I sends, armies under Paskevich to crush Magyar independence. Holy Alliance memory and fear of European revolution justify the intervention in Russian official language.
Military decision
Russian mass and Austrian reconstitution overwhelm the Hungarian field armies; Világos follows. The intervention is the largest military fact of 1849 in east-central Europe and binds Austria’s survival to tsarist aid—with later diplomatic costs in the Crimean decade when Austria “repays” with ingratitude in Russian eyes.
Aftermath
Haynau’s repression and Bach’s administration build on a victory Russians claim a share in. Prefer nicholas-i, hungarian-war-independence-1848-49, kossuth.

events/schleswig-holstein-war-1864.title: Schleswig-Holstein War 1864
events/schleswig-holstein-war-1864.content:
Schleswig-Holstein War 1864
The Schleswig-Holstein War of 1864 is the Prussian-Austrian campaign against Denmark over the Elbe duchies—read in Sybel’s foundation history and Treitschke’s German history as the first of the wars that revise northern Europe under Prussian leadership and as the military end of a long legal-national quarrel.
Legal-national quarrel
Schleswig and Holstein sit where Danish royal law, German federal claims, and national agitation meet. Succession crisis and Danish constitutional moves to bind Schleswig more tightly to the kingdom detonate responses in the Confederation and in Berlin. The file is older than Bismarck; 1864 is the year cabinets choose arms.
Allied campaign
Prussia and Austria fight as German allies against Denmark. Düppel (Dybøl) becomes the emblematic storm in German national narrative; siege and field operations break Danish resistance. The political result is cession of the duchies. Contemporary German historians linger on military virtue and on the humiliation of the Danish unitary claim.
Gastein and the unstable prize
Administration of the conquered duchies is partitioned between the two German powers at Gastein—an unstable condominium. Cooperation against Denmark becomes competition over the spoils, preparing the road to the 1866 Austro-Prussian conflict. Sybel’s arc makes 1864 a necessary first act of Reich foundation, not a closed local war.
Deposit discipline
This page follows Sybel and Treitschke’s German framing. It does not import later textbook generalities beyond what those deposits carry. Pair with Bismarck, Confederation, and Zollverein pages for the political economy of Prussian leadership.
Federal and Prussian double track
German national agitation wants the duchies; Prussian policy wants them in a form that extends Prussian power. Austria joins to avoid isolation in German opinion and to keep a hand on the settlement. Sybel’s foundation story stresses the outcome that matters for Reich-building: Denmark is expelled, and the German powers hold the gate of the north.
From allied victory to fraternal war
The speed with which Gastein’s condominium turns poisonous is part of the 1864 meaning. Shared trophies without shared hierarchy recreate dualism’s old German problem in a new province. Readers of Sybel are meant to see 1866 already latent in the victory parade of 1864.
German powers against Denmark
Sybel’s Begründung volumes narrate the 1864 war as Prussia and Austria jointly executing the German national claim on the duchies against the November Constitution Danish policy—military success under Wrangel/Moltke’s era organisation, London diplomacy, and the occupation settlement that later becomes the Austro-Prussian quarrel.
Dualism inside victory
Joint victory hides opposite aims: Austria’s confederal habits versus Prussia’s exclusive grip. Gastein’s later condominium is already latent in 1864’s trophy problem. Zollverein and annexation conditions appear in Prussian demand lists Sybel preserves.
Placement
Edge of the wiki’s chronological charter but present in Sybel deposits used throughout the German spine. Prefer bismarck, zollverein, german-confederation.

events/silvesterpatent-1851.title: Silvesterpatent (1851)
events/silvesterpatent-1851.content:
Silvesterpatent (1851)
The Silvesterpatent (DE Silvesterpatent (“New Year’s Eve Patent”); 31 December 1851) was the package of imperial decrees by which Francis Joseph extinguished the stillborn March Constitution of 1849 and inaugurated open absolutism after 1848. Friedjung makes Karl Friedrich von Kübeck the intellectual author and Alexander Bach the administrative beneficiary: constitutional promises died; the unitary bureaucratic empire remained.
From March 1849 to Silvester
The Märzverfassung (DE Märzverfassung (“March Constitution”)) of 4 March 1849 had been Schwarzenberg’s answer to Kremsier: a single imperial crown, central parliament promised, historic crowns subordinated, Hungary declared integral to the unitary state. It was octroyed while the Hungarian war continued and never truly lived as a parliamentary regime. After Világos, the court faced a choice — animate the constitution with elections and ministers responsible to a Reichstag, or rule through army, police, and bureaucracy alone. Kübeck, recalled to influence as president of the rebuilt Reichsrat (DE Reichsrat (“Imperial Council”)), argued that 1848’s paper machinery was incompatible with monarchical salvation. Schwarzenberg still covered the transition; Bach’s interior held the administrative levers.
Content of the decrees
The Silvester acts suspended and then discarded the constitutional apparatus: no functioning imperial representative body of the 1849 type; government by emperor and ministers; the Reichsrat reduced to an advisory council of notables under Kübeck rather than a legislature. What survived was the administrative programme already in train — fusion of the kingdom of Hungary into the imperial structure, extension of Austrian judicial and political organisation, German as the language of command, continuation of peasant emancipation’s legal aftermath. Friedjung stresses the irony: the unitary state that liberals had partly imagined in 1848–49 was realised as police absolutism without the liberties that had justified unity.
Political meaning
For Francis Joseph, aged twenty-one at Silvester, the patent was a declaration of personal rule that he would not relinquish until war and finance forced the October Diploma. For Bach it cleared obstacles to systematic interior reform. For Kübeck it was the triumph of an older bureaucratic absolutism over “advocate” constitutionalism — though he soon found Bach’s democratic past and clerical alliances new enemies inside the victory. Metternich’s circle noted that the monarchy had abandoned even the appearance of the Rechtsstaat promised in 1849. Magyar passive resistance under Deák treated Silvester as final proof that Vienna had renounced lawful dualism.
Aftermath
The 1850s — Concordat, criminal code, Kempen’s police, the unfinished German condominium after Olmütz — unfolded under Silvester’s legal sky. Only Magenta, Solferino, and bankruptcy reopened the constitutional file. In wiki sequence Silvester stands between military reconquest and the Bach system’s full bloom; it is the juristic death certificate of Kremsier and of the March charter alike.

events/spanish-expedition-1823.title: Spanish expedition (1823)
events/spanish-expedition-1823.content:
Spanish expedition (1823)
The French expédition d’Espagne (“expedition to Spain”) of 1823 was the military intervention by which a Bourbon army, acting in the climate of the European congress system after Verona, restored Ferdinand VII to unrestricted power against the Spanish constitutional regime. In French parliamentary memory it became the great external success of the Villèle years and a proof, for ultras, that the restored monarchy could still make war in the name of legitimacy.
European and French setting
After the assassination of the duc de Berry and the rightward shift of 1820–22, French royalists looked on the Spanish revolution and the Cadiz constitution as a neighbouring fire. The congress diplomacy of the Holy Alliance powers treated intervention as a monarchical duty; France supplied the army. Villèle’s government had to balance ultra enthusiasm, liberal fear of a new crusade, and the fiscal cost of a campaign beyond the Pyrenees.
Campaign outline
French forces crossed into Spain under the duc d’Angoulême. The symbolic climax in French narratives was the taking of the Trocadéro forts at Cadiz, which broke the last serious constitutional resistance and delivered Ferdinand from constraint. Delord, writing later under the Second Empire, still treats the expedition among the military memories that Bonapartists and royalists contested: a Bourbon victory without Napoleon, used in pamphlets and street legend as a counter-weight to imperial glory.
Political consequences in France
Success strengthened Villèle and the court party. It fed the confidence that later accompanied Charles X’s accession and the more adventurous domestic laws of the mid-1820s. Liberals read the same events as proof that the Charter monarchy would export counter-revolution. The expedition did not create a stable Spanish settlement; Ferdinand’s restored absolutism disappointed even some of its patrons. In France, however, 1823 remained a date of Right triumph between the Berry crisis and the eventual shipwreck of 1830.

events/troppau-laibach-verona.title: Troppau, Laibach, Verona
events/troppau-laibach-verona.content:
Troppau, Laibach, Verona
Troppau, Laibach, and Verona are the early-1820s congresses at which the continental great powers, under Metternich’s working chairmanship, articulate and execute intervention against constitutional revolutions in Italy and Spain—the practical peak of Restoration conference police.
Troppau: principle of exclusion and force
Confronting the revolutionary wave after 1820, the powers draft language that states undergoing illegal change may be cast out of the European alliance and restored by arms. Britain’s reservations already limit universal solidarity; Austria, Russia, and Prussia form the interventionist core. The conference habit of 1815 becomes a doctrine of counter-revolution.
Laibach: Italy as military file
Laibach turns protocol into march. Austrian intervention destroys the Neapolitan constitutional regime and reasserts Habsburg guardianship over the peninsula’s dynasties. For Italian liberal memory the congress is the international veto on national constitutions; for Springer’s Austrian state narrative it is necessary police in the security glacis.
Verona: Spain and the wider system
Verona continues the method for Spain and residual Italian questions. French arms later execute the Spanish restoration under the political umbrella of monarchical Europe. Holy Alliance idiom and cabinet interest mix; constitutional movements lose the round.
Long arc
These meetings teach that 1815 will be defended by conference and army. 1830 and 1848 test the lesson. Inside the wiki the triple congress anchors metternich-system and holy-alliance with dates and places rather than metaphor alone.
Britain’s half-distance
Castlereagh’s and later British caution matters because it shows the system’s incomplete membership. London will not underwrite a general right of continental interference in the same religious-monarchical language Petersburg prefers. The interventions still proceed; they proceed with a visible crack in the alliance chorus. Treitschke and Springer register that crack without dissolving the fact of Austrian and French marches.
Italian and Spanish outcomes as precedent
What governments learn is practical: constitutions born of barracks revolts can be reversed when a great power’s army is free. What oppositions learn is equally practical: without a protecting great power of their own, legal charters are provisional. 1848 will remember both lessons—sometimes by trying to seize the army first, sometimes by hunting a French or Piedmontese guarantor.

events/vienna-march-1848.title: Vienna March 1848
events/vienna-march-1848.content:
Vienna March 1848
The Wiener Märzrevolution (“Vienna March Revolution”) of 1848 ended the Metternich era in the Habsburg capital and opened the revolutionary year across the Austrian lands. Within days of the February revolution in Paris, petitions of Viennese burghers, student agitation, and the liberal opposition in the Lower Austrian diet produced street fighting on 13 March, the resignation of Metternich, and imperial promises of constitution and reform. Friedjung, Springer, and Helfert treat the March days as both a local municipal-military crisis and the signal that the polyglot monarchy’s old system could no longer rule by delay.
Prelude
Before 1848 the Lower Austrian estates and the Viennese bourgeoisie had pressed for publicity, administrative reform, and relief from censorship without yet demanding a modern parliament for the whole empire. News from Paris and from the Italian and German states raised expectations. On 6 March burgher petitions circulated; by mid-March the combination of students, middle-class liberals, and workers in the suburbs outran the police. The Staatskonferenz (“State Conference”) under the weak Emperor Ferdinand lacked a soldier-statesman ready to fire on the capital as Windischgrätz would later do.
13–15 March
On 13 March crowds and National Guard formations forced the crisis; Metternich resigned and left Vienna. The court granted freedom of the press and the prospect of a constitution. Troops and burghers negotiated an uneasy order. On 15 March constitutional promises were repeated; the fall of the chancellor was already irreversible. The March days did not yet create a single Austrian nation-state programme: they removed the person and system that had blocked all programmes, Magyar, German-liberal, and Slav alike.
April–May sequel
The Pillersdorfsche Verfassung (“Pillersdorf constitution”) of 25 April attempted a monarchical constitution from above and was rejected by democratic Vienna. The rising of 15 May and the formation of the Wessenberg–Doblhoff ministry, with Alexander Bach as justice minister, shifted power toward a more parliamentary course. The Austrian Reichstag (“constituent assembly”) later abolished the feudal Frohnden (“robot / forced labour dues”) — the social measure that outlasted many political forms of the year. Suppression of the 14 September rising showed that order and revolution still contended inside the city months after Metternich’s flight.
Wider meaning
For Hungary the Vienna March enabled the April Laws and the Batthyány ministry; for Prague and the Slav Congress it opened a contest over federal reform; for Germany it was the shock that made the Frankfurt National Assembly conceivable. The March victory was incomplete: the dynasty, the army, and the non-German nationalities remained. October would reverse the capital’s revolution by siege; December would place Francis Joseph on the throne. March remains the hinge from Vormärz to open civil war.

events/vienna-october-1848.title: Vienna October 1848
events/vienna-october-1848.content:
Vienna October 1848
Vienna’s October 1848 rising is the capital’s second great revolutionary crisis of the year—Latour’s murder, the court’s flight, Windischgrätz’s siege and reconquest—after which the Austrian monarchy’s centre is held by the army rather than by March ministries. Springer and Friedjung make it the hinge between hopeful constitutional spring and military-bureaucratic winter.
From March promises to autumn rupture
March drove Metternich out and opened constitutional language. Summer brought war in Italy and Hungary, radicalization in the capital, and a court hunting military instruments. October detonates when popular radicalism, the fate of troops ordered toward the Hungarian theatre, and collapsed trust between city and dynasty coincide.
Latour, flight, and civic revolution
The lynching of War Minister Latour is the rising’s indelible signature in Austrian narrative. The court abandons the city; revolutionary authorities try to hold Vienna as a political actor in the empire’s civil wars. Barricades and committees recall Paris and Milan, but the opponent is now the dynasty’s field army returning from other victories.
Windischgrätz reconquers the capital
Windischgrätz—already emblem of Prague’s suppression—invests and takes Vienna. Bombardment, street fighting, and political executions restore imperial control at a moral price the liberal capital never forgets. Military victory clears the ground for Francis Joseph’s early course and for the winter war against Hungary.
Aftermath
With Vienna held, the monarchy can treat Hungarian resistance as rebellion rather than as partner negotiation. Russian intervention in 1849 completes the counter-revolutionary arc. Constitutional experiments will return in Diploma and Patent forms; October ends the hope that the streets of Vienna could dictate a liberal empire in 1848.
Capital and countryside inverted
October reverses March’s image of Vienna leading the empire into liberty. The reconquered capital becomes proof that the dynasty’s sword can retake the political centre. Provincial and Hungarian theatres continue, but the symbolic head is secured for counter-revolution.
Terror and legality
Courts-martial and exemplary punishments after the siege enter liberal martyr catalogues and conservative order catalogues alike. Friedjung’s later history needs that darkness to explain why constitutional experiments of the 1860s arrive freighted with distrust.

events/villafranca-1859.title: Villafranca armistice (1859)
events/villafranca-1859.content:
Villafranca armistice (1859)
The preliminari di Villafranca (“Villafranca preliminaries”) of 11 July 1859 ended the Franco-Austrian war in Italy after Magenta and Solferino without the full expulsion of Austria from the peninsula that Plombières had contemplated. Tivaroni’s chapter “Villafranca” is the principal narrative in this corpus.
After two victories
Even after Magenta and Solferino, Tivaroni notes, a march on Vienna was not possible. Napoleon III sent an autograph letter proposing a suspension of arms and a meeting of the two emperors at Villafranca, Fleury letting Napoleon’s ideas for peace preliminaries filter through. Francis Joseph is reported surprised at the offer. About three hours at Villafranca fixed an armistice running to 15 August; La Marmora telegraphed the suspension to Cavour.
The interview
On 11 July the emperors met in the house Gandini-Morelli on the main road, in a first-floor salon. Napoleon accompanied Francis Joseph, who had come out beyond Villafranca to meet him. In Bazancourt’s campaign history as cited by Tivaroni, Francis Joseph spontaneously offered Lombardy less Mantua and Peschiera—the core territorial cession that left the Quadrilateral and Venetia in Austrian hands and checked the maximum Italian programme.
Cavour’s fury
Cavour reached the king’s headquarters at Monzambano on the evening of the 10th knowing nothing certain of what would follow. The settlement produced his most famous outburst (preserved via Kossuth’s emigration writings in French and Italian forms): he would take Solaro della Margherita with one hand and Mazzini with the other, make himself conspirator and revolutionary, but this treaty would not be executed—no, a thousand times no. The cry marks the collision between cabinet peace and national war aims. He left office; central Italy’s subsequent annexations and the 1860 southern revolution reopened by force and plebiscite what Villafranca had frozen. Saffi could later argue that the peace had at least saved Italy from becoming Napoleon’s absolute dependency—an interpretation that shows how bitterly contemporaries weighed the same act.
Place in the corpus
Villafranca is the brake on 1859: Lombardy transferred (via France) toward Piedmont, Venetia retained by Austria, confederation schemes and papal presidency floated in the wider diplomatic chatter, and Italian unitarists forced onto the road of central-Italian votes and Garibaldi’s 1860 war.

events/zollverein-founding-1834.title: Founding of the Zollverein (1834)
events/zollverein-founding-1834.content:
Founding of the Zollverein (1834)
The German Customs Union (Zollverein) that took effect at the beginning of 1834 joined Prussian tariff territory with a growing ring of German states—Treitschke’s institutional prehistory, List’s agitation, and later Sybel’s political use of the Union all treat 1834 as a hinge between economic integration and Prussian leadership.
Prehistory in the deposits
Treitschke’s third volume carries a chapter on “the tariff war and the first customs unions,” with beilagen on Nebenius and the German Zollverein and on Motz’s correspondence. He stresses how party myths later clouded the real history, and recalls that Hardenberg’s official language to List and others in 1819 already spoke of consultation on trade—words that stood in the newspapers long before Aegidi’s 1865 publication of Bernstorff instructions was hailed as a revelation. List’s own career, in the introduction to Das nationale System, is signed by enthusiastic entry for the Zollverein idea: the German Commercial and Industrial Association of 1819, dismissal from Württemberg service (1820), chamber agitation, and condemnation in 1822. His unfinished masterwork’s first volume is subtitled international trade, commercial policy, and the German Zollverein.
1834 as system
The treaties that brought the Union into force created a common external tariff and internal free trade among members while Austria remained outside. That geometry—Prussia-centered economic Germany without Habsburg participation—is the fact Sybel still assumes in the 1860s when Bismarck’s February demands require Schleswig-Holstein’s entry into the Zollverein and Prussian tariff system. The founding is thus not only a finance measure; it is the long economic premise of kleindeutsch politics.
Entry into force
Treitschke dates the practical gathering of the main Prussian-led customs treaties into the Zollverein’s 1834 operation after years of bilateral and regional preliminaries. Toll barriers inside the member bloc fall; a common external tariff and revenue-sharing rules begin to train south and central German states into Prussian administrative rhythms.
Who is in, who is out
Austria stands outside; Hanover and some north-German configurations remain problems for later rounds; free cities and Mecklenburg paths differ. List’s agitation and official Prussian policy converge on the same map from different motives—national economy versus state power and revenue.
Political meaning
The founding is an event with a date and a concept with a long afterlife. Prefer zollverein for structure; this page marks the 1834 hinge Treitschke and List both treat as epochal for material Germany.

index.title: Rest of Europe 1800–1865
index.content:
Rest of Europe 1800–1865
A narrative-research knowledge base on continental European history from the Napoleonic settlement through 1865 (eve of the Austro-Prussian War). The United Kingdom is a separate wiki. Pages are grounded in the deposited source corpus — German national narrative sources (Treitschke, Sybel, List), Austrian revolutionary and absolutist sources (Springer, Friedjung, Helfert), Italian Risorgimento (La Farina, Tivaroni), French parliamentary and imperial history (Duvergier, Delord, Ollivier), Hungarian reform (Grünwald, Springer), and Russian nineteenth-century lectures (Kornilov).
Narrative arc
Napoleonic Italy and the Congress of Vienna reset the peninsula and the Germanies under Austrian presidency while Prussia prepared the commercial path of the Zollverein (1834). The Concert of Europe and Holy Alliance framed legitimacy; Troppau–Laibach–Verona turned congress diplomacy into intervention after 1820. Alexander I’s Russia mixed reform openings and alliance politics; Decembrists, then Nicholas I and Official Nationality (Uvarov), closed the door. Restoration France lived under the Charte and the Doctrinaires; the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe, Guizot, and Thiers ran the pays légal until February 1848. Carlsbad, Burschenschaften, and Hambach marked the German Vormärz; List’s national system theorized protection behind customs unity. The Rhine crisis of 1840 tested Orléanist foreign policy and German national feeling together.
1848–49 broke the Metternich system: Paris in February and the June Days (National Workshops, Cavaignac); Vienna’s March and October; Milan’s Five Days; Hungary’s April Laws, Batthyány, Széchenyi’s reform legacy, war of independence, Jelačić and Windischgrätz, Görgei and Világos; Frankfurt’s failed constitution; Rome’s republic and the death of neo-Guelphism; Novara, Charles Albert’s abdication, and d’Azeglio’s Piedmont under the Statuto; Russian intervention in Hungary. Schwarzenberg and the young Francis Joseph rebuilt power; Radowitz’s Erfurt Union failed at Olmütz (Manteuffel); the Silvesterpatent, Kübeck, and Bach defined absolutism after 1848, sealed spiritually by the Concordat of 1855.
The 1850s–60s reopened national questions. The Crimean War isolated Russia and seated Sardinia at Paris; Orsini and Plombières led to Magenta and Solferino, Villafranca, the Thousand, Gaeta, and the Kingdom of Italy (1861) under Cavour, Victor Emmanuel, Garibaldi, then Ricasoli, Farini, and Rattazzi — Roman question still open, Ferdinand II’s Naples gone. Austria’s October Diploma and February Patent began constitutional retreat from Bach’s system. Bismarck’s conflict ministry under Wilhelm I and Roon, the Schleswig-Holstein war of 1864, and Gastein reopened dualism (kleindeutsch / großdeutsch). Alexander II’s Emancipation Manifesto (1861) opened the Great Reforms. France’s Second Empire moved from coup authoritarian core (Morny, Persigny) toward talk of a liberal Empire.
How to read

Start with major events (Vienna 1815; congress intervention; 1830; 1848 clusters; Crimea; 1859–61 Italy; Austrian patents; 1864 Denmark).
Read entities as continuous political biographies tied to those crises.
Use concepts for structures that span decades (Metternich system, Zollverein, Bach system, Charte, Risorgimento, nationality question, Official Nationality, Napoleonic Italy).
Every entity/event/concept page ends with a Sources section pointing at the underlying books.
Native-language glosses follow conventions-sources-and-glosses.
