sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t1.title: Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome I
sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t1.content:
Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome I
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire illustrée du second empire. — Tome premier. — Nouvelle édition. — Paris: Librairie Germer Baillière et Cie, 108, boulevard Saint-Germain, 1880 (printer: Coulommiers, Typographie Paul Brodard). 121 gravures dans le texte.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous narrative, not memoir. This is the illustrated edition of the same multi-tome work originally published by Baillière 1869–75 (see Tome II in this wiki). The present volume opens with an Introduction tracing the Bonapartist tradition from 1814, covers the Restoration and July Monarchy periods of Bonapartist conspiracy, the 1848 revolution, Louis-Napoléon’s election as President, the conflict with the Constituent and Legislative Assemblies, the coup d’état of 2 December 1851, the establishment of the Empire, and the early years of the reign through the Crimean War and Congress of Paris (1856). Body text runs approximately 596 printed pages; table of contents follows.
Core chronological span is 1814–1856, but the narrative weight falls on 1848–1856 — the February Revolution, the presidency, the coup, the consolidation of the authoritarian Empire, and the Crimean War. The introductory chapters on Bonapartism under the Restoration and July Monarchy supply the pre-history of the movement that carried Louis-Napoléon to power.
OCR from local Anna’s Archive UCAL scan (OCLC 7058591; Baillière [1880–83]). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through table; internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves and rear library plates dropped.
Chapters
Introduction — Le Bonapartisme
Chapitre I — Le bonapartisme et la Restauration (1814–1830)
The Bonaparte family after Waterloo, dispersion of the brothers, the duc de Reichstadt, Queen Hortense, beginnings of the alliance between Bonapartism and the republican party.
Treaty of Fontainebleau (11 April 1814); the family’s disbelief in the durability of the Restoration. Joseph in America, Lucien in Rome, Jérôme in Germany, Eugène de Beauharnais as duc de Leuchtenberg. The duc de Reichstadt. Mme Letizia at Rome. Napoleon’s sisters — Caroline, Elisa, Pauline. Queen Hortense: her disputes with her husband, her conduct after Waterloo. Beginnings of the alliance between Bonapartism and the republican party.
Chapitre II — Le bonapartisme et la monarchie de Juillet — La tentative de Strasbourg (1830–1836)
Bonapartism in 1830, the Bonaparte and Orléans families, the Strasbourg attempt.
Danger for the republican party of an alliance with the Bonapartists. The Chamber votes to maintain the 1816 legislation against the Bonapartes. Hortense and her sons in the Romagna insurrection. Death of the elder son. Hortense received by Louis-Philippe. Bonapartist demonstrations at the Vendôme column. Louis-Napoléon protests against being suspected of coveting the Belgian throne. Departure for Arenenberg. Publications of the prince. Fialin de Persigny. The Strasbourg attempt. Louis-Napoléon sent to America.
Chapitre III — Le bonapartisme et la monarchie de Juillet — Tentative de Boulogne (1836–1840)
The Boulogne landing, Ham imprisonment, escape.
Severe opinion of the Bonaparte family on the Strasbourg attempt. Prince Jérôme solicits return to France; Thiers transmits the refusal. Louis-Napoléon in Switzerland; the French government demands his expulsion. Arrival in England; publication of Idées napoléoniennes. Bonapartist propaganda of the prince de Crouy-Chanel. The club des culottes de peau and club des cotillons. Formation of Louis-Napoléon’s military household. Return of Napoleon I’s ashes. The Boulogne attempt. Trial before the Cour des pairs. Barbès’s attempt. Persigny boasts of having fired on an officer. Ham captivity. Louis-Napoléon as collaborator of republican newspapers. Literary celebrities of the epoch in contact with the prisoner. He writes to Louis-Philippe asking permission to see his sick father. Escape from Ham. Prince Jérôme writes again to Thiers and is allowed to reside in France for three months. Death of the ex-king of Holland.
Chapitre IV — Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte est-il fils du roi Louis?
The paternity question: Louis’s marriage to Hortense de Beauharnais, the hereditary senatus-consultum, the reign in Holland, the legal dispute after the Empire.
Louis marries Hortense against his will — Duroc had refused her despite the First Consul’s insistence. The senatus-consultum on imperial hereditary succession. Louis becomes king of Holland. Persistent incompatibility between Louis and his wife. Hortense leaves Holland. After the fall of the Empire, Louis sues his wife before the Seine tribunal and obtains custody of the elder son. Louis’s letter to the Pope regretting his elder son’s participation in the Romagna insurrection, and disavowing paternity of the second son. Timid and irresolute character of Louis-Napoléon. Striking resemblance between Morny and Louis-Napoléon. Letters from Louis showing intermittent paternal affection. Louis’s testament declaring Louis-Napoléon his son.
Chapitre V — Le bonapartisme et la Révolution de février (1848)
Louis Bonaparte’s arrival in Paris, his letter to the provisional government, Bonapartist propaganda, election to the Assembly.
The republican party at the beginning of 1848 hesitates to ally with the Bonapartists. Louis Bonaparte arrives in Paris; writes to the provisional government; departs for England. Bonapartist propaganda; the bonnets à poils demonstration. The first-hour Bonapartists. Louis-Napoléon’s candidacy; elected in four departments. Agitation and troubles over the nomination. Assembly debate on validation: speeches of Cavaignac, Jules Favre, Lamartine, Buchez, Viellard, Ledru-Rollin. Louis-Napoléon validated; he resigns as representative. Bonapartism emerges strengthened.
Chapitre VI — L’élection du Président de la République
National workshops, the June insurrection, Cavaignac’s executive power, the presidential election.
The national workshops; Trélat’s attitude as minister of public works; the government tries to force workers to leave Paris. Bonapartists foment revolt. Falloux as rapporteur. Tumult on the place du Panthéon. Dissolution of the national workshops pronounced. The June insurrection; character of street warfare; protracted struggle. General Cavaignac named head of the executive power. The National Assembly’s error in not reserving the right to elect its own president. Grévy demands suppression of the presidency. Lamartine’s speech. Thiers’s speech: he turns decisively against the Republic. Marshal Bugeaud, General Changarnier, Dufaure. Louis-Napoléon elected President. He swears fidelity to the Republic. Cavaignac and his government.
Chapitre VII — Le bonapartisme et l’Assemblée constituante
Formation of the 20 December cabinet, the 29 January crisis, the Roman question, the end of the Constituante.
Formation of the 20 December cabinet: Odilon-Barrot as chief, Léon Faucher, Tracy, Falloux, Bixio, Passy, Léon de Malleville, Drouyn de Lhuys, Boulay de la Meurthe as vice-president. Resignation of Malleville and Bixio. The 29 January crisis; Changarnier’s attitude. Suicide of the Constituent Assembly. The Roman question: political, military, and economic situation of the Roman Republic. Assembly’s opposition to the Roman expedition. Ledru-Rollin demands the impeachment of the President. Napoléon-Jérôme Bonaparte attacks the President’s policy. Last session of the Constituent Assembly.
Chapitre VIII — Le treize juin (1849)
The Legislative Assembly, the rue de Poitiers committee, the 13 June demonstration.
Legitimist, Bonapartist, Orleanist pamphlets. Composition of the new ministry under Odilon-Barrot. Emotion produced by the news from Rome. Numerous protests. Ledru-Rollin’s speech: he declares he will defend the Constitution even by arms. The 13 June journée — a mere scuffle. Paris placed under siege. Faults of Ledru-Rollin and his friends.
Chapitre IX — La révision de la Constitution (1849–1850)
Consequences of 13 June, the Ham speech, the 31 October message, the Falloux Law, the 31 May electoral law.
The Ham speech. The 31 October message. Letter to Edgar Ney. Dismissal of the Odilon-Barrot ministry. Rouher minister of justice; Fould minister of finance. Law on liberty of teaching — the singular alliance of Thiers and Montalembert. Le Verrier’s proposal to move the École Polytechnique to Meudon. Fear caused by partial Paris elections. The Eugène Sue candidacy. The 31 May law. The President travels through the departments. Message of 12 November.
Chapitre X — Conflits entre l’Assemblée et le Président de la République
Publication of Changarnier’s instructions, destitution of Changarnier, the transitory cabinet.
Publication of the instructions given by Changarnier to the Paris army chiefs. Thiers’s speech. The day of defiance against the ministry. Dismissal of General Changarnier. The men of action are lacking. Order of the day. Letter of Louis Bonaparte to Dupin. The transitory cabinet. The Right threatens the President with refusal of a salary increase. Montalembert’s speech. Letter of the comte de Chambord. Law on the National Guard. Suspension of Michelet’s course.
Chapitre XI — La révision de la Constitution (1851)
Five revision proposals, the 14 July debate, rejection, the Saint-Arnaud ministry.
Five revision proposals are before the Assembly. Opening of discussion on 14 July 1851: speeches of Baroche, Falloux, Cavaignac, Michel (de Bourges), Berryer, Dufaure, Odilon-Barrot. Rejection of the revision proposals. Imprudent and threatening attitude of the revolutionary party. Louis-Napoléon’s speech at the inauguration of the Halles. Assembly vacation. The coup d’état project abandoned. Recall of the 31 May law. Formation of a cabinet of devotion. General Leroy de Saint-Arnaud, minister of war. Reading of a presidential message on 4 November 1851 to the Assembly. Louis-Napoléon’s speech to French exhibitors at the London Exhibition. Dangerous illusions of the republican party.
Chapitre XII — La proposition des questeurs
The questors’ proposal to secure the Assembly against a coup, debate, rejection.
The questors’ proposition. The minister of war, interrogated, first sides with the Commission, then retracts. Uncertainty of part of the Assembly. Discussion of the proposition. Amendment of Broglie, Daru, etc. Colonel Charras supports the proposition. Michel de Bourges combats it. Hypocritical declaration of the minister of war. The proposition is rejected. The Montagnards. The socialists. The Right. The executive power profits from the Assembly’s errors.
Chapitre XIII — La conspiration
The Bonapartist conspiracy — Persigny and Changarnier, Fleury in Algeria, Saint-Arnaud’s hesitation.
The Bonapartist conspiracy. The President protests his respect for legality at every instant. The Strasbourg and Boulogne precedents. The Bonapartist programme. Persigny at Changarnier’s. Fleury in Algeria. The President’s speeches become veritable appeals for his re-election. Graduation of his attacks. Message of 4 January 1851. Did the Assembly wish to overthrow the President? Message of 4 November 1851. Louis Bonaparte calumniates the Assembly. Captation of the army. Mission of Commandant Fleury in Algeria. The Kabylie expedition resolved to create popularity for Saint-Arnaud. Canrobert’s hesitation. Change of the Paris troops. Espinasse tells Saint-Arnaud he is ready.
Chapitre XIV — La nuit du 1er au 2 décembre
The evening at the Élysée, the arrests of generals and deputies.
The evening of 1 December 1851 at the Élysée. Arrival of Vieyra. Morny at the Opéra-Comique. The conspirators meet at the Élysée. The Imprimerie nationale. The police commissioners summoned to the prefecture; they receive Maupas’s final instructions. Arrests of General Cavaignac, General Changarnier, General Lamoricière, General Bedeau, Colonel Charras, Thiers, Greppo, Roger (du Nord). Persigny at the École militaire. Espinasse marches on the Palais Bourbon. Lieutenant-Colonel Niol’s noble threat to Espinasse. Arrest of General Le Flo and Baze. Morny takes possession of the ministry of the interior. Maupas’s dispatch to Louis-Napoléon.
Chapitre XV — Le 2 décembre
The coup d’état proclaimed, the proclamations and decrees, the deputies’ resistance.
The Parisian population learns of the coup from reading the proclamations and decrees. Proclamation to the army. Action of the Catholic associations in favour of the coup. The people have no means of learning the situation following the suppression of the newspapers. Meeting of the representatives at Yvan’s and at Odilon-Barrot’s. The President declared deposed; the Haute Cour convened. Appeal to the conseils généraux. Weakness of President Dupin. Meeting at Daru’s. Arrest of representatives on the place de Bourgogne and at Crémieux’s. In the morning at the Élysée, first apprehensions. Louis Bonaparte shows himself to the population.
Chapitre XVI — La résistance légale
The deputies at the mairie of the Xe arrondissement, the proclamation of déchéance.
The deputies assemble at the mairie of the Xe arrondissement. They pronounce the déchéance of Louis-Napoléon. They exhort the soldiers to respect the Constitution and summon them to defend it. The soldiers declare they recognise only passive obedience to their chiefs. Berryer’s allocution to the crowd. Two police commissioners order the Assembly to disperse. Magnan orders the mairie to be occupied. The deputies arrested and led to the caserne du quai d’Orsay. The deputies in the prison van. The Assembly of the Xe arrondissement has done its duty. The Haute Cour obliged to convene itself. Efforts of several representatives to rouse the people. Attempts to organise resistance. Appeal to the people by Victor Hugo. Michel (de Bourges) at the Balcon du restaurant Bonvalet.
Chapitre XVII — La journée du 3 décembre
The night of 2–3 December, Victor Hugo’s appeal, the barricades, Baudin’s death.
The night of 2–3 December. Victor Hugo appeals to the people in the name of the Montagne. The wall of the rue Notre-Dame-de-Lorette. The Commission consultative. Convocation of the people in their comices. Formation of the new cabinet. The representatives refuse to be freed by force. The Montagnard representatives at the faubourg Saint-Antoine; they call the people to arms. A barricade is formed. Death of Baudin. New and useless appeal to arms. Rumours unfavourable to the coup. Second hearing of the Haute Cour; a police commissioner orders it to disperse. The Temple quarter becomes covered in barricades. The Parisian population begins to stir. Proclamation of Saint-Arnaud. Meeting at Marie’s. Meeting at Landrin’s. Colonel Rochefort’s trap. Charge of the lancers in the rues Taitbout and de la Chaussée-d’Antin. Anxiety of the Bonapartists.
Chapitre XVIII — Les fusillades du 4 décembre
The barricades of 4 December, the fusillades on the boulevards.
The barricades of 4 December. Maupas’s anxieties. Demonstration at the mairie of the IIe arrondissement. The barricade of the boulevard Poissonnière. Occupation of the boulevard by the troops. Fusillades on the boulevards. Invasion of the maison Frascati. The first victims of the day. Irruption of the troops into the Cercle du Commerce. The barricades of the porte Saint-Denis. The battery of the boulevard Bonne-Nouvelle opens fire. Fusillade from the faubourg Poissonnière to the Chaussée-d’Antin. Acts of savagery by the soldiers. Fusillades on the Left Bank.
Chapitre XIX — La nuit du 4 au 5 décembre
Night executions, arbitrary arrests, Delahode the informer.
General terror of the Parisians. Lirieux is handed over to the gendarmes who prepare to shoot him; saved by a fortunate accident. Nocturnal executions. Cruel treatment of alleged insurgents. Arrests at the Divan de la rue Lepelletier. The informer Delahode designates the journalists to be arrested. Nocturnal feasts of the soldiers on the boulevards. Secret executions.
Chapitre XX — L’insurrection dans les départements
Secret societies, the Var, Basses-Alpes, Vaucluse, Bédarieux, Marmande, Clamecy.
Secret societies in the departments. Marseille does not rise at the news of the coup. Armed uprisings in the Var department. Summary executions. Martin Bidouré shot twice. Executions at Lorgues. The Basses-Alpes department. Uprisings in the Apt arrondissement, Vaucluse. The canton of Crest. Resistance in the Hérault department. The Bédarieux affair. Resistance at Marmande. Resistance in the East and the Centre. The Nièvre department. Clamecy.
Chapitre XXI — La proscription
The 5 December decree, military commissions, state of siege, deportation, the pontons.
Decree of 5 December 1851. Proclamation of 8 December and its contradiction. Formation of military commissions. State of siege declared in thirty-two departments. Arrests and expulsions. Prisoners packed into casemates; assimilated to common thieves. Prévôtale procedure. The three categories. Arbitrary power confounds all authorities. The highways fill with chains. Ill-treatment of prisoners. Decree of 7 January 1852. Representatives deported, expelled, or provisionally removed. Departure of the first convoy on 9 January. Prisoners aboard the Canada; their sufferings. Horrible diseases on board. Situation of the republican party. Arrests on the most frivolous pretexts. The mixed commissions. Prohibition of associations. The proscribed in Switzerland, Belgium, Italy, Spain, America.
Chapitre XXII — Les décrets du 22 janvier
The plebiscite, the eagles restored, the Constitution promulgated, the Orléans property decree.
Absence of liberty during the vote on the plebiscite. Result of the vote. Baroche’s allocution. The Prince-President’s reply. The archbishop of Paris addresses a few words. Restoration of the eagles on the flags. Promulgation of the Constitution. Organic law of the press. The Empire re-established indirectly. Emotion caused by the 22 January decrees. Employment of the revenues of the Orléans family property. Dupin resigns as procureur général. Montalembert withdraws from the Commission consultative. Gasparin and Rambuteau refuse to enter the Senate. The administration of the domaines takes possession of Neuilly and Monceaux by force. The question brought before the Conseil d’État. Baroche hampers the freedom of this body; the government wins by a single vote. Punishment of those who voted against. End of the dictatorial period.
Chapitre XXIII — Ave Caesar
Distribution of the eagles (10 May 1852), the Bordeaux speech (“L’Empire, c’est la paix”), the plebiscite of 21 November, the proclamation of the Empire.
Distribution of the eagles to the army, 10 May 1852. Allocution of the Prince-President. 7 July 1852: elections of municipal and general councillors. 17 July: inauguration of the Strasbourg railway. The Prince departs for the Midi. 9 October: the Bordeaux speech: “L’Empire, c’est la paix.” The Prince’s return to Paris. Royal reception; Louis Bonaparte and Morny embrace before the crowd. The curé of the Madeleine awaits at the church door. Salute to the Emperor. The re-establishment of the Empire decided. Convocation of the Senate. Plebiscite of 21 November. Gathering of the great corps of state at the château de Saint-Cloud. Billault’s speech. The Prince-President’s reply: the Republic alone can save liberty. Faults of the republican party.
L’Empire
Chapitre I — L’Empire et l’Europe
Proclamation of the Empire in Paris, the imperial family, the new right, the Eastern question, the Holy Places quarrel.
The Emperor at the Tuileries. Proclamation of the Empire at Saint-Cloud. Proclamation of the Empire at the Hôtel-de-Ville. The imperial family. The Empire before Europe. The new right. Hostility of the English press against the Emperor. Hostility of Emperor Nicholas. The question of the Holy Places. French devotion and Russian devotion. The Tsar decides to recognise Napoleon III. Dispositions of Austria and Prussia. Persigny’s mission to Prussia. Saxe and Bavaria.
Chapitre II — Le mariage de l’Empereur
The Montijo marriage, the civil and religious ceremonies, the Empress’s education and role.
Prince Jérôme advises his nephew to marry. The royal marriage and the national marriage. Mlle de Montijo; she is the queen of the Presidency fetes. Le Moniteur announces the Emperor’s marriage to Mlle de Montijo. Nuptial manifesto: representing a new principle, he must conserve that character in marrying. The father of Mlle de Montijo. Signature of the contract in the salle des Maréchaux. Civil marriage ceremony. Religious marriage at Notre-Dame. Presentation at the Tuileries. The Imperatrice’s difficult task. The 1 January reception. The official press and La Guéronnière. Portrait of the Empress by La Guéronnière; she is poorly prepared by her education.
Chapitre III — Commencement de la guerre de Crimée
The Eastern question, Menshikov’s mission, the Sinope battle, the Franco-English alliance.
Nesselrode’s memorandum. Nicholas’s overtures to Sir Hamilton Seymour eight years after. The sick man. Russia refuses to come to an understanding with France. Menshikov’s mission; he modifies his demands. Aali-Pasha and Fuad-Pasha. Dispositions of the powers. Passage of the Pruth by the Russians on 22 May 1853. Vienna conference. Nicholas I and Franz-Joseph. Austria separates from Russia. Orlov’s mission to Vienna: he asks for Austrian neutrality; Austrian refusal. The king of Prussia and his dispositions. The Russian fleet leaves Sebastopol. Battle of Sinope. Dispatch of English troops to Malta. Signature of the Franco-English treaty on 10 April 1854. Allied landing at the Piraeus on 25 May 1854. The programme of the four guarantees. Operations in the Baltic. Taking of Bomarsund.
Chapitre IV — La bataille de l’Alma
Lord Raglan and Maréchal Saint-Arnaud, the landing at Gallipoli, the siege of Sebastopol resolved, the Alma.
First troop deployment. Disembarkation point fixed at Gallipoli. The expeditionary chiefs have no plan. First appearance of cholera. Inaction and impatience of the army. The Dobroutscha expedition forced to retreat. Lack of remedies and transport for the sick. Disastrous retreat to Varna. Recrudescence of cholera. The expedition loses more than half its effectives. Bombardment of Odessa. The siege of Sebastopol resolved. Proclamation to the army. Council of war held on board La Ville de Paris. Occupation of Eupatoria. Saint-Arnaud wants to attack Fort Constantine. Inaction of Prince Menshikov. Menshikov takes a defensive position on the heights of the Alma. March and battle plan of the allies. Slowness of the English delays their first movement. Bosquet’s turning movement. The French appear on the Russian left. Complete victory for the allies. News of the taking of Sebastopol spreads to Constantinople and Paris. General disappointment. Death of Maréchal Saint-Arnaud.
Chapitre V — Balaklava et Inkermann
Allied positions, the battles, the Crimean winter.
Positions of the allies after the Alma. General Canrobert. March of the allies on Sebastopol. Battle of Balaklava. Battle of Inkermann. General Gortschakoff succeeds Menshikov as Russian commander-in-chief. Recrudescence of cholera at the start of winter. Appearance of scurvy.
Chapitre VI — Fin de la guerre de Crimée
The Piedmontese contingent, the death of Nicholas I, the Vienna conferences, the fall of Sebastopol.
A Piedmontese army corps joins the allies in the Crimea. Death of Nicholas I. The Vienna conferences. Fault committed by Drouyn de Lhuys; he is replaced by Walewski at the foreign ministry. Slowness of the Sebastopol siege. Public impatience. General Pélissier replaces Canrobert as commander-in-chief. Failure of the first assault. Combat of the Tchernaïa. Taking of Sebastopol. Canrobert’s mission to Sweden. Alexander II’s proclamation to his army. Napoleon III’s speech at the closing of the Exposition. The king of Sardinia and Cavour at Paris. Acceptance of the four guarantees by Russia. The unpeaceable dispositions of England. Menacing language of the English press. Panic on the Bourse. The brochure on the Congress. Austrian propositions to Russia. Russian counter-propositions. Isolation of this power. Alexander II decides to make peace.
Chapitre VII — Le Congrès de Paris
The Congress sits at the Quai d’Orsay, the Italian question raised, the Empire at its apogee.
The Congress meets in Paris on 21 February 1856 under the presidency of Walewski. It sits at the Hôtel du ministère des affaires étrangères. Etiquette difficulties. Prussia admitted to the Congress. Walewski’s propositions. Reply of the plenipotentiaries. Le Constitutionnel declares there will be no prorogation of the armistice. Note of the Moniteur on industrial affairs. Session of 8 April. Walewski calls the Congress’s attention to the situation of Italy. Napoleon III receives the plenipotentiaries at the Tuileries. The Empire is at its apogee.
Notes
Series: Histoire illustrée du second empire by Taxile Delord; this is the Tome premier of the illustrated edition (Baillière [1880–83]), corresponding to an expanded and illustrated version of the first volume of the original 1869–75 Baillière set (OCLC 6266334). Tome II of the original edition is in this wiki; the illustrated Tomes III–IV and original Tome V exist elsewhere in the corpus. Placement: Rest of Europe 1800–1865 wiki — the volume’s core is 1848–1856 (Second Republic, coup, early Empire, Crimean War). The later Empire (1859 Italian war, 1860s liberalisation) is handled by Tome II and later volumes. Voice: Contemporary republican narrative history; represent what Delord states, without modern scholarly reframing. Illustrations: 121 wood engravings in the text (not preserved in this raw OCR).
Related in corpus: Ollivier L’Empire libéral tomes V and VII (participant memoir-history of later imperial years) sit under the same French Second Empire shelf in this wiki. Raw: delord-histoire-second-empire-t1.txt.
Notes on form
Bullet inventory flattened to continuous English narration (2026-08-16). Prefer native term (“English”) glosses on institutional keywords when thickening from raw.

sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t2.content:
Delord — Histoire du second empire, Tome II
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire du second empire (1848–1869). — Tome deuxième. — Paris: Germer Baillière, libraire-éditeur, rue de l’École-de-Médecine, 17, 1870. Printer: Imprimerie Émile Martinet, rue Mignon, 2. London / Madrid / New-York Baillière houses listed on the title-page.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous Histoire, not memoir. The series band is 1848–1869. This volume carries the running title L’Empire (suite) and is the second tome of the set (tomes I and III+ are not yet in this raw corpus). Body text runs through printed p. 721 (Fin du deuxième volume); table of contents follows. The closing paragraph points forward to the next volume for the Empire’s search for force after Italian war and internal weakness.
Core chronological span is the authoritarian Empire from the aftermath of 2 December 1851 through the Italian war of 1859 and interior politics into early–mid 1860 (Thouvenel at Foreign Affairs, commercial treaty programme of 5 January, Lamoricière at Rome). Thematic chapters on parties, press, clergy, Academy, and proscrits cover 1848–1859 as backstory to the same years.
OCR from local Anna’s Archive scan set (OCLC 6266334; Baillière 1869–75). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through table; internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves dropped.
Chapters
Chapitre I — La loi de régence (1856)
Financial fever, Haussmann’s Paris, Imperial Prince’s baptism, senatus-consult on the regency.
Agiotage and sudden swings of the public funds after government, municipal, and railway borrowings; Emperor’s moralising letters to Ponsard and Oscar de Vallée; Bank of France discount at 6 per cent; poor cereal harvest; monetary and food crisis; rent crisis in rebuilt Paris. Haussmann takes the prefecture of the Seine (from July 1854 appointment narrative); floods and the Emperor’s tour of inundated departments; “Paris césarien”; foreign princes; baptism of the Prince imperial and the golden rose for the Empress. Political situation of the Senate; Moniteur warning; opposition to the carriage tax; presentation and lively discussion of the organic senatus-consult on the regency (8 July 1856); oath of regency and La Valette’s failed amendment to bind the regent to the Concordat and liberty of cults; unanimous adoption.
Chapitre II — Le parti républicain (1852–1857)
Repression after the coup, prisons and pontons, plots and attentats, moral state of the party.
2 December 1851 as a blow not only to liberty but to workers’ associations (Castors, fraternal societies, sociétaire butcheries and bakeries dissolved across the departments). Approximate scale of arrests and mixed commissions; departmental prisons, internments, transportation to Algeria, pontons (Canada, Duguesclin), Cayenne; impossibility of a complete statistical account. Deaths and funerals of Armand Marrast and Lamennais under police constraint. Conspiracies and scares: Reine-Blanche, Marseille infernal machine, Hippodrome and Opéra-Comique plots; Pianori’s attentat, trial, and execution; Bellemare; Guinard; Pérenches; Angers échauffourée; Marianne; further departmental arrests. Moral condition of the republican party under the Empire.
Chapitre III — La légitimité — L’orléanisme (c. 1850–1857)
Legitimist organisation around the comte de Chambord, Orleanist politics, fusion, and decline of pure royalism.
Wiesbaden manifesto; Chambord’s mandatories (Lévis, Des Cars, Pastoret, Saint-Priest, Berryer); majority rally to the Empire and defections (La Rochejacquelein, Mouchy, Pastoret). Government measures against legitimist correspondents; arrests and the Correspondants trial; Vincennes plot; Ligue fédérale; Jockey-Club and legitimacy; Chambord and the Crédit foncier; legitimists and Russia. Orleanism versus legitimacy; stathoudérat idea; Bulletin français trial at Brussels; decrees of 24 January at the Conseil d’État; Bocher trial; origins of fusion; Chambord–Nemours interview at Vienna; death of the last “Louis XVII”; Bonapartist pamphlets and Troplong against fusion.
Chapitre IV — Le journalisme (1851–1857)
Press law after the coup, authorised papers, government and opposition organs, clerical and light press.
Public opinion and the French press compared with the English; cheap press, advertising, Girardin’s reforms, Duveyrier’s régie générale des annonces, the roman-feuilleton. Press the day after the coup; new legislation; precautions against French and foreign papers; authorised list. Government papers: Mirès buys the Constitutionnel (Morny and Véron’s share at 1,200,000 francs); Arthur de La Guéronnière at Constitutionnel and Pays; Delamarre and La Patrie. Opposition: Havin and Le Siècle; Journal des Débats (Bertin, Saint-Marc Girardin, de Sacy); Assemblée nationale; Lourdoueix and the Gazette de France; Laurentie and L’Union; Veuillot and L’Univers. Girardin under the administrative regime; Villemessant’s Figaro; chronicle and clerical press.
Chapitre V — Le clergé (1848–1857)
Church and Empire, Sibour, classical studies quarrel, Concordat politics, Immaculate Conception.
Religious quarrels reborn with the Empire; July Monarchy and February Revolution vis-à-vis the Church; Falloux-era public instruction law; congregations working for the imperial foundation; Sibour as archbishop of Paris; alliance of philosophy and religion; fête des Écoles. Classical studies dispute between L’Univers and the archbishop; part of the episcopate for Veuillot; encyclical of 21 March 1853; defeat of the archbishop of Paris. Conditions the Pope attaches to any journey for Napoleon III’s sacre; surveillance of the pulpit; Lacordaire at Saint-Roch; liberal Catholics and ultramontanes; proclamation of the Immaculate Conception.
Chapitre VI — L’Académie — L’Université — La littérature (1850–1857)
Academic politics, Fortoul’s university reform, literary ralliés.
Opposition and parties inside the Academy; receptions of Montalembert, Musset, Dupanloup; moral prize split between Père Gratry and Jules Simon; Berryer’s refusal of the traditional visit to the Emperor (correspondence with Mocquard); secret sittings; Broglie; Laboremus; de Sacy; deaths of Molé; Falloux; Guizot’s influence; new class of the Academy of moral and political sciences by decree; reform decree. Salons. Fortoul as minister of public instruction; university reform; Dumas replaces Thiers as vice-president of the Conseil général de l’instruction publique; suppression of philosophy teaching in the lycées; bifurcation; death of Fortoul. Literature: few writers rally to the Empire — Sainte-Beuve, Mérimée, Théophile Gautier among those named.
Chapitre VII — 1857
Sibour’s murder, last legislature of 1852–57, elections, deaths of Béranger and Cavaignac.
Opening of 1857 marked by the assassination of Archbishop Sibour by the interdicted priest Verger; trial and execution. Last session of the 1852–57 legislature: free trade versus protection; 100,000-franc dotation to Marshal Pélissier; military code revision and rejection of attenuating circumstances; renewal of the Bank of France privilege (Devinck, Königswarter); transatlantic mail steamers; great works of Paris; tax on immovable property; Grand-Central; purchase of Longwood. Elections; death of Béranger; inauguration of the Louvre; death of General Cavaignac; opening of the new session, verification of powers, contested elections, Migeon affair; close of 1857.
Chapitre VIII — 1858 (Attentat d’Orsini)
14 January bombs, trial, letters to the Emperor, execution.
New Year diplomatic reception at the Tuileries; nuncio’s speech and the Emperor’s reply; general calm before the blow. Orsini’s antecedents and English sojourn; search for accomplices; bomb manufacture; Orsini and Pieri in Paris; police failures; date fixed for 14 January; Pieri’s arrest on the rue Le Peletier sidewalk does not alter ordinary precautions. Triple explosion; Emperor, Empress, General Roguet; the Emperor at the Opéra; mood of the boulevards; return to the Tuileries; arrests. Trial of Orsini and accomplices; Orsini’s letter to the Emperor; whether pardon was ever seriously considered; testament and last letter; execution.
Chapitre IX — 1858 (After Orsini)
Loi de sûreté générale, Espinasse, partial Paris elections, Montalembert trial.
Government attitude after the attentat; suppression of the Revue de Paris and the Spectateur; great military commands; Empress designated regent; privy council; colonels’ addresses; threats toward England; Milner-Gibson motion and Palmerston’s resignation. Discussion of the general security law in the Corps législatif; General Espinasse minister of the interior and general security; transportations of 1858. Partial Paris elections: Jules Favre, Ernest Picard, Perrot. Rest of the session: military exemption law, budget, nobility law, Paris works; renewal of conseils généraux; circular on charities that helps bring Espinasse down; Delangle succeeds; Prince Napoléon minister of Algeria and the colonies; Cherbourg visit; Montalembert trial; death of the duchess of Orléans.
Chapitre X — Commencement de la guerre d’Italie (1859)
Plombières to Magenta and the entry into Milan.
Moral situation of the Empire and the need to “do something”; hesitation between Poland and Italy; choice of the Italian war. Sardinia and Italy; Cavour summoned to Plombières; 1 January reception; marriage of Prince Napoléon to the princess of Savoy; opening speech of the legislative session; how Paris and France learn that war is likely; Corps législatif debate (Brame, Picard). Italian situation: duchies, Naples, muratism. Government efforts to soothe opinion (Moniteur note, Congress talk); Cavour’s alarms; military preparations; public opinion; Empress declared regent; Austrian ultimatum; Emperor’s departure for the army. First operations: Montebello, Palestro, Turbigo; battle of Magenta; French entry into Milan.
Chapitre XI — 1859 (Solferino, Villafranca, Zurich)
From the Mincio to the preliminaries of peace and the Italian settlement.
Austrian retreat behind the Mincio; field works at Melegnano; combat and taking of Melegnano; French uncertainty and Godard’s balloon ascent; the Austrian emperor takes command; unexpected meeting of the armies; village of Solferino; battle of Solferino. Interview of Villafranca; Cavour at headquarters and his resignation; Emperor’s return to Paris and speech to the great bodies of state; Treaty of Zurich; Italy and the papacy.
Chapitre XII — Les proscrits (1848–1859)
Exile communities and the amnesty of 13 August 1859.
Refugees of 1848–49; proscription in Belgium (rigour of the Belgian government, daily life); England 1848–59 (La Voix du Proscrit, le Proscrit); societies after 1851 (Commune révolutionnaire, la Révolution); Barthélemy–Cournet duel; expulsion from Jersey; proscrits in Switzerland, Italy, Spain. Partial amnesties; decree of amnesty of 13 August 1859; debate whether proscrits should accept; return of the exiles. Chapter frame: an Empire victorious in two campaigns and aiming at European autocracy cannot appear to tremble before a handful of republicans — hence the political necessity of amnesty.
Chapitre XIII — Politique intérieure (1859–1860)
After the Italian war: press amnesty, cabinets, commercial treaty programme, Rome, “faiblesse de l’Empire dictatorial.”
Addresses of the conseils généraux (22 August) congratulating a war they had disapproved; press amnesty; Moroccan expedition; creation of L’Opinion nationale; embarrassments of imperial policy in Italy; China expedition; Billault replaces the duke of Padoue at the interior; signature and uselessness of the Treaty of Zurich; close of 1859. Thouvenel succeeds Walewski at Foreign Affairs (4 January 1860); interior embarrassments; programme of 5 January; commercial treaty; legislative session and contested elections (de Ferrière, de Dalmas); Italian affairs debate; Emperor’s letter to the Pope; encyclical of 19 January; Lacordaire at the French Academy; Thouvenel dispatch; Siècle suit against the bishop of Orléans; Lamoricière commander of the papal army; white cockade in Rome. Closing meditation on the weakness of the dictatorial Empire: youth and the schools hostile to the regime of 2 December; Corps législatif impatient of a role limited to sanctioning ministerial texts; the antithesis of Italian liberty restored by a government that suppresses liberty in France; the exhausted Empire asks where it will find the force to prolong its existence — answer deferred to the following volume.
Notes
Series: Histoire du second empire (1848–1869) by Taxile Delord; multi-tome Baillière set (imprints 1869–75 in the AA bundle metadata). This raw file is tome II only (1870 title-page). Tome V (1874; 1867–1869) is in the 1866–1919 wiki. Tomes I, III, IV, and VI+ are not yet extracted into this wiki corpus. Placement: Rest of Europe 1800–1865 wiki — bulk of the volume is 1851–1860 authoritarian Empire; Italian war and early 1860 close the book. Later Delord tomes (Tome V) sit in 1866–1919. Voice: Contemporary republican narrative history; represent what Delord states, without modern scholarly reframing. Related in corpus: Ollivier L’Empire libéral tomes V and VII (participant memoir-history covering later imperial years) sit under the same French Second Empire shelf in this wiki; Tome V Delord continues the series into 1867–69 beside Ollivier XI and Sybel VII in the later wiki.

sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t3.title: Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome III
sources/delord-histoire-second-empire-t3.content:
Delord — Histoire illustrée du second empire, Tome III
Taxile Delord (1815–1877) — Histoire illustrée du second empire. — Tome troisième. — Nouvelle édition. — Paris: Librairie Germer Baillière et Cie, 108, boulevard Saint-Germain, 1880 (printer: Coulommiers, Typographie Paul Brodard). 72 gravures dans le texte; 17 têtes de chapitre ou culs-de-lampe.
Republican journalist and deputy (Siècle), Delord writes a contemporary opposition history of the Second Empire as a continuous narrative, not memoir. This is the illustrated edition (Baillière [1880–83]) of the same multi-tome work originally published 1869–75. The present volume opens with the legislature of 1857–1863 (session of 1858, Orsini aftermath, law of sûreté générale) and carries the narrative through the Italian war’s later phases, the China and Syria expeditions, the Mexican expedition, the great elections of 1863, and into early 1864 (Carnot and Garnier-Pagès elected in Paris, foundation of the International, the 15 September Convention with Italy).
Core chronological span is 1857–1864 — the later authoritarian Empire, the liberal turn of the 1860 decree, the Italian unification crisis (Castelfidardo, Garibaldi’s conquest of the Two Sicilies), the Polish insurrection of 1863, the Danish question and the rise of Bismarck, and the beginnings of the Mexican adventure. The volume closes with the elections of 1863–64 and the first steps toward the liberal Empire.
OCR from local Anna’s Archive scan set (OCLC 7058591; Baillière [1880–83]). Cleaned raw keeps title-page through table of contents; internal double-spaces collapsed; front blank library leaves dropped.
Chapters
Chapitre I — Législature de 1857 à 1863
Sessions of 1858–1863: verification of powers, Migeon affair, law of sûreté générale, law on titles of nobility, the Paris works, the budget commission and the Conseil d’État. Session of 1859: the 500-million loan, clericals demand guarantees, Jules Favre speaks in the Corps législatif. Brame’s proposition, the Grand Central, annexation of the banlieue. Session of 1860: contested elections, official candidacy, the commercial treaty, financial speciality, loans to industry. Session of 1861: imperial discourse to Senate and Corps législatif, Troplong’s report on the senatus-consult, Prince Napoléon’s speech, the cardinals’ amendment rejected, Dupin and the press, stamp on the roman-feuilleton. Session of 1862: address discussed in Senate (religious question, Persigny called Polignac, Rome), La Guéronnière and Prince Napoléon, Mexico. Corps législatif: thirty-year obligations, the Palikao endowment, the commercial-free-trade inquiry, income-tax proposal by Granier de Cassagnac and Roques-Salvaza. Opening of the 1863 session: Emperor’s retrospective review since 1857, Thouvenel’s speech, Billault, Darimon petition, Ollivier’s discourse, Baroche’s reply, Mexico debate (Jules Favre, Jérôme David), modification of the Penal Code.
Chapitre II — Suite de la Guerre d’Italie
January 1860 reception, the brochure Le Pape et le Congrès, the 5 January programme, the commercial treaty with England (Michel Chevalier and Richard Cobden), cession of Nice and Savoy to France, Thouvenel’s dispatch, Napoleon III’s letter to Persigny. Weakness of the dictatorial Empire.
Chapitre III — Expéditions de Chine et de Syrie
China expedition: causes, Treaty of Tien-tsin, delay in ratification, Anglo-French expedition (Lord Elgin and Baron Gros), taking of the Pei-ho forts, Pa-li-kao battle, flight of the Emperor of China to Manchuria, capture and pillage of the Summer Palace, destruction of the Summer Palace, Prince Hong-kong and General Ignatieff bring the Chinese government to sign peace, return of the army, preparations for the Cochinchina expedition. Syria expedition: the Lebanon, state of the Orient since the Sepoy revolt and the Crimean War, the massacres of the Lebanon and of Damascus, news reaches France, Napoleon III prepares to succour the Christians of Syria, diplomatic preliminaries, resistance of Turkey, difficulties raised by England and Russia, Piedmont excluded from negotiations, Fuad-Pasha at Beirut and Damascus, slowness of repression, indemnity, result of the expedition at the end of 1860.*
Chapitre IV — Castelfidardo
Impotence of the Villafranca convention. Imperial policy shifts in a sense favourable to Italy; the brochure Le Pape et le Congrès; difficulties raised by the proposal for a congress; the four propositions. Annexation of Savoy and Nice to France. Expedition to Sicily. Chambéry interview. Preparations for war; Piedmontese troops enter Pontifical territory. Battle of Castelfidardo. The kingdom of Naples and its interior situation. Attempts at alliance between Naples and Piedmont. Garibaldi crosses the strait. Conquest of the Two Sicilies by Garibaldi. Victor-Emmanuel enters Naples. Francis II at Gaeta, his capitulation and retreat to Rome.
Chapitre V — 1860–1861
The decree of 24 November; its causes. 1 January reception at the Tuileries. Application of the decentralization decree to the city of Paris. Rumours of dissolution of the Corps législatif. Rivalry of Persigny and Haussmann. Reception of Father Lacordaire at the French Academy; the Empress attends. Arrest of financier Mirès; Delangle’s report. The duc d’Aumale’s brochure: Lettre sur l’histoire de France. Seizure of the duc de Broglie’s Vues sur le gouvernement de la France. The Blanqui trial. Inauguration of the boulevard Malesherbes. The 25 millions for chemins vicinaux. Transformation of Paris. Industrial and financial crisis. The thirty-year obligations. Fould’s memoir addressed to the Emperor. Stockbrokers seek authorization for a statue of the Emperor. The Plassiart trial.
Chapitre VI — La Question des Duchés
Illness of the king of Prussia; the heir presumptive assumes the regency. Napoleon III and the regent of Prussia at Baden. Bismarck named Prussian ambassador at St Petersburg. Accession of Wilhelm I. Army reform. Awakening of unitary spirit. The Backer attentat and its influence on the king. Coronation of the king of Prussia. The principle of nationalities and the question of the Duchies. Effect of the February Revolution on Germany. The campaign of the free corps. London conference. The Danish question subsides but the regent of Prussia revives it in 1859. Denmark counts on France and England. State of Poland. Troubles at Warsaw. Address to the Emperor. Dissolution of the agricultural society. Death of Prince Adam Czartoriski. England, Austria, Prussia, France and the insurrection; discourse of Prince Napoléon.
Chapitre VII — Mort de Cavour
Rome declared capital of Italy. Cavour’s illness and death. Italy recognized by Napoleon III. Ricasoli succeeds Cavour. United States: the slavery question, election of Lincoln, the War of Secession. End of the Syria expedition and its results.
Chapitre VIII — L’Année 1862
1 January reception at the Tuileries. Fould’s financial programme. Trials and arrests. Société du Prince impérial. Imperial letter on the Roman question. Imperial voyage through central France. Morny created duke. Reversal of imperial policy on the Roman question: Thouvenel resigns, Drouyn de Lhuys replaces him. Napoleon III and mediation in the United States. Prohibition of the rue de la Paix conferences. Polemic over Le Fils de Giboyer. Inauguration of the boulevard du Prince-Eugène. Budberg, Russian ambassador, presents credentials. Imperial discourse. Subscription for cotton workers. Revival of the title of chevalier.
Chapitre IX — La Presse et le Clergé (1860–1862)
Expulsion of Ganesco (editor of the Courrier du dimanche). Difficulty over the reporting of judicial debates. Obscurity of the senatus-consult. Leymarie’s attempts to buy the Courrier de Paris; Billault and d’Haussonville. Hippolyte Castille as editor-in-chief; replaced by Clément Duvernois. Persigny and the press. Masson’s brochure finds no printer. Les Muses d’État. Laprade removed. Millaud buys La Presse; mass resignation of editors. The clergy and King Jérôme. Mandements and funeral ceremonies. La France, Rome et l’Italie by La Guéronnière. Bishop of Poitiers deféré as d’abus to the Conseil d’État. Religious proselytism; Lille trial. The Société de Saint-Vincent de Paul: the government and the society; Persigny’s circular; Rouland’s circular. Suppression of religious houses. Renan named to the Hebrew chair at the Collège de France; his destitution. The jubilee of Toulouse.
Chapitre X — Expédition du Mexique (1858–1861)
Mexico under Spanish domination; the war of independence; Iturbide’s empire and its fall. Effect of pronunciamentos. Formation of the liberal party; Mexico and Santa Anna; triumph of the liberal party; Juarez presidency. Struggle between the liberal party and the clerical party. The Jecker loan. The Mexican republic and the European powers. The monarchical Mexican party abroad; it surrounds the Emperor and Empress; Morny’s support. The Jecker bonds. Dubois de Saligny replaces Gabriac; he begins with the Jecker claim. Juarez forced to suspend customs payments. Spain, England, and France. The United States.
Chapitre XI — Les Français au Mexique
Diplomatic negotiations; the London convention. The Spanish arrive before the English and French at Mexico; they occupy Vera-Cruz. Preliminaries of La Soledad. Manifesto of the allied commissioners; their rupture. Conference of Orizaba; the conference separates. Denunciation of the rupture. Attack on Orizaba by General Lorencez. Pronunciamento of the city in favour of Almonte. March on Puebla; French army repulsed. Period Lorencez; reinforcements sent. General Forey replaces Lorencez. Public opinion and Mexico at the end of 1862.
Chapitre XII — Les Élections dans les Départements
Early 1863; the cotton crisis. Distribution of rewards to French exhibitors at London. Prohibition of public readings for the benefit of workers of the Seine-Inférieure. Seizure of the Histoire de la maison de Condé. Moniteur note on parliamentary reporting. Academy election: Bishop Dupanloup and Littré. The 1863 elections in the departments. Garnier-Pagès’s tour. State of opinion in the great cities. Thiers’s candidacy; the oath question. The Union libérale. The Catholic party. Legitimism and Orleanism. Official candidacy. Result of the departmental elections.
Chapitre XIII — Les Élections à Paris
Republican party in Paris; its divisions; abstention; the party of the Siècle; the party of 1848; the party of new men; the party of the Cinq. Rivalries between candidates in the 5th circonscription; Havin and Ernest Picard. The central committee; Carnot’s meeting; failure to found a central committee. Government opposition to meetings. Moniteur note. Thiers’s candidacy; the Siècle does not accept it. First opposition list: Havin, Laboulaye, Ollivier, Ernest Picard, Jules Favre, Guéroult, Darimon, Jules Simon, Pelletan. Laboulaye withdraws in favour of Thiers. The Siècle decides to support Thiers. Persigny’s maladroitness in combating the candidacy; his circular to prefects; his letter to the prefect of the Seine. Paris elects the entire opposition list. Effect of the 31 May vote on Europe. Persigny forced to resign. Ministerial change. Billault minister of state; his death; Rouher replaces him. Empress’s voyage to Spain. Napoleon III proposes a congress to the powers; 300-million loan; congress aborted. End of 1863.
Chapitre XIV — Le Nouveau Cabinet
Persigny forced to resign. A new ministry forms: Billault, Boudet, Duruy, Behic, Rouher. Morny’s letter. Billault’s death; difficulty finding his successor; two possible men: Rouher and Baroche. Rouher: his beginnings, Minister of the President under the coup d’état, resignation as garde des sceaux over the 22 January decrees, president of section at the Conseil d’État, entry into the cabinet in 1855 as minister of agriculture, commerce and public works; replaces Billault at the ministry of state.
Chapitre XV — Napoléon III et l’Europe
Polish affairs. Grand Duke Constantine named viceroy of Poland. Attempts on Wielopolski and the Grand Duke. The Polish insurrection; repression by Mouraview; the cabinets of the Tuileries, London, and Vienna. Negotiations with Russia; Prince Gortschakoff ends them cavalierly. The princes’ day at Frankfurt. Influence on the Polish question and the Danish question. Denmark’s situation in 1862. The Gotha dispatch. Concessions of Christian VIII; Prussia and Austria reject them. Imprudence of passages in the Emperor’s opening speeches. Congress rendered impossible by England. Bismarck and England. The European concert and Denmark. Dismemberment of the Danish monarchy. Treaty of Vienna.
Chapitre XVI — Maximilien au Mexique
Siege of Puebla. Combat of San-Lorenzo. French entry into Mexico City. The triumvirate. Convocation of a constituent assembly. A deputation carries the offer of the crown to Maximilian. The council of regency. Establishment of martial courts; the contre-guérilla; military and administrative cruelties. Marshal Forey replaced by General Bazaine; Dubois de Saligny by Montholon. Arrival of the Mexican deputation at Miramar. Maximilian’s hesitations. Napoleon III’s impatience; he summons Maximilian and his wife to Paris; convention of 12 March. Further hesitations. Voyage of General Frossard to Miramar. The Archduchess Charlotte at Vienna. Treaty of Miramar; its three secret articles. Maximilian and Charlotte depart for Mexico; they stop at Rome. Arrival at Vera-Cruz; general indifference. Journey from Vera-Cruz to Mexico. Official reception. Installation of the imperial household.
Chapitre XVII — L’Année 1864
Beginning of 1864. Receptions at the Tuileries. Arrest of four Italians. Partial elections at Paris. Committee of electoral reform. Candidacies in the 1st circonscription (Pasquet, Carnot, Laboulaye, Pinard); in the 5th circonscription (Garnier-Pagès, Bancel, Bac, Renan, Vautrain, Hugelmann, Morin, Alix, Jules Ferry). Tolain, worker’s candidate. Carnot and Garnier-Pagès elected. Prohibition of public readings for the benefit of the Poles. Prohibition of the banquet in honour of Shakespeare. Dufaure received at the French Academy. Trial of the Thirteen. Foundation of the International Workingmen’s Association. Convention of 15 September. Vuitry minister presiding the Conseil d’État. Persigny’s letter to Girardin; the government rebukes it. Encyclopaedia of 8 December. Voltaire’s heart at the Bibliothèque nationale. Prince Napoléon vice-president of the privy council.
Notes
Series: Histoire illustrée du second empire by Taxile Delord; this is the Tome troisième of the illustrated edition (Baillière [1880–83]), corresponding to the third volume of the original 1869–75 Baillière set (OCLC 6266334). Tome II of the original edition is in this wiki; Tome IV and Tome V sit in the 1866–1919 wiki. Placement: Rest of Europe 1800–1865 wiki — the volume covers 1857–1864, from the later authoritarian Empire through the liberal turn and the Italian, Chinese, Syrian, and Mexican expeditions. The later 1865–1867 period (Sadowa, end of the Mexican expedition) is covered by Tome IV and Tome V in the 1866–1919 wiki. Voice: Contemporary republican narrative history; represent what Delord states, without modern scholarly reframing. Illustrations: 72 wood engravings in the text plus 17 decorative headpieces and tailpieces (not preserved in this raw OCR).
Related in corpus: Ollivier L’Empire libéral tomes V and VII (participant memoir-history of later imperial years) sit under the same French Second Empire shelf in this wiki. Raw: delord-histoire-second-empire-t3.txt.

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome I
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome I
Prosper Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome premier (“First Volume”). — Second edition. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, rue Vivienne, 2 bis, et boulevard des Italiens, 15 (Librairie Nouvelle), 1870. — 640 files, 24,450 lines (~1.34 MB in the cleaned raw).
Duvergier de Hauranne, an Orléanist deputy and member of the Tiers Parti (“Third Party”) under the July Monarchy (académicien, 1871), writes a doctrinal history of the parliamentary regime in France centred on the constitutional practice of 1814–1848. This tome premier (“first volume”) covers the revolutionary origins of representation (in the Introduction) and then the first parliamentary episode in French history — the Restauration de 1814 et les Cent-Jours (“the Restoration of 1814 and the Hundred Days”) — ending on the eve of the Second Restoration. The sequel (1815–1848) occupies the later volumes.
The Préface (“preface”) is a manifesto for the strict definition of parliamentary government — that in which “the last word belongs to parliament, that is to say the nation” — against the prevailing confusion between “representative government” (mere form) and “parliamentary government” (substance). Duvergier claims thirty-four years of existence for this regime in France, and maintains that between parliamentary and absolute government there exist only “factitious, incoherent, dangerous combinations, which lead fatally to coups d’état or insurrections.”
The Introduction (pages 1–403 of the printing, nearly half the volume) goes back as far as the États généraux (“Estates-General”) of 1789 to trace the genesis of representative institutions through the Revolution, the Directory, and the Empire — not as a retrospective teleological narrative but as the archaeology of the principles the Restoration would have to wield.
OCR from Anna’s Archive (scan of a Harvard College Library copy, Widener; shelfmark Fr 1632.8.2). Cleaned raws: internal double-spacings collapsed; flyleaves and library stamps discarded.
Introduction
Chapter I — Opening of the Estates-General
Reply to the detractors of the Constituent Assembly. The old French constitution. Cahiers (grievance-books) of the three orders. Intentions and conduct of King Louis XVI. The declaration of 23 June. Revolution of 14 July. State of opinions and parties in the Assembly. Theory of the division of powers. Sieyès, Mounier, Mirabeau.
Chapter II — 1789-1791
First constitutional committee. Declaration of Rights. Reports of Lally-Tollendal and Mounier. Question of the two Chambers. Question of the royal veto. Fundamental error of the Constituent Assembly. Nomination and recall of ministers. Incompatibility of ministerial with legislative functions. Organisation of the Corps législatif (Legislative Body). Right to elect and to be elected. Departmental and municipal organisation. Judicial organisation. Maintenance of public order. Right of peace and war. Individual liberties and guarantees.
Chapter III — 1791
State of minds. Clubs and newspapers. Mirabeau. The non-re-eligible members of the Assembly. Speeches of Duport and Cazalès. Flight and arrest of the king. New situation. Schism in the Jacobin club. Barnave and Robespierre. Conduct of the Right. Revision and acceptance of the constitution. End of the Constituent Assembly.
Chapter IV — Legislative Assembly — 1791-1792
Situation. Influence of the vices of the Constitution on events. Difficulty of forming a ministry. First applications of the suspensive veto. Narbonne ministry and Girondin ministry. Disposition of the public force. 20 June and 10 August. Imprisonment of the king and enslavement of the Legislative Assembly.
Chapter V — National Convention — 1792-1794
Proclamation of the Republic. Struggle of parties. Report of Condorcet. Declaration of Rights. Girondin constitution. Montagnard constitution. Robespierre. Constitutional theory of Saint-Just. Discussion of the Girondin constitution interrupted by 31 May. Report of Hérault-Séchelles. Vote, proclamation, and suspension of the Montagnard constitution. Organisation of the revolutionary government. The Terror. Robespierre and Saint-Just. Revolution of 9 Thermidor.
Chapter VI — 1794-1795
New constitutional committee. Reports of Boissy-d’Anglas and Daunou. Thibaudeau. Discussion. Plan of Sieyès and complete failure of that plan. Constitution of Year III. Decrees keeping two-thirds of the Convention’s members in the new Corps législatif. Insurrection of 13 Vendémiaire. Consequences of that insurrection. Nomination of the Directory and end of the Convention.
Chapter VII — 1795-1799
Origin of the conflict between the Directory and the Councils. Conduct of the Directory on the occasion of the conspiracies of Babeuf and Brothier. Elections of Year V. Shift of the majority. Conventionnel party. Clichy party. Constitutional party. Division in the Directory. Open struggle between the Directory’s majority and the Councils’ majority. Coup d’État of 18 Fructidor. Suspension of all liberties. Decrees of deportation. Carnot and Sieyès. Elections of Year VI. New coup d’état. Awakening of public opinion. Elections of Year VIII. Coalition against the Directory. Nomination of Sieyès. Projects and speeches of Sieyès.
Chapter VIII — 1799-1804
Constitution of Year VIII. Sieyès and Bonaparte. Destruction of the parliamentary institutions. Administrative centralisation. Opposition of the Tribunat and the Corps législatif. Complaisance of the Senate. Infernal machine. Deportation of one hundred and thirty-two suspects. Lists of notability. Consulate for life. Purge of the Tribunat and the Corps législatif. Sénatus-consulte (decree of the Senate) of Year X. Electoral colleges. Individual liberty and liberty of the press. Conspiracy of Georges Cadoudal. Projects of the First Consul. Sénatus-consulte of Year XII. The Empire.
Chapter IX — 1804-1813
Omnipotence of the emperor. Sénatus-consultes substituted for laws. Special tribunals. Suppression of the Tribunat. Organisation of the imperial nobility. Re-establishment of majorats and substitutions. Decree on state prisons. Decree on the press. Confiscations and attacks on property. Council of 1811 and imprisonment of three bishops. Taxes levied without the Corps législatif’s concurrence. Malet conspiracy. Nullification of a criminal judgment. Conclusion.
Main text — 1814-1815
Chapter I — End of the Empire — 1813-1814

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome X
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome dixième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1871. — Final volume of the series, from the Polignac ministry through the July Revolution.
This tenth volume covers 1829–1830. It opens with the Polignac cabinet confronting the chambers, follows the conflict of the bishops and Rome, the address of the 221, the dissolution and elections of 1830, the Four Ordinances of July, the Three Glorious Days, the fall of Charles X, and the advent of Louis-Philippe. Duvergier writes as a participant-observer of the parliamentary school: the Revolution of 1830 is for him the forced execution of the Charte (“Charter”) against a king who tried to empty it by article 14. The volume is both chronicle and civic lesson.
OCR from a major library scan. Raw cleaned (~1.45 Mo).
Chapter XLII — The Bishops and the Court of Rome (1828–1829)
Resistance of the bishops and their protest place the Martignac and early Polignac governments in embarrassment. M. Lassagni is sent to Rome; Cottu writes against the electoral law. The king’s journey in eastern France; Lassagni’s success; fury of Royalist journals; submission of the bishops. The Morea expedition and public impatience in the departments show liberal discontent with a foreign policy that seems glorious yet irrelevant to domestic liberty. A ministerial memoir to the king at first has no result. Newspaper polemics intensify; dismissals; trials of the Gazette de France and of Béranger. The conflict with the bishops ends; Netherlands affairs and the Belgian Catholic-liberal coalition; Don Miguel proclaimed in Portugal; Russian setbacks in the East; Greek affairs. Chateaubriand at Rome. Illness of de la Ferronnays; Polignac called to Paris by the king; he fails to find colleagues at first. Portalis interim at Foreign Affairs. Situation of parties on the eve of the session; convocation of the chambers; discussion of municipal and departmental laws; rumours. Duvergier uses the Roman and episcopal crisis to show that even the clergy cannot be governed by pure court will without negotiation — a lesson Charles X will not apply to the political chambers.
Chapter XLIII — The Session and the Address of the 221 (1830)
The session opens under Polignac. The king’s speech asserts royal prerogative; the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”) answers with the famous address of the 221 deputies declaring that the ministry does not have the confidence of the nation. Royer-Collard, as president, embodies Doctrinaire gravity; Guizot, Thiers’s friends in the press, and the left liberals unite on the constitutional point: the king reigns but the ministry must answer to the chamber. Charles X receives the address coldly and dissolves. Duvergier analyses article 14 of the Charter — the disputed clause on ordinances for the security of the state — as the legal battlefield. Public meetings, electoral committees, and the association for refusal of taxes prepare the country for a struggle that is still, in liberal minds, legal and parliamentary rather than revolutionary.
Chapter XLIV — The Elections of 1830
Dissolution sends the country to the polls under the double vote and septennial rules still in force. The campaign is a referendum on Polignac. Liberal organisation in Paris and the provinces, the role of the National (Thiers, Mignet, Carrel), and Ultra efforts through prefects and clergy fill Duvergier’s pages. The result is a reinforced opposition: the 221 return stronger. The king and Polignac refuse the plain meaning of the vote. Military expeditions (Algiers) are used to distract opinion; Duvergier notes the capture of Algiers as a colonial success that cannot save a domestic coup. The court prepares extraordinary measures while still speaking the language of the Charter.
Chapter XLV — The Address and the Ordinances (July 1830)
After the elections the ministry reports to the king. Confidence of the ministers contrasts with the agitation of journalists. Meetings at Dupin’s and in the offices of the National prepare resistance. The Four Ordinances of 25 July 1830 suspend freedom of the press, dissolve the new chamber before it meets, alter the electoral law without the chambers, and convoke a rump electorate — a coup d’État (“coup d’état”) in the form of ordinances. Publication and the report to the king; journalists’ protest drafted in legal terms; printers and deputies hesitate then stiffen. Duvergier insists on the lawyers’ and journalists’ first response: not yet revolution, but refusal to obey illegal ordinances.
Chapter XLVI — The July Revolution (1830)
Street fighting of the Trois Glorieuses (“Three Glorious Days”) — 27, 28, 29 July — transforms legal resistance into insurrection. Barricades, the tricolour, defections in the line, the hesitation of Marmont, the poltroonery or panic of parts of the court, the courage of polytechnicians and workers fill the narrative. Charles X withdraws ordinances too late, then abdicates in favour of the child duc de Bordeaux with the duc d’Angoulême’s renunciation — a combination Paris will not accept. The Hôtel de Ville (“City Hall”), Lafayette, the duc d’Orléans as lieutenant-general, and the revision of the Charter into the Charter of 1830 close the Restoration. Duvergier’s final judgment is parliamentary: a king who dissolves the contract cannot appeal to its letter; the July monarchy inherits the task of making ministerial responsibility real. The ten-volume history ends where a new experiment in parliamentary government begins.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Tome 10 closes or crowns the same series’ later July Monarchy span—treat as sibling to t9 for endgame ministries and the fall.
End of the Charter world
Ministerial last reshuffles, opposition convergence, and the collapse sequence as Duvergier preserves debates and public acts.
Method
Duvergier is denser in parliamentary paper than Delord; prefer him for quotations of chamber language, Delord for Empire narrative prose.
Compilation rules for this file

Enlarge entities only with facts present in the matching raw deposit for this source.
Keep contemporary vocabulary; gloss DE/FR/IT/HU/RU on first emphasis.
Prefer linking existing E/E/C pages over creating micro-duplicates.
If a chapter summary here outruns what raw OCR can verify on a point, cut the claim rather than pad.

Scope: Polignac ministry; bishops and Rome; address of the 221; elections of 1830; Four Ordinances; Three Glorious Days; accession of Louis-Philippe. Notable figures: Polignac, Charles X, Royer-Collard, Guizot, Thiers, Carrel, Lafayette, Louis-Philippe, Marmont, Dupin.
Placement: Rest of Europe 1800-1865; climax of the Restoration. Corpus: Tenth of ten; chapters XLII–XLVI. Raw: duvergier-gouvernement-parlementaire-t10.txt.

Duvergier de Hauranne, an Orléanist deputy and member of the Tiers Parti (“Third Party”) under the July Monarchy (académicien, 1871), writes a doctrinal history of the parliamentary regime in France centred on the constitutional practice of 1814–1848. This tome deuxième (“second volume”) covers the Première Restauration et les Cent-Jours (“the First Restoration and the Hundred Days,” 1814–1815) — exactly the same period as the main body of Tome I (2nd edition, 1870), but in the first edition (1857).
The volume is divided into eight chapters forming a continuous narrative sequence from the fall of the Empire (end of 1813) to the last intrigues of Ghent and Paris on the eve of Waterloo (June 1815). The material is identical to that of Chapters I–VIII of Tome I (2nd ed.), but without the retrospective Introduction (1789–1813) that occupies nearly half of the first volume.

Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome III
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome troisième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, libraires-éditeurs, rue Vivienne, 2 bis, 1859 (droits de reproduction et de traduction réservés). — 570 fichiers, 21,054 lignes (~1.18 Mo en brut nettoyé).
This third volume of Duvergier de Hauranne’s parliamentary history of France opens with an Avertissement (Preface) in which the author acknowledges the warm reception given to the first two volumes and explains the delay in publication. He benefited from new communications, notably the papers of Élie Decazes made available through M. Forgues, which shed light on the pivotal ministries in which Decazes was the most influential member. The preface closes with the author’s intention to cover the legislative sessions of 1816, 1817 and 1818 in the next volume.
The volume covers the period from the Chamber of Representatives of the Hundred Days through the dissolution of the Chambre introuvable by the Ordonnance of 5 September 1816 — a crucial phase in which the nature of the Restoration regime was determined.
OCR from Anna’s Archive (scan of a copy held by the Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Facultad de Derecho; shelfmark presumably from the Complutense collections). Raw text cleaned: internal double-spaces collapsed; library plates and blank pages discarded.

Napoleon’s departure. Reports from the ministers of the interior, foreign affairs and police. The Leguevel proposal. Motion by MM. Dupin and Mourgues. Appointment of a commission to revise the imperial constitutions. Napoleon’s precipitate return after the Battle of Waterloo. General consternation and calls for abdication. Suspension of individual liberty. Napoleon’s departure for Malmaison. Probable aims of Fouché.
Chapter X — The Second Restoration (1815)
State of opinion at Ghent. Mons and Cambrai. The comte d’Artois and Talleyrand. The Proclamation of Cambrai. French plenipotentiaries at Laon and Haguenau. Unfortunate misunderstanding. Wellington and Blücher. Fouché’s intrigues. Vitrolles and Marshal Davout. Proposal to recall Louis XVIII. Grand council of government. Adjournment. Napoleon at Malmaison. Fouché’s secret negotiation with the Duke of Wellington. False hopes of the Chamber of Representatives. Constitutional act. Address to the army. Letter from Marshal Davout. Napoleon offers to lead the army; refusal. Napoleon’s departure for Rochefort. Vitrolles’s mission to Davout’s headquarters. Violent scene. Fouché imperturbable. Disquiet and mistrust of the Chamber of Representatives. Brochure by Malleville. Address to the French people. Exasperation of the army. Indifference of the population. Interview of the French commissioners with Wellington. Grand council of war. Capitulation of Paris. Louis XVIII at Roye and Saint-Denis. Fouché’s interview with Wellington. Fouché becomes minister of Louis XVIII. Declaration of principles by the Chamber of Representatives. Resignation of the executive commission. Entry of the Allies into Paris. Dissolution of both Chambers. Entry of Louis XVIII into Paris. Napoleon’s embarkation at Rochefort.
Chapter XI — The First Ministry (1815)
Formation of the ministry. Summoning of a new Chamber. Articles of the Charter submitted for revision. The Chamber of Peers. External and internal difficulties. Conduct of the foreign armies in Paris and the departments. Looting of the Musée. Plans for the dismemberment of France. Disbanding of the army. Violent royalist reaction. Massacres and terror in the Midi. Anarchy in the West. Ordinance of 24 July. Proscription lists. The king’s proclamation against the assassins of the Midi. Royalist pamphlets and newspapers. Elections. Triumph of the Ultra-Royalists. Fouché’s reports. His forced resignation. Ultimatum of the foreign powers. Talleyrand’s resignation accepted by Louis XVIII. Fouché’s departure. Formation of the new ministry: the duc de Richelieu and Decazes. Minor concessions made to the duc de Richelieu. Signature of the new peace treaty. Opinion of England on this treaty.
Chapter XII — The Chambre introuvable (1815)
Opening of the session. The king’s speech and addresses from both Chambers. First parliamentary sittings. Law of general security (loi de sûreté générale). Law on seditious cries (loi des cris séditieux). Discussion and adoption of these two laws. Law of provost courts (loi des cours prévôtales). Proposal against the irremovability of the magistrature. Speech by Royer-Collard. State of opinion in France. Trial of Marshal Ney. Presentation of the amnesty law. Escape of Lavalette and anger of the Ultra-Royalist party. Corbière’s report and discussion of the amnesty law. Speeches by La Bourdonnaie, Royer-Collard and de Serre. Rejection of the proposed categories and confiscations by the commission. Banishment of the regicides. Conviction of Travot. Individual proposals. Endowment of the clergy. Civil registers. The University. Definitive constitution of the Ultra-Royalist majority. The court and the ministry. Electoral law. Villèle’s report. Question of integral renewal. Principle of parliamentary government, combated by Royer-Collard, de Serre and Decazes, defended by La Bourdonnaie, Villèle and Corbière. Defeat of the ministry. Budget. Question of the arrears and the clergy’s woodlands. Capitulation of the ministry. Anxieties of foreign diplomacy; letter from the Duke of Wellington to the king. Rejection of the electoral law by the Chamber of Peers. New bill. Violent rupture between the ministry and the majority. Garnier’s report on the budget. Kergorlay’s report on the clergy endowment. Speech by de Serre. Abrupt close of the session. Character of the Chamber of 1815.
Chapter XIII — The Ordinance of 5 September (1816)
(Classified as Chapter XII in the OCR but correctly numbered XIII in the Table of Contents.)
State of the parties. New political trials. The exiled Nain jaune. The duc d’Orléans and the prince of Orange. Ministerial crisis. Vaublanc replaced by Lainé. Insurrection at Grenoble. Merciless repression. Trial of the patriots of 1816. Conviction and execution of Chartran and Mouton-Duvernet. Religious missions and processions. Hopes and intrigues of the Ultra-Royalists in Paris and the departments. Preliminary steps towards the Ordinance of 5 September. Decazes and Richelieu. Intervention of the foreign powers. The king’s hesitation. Notes by Decazes, Pasquier and Guizot in favour of dissolution. Dissolution settled in principle. Secondary difficulties. Lainé’s plan. Blindness of Monsieur’s party. First secret note. New hesitations of the king and fresh efforts by Decazes. The Ordinance of 5 September. Stupefaction and anger of the Ultra-Royalists. Public joy. Monarchie selon la Charte by Chateaubriand; seizure of the book and dismissal of the author. Judgment of foreign governments and peoples on the dissolution. Electoral struggle. Embarrassment of public officials. Personal intervention of the king. Result of the elections. Situation of the ministry. Speech by Séguier. Political writings: Villemain, La Luzerne, Saint-Roman, Lourdoueix, Guizot, Sesmaisons and Montlosier.
Notes
Series: Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848; this third volume covers June–September 1815 through September 1816 (from the Hundred Days dissolution through the dissolution of the Chambre introuvable). Avertissement: The preface explains that new materials — notably the papers of Élie Decazes — allowed Duvergier to treat the Decazes ministries with greater authority. He promises forthcoming treatment of the sessions of 1816, 1817 and 1818 in the next volume. Edition: First edition (Michel Lévy Frères, Paris, 1859). Unlike Tomes I and II which are second and first editions respectively, this volume is the original 1859 printing. Scope: The volume is the first of two covering the actual Restoration (Tome I covered the Introduction through 1789-1813 and the early Restoration 1814-1815). Tome III begins with the Hundred Days Parliament (Chambre des Représentants) and ends with Louis XVIII’s dissolution of the Ultra-Royalist Chamber in September 1816 — the decisive moment when the king chose the moderate/constitutional path over Ultra reaction.
Placement: Rest of Europe 1800-1865 wiki. Chronologically the volume covers 1815-1816, entirely within the early Restoration period. Corpus: This volume sits alongside Delord (Histoire du second empire) and the other Duvergier volumes as French constitutional history sources. Duvergier writes as an Orléanist liberal — a partisan of parliamentary government in the English mode, hostile to both Ultra-Royalist reaction and Bonapartist authoritarianism. Raw: duvergier-gouvernement-parlementaire-t3.txt.
Notes on form
