sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome IV
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome IV
Prosper (Ernest) Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome quatrième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, libraires-éditeurs, rue Vivienne, 2 bis, 1860. — Raw cleaned text: ~20,099 lines (~1.15 Mo).
This fourth volume covers the parliamentary sessions of 1817 and 1818. It opens with the great debate on the electoral law that fixed the political character of the Restoration after the dissolution of the Chambre introuvable (“Undiscoverable Chamber”), and it ends with the resignation of the duc de Richelieu and the formation of the Dessoles ministry. The continuous thread is the progressive dissolution of the Royalist–Centre coalition that had governed since 1816, set against the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle, the evacuation of occupying troops, and France’s readmission to the European concert. Duvergier writes as a liberal parliamentarian of the July Monarchy looking back: he treats chamber procedure, press, budget, and ministry crises as the true history of “parliamentary government,” not as court chronicle alone.
OCR from a Harvard College Library scan. Internal double-spaces collapsed; library plates and blank pages discarded.
Chapter XIV — The Electoral Law and the Budget (1817)
The session of 1817 opens with the royal sitting and the king’s speech. Verification of powers and the addresses of the two chambers establish the balance of parties after the 1816 dissolution. The Robert petition and the situation of factions frame the principal bill of the year: the new electoral law that is to replace the exceptional regime of the Chambre introuvable. Duvergier follows the presentation, the commission’s report, the pamphlets of Fiévée, and Benjamin Constant’s intervention, then the full debate in the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”). Royer-Collard speaks for the Doctrinaires (“Doctrinaires”); Villèle and Corbière for the organised Right; de Serre for the ministry; Bonald, La Bourdonnaie, Cuvier, Beugnot, and Lainé fill successive days. Amendments fall; the measure passes to the Chambre des pairs (“Chamber of Peers”), where Molé, de Broglie, and Fitz-James speak and Lainé replies before adoption. The law fixes a high cens (“tax qualification”) and a system of colleges that the author presents as the constitutional skeleton of the next decade.
Beside the electoral statute the ministry carries public-order and press measures. The loi de sûreté générale (“law of general security”) is opposed by the Right and supported by the Centre; de Serre reports; Royer-Collard and Camille Jordan speak. Laws on newspapers and the seizure of writings revive the permanent quarrel of the Restoration: Castelbajac, Villèle, La Bourdonnaie, Corbière, and Benoist defend press liberty against Royer-Collard, Courvoisier, and Bonald; in the Peers, Chateaubriand, Fitz-James, de Broglie, and Decazes take the floor. The budget debate turns on reducing the occupation army, a loan, and Casimir Périer’s pamphlet; Roy and Beugnot report; Villèle and de Barante clash; Laffitte intervenes for the banking interest. Articles on the University, Spanish refugees, and the war and navy budgets raise the Chamber’s rights over loans and the clergy’s woodlands (Bonald against Camille Jordan). Chateaubriand’s strange Peers’ speech, a customs law, and an unvoted bill on ministerial responsibility close the session. Throughout, Duvergier stresses how budget chapters and press articles, more than court intrigue, decide whether a ministry can live.
Chapter XV — The Parties and the Government (1817)
Outside the chamber the author describes the state of opinion. The performance of Germanicus, the coalition’s pressure on France, the unexpected return of the comte de Blacas, and the concordat affair show how diplomacy and religion still cut across parliamentary lines. The Lyon rising, press trials, Benjamin Constant’s pamphlet, and the journalism of Comte and Dunoyer fill the pamphlet war. Inside the ministry the concordat alarms the cabinet; the duc de Feltre and Dubouchage give way to Marshal Gouvion-Saint-Cyr and Molé — a reconstruction that Duvergier reads as Decazes’s growing weight beside Richelieu. As elections approach, newspapers and pamphlets multiply (Constant, de Pradt). Paris sees a hard fight between ministerial and independent lists. Madame de Staël dies; the layette affair and the positions of the duc d’Angoulême and the duc d’Orléans close the chapter’s social-political tableau. The author’s claim is that “parties” now exist as durable organisations of press, salon, and electoral college, not merely as court coteries.
Chapter XVI — Session of 1817 (1817–1818)
The next session opens with the king’s speech, first votes, and a majority already in dissent from parts of the cabinet. New rules of procedure accompany press laws and a heated debate in which Camille Jordan attacks “bastard constitutionalism.” The jury question divides Decazes and Lainé; Royer-Collard, Courvoisier, Corbière, and Lainé speak; the newspaper law passes, the jury is rejected, the press law is adopted in the Deputies then rejected by the Peers after Chateaubriand’s pamphlet and the clearer grouping of the Doctrinaires. Leaders of the Right meet Decazes in corridors that Duvergier treats as half the constitution.
The recruitment law occupies a great debate: Camille Jordan on the annual vote, Royer-Collard on veteran legionaries, Salaberry, a fight over promotion, and a powerful speech by the minister of war that carries the law. A letter from Monsieur to the king and the king’s reply shadow the Peers’ discussion of recruitment — a reminder that the heir’s household remains a political power. The concordat law meets vigorous opposition, episcopal discontent, and Marcellus’s letters to the pope before the ministry abandons the project. Budget debate (Bignon), the Lyon affair (La Bourdonnaie and Camille Jordan), and foreign liquidations fill the close of the session. Semi-periodical journals — La Minerve, Le Publiciste, Le Spectateur, La Bibliothèque historique — and press trials (Marchangy, Fiévée, Comte, Dunoyer) mark the extra-parliamentary struggle. Duvergier’s method is to interleave chamber days with newspaper trials so that “public opinion” appears as a second chamber.
Chapter XVII — The Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle (1818)
The narrative widens to Europe. German efforts toward representative institutions, sovereign resistance, and the Bavarian and Baden constitutions frame anxiety in Paris and London over Alexander I’s liberalism and a secret note. Monsieur, Vitrolles, and Chateaubriand appear in a Royalist conspiracy story with the duc de Raguse and General Canuel — an episode Duvergier uses to show how the Right still dreamed of extra-parliamentary solutions. Reform of the Garde nationale (“National Guard”) removes supreme command from Monsieur, a deliberate reduction of the heir’s military prestige.
Richelieu leaves for Aix-la-Chapelle, meets Castlereagh at Spa, and opens with Alexander on liberating French territory and settling the occupation debt. The question of a quadruple or quintuple alliance divides cabinets: whether France is to re-enter as equal or remain supervised. Alexander and the King of Prussia visit Paris; Alexander converses with Louis XVIII; France is invited back into the European alliance by protocol and declaration. A financial crisis forces a supplementary convention. The duc d’Angoulême’s journey to Metz and Aix, the effect of French elections on the sovereigns, a Bonapartist plot, and Richelieu’s return end the congress narrative. For Duvergier, Aix is both a diplomatic triumph and the last moment when Richelieu’s personal European credit still holds a fractured domestic majority together.
Chapter XVIII — Dissolution of the Ministry (1818)
Divisions inside the majority and inside the ministry drive Richelieu toward retirement. Lainé and Decazes pull in different directions; Richelieu’s irritation against Gouvion-Saint-Cyr over the Royal Guard; imprudent clerical demonstrations and missionaries; the writings of Montlosier and Camille Jordan set the tone. Le Conservateur is founded as an Ultra organ of high literary quality. Election preliminaries and pamphlets divide the camps; ministers grow anxious; Richelieu plans reconciliation with Monsieur and corresponds with colleagues from the congress road.
On his return the Beausset coalition scores a first success; Ravez is elected president of the Deputies; the ministers resign. The king tries to keep Richelieu, who sets conditions the Right will not accept; attempts at a Richelieu–Villèle ministry fail; Richelieu retires definitively. General Dessoles forms a ministry after further difficulties, with Decazes as the real political centre. Duvergier closes with the effect on public opinion and general reflections on the parliamentary crisis: a ministry that loses the chamber’s confidence must yield, yet under the Charte (“Charter”) the king still chooses and dismisses — the unresolved tension of the whole Restoration.
Notes
Series: Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848; Tome IV covers 1817–1818 from the electoral law through the first Richelieu ministry’s fall. Edition: Michel Lévy Frères, Paris, 1860. Harvard College Library copy. Scope: Full two-year parliament including Aix-la-Chapelle and the Dessoles succession after the 1817 leftward electoral shift fractured the post-Chambre introuvable coalition. Notable figures: Benjamin Constant, Royer-Collard, Decazes, Pasquier, Laffitte, Camille Jordan, Chateaubriand, and the Doctrinaires (Guizot, de Broglie, Barante).
Placement: Rest of Europe 1800-1865 wiki; early Restoration. Corpus: Fourth of ten volumes; chapters XIV–XVIII follow Tome III. Raw: duvergier-gouvernement-parlementaire-t4.txt.

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome V
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome V
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome cinquième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, libraires-éditeurs, rue Vivienne, 2 bis, 1862. — 604 fichiers, 22,523 lignes (~1.25 Mo en brut nettoyé).
This fifth volume covers 1819–1820, the sharpest reversal of the Restoration’s middle years. It opens with the liberal triumph of the 1819 press laws and something approaching genuine press freedom under Decazes and de Serre; it closes with the assassination of the duc de Berry, the fall of Decazes, Richelieu’s return on Ultra terms, and the exceptional laws crowned by the loi du double vote (“law of the double vote”). Duvergier’s thesis is parliamentary: liberty of the press and electoral honesty cannot survive when court, diplomacy, and a dynastic murder push the Charte (“Charter”) toward exceptional rule.
OCR from a New York Public Library scan. Raw text cleaned: internal double-spaces collapsed; library plates and blank pages discarded.
Chapter XIX — The Press Laws (1819)
The chapter opens on the progress of the liberal spirit, religious liberty, and freedom of the press. First debates map the parties in the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”). The dotation (“endowment”) of the duc de Richelieu, the right of petition, and the loi de l’année financière (“financial-year law”) meet vigorous opposition from the Right. De Serre delivers a brilliant speech; first cracks appear inside the ministry. Inaction follows the proposition Barthélemy (“Barthélemy proposition”) and public agitation. La Minerve and Le Conservateur set the journalistic poles of Left and Ultra Right.
In the Chambre des pairs (“Chamber of Peers”) the Barthélemy proposition is adopted and the financial-year law rejected; sixty new peers are created to secure the government majority, angering the Royalist party and fueling violent polemics. By-elections follow. In the Deputies La Bourdonnaie, Royer-Collard, Lainé, Sainte-Aulaire, and Villèle speak; de Serre’s energetic reply has a prodigious effect and becomes one of the volume’s set-pieces. The new press laws are presented; Courvoisier reports; heated debates proceed largely without the Right, which abstains in calculated hostility. Benjamin Constant speaks; de Serre admirably defends the main provisions. Responsibility of printers, outrages against public morality, immunity of deputies, the jury question, and proof in cases of defamation against public officials occupy successive sittings. Officials resist; Royer-Collard and de Serre answer; Bignon adds piquant observations. Cautionnement (“security deposit”) for newspapers is debated as the fiscal bridle on journalism; Constant speaks; de Serre remarks on the Convention. De Broglie reports in the Peers; stormy debates end with the suppression of censure (“censorship”) and adoption of the three laws — the high-water mark of Decazes’s liberal experiment.
Duvergier then surveys the attitude and organisation of the parties, old and new newspapers, the law of accounts, and loans, with Casimir Périer, Laffitte, Pasquier, and Delessert. A petition for the bannis (“exiles”) exposes ministerial uncertainty; de Serre’s memorable speech resonates abroad and is read in foreign cabinets as a sign of French liberal consolidation. Violent press commentaries mark a rupture between the Left and the ministry once the Left judges Decazes too timid. In the budget debate La Bourdonnaie attacks; de Serre and General Grenier reply; Marshal Gouvion-Saint-Cyr speaks. Bignon’s “secret” and a parliamentary incident follow. A new de Serre speech on the exiles and debate on the comité directeur (“steering committee”) bring Courvoisier, Corbière, Constant, Royer-Collard, and a skilful speech by Manuel. The revenue budget, the School of Law, Bavoux, and disorders at Grenoble prepare the first application of the press laws and the end of the session. The author’s art is to show how a session that seemed to entrench liberty already contained the personnel and press wars that would destroy it.
Chapter XX — New Crisis (1819)
Ministerial embarrassment deepens under hostility from diplomacy and the court and the violence of the newspapers. Rumours of a coup d’État (“coup d’état”) circulate in salons and chancelleries. A project of great electoral reform is discussed in the press as either remedy or provocation. Press trials continue even under the new laws. The Brothers of the Christian Doctrine and the Concordat occupy Portalis at Rome in negotiation with Cardinal Consalvi. A papal letter to the bishops, writings on the Concordat (including de Pradt), episcopal discontent, an assembly of bishops, and their letter to the pope anger Louis XVIII, who dislikes episcopal collective politics. Negotiations resume; a provisional arrangement with the court of Rome and the bishops’ adhesion close the ecclesiastical crisis for the moment without healing the mistrust between Gallican crown and ultramontane clergy.
Electoral preliminaries follow Royer-Collard’s resignation from positions that had linked the Doctrinaires to the ministry. Elections bring defeats for the ministry and the Right; the election of Grégoire — the former Conventionnel — produces a moral and political shock exploited by Ultras as proof that liberalism ends in regicide. Duvergier paints the state of Germany under the Carlsbad Decrees, the murder of Kotzebue, and reaction across the Confederation, so that French readers see Decazes’s experiment against a European background of police and press repression. In France the ministry is shaken; Decazes’s position weakens; court and diplomatic pressure mount. The volume’s political temperature rises toward the catastrophe of early 1820.
Chapter XXI — Assassination of the duc de Berry (1820)
The session opens amid press polemics and the Isère election; Lainé, Benjamin Constant, and others already fight over the meaning of Grégoire’s return when, on 13 February 1820, Louvel strikes the duc de Berry as he leaves the Opéra. Duvergier narrates the crime, the dying prince’s agony, the court’s grief, and the immediate political exploitation of the murder. The Ultra-Royalist press holds Decazes responsible for a system that supposedly armed assassins by weakening religion and authority. The ministry falters; exceptional measures are demanded as the price of any continued government. The duchesse de Berry’s courage is recorded; the later birth of the duc de Bordeaux (the enfant du miracle) is prepared in the surrounding narrative as the dynastic answer to the crime. Decazes’s fall becomes inevitable as Richelieu is recalled and Villèle’s friends prepare to exact the price of Royalist support. Duvergier insists that the murder did not create Ultra strength so much as remove the last barrier to using the chamber majority against the liberal experiment of 1819.
Chapter XXII — The Law of the Double Vote (1820)
Under the second Richelieu ministry the chambers confront exceptional legislation: suspension of individual liberty, a new press regime, and above all the loi du double vote (“law of the double vote”), which gave the wealthiest electors a second vote in departmental colleges and weighted representation toward landed property. Duvergier follows the presentation, the commission, and the stormy debates day by day. De Serre, architect of the 1819 press laws, now defends exception after Berry’s death — the central biographical arc of the volume and, for the author, a tragic illustration of how fear converts liberals into instruments of reaction. Royer-Collard, Benjamin Constant, General Foy (in a notable parliamentary début), Camille Jordan, Manuel, Pasquier, Lainé, and La Bourdonnaie fill the lists. The law passes amid liberal fury and Royalist triumph. Civil disturbances and the first conspiracies of the Restoration’s middle years close the volume’s drama. The double vote becomes, in Duvergier’s later volumes, the original sin of the electoral system that the July Revolution will have to overthrow.
Notes
Edition: First published 1862 (Michel Lévy Frères, Paris). Printing by Simon Raçon et Comp., rue d’Erfurth. NYPL copy. Scope: Reversal of Decazes’s liberal experiment — press laws of 1819, election of the regicide Grégoire, Carlsbad Decrees and German reaction, assassination of the duc de Berry, fall of Decazes, return of Richelieu with Ultra-Royalist support, and the exceptional laws culminating in the double vote. Notable figures: De Serre (central arc), Decazes, Villèle, Royer-Collard, Benjamin Constant, General Foy, Camille Jordan, Chateaubriand, Manuel, Pasquier, Lainé, La Bourdonnaie. Placement: Rest of Europe 1800-1865 wiki. Chronologically 1819–1820.
Corpus: Fifth of ten volumes; chapters XIX–XXII follow XVIII of Tome IV. Raw: duvergier-gouvernement-parlementaire-t5.txt.
Notes on form

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VI
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VI
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome sixième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1864. — 676 fichiers, 25,469 lignes (~1.40 Mo).
This sixth volume covers 1820–1822, the passage from Richelieu’s moderate royalism to Ultra-Royalist ascendancy under Villèle. It opens after the duc de Berry’s assassination, traces first conspiracies and secret societies, the European congresses of Troppau and Laybach, the slow death of Richelieu’s second ministry, the fall of the Centre in December 1821, and consolidation of the Ultra programme under Villèle and Corbière, culminating in the new press laws of 1822. France’s diplomatic subordination to Metternich is treated as the external face of the same defeat of parliamentary liberalism.
OCR from a University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign scan. Raw text cleaned.
Chapter XXII — First Conspiracies (1820)
The Royalist party triumphs in the aftermath of the exceptional laws. Destitutions and brochures accompany the convocation of electoral colleges under the new double-vote system. Royer-Collard writes; Madier de Montjau appears; press trials continue. De Pradt and Clausel de Coussergues’s factum against Decazes feed opinion still hungry for scapegoats. Secret societies and the comité directeur (“steering committee”) prepare military conspiracy (19 August) — the first serious attempt to overthrow the restored monarchy by force since 1815. Decazes and Camille Jordan figure in the approach to the elections even as Decazes’s formal power has ended.
Political writings by Kératry, Benjamin Constant, Guizot, Fiévée, Donnadieu, and Saint-Simon map the camps from liberal constitutionalism to early socialist speculation. The birth of the duc de Bordeaux produces public joy and Royalist imprudence; a project to dissolve the Chamber definitively is set aside because the double-vote elections already promise a docile majority. Electoral disturbances and a riot at Saumur (Benjamin Constant threatened) precede liberal defeat and the rediscovery of a new Chambre introuvable (“Undiscoverable Chamber”) spirit. Political trials; Madier de Montjau censured; Villèle called to Paris. Negotiations with the Right break and resume. Madame du Cayla’s rising favour at court becomes a political fact Duvergier does not omit. Richelieu offers Villèle and Corbière entry to the Council; they refuse until the price is higher. The session opens with the king’s speech; Chateaubriand intervenes as the literary sword of the Ultras. Corbière becomes director of public instruction; Villèle and Lainé ministers without portfolio. The réunion Piet (“Piet meeting”) gains preponderant influence over the Ultra deputies; a project of disbanding the Garde nationale (“National Guard”) is aired as revenge on a force associated with 1789 and 1815 liberalism.
Chapter XXIII — The Congress and the Chambers (1820–1821)
Europe at the beginning of 1820: the Spanish revolution shakes cabinets. Metternich, Castlereagh, and Alexander I react; the Neapolitan revolution forces preliminary negotiations. France proposes a congress accepted by Russia despite English and Austrian reservations. At Troppau the sovereigns gather; Metternich’s programme and intrigues win Alexander away from earlier liberal phrases. A preliminary protocol and letter to the King of Naples are prepared without France and England; both powers answer in discontent. Complete Metternichian success follows agitation at Naples and the king’s departure for Laybach.
In the Chambre des députés first debates, the address, and the law of provisional twelfths expose divisions in the Royalist party between those who want pure reaction and those who still speak the language of the Charte. A petard explodes in the king’s apartments; Royalist newspapers rage and demand more police. Camille Jordan’s last speech and painful discoveries for the Royalists lead to heated petition debates and even praise of the tricolour cockade from opposition benches. At Laybach the English circular, French instructions, de Blacas’s proud attitude, and de la Ferronnays’s conversation with Alexander form what Duvergier calls a diplomatic comedy: French plenipotentiaries sign congress acts that the ministry does not clearly disavow. Gallo appears before the congress; any liberal constitution at Naples is excluded. Naples refuses to submit; the congress closes. France protests in a verbal note; the three absolute courts are discontented. De Pradt and Bignon write; Pasquier refuses explanations in the Chamber; violent debates, electoral districts, and petitions fill the winter. De Serre speaks with declining force as health fails; Decazes returns to the wings; the August trials and the Piedmontese revolution close the European half of the chapter. The author’s judgment is harsh: France neither led liberal Europe nor honestly joined the Holy Alliance, and lost credit with both.
Chapter XXIV — Session of 1821
Parliamentary work continues under mounting Ultra pressure. Duvergier follows verification of powers, addresses, and the slow isolation of the Centre. Budget and administrative questions interleave with foreign news of Austrian intervention in Italy and the restoration of absolute princes. Liberal orators — Constant, Manuel, Foy — sharpen attacks on a ministry that will neither fight Metternich nor satisfy Villèle. Royalist majorities harden in the departmental colleges of the double vote. The ministry’s ambiguities between European reaction and French constitutional forms become unsustainable; every budget chapter becomes a confidence vote.
Chapter XXV — Fall of the Richelieu Ministry (1821)
Richelieu’s second ministry disintegrates under court favour, Madame du Cayla’s influence, and Villèle’s patient organisation of the Right. Resignations and reconstructions fail. In December 1821 power passes to Villèle. Duvergier narrates the personal and factional dimensions of the transfer: Corbière, Montmorency, and the Ultra press claim victory; liberals organise for long opposition in press and secret society alike. Napoleon’s death at St Helena echoes in French opinion — Bonapartist emotion without altering the Ultra course. The Centre, which had been the parliamentary ballast of 1816–1820, ceases to be a governing force.
Chapter XXVI — New Press Laws (1822)
The Villèle–Corbière system moves to tame the press. New press laws restore restraints that 1819 had loosened: cautionnement (“security deposit”), offences of tendency, and procedure favourable to authority. Debates revive the 1819 arguments in reverse; de Serre’s old phrases are thrown back at a chamber that no longer wants them. Young liberal journalism (Thiers, Mignet) appears beside Constant and Foy, preparing the historical and newspaper culture of the next reign. The Charbonnerie (“Carbonari-style secret society”) under Lafayette and others organises military and civilian networks that the courts will soon strike in the trials of La Rochelle and Saumur. The volume ends with Ultra consolidation and liberal conspiracy as twin facts of 1822 — parliament narrowed, street and barracks tempted.
Notes
Edition: 1864, Michel Lévy Frères, Paris. UIUC copy. Scope: (1) Royalist reaction of 1820 and first secret societies; (2) Troppau and Laybach, Neapolitan and Piedmontese revolutions, French diplomatic subordination to Metternich; (3) death of the Richelieu ministry and transfer to Villèle, with new press regime. Birth of the duc de Bordeaux; death of Napoleon; organisation of the Charbonnerie. Notable figures: De Serre (declining health), Pasquier, Royer-Collard, Constant, Manuel, Foy, Lafayette, Chateaubriand, Villèle, Corbière; Metternich, Alexander I, Castlereagh, Ferdinand I of Naples; Thiers and Mignet emerging. Placement: Rest of Europe 1800-1865 wiki; 1820–1822.
Corpus: Sixth of ten; chapters XXII–XXVI follow Tome V. Raw: duvergier-gouvernement-parlementaire-t6.txt.

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VII
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VII
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome septième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1865. — 632 fichiers, 23,577 lignes (~1.30 Mo).
This seventh volume covers 1822–1824, Ultra consolidation under Villèle. It opens with the financial session of 1822 and Charbonnerie trials, traces the Congress of Verona and French intervention in Spain, describes the Spanish War of the cent mille fils de Saint Louis (“Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis”), covers the 1823 dissolution, and closes with the Villèle–Chateaubriand rivalry and the latter’s dismissal. Louis XVIII’s final years end on the eve of the septennial law that will lock in a long chamber.
OCR from Universidad Complutense de Madrid (Menéndez Pelayo). Raw cleaned.
Chapter XXVII — The Financial Session (1822)
Parties distrust each other. Elections bring liberal successes in Paris even under the double vote. The duc de Richelieu dies, removing the last great moderate of the first Restoration generation. The session opens with verification of powers, electoral manoeuvres, nomination of the bureau, and the address. Royalist pretensions frame a customs law and a first political debate. Affairs of Béfort, La Rochelle, and Saumur; arrest of Berton; the Colmar ambush; Colonel Caron — the judicial war on the Charbonnerie (“Carbonari-style secret society”) enters the chamber through petitions and interpellations. Guizot writes on the death penalty in political matters. Petitions and the budget bring Benjamin Constant, Bignon, Laffitte, and Villèle. An incident on the Colmar ambush embroils Constant, Foy, Lafayette, and Manuel in tumult. Foreign affairs: European state, attempted counter-revolution, constitutional victory abroad. Bignon and Bonald speak; Royer-Collard delivers a brilliant speech on the Revolution as définitif (“definitive”) — a Doctrinaire claim that 1789’s civil results cannot be undone even if 1793 is condemned. Public instruction pits Corbière against Royer-Collard. Constant on the police; Demarçay on the army; violent debate. Accusation in the Saumur affair; deputies called to testify. Courvoisier’s report on Béfort and La Rochelle; tumultuous sessions; Royer-Collard, Courvoisier, Manuel; rejection; public emotion; end of session.
Chapter XXVIII — The Congress of Verona (1822)
Trials of Béfort and Colmar; execution of Caron. La Rochelle trial: noble attitude of the four accused sergeants; condemnation. Saumur trial: Mangin’s violent prosecution; Berton and accomplices condemned. A Charbonnerie congress at Bordeaux; press trials; Koechlin and Constant; charge of calumny against Mangin. Execution of the four sergeants of La Rochelle leaves a profound liberal martyrdom that Duvergier treats as a founding memory of the opposition.
At Verona Metternich meets Wellington; France is represented by Montmorency and Chateaubriand. Negotiations of the French plenipotentiaries; a Spanish war proposal is at first disapproved in Paris; a verbal note is presented. Discussions, intrigues, and resolutions mark reaction’s progress. Trial of the Tablettes; Royalist newspaper anger. Montmorency returns; dissidence in council; Chateaubriand becomes ambassador to England then returns to the decisive role. Villèle asks delay from Verona and is refused. End of congress; rupture between Villèle and Montmorency; Montmorency resigns. Louis XVIII sides with Villèle; English mediation is refused. Madame du Cayla and Sosthènes de La Rochefoucauld work the court; despatch to Lagarde. The author’s point is that Verona commits France to armed counter-revolution in Spain while the cabinet at home is already splitting over who will claim the glory.
Chapter XXIX — The Spanish War (1823)
Opinion is inflamed. A new Charbonnerie congress; Lord FitzRoy Somerset’s mission; events in Madrid. Chateaubriand and Canning duel in despatches; Royalist exasperation; rupture with Spain; division in council. Address of the Chambre des pairs (“Chamber of Peers”); de Barante’s amendment; Daru; Talleyrand’s cold wisdom. Address of the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”); La Bourdonnaie and Delalot; Villèle’s imprudent word; the young Duvergier de Hauranne and Foy on the opposition benches. Canning’s letter to Monsieur; press trials; budget. The army of the Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis crosses into Spain under the duc d’Angoulême. Duvergier follows military and diplomatic phases, liberal opposition at home, and the restoration of Ferdinand VII’s absolute power — a short victorious war that strengthens Villèle, flatters the court, and deepens liberal bitterness without solving the structural conflict of the Charte.
Chapter XXX — Dissolution of the Chamber (1823)
After victory Villèle dissolves to obtain a more docile chamber. The electoral struggle, Ultra organisation, and liberal weakness under the double vote produce a Royalist majority. Duvergier narrates Manuel’s violent expulsion from the Deputies — a set-piece of parliamentary brutality that becomes a liberal legend and a stain on the session. The new chamber prepares the legislative instruments of Ultra dominance: long duration, indemnity projects, religious bills.
Chapter XXXI — Villèle and Chateaubriand (1824)
Rivalry between the president of the council and the foreign minister breaks into the open. Chateaubriand’s European prestige and the Journal des Débats confront Villèle’s parliamentary machine. Dismissal of Chateaubriand is a cause célèbre that permanently alienates the Débats from the Ultra party and gives the opposition a great pen. Ouvrard’s financial operations appear as a running wound in public finance. The septennial law that will frame the next decade is prepared as Louis XVIII’s death approaches — locking a chamber for seven years and reducing the electoral check that even the double vote still allowed every year.

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VIII
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome VIII
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome huitième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1867. — Raw cleaned text of several hundred pages covering the last months of Louis XVIII and the first years of Charles X.
This eighth volume runs from 1824 to 1827. It opens with the death of Louis XVIII and the accession of Charles X, follows the loi du septennat (“septennial law”) that locked the Ultra chamber for seven years, the indemnity of the émigrés (“émigrés”), the law of sacrilege, the coronation at Reims, the ministry’s religious and financial programme, the rising power of the Congrégation (“Congregation”) and Jesuit controversy, and ends with the growing opposition that will culminate in the liberal victory of 1827 and Villèle’s fall in the next volume. Duvergier treats Charles X’s reign as the test of whether a king who still thinks in terms of 1789’s undoing can live inside the Charte (“Charter”) he has sworn.
OCR from a university library scan. Internal double-spaces collapsed; library plates discarded.
Chapter XXXII — Death of Louis XVIII (1824)
As the Chambre des pairs (“Chamber of Peers”) rejects a law on rentes, the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”) adopts other financial bills. Louis XVIII’s health declines; court factions prepare the succession. The king dies in September 1824 after a reign that Duvergier judges as the only period when genuine parliamentary government seemed possible under the Restoration. Charles X, formerly Monsieur, takes the oath to the Charter amid liberal hope that the old count of Artois will reign as a constitutional king. The early addresses of the chambers, the tone of the press, and Villèle’s careful management create a brief honeymoon. Chateaubriand, still alienated since his dismissal, watches from the Journal des Débats. The septennat is carried: deputies elected under the double vote will sit for seven years, removing the annual electoral check that had still disciplined ministries. Duvergier marks this as the constitutional hinge of the reign — a long Ultra chamber under a king who listens to priests and old émigrés more than to the Centre.
Chapter XXXIII — The Emigré Indemnity and Sacrilege (1825)
Villèle’s great social-financial measure is the milliard des émigrés (“émigré billion”) — indemnity for properties confiscated in the Revolution, financed by a conversion of rentes that hits the bourgeois rentier. Debates are passionate: Foy, Constant, Royer-Collard, and the liberal press denounce a transfer of wealth to the old nobility; Villèle and the Right defend justice and social peace. The law of sacrilege (loi du sacrilège) restores extreme penalties for profanation of consecrated hosts, a symbolic restoration of altar beside throne that liberals read as a return to theocratic justice. In the Peers and Deputies the opposition fights article by article; Bonald and the Ultras exalt religion; Casimir Périer and bankers defend the modern credit system against the rente conversion. The laws pass. Duvergier’s narrative links them: the same majority that pays the émigrés criminalises the Revolution’s irreligion, and both measures alienate the urban electorate that will vote against Villèle in 1827.
Chapter XXXIV — Coronation of Charles X (1825)
The coronation at Reims revives medieval ceremonial — holy ampulla, knights of the Holy Spirit, the king touching for scrofula. Duvergier describes the pageant and the political reading: Charles X presents himself as Most Christian King more than as king of the Charter. Liberal newspapers contrast the ceremony with English constitutional coronations; Ultra papers celebrate the reborn alliance of throne and altar. The Congrégation and Jesuit colleges become public issues; Montlosier’s writings against Jesuit influence open a long pamphlet war. Municipal and departmental administration, press seizures, and the police of Corbière fill the ordinary work of government while the court multiplies religious processions. The author notes that foreign cabinets watch Reims with irony: Metternich prefers quiet police to crusading kings, and Canning’s England has no taste for a French theocratic revival.
Chapter XXXV — Religious Struggle and Finance (1826)
The session turns on church and money. Bills affecting the religious orders, the rights of the University against ecclesiastical colleges, and the status of the Jesuits produce Royer-Collard’s great speeches on Gallican liberties and civil society. The Right answers with petitions and episcopal memoirs. Financial debate revisits the rente conversion’s effects; Laffitte and Casimir Périer speak for commercial France. Press trials multiply; the Constitutionnel and Courrier français fight cautionnement (“security deposit”) and jury questions. Local elections begin to show liberal gains even under the double vote. Duvergier interleaves chamber days with salon and newspaper wars so that “public opinion” appears as a second legislature already undoing Villèle’s majority in spirit.
Chapter XXXVI — Toward the Elections of 1827
Villèle attempts to strengthen the upper house and tighten press control as opposition grows. Projects touching the Peers and the press unite Doctrinaires, left liberals, and the Chateaubriand Débats against the ministry. The garde nationale (“National Guard”) of Paris, reviewed by the king, shouts “Down with the ministers!” — a public humiliation Duvergier records as the street verdict on Ultra rule. Dissolution and new elections are prepared. The volume ends on the eve of the liberal electoral victory that will force Villèle’s resignation in January 1828. The political lesson drawn is that even a septennial chamber and double vote cannot permanently govern against the press, the cities, and a king who multiplies religious provocations.

sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.title: Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome IX
sources/duvergier-gouvernement-parlement.content:
Duvergier de Hauranne — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, Tome IX
Ernest Duvergier de Hauranne (1798–1881) — Histoire du gouvernement parlementaire en France, 1814-1848, précédée d’une Introduction. — Tome neuvième. — Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1869. — Large volume on the Martignac interlude and the approach of Polignac.
This ninth volume covers 1827–1829. It opens with the elections that defeat Villèle, narrates the short Martignac ministry’s attempt at moderate reform (press, elections, administration), the king’s distrust of any liberal concession, the failure of Martignac’s bills in a chamber still full of Ultras and an opposition that wants more, and the summons of the prince de Polignac — the appointment that will lead to the ordinances of 1830. Duvergier presents Martignac as the last serious effort to make the Restoration live inside the Charte (“Charter”) before Charles X chooses open conflict.
OCR cleaned; library plates discarded.
Chapter XXXVII — Fall of Villèle (1827–1828)
The elections of November 1827 return a majority hostile to Villèle. Paris and the great cities vote liberal; even under the double vote the departmental colleges cannot save the ministry. The garde nationale episode and press campaign have done their work. Villèle resigns in January 1828. Duvergier analyses the Ultra party’s bitterness: they blame not only the opposition but the king’s hesitation and the half-measures of the late session. Chateaubriand’s friends claim moral victory; the Doctrinaires prepare to support a centrist cabinet if one can be formed without humiliating the crown.
Chapter XXXVIII — The Martignac Ministry (1828)
Charles X calls a ministry of moderate Royalists: Martignac at the Interior, Portalis, Roy, de la Ferronnays at Foreign Affairs, and others who speak the language of the Charter without being liberals of 1819. The programme is conciliation: freer press practice, administrative reform, a less clerical public instruction, careful foreign policy after Navarino and Greek affairs. Addresses of the Chambre des députés (“Chamber of Deputies”) and Chambre des pairs (“Chamber of Peers”) test the new tone. Duvergier follows Martignac’s speeches — polished, legal, and sincere — and the king’s private resistance. Bishops and the Congrégation distrust the ministry; the extreme Left finds it too timid. The author’s sympathy is clear: Martignac is the parliamentary path not taken.
Chapter XXXIX — Bills on the Press and the Communes (1828–1829)
Martignac presents laws on the press and on municipal and departmental organisation intended to broaden participation without manhood suffrage. Debates revive the great themes of the Restoration: cautionnement (“security deposit”), jury, offences of tendency, the rights of elected councils against prefects. Royer-Collard and the Doctrinaires support measured reform; La Bourdonnaie and the Ultra remnant fight every article; Benjamin Constant and the left push for more. Foreign news — Greek independence, Russian war with Turkey, Belgian Catholic-liberal union in the Netherlands — frames the French discussion. Several bills pass in compromised form; others stall. The ministry loses ground as the king listens to Polignac and the salon of the ultra court.
Chapter XL — Crisis of the Martignac Cabinet (1829)
Budget fights and incidental interpellations erode the majority. Martignac’s attempt to remodel the administration alarms office-holders of the Villèle years. The king refuses further concessions on the Jesuits and the University. Duvergier narrates the personal audiences, the queen’s circle, and the return of Polignac from the London embassy as a political event. The chamber’s address grows bolder; the ministry, caught between crown and opposition, cannot dissolve without the king’s will and cannot govern with a half-hostile house. Resignation becomes inevitable. The volume insists that constitutional monarchy died not in July 1830 alone but when Charles X discarded Martignac.
Chapter XLI — Polignac Called (1829)
In August 1829 the prince de Polignac forms a ministry of decided Royalists: La Bourdonnaie, Bourmont, and colleagues identified with the extreme Right. The liberal press explodes; the Journal des Débats and the Constitutionnel treat the appointment as a declaration of war on the Charter. Associations for the refusal of tax in case of a coup d’État (“coup d’état”) begin to form. Duvergier closes the volume on this electric atmosphere: a chamber still legally elected under the septennial law faces a ministry that does not represent it, and a king who believes he may govern by article 14 of the Charter without the chambers’ consent. The road to the July Ordinances is open.

sources/friedjung-oesterreich-1848-60-vo.title: Friedjung — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860, Vol. I: Die Jahre der Revolution und der Reform 1848 bis 1851
sources/friedjung-oesterreich-1848-60-vo.content:
Friedjung — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860, Vol. I: Die Jahre der Revolution und der Reform 1848 bis 1851
Heinrich Friedjung (1851–1920) — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860. Erster Band: Die Jahre der Revolution und der Reform 1848 bis 1851. — Stuttgart and Berlin: J. G. Cotta’sche Buchhandlung, 4th edition, 1918 (first published 1908).
The first of two volumes of Friedjung’s classic narrative of Austria from the revolution of 1848 to the eve of the new era of 1860. The present volume carries the story from the collapse of the Metternich system through the March revolution in Vienna, the revolutionary movement in Hungary and the October revolution, the accession of Francis Joseph, the constitutional labors at Vienna, Frankfurt, and Kremsier, the winter campaign in Hungary, the subjugation of Hungary, the constitution of 4 March 1849, and the administrative, economic, and agrarian reforms, down to the revocation of the constitution on 31 December 1851 and the restoration of absolutism.
Friedjung’s account is a Liberal-national one, written with the materials of the Vienna and Hungarian archives and informed by his own experience of the nationalities question. The opening book interprets the Metternich system not as mere doctrine of legitimacy but as the practical defense of a polyglot monarchy against liberal and national dissolution; the narrative then follows the revolution as the collision between the imperial idea of a united Austria and the competing nationalisms, above all the Magyar. Throughout, Alexander Bach figures as a central, ambiguous personality — the revolutionary advocate who became the architect of the restored absolutism.
The volume is approximately 520 pages of text (plus a register), extracted from a Michigan State University scan (Anna’s Archive), 554 scanned pages. A detailed Inhalt des ersten Bandes opens the volume, and it closes with an appendix of eleven documents, including the protocol of the State Conference of 14 March 1848, rescripts of Emperor Ferdinand, Bach’s memorandum on the Hungarian-Croatian crisis, and the trial of Count Batthyány.
Content Summary
Einleitung — Introduction
Friedjung’s preface situating the work within the history of the monarchy and the nationality conflict.
Erstes Buch — Vor der Revolution (Before the Revolution)
The Metternich system as the result of Austria’s internal condition: the opposition of Archdukes Karl and Johann, Emperor Francis’s failure to settle the succession, the State Conference under Ferdinand, Metternich on Hungary, neglected reforms, the plans of Archduchess Sophie for the elevation of Archduke Francis Joseph, and the notion of summoning an imperial representative body.
Zweites Buch — Die Wiener Märzrevolution (The Vienna March Revolution)
The Austrian diets before 1848 and the liberal opposition in the Lower Austrian diet; the petition of the Viennese burghers of 6 March, the rising of 13 March, the resignation of Metternich, the granting of a constitution on 15 March, the Pillersdorf constitution of 25 April, the democratic rising of 15 May, the Wessenberg–Doblhoff ministry with Bach as justice minister, the abolition of the feudal Frohnden by the Austrian Reichstag, and the suppression of the rising of 14 September.
Drittes Buch — Ungarn und die Oktoberrevolution (Hungary and the October Revolution)
Count Széchenyi, Kossuth, Deák, and Count Batthyány; Kossuth’s speech of 3 March 1848; the Palatine Archduke Stephen’s part in securing a responsible Hungarian ministry; Batthyány named minister-president; the appointment of Jellačić as Ban of Croatia; the Hungarian April constitution of 1848; Kossuth’s finance speeches against Austria; Windischgrätz’s suppression of the Whitsun rising in Prague; the Serb rising against Hungary; the deposition and reinstatement of Jellačić; the Hungarian Reichstag’s war measures; the murder of General Lamberg at Pest; the rising in Vienna on 6 October and the murder of the war minister Latour; Windischgrätz’s march on Vienna and the reconquest of the city; the executions of Messenhauser and Robert Blum.
Viertes Buch — Thronbesteigung Kaiser Franz Josephs (The Accession of Emperor Francis Joseph)
The position of the army; the plans of Windischgrätz; the formation of the Schwarzenberg–Stadion ministry; the character of Schwarzenberg; Stadion and Bach as members; Archduchess Sophie and her relations with Metternich; the youth and education of Francis Joseph under his tutor Count Bombelles; the necessity of Ferdinand’s abdication; and the accession of Francis Joseph (2 December 1848).
Fünftes Buch — Verfassungsarbeit in Wien, Frankfurt, Kremsier. Winterfeldzug in Ungarn (Constitutional Labor in Vienna, Frankfurt, and Kremsier. The Winter Campaign in Hungary)
I. Die österreichische Frage in Frankfurt — the Austrian question at Frankfurt; Schmerling president of the imperial ministry; the German constitutional draft demanding personal union between Austria and Hungary; the proposals of Gagern. II. Der Winterfeldzug in Ungarn — the Hungarian diet declaring Ferdinand’s abdication invalid; the defection of imperial troops to the Hungarian cause; Windischgrätz’s invasion of Hungary; Arthur Görgei; the capture of Ofen-Pest; the concentration of Hungarian forces under Dembinski; the indecisive battle of Kápolna. III. Stadion, Schwarzenberg, Windischgrätz — Stadion’s constitutional drafts; the unity of the Empire; the free commune; Trade Minister Bruck; the ministerial deliberations on the future constitution; Windischgrätz against Stadion’s plans; Bach’s memorandum; the liberal-centralist and aristocratic conceptions of the state. IV. Die Kremsierer Verfassung — the idea of popular sovereignty; Bach in the Kremsier Reichstag; the relation of state to provinces and districts; the opposition of Palacký and Rieger; the adoption of the constitutional draft in committee; Stadion’s arrival at Kremsier and the dissolution of the Reichstag.
V. Die oktroyierte Verfassung — the imposed unitary constitution of 4 March 1849; unity of the customs territory; the strengthening of the monarchical power; partial recognition of the Hungarian constitution; the narrow civil liberties; the Grundentlastung (redemption of feudal burdens); Stadion’s illness and resignation.
Sechstes Buch — Die österreichische Frage im Frankfurter Parlament (The Austrian Question in the Frankfurt Parliament)
The revival of Austria’s strength; German particularism; the formation of the Gagern imperial ministry; Schmerling as Austria’s plenipotentiary at Frankfurt; the first reading of the German imperial constitution; the Austrian memoranda of 18 December 1848 and 17 January 1849; the victory of the Prussian ministry over the king; Schwarzenberg demanding the entry of the whole of Austria into the German Confederation; Schmerling’s resignation; the decline of the Greater German party, the election of the King of Prussia as German Emperor, and the refusal of the imperial crown.
Siebentes Buch — Unterwerfung Ungarns (The Subjugation of Hungary)
Windischgrätz’s inactivity; Görgei made Hungarian commander-in-chief; the second Hungarian advance on Pest; Görgei’s march to relieve Komorn; Windischgrätz relieved of command; the Austrians evacuate Hungary; the war in Transylvania and southern Hungary; the storming of Ofen; the deposition of the House of Habsburg by the Debrecen diet; the strength of the Hungarian army; the Russian intervention; Görgei’s capitulation at Világos; the execution of the thirteen Hungarian generals; the execution of Batthyány; the severity of the military judgments.
Achtes Buch — Militärdiktatur und Finanznot (Military Dictatorship and Financial Distress)
The position of the generals and the army in the state; the return of the court to Vienna; the reconstitution of the ministry with Bach as minister of the interior; the ruin of the currency; Finance Minister Philipp Krauß; the deficit and the rising war budget; the income tax; Kübeck’s influence; Baumgartner as trade and finance minister; the state of siege, executions, and police vexations; Hungary’s Honvéd officers in the imperial army; Austria in the public opinion of Europe.
Neuntes Buch — Die Verfassung vom 4. März 1849 und die Nationalitäten (The Constitution of 4 March 1849 and the Nationalities)
The repeated promise to execute the constitution; Bach’s circular of 15 August 1849; the ministry’s proposal of 29 December 1849 for the creation of provincial representative bodies; Stadion’s diet statutes and the curial franchise; the favor shown to the bourgeoisie; the Galician provincial ordinance under Statthalter Goluchowski; opinion in German Austria and the democratic party; party life in Bohemia, the Slovanská lípa (“Slavic Linden” — a Czech national society), the vacillation of the Czechs between historical and natural right, the conspiracy of May 1849, Havlíček and Palacký, the decline of Palacký’s party; the nationality policy of the government, the German state language before 1848, the principle of equal rights, and the Reichsidee (“imperial idea”).
Zehntes Buch — Reform der Staatsverwaltung (Reform of the State Administration)
Bruck and the reform of commercial policy; the creation of a unified customs territory and the transition from the prohibitive system to a moderate protective tariff; the plan of a customs union with the German Zollverein; railway building and the Semmering railway; reform of the political administration; the patrimonial jurisdiction before 1848; Schmerling and the reform of the judiciary; the creation of the Supreme Court; Bach and the administrative reform, the end of collegiate procedure, the district offices, and the communal law of 17 March 1849; the establishment of the gendarmerie; the educational reform under Leo Thun.
Elftes Buch — Sozialpolitik und Agrarreform (Social Policy and Agrarian Reform)
The national and social forces in Austria; the bureaucracy; the German bourgeoisie as carrier of the Reichsgedanke (“imperial idea”); the petty bourgeoisie and the working class in 1848; the end of the privileged position of the nobility; the successes of economic liberalism; agrarian conditions before 1848 and the agrarian reforms of Joseph II; the height of the Frohnden before 1848; the Grundentlastung; the law of 4 March 1849 and the redemption payments; the redemption of servitudes in Hungary; the closed farmsteads (geschlossene Bauernhöfe) of Austria; Windischgrätz and the nobility against the Grundentlastung; the crown for the liberation of the soil; the historical merit of the reformers.
Zwölftes Buch — Das Schicksal Ungarns. Das Provisorium (The Fate of Hungary. The Provisional Arrangement)
Opinion in Hungary during the revolutionary war; Windischgrätz’s conservative administration; the memorandum of Count Dessewffy; Geringer as imperial commissioner; the provisional organization of 17 October 1849; judicial reform in Hungary; the diminution of Hungary’s territory and the five military districts; the first Austrian officials in Hungary; the German officials; the old-conservative party and its address of 7 April 1850; Francis Deák and his circle, Baron Eötvös, Baron Kemény, and Deák’s silence; the position of the Magyars toward a united imperial diet.
Dreizehntes Buch — Zentralisation und Germanisation in Ungarn (Centralization and Germanization in Hungary)
Haynau as head of the administration of Hungary, his arbitrariness and dismissal; Geringer as statthalter; Hungary divided into five administrative districts; Archduke Albrecht as military and civil governor; Bach for full centralization in Hungary; Transylvania under General Wohlgemuth and the organization of 12 May 1851; the wishes of the Rumanians and the Saxons, the destruction of the Saxon Königsboden and of Saxon autonomy; southern Hungary, Jellačić’s pan-South-Slav wishes, the boundary between Croatia and the Banat, and the Swabians of southern Hungary; Croatia, the Military Frontier, and Jellačić’s work for Croatian autonomy; the trials of the Slavic spokesmen and the fate of the Rumanian leader Iancu; the imperial journey to Hungary in 1852; the struggle between the old conservatives and Bach.
Vierzehntes Buch — Widerruf der österreichischen Verfassung (The Revocation of the Austrian Constitution)
The dispute over the best constitution for the monarchy; the arguments for absolutism; Metternich in England and Belgium and his dissatisfaction with the ministry; Kübeck’s formation and views, his mission to Frankfurt, and his advocacy of absolutism; Schwarzenberg’s decision to abolish the “Mistverfassung” (the “muck constitution”); the creation of the Reichsrat (Staatsrat); police pressure and the mishandling of the press; Schmerling’s resignation; the administrative banishments, including Havlíček’s; Kübeck’s interviews with the emperor; Bach at the crossroads; the ministerial council of 17 August 1851; the decrees of 20 August 1851; the commission for the revision of the constitution; the coup d’état of Prince Napoleon of 2 December 1851; the imperial patent of 31 December 1851 revoking the constitution; and the social and political significance of the return to absolutism.
Anhang — Appendix
Eleven documents: the protocol of the State Conference of 14 March 1848; rescripts of Emperor Ferdinand of 17 and 18 March 1848; Alexander Bach’s “Punkte der Ausgleichung der ungarisch-kroatischen Wirren” (summer 1848); Bach to Baron Doblhoff (end of September and 7 October 1848); Wessenberg on Archduchess Sophie; H. v. Sybel on the policy of Prince Schwarzenberg; extracts from Schmerling’s reports from Frankfurt; extracts from Prokesch-Osten’s reports from Berlin; the trial of Count Batthyány; and Bach’s memorandum on the Austrian constitution (autumn 1851). The volume closes with a Register (index).

sources/friedjung-oesterreich-1848-60-vo.title: Friedjung — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860, Vol. II: Die deutsche Politik des Fürsten Schwarzenberg und die Reaktion 1849–1860
sources/friedjung-oesterreich-1848-60-vo.content:
Friedjung — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860, Vol. II: Die deutsche Politik des Fürsten Schwarzenberg und die Reaktion 1849–1860
Heinrich Friedjung (1851–1920) — Österreich von 1848 bis 1860. Zweiter Band, Erste Abteilung. — Stuttgart and Berlin: J. G. Cotta’sche Buchhandlung, 3rd edition, 1912 (first published 1908).
The second volume of Friedjung’s narrative of Austria from 1848 to 1860, covering the years from the spring of 1849 to the middle of the 1850s. (The volume is labelled Erste Abteilung — the First Division — of the second volume; a further section carried the story into the later 1850s.) The narrative opens with the German policy of Prince Felix Schwarzenberg — the rejection of the Prussian attempt at a federal state, the rise and fall of the Erfurt Union, the Four-Kings’ alliance, the two meetings at Warsaw, the collision over Holstein and Hesse-Cassel, and the Punktation of Olmütz (1850) — and proceeds to Schwarzenberg’s death, the reaction under Kübeck and Bach, the Crimean War, and then a broad series of studies of the monarchy in the 1850s: the emperor and the court, the social structure, intellectual life, the theatre, the visual arts and the Vienna city expansion, and the church question down to the fall of Josephinism and the Concordat of 1855.
The volume is approximately 570 pages of text, extracted from a Michigan State University scan (Anna’s Archive), 598 scanned pages. A full table of contents (Inhalt) opens the volume, and it closes with three appendices of documents: letters of Prince Felix Schwarzenberg (Nos. 1–28), acta of 1850–1852, and a note on an alleged saying of Schwarzenberg, “Avilir puis démolir” (to debase and then to demolish).
Content Summary
Einleitung — Introduction
The opening of the second volume, carrying the reader from the position reached at the close of Vol. I.
Erstes Buch — Die deutsche Politik des Fürsten Schwarzenberg (April 1849 bis Mai 1850) (The German Policy of Prince Schwarzenberg, April 1849 to May 1850)
I. Die deutsche Kaiserkrone — the German imperial crown; the offer of the crown to Emperor Francis of Austria in 1814 and its refusal; the decision of 1849. II. Der preußisch deutsche Bundesstaat — the Prussian note of 9 May 1849 proposing a federal state (the German Union); the Prussian-German constitution of 28 May; the defeat of the Austrian army in Hungary; Schwarzenberg’s rejection of the Prussian proposal. III. Radowitz und seine Gegner — Radowitz and his opponents. IV. Das großdeutsche Programm Österreichs — the Greater-German program of Austria; the capitulation of the Hungarian army; the mediating influence of the Tsar; the meeting of Francis Joseph and Frederick William IV at Teplitz (9 September); the Austro-Prussian treaty of 30 September on the provisional central authority; the elections for the Erfurt parliament; the “Seventy-Million-Reich.”.
V. Das Vier-Königsbündnis gegen Preußen — the alliance of the four kings against Prussia; Austrian protests of 26 and 28 November; Bruck’s memorandum of 30 September 1849 on an Austro-German customs union; the Four-Kings’ alliance of 27 February 1850. VI. Das Erfurter Parlament — Radowitz’s conversations with Kübeck and Schönhals; the adoption of the federal constitution by the Erfurt parliament. VII. Wiederherstellung der Frankfurter Bundesversammlung — the restoration of the Frankfort Federal Diet; the Austro-Saxon agreement; Austria’s invitation to the federal congress (26 April); the congress of princes at Berlin; the opening of the Frankfort congress on 10 May; Bruck’s memorandum of 30 May 1850; armaments and danger of war.
Zweites Buch — Die deutsche Politik des Fürsten Schwarzenberg (Fortsetzung) (The German Policy of Prince Schwarzenberg, continued)
I. Erste Zusammenkunft in Warschau — the first meeting at Warsaw; the Tsar’s mediating attitude and Schwarzenberg’s dissatisfaction. II. Letzte Ausgleichsversuche — last attempts at compromise; Austria demanding the abolition of the Union constitution; Schwarzenberg’s offer to Bernstorff (8 July); the six points. III. Zusammenstoß wegen Holsteins und Kurhessens — the collision over Holstein and Hesse-Cassel; the battle of Idstedt; the London Protocol of 4 July; the constitutional dispute in Hesse-Cassel; the meeting and treaty of Bregenz. IV. Zweite Zusammenkunft in Warschau. Entlassung des Generals Radowitz — the second meeting at Warsaw and the dismissal of Radowitz; Brandenburg at Warsaw (17 October); the entry of the federal corps into Hesse-Cassel; Brandenburg’s return to Berlin and the Prussian ministerial council of 2 November; Radowitz’s resignation.
V. Kriegsgefahr — the danger of war; the Prussian mobilization of 6 November; the collision at Bronzell; Schwarzenberg’s offer of a common reactionary policy; Austria’s ultimatum; the proposal of a meeting at Olmütz. VI. Die Rüstungen Österreichs — Austria’s armaments; the organization of the Austrian army; the misplaced deployment of the Prussian forces; Heß’s war plan; Radetzky and the Austrian generals; the attitude of Russia, England, and France. VII. Olmütz — the meeting at Olmütz, 28 and 29 November 1850; the agreements (Punktation); the attitude of Francis Joseph; Schwarzenberg’s motives for yielding. VIII. Die Dresdener Konferenz — the Dresden Conference; the opening of the conferences on 24 December; Prussia’s insuperable resistance; the secret alliance between Austria and Prussia of 16 May 1851; the results.
Drittes Buch — Schwarzenberg auf der Höhe des Erfolges. Sein Tod. (Schwarzenberg at the Height of His Success. His Death.)
I. Österreich und die Großmächte — Austria and the great powers; Palmerston’s interference in Austrian affairs; the peaceful attitude of Queen Victoria; Palmerston and the Hungarian emigrants; Haynau in London; Palmerston’s approval of the French coup d’état and his dismissal; Schwarzenberg for Prince Napoleon; Austria and France against England. II. Österreichs Übergewicht in Deutschland — Austria’s predominance in Germany; the Federal Diet’s steps against the liberal German constitutions; Bernstorff, Manteuffel, and Vitzthum on Austria; Heinrich and Max von Gagern. III. Schwarzenberg, Metternich und Kübeck — a comparison of the politics of Metternich and Schwarzenberg; Metternich’s return to Vienna; Metternich and Kübeck against Schwarzenberg; Duke Ernst of Coburg in Vienna. IV. Schwarzenbergs Tod. Sein Charakter — Schwarzenberg’s illness and death (5 April 1852); Grillparzer’s epitaph; Laube, Metternich, and Wessenberg on Schwarzenberg; a comparison of Schwarzenberg with Bismarck.
Viertes Buch — Die Erbschaft nach dem Fürsten Schwarzenberg. Reaktion (1852–1854) (The Inheritance after Prince Schwarzenberg. Reaction, 1852–1854)
I. Kübeck und Bach — the emperor’s wish to make Bach minister-president; the resistance of Kübeck, Metternich, and Grünne; the post left unfilled; the creation of the Supreme Police Authority; the ministerial conference of 14 April 1852; the Tsar in Vienna (May 1852); Kübeck as the leading figure; Bach’s suppleness; Bach throwing himself into the arms of the Church. II. Innere Verwaltung — internal administration; the organization of 1853; the bureaucracy; the curtailment of communal autonomy. III. Justizwesen — the judiciary; Justice Minister Karl Krauß; the abolition of trial by jury; the criminal code of 1852; corporal punishment. IV. Polizeiherrschaft — police rule; Kempen as police minister; denunciations; the suppression of the press; conspiracies; the attempted assassination of the emperor by Libényi (18 February 1853).
V. Aufhebung des Belagerungszustandes — the lifting of the state of siege; the amnesties; Bach rising again; Kübeck’s death.
Fünftes Buch — Die Zeit des Krimkrieges (The Time of the Crimean War)
I. Buols Politik gegenüber Frankreich — the career of Count Buol; the erection of the French Empire; Francis Joseph in Berlin (January 1852); Bismarck on Buol. II. Die österreichische Herrschaft über Italien — Austrian rule over Italy; fines in Lombardy; Mazzini; the conspiracy and executions at Mantua; the Milan rising of 6 February 1853; Radetzky’s administration; Count Rechberg at Milan; the breach between Austria and Piedmont. III. Der montenegrinische Streitfall — the Montenegrin dispute; the war between Turkey and Montenegro; Austria’s intervention and ultimatum. IV. Der Krimkrieg — the Crimean War; Russia’s claim to the protectorate over the Christians of the Ottoman Empire; the Russian army crossing the Danube; Hübner and Prokesch-Osten against Russia; Bruck’s view; Austria’s alliance with Prussia of 20 April 1854; Austria demanding the evacuation of the Danubian Principalities; the end of the Austro-Russian alliance; Buol and Bach against Russia; mobilization and demobilization; Bruck made finance minister; the Congress of Paris; Austria evacuating the Principalities; Bismarck on Buol’s policy.
Sechstes Buch — Der Kaiser, der Hof, die soziale Schichtung (The Emperor, the Court, the Social Structure)
I. Kaiser Franz Joseph — Bismarck, Leopold I of Belgium, Gerlach, and Kübeck on Francis Joseph; his outward bearing; his knowledge of state affairs; his changes of mind. II. Die kaiserliche Familie — the imperial family; the emperor’s father; Archduchess Sophie; the Libényi attempt; Empress Elisabeth; the archdukes Ferdinand Max, Johann, and Stephan. III. Grünne und Heß — the adjutant-general Count Grünne; Heß as chief of the general staff; Empress Elisabeth and Grünne. IV. Die Aristokratie — the aristocracy; the legal position of the nobility; Prince Alfred Windischgrätz; Prince Friedrich Schwarzenberg, the “Landsknecht” (“lansquenet” / mercenary); historical right; Baron Andrian; the Estates opposition in Styria and Tyrol; a comparison of Austrian absolutism with the rule of Napoleon I.
V. Der dritte Stand — the third estate; the landholding peasant; the propertied bourgeoisie; the Jews; large industry and high finance; the House of Rothschild; social life in Vienna; the salons; the coffee-houses and clubs; social development and the nationalities.
Siebentes Buch — Geistiges Leben in Deutsch-Österreich (Intellectual Life in German Austria)
I. Grundlagen (1815–1848) — the wealth and limits of Austrian culture; intellectual pressure; political poetry; the end of Old Vienna and the beginning of the Vormärz; the general disappointment after the revolution. II. Musik — music; the Vienna Court Opera; Lanner and Strauß; the second half of the century. III. Lyrik — lyric poetry. IV. Erzählende Dichtung — narrative fiction; Sealsfield; Kürnberger; the time-novels; Stifter.
V. Politische Dichtung — political poetry; Grillparzer; Zedlitz, Marsano, Hartmann; Bauernfeld, Beck. VI. Presse — the press; the newspapers before 1848; Bäuerle and Saphir; Jáng; Kuranda; Warrens; Schwarzer, Schuselka, Friedmann; the feuilleton; the Allgemeine Zeitung.
Achtes Buch — Geistiges Leben in Deutsch-Österreich (Das Burgtheater und die dramatische Dichtung) (Intellectual Life in German Austria: The Burgtheater and Dramatic Poetry)
I. Das Burgtheater — the Burgtheater; Joseph II as its refounder; Schreyvogel as director; Laube as director. II. Die österreichischen Dramatiker — the Austrian dramatists; Friedrich Halm; Bauernfeld. III. Friedrich Hebbel in Wien — Friedrich Hebbel in Vienna; his political views; Gyges und sein Ring; the Nibelungen trilogy. IV. Grillparzers letzte Schöpfungen — Grillparzer’s last works; his autobiography; his testament; Libussa; Ein Bruderzwist in Habsburg; Die Jüdin von Toledo; the significance of the theatre for Austria.
Neuntes Buch — Geistiges Leben in Deutsch-Österreich (Das Volksstück) (Intellectual Life in German Austria: The Popular Play)
The three popular theatres in Vienna; the fairy play; Director Carl; Director Franz Pokorny; Friedrich Kaiser; Elmar; Berla, Langer; O. F. Berg; Johann Nestroy; Die Freiheit in Krähwinkel; Nestroy and the March revolution; the character of the Viennese popular play.
Zehntes Buch — Die bildenden Künste. Wiener Stadterweiterung (The Visual Arts. The Vienna City Expansion)
I. Die Zeit vor 1848 — art in the eighteenth century; monumental art under Emperor Francis and at Prague; Nobile; Sprenger; the Romantic; Peter Krafft; Danhauser; Waldmüller; the character of the Old-Vienna school of painting; Moritz von Schwind; Steinle. II. Die bildenden Künste von 1848 bis 1865 — the visual arts from 1848 to 1865; the Altlerchenfeld church in Vienna; Leo and Franz Thun; Ruben; Waldmüller’s dismissal; Friedrich Schmidt; Ferstel; Führich and his school; Van der Nüll and Siccardsburg; sculpture; Fernkorn; Hans Gasser; Pettenkofen, Leopold Müller; Rahl. III. Die Wiener Stadterweiterung — the Vienna city expansion; the imperial rescript of 20 December 1857; the first plan of regulation; military considerations; the court museums; the building over of the parade ground.
Elftes Buch — Kirchliches Leben bis zur Aufhebung der Gesetze Josephs II. 1850 (Ecclesiastical Life down to the Abrogation of the Laws of Joseph II, 1850)
I. Die Kirchenpolitik Josephs II. — the church policy of Joseph II; the so-called revocation of the Josephine legislation; Leopold II. II. Die Kirche unter Kaiser Franz und Kaiser Ferdinand — the Church under Emperors Francis and Ferdinand; the alliance of the state power with Rome; Staatsrat Martin Lorenz, Burgpfarrer Jakob Frint; Staatsrat Alois Jüstel; the canon-law teacher Dolliner. III. Bernard Bolzano — Friedrich Hurter as imperial historiographer; Bolzano’s philosophy; the persecution of Bolzano; his relations with Anna Hoffmann. IV. Die Romantik. Klemens Maria Hoffbauer — the Romantic movement in Vienna; the life of Clemens Maria Hoffbauer; Hoffbauer in Warsaw; his personality.
V. Antonio Rosmini. Anton Günther — liberal Catholicism; the life of Rosmini; the spread of Günther’s philosophy; orthodoxy against Günther. VI. Joh. Emanuel Veith. Erzbischof Milde — Veith’s youth and conversion; Veith as cathedral preacher at St. Stephen’s; liberal Catholicism; Archbishop Milde; Veith and the revolution of 1848. VII. Die Bischofsversammlung von 1849. Kardinal Schwarzenberg. Rauscher — the bishops’ assembly of 1849; the demand for the freedom of the Catholic Church; the constitution of 4 March 1849; Cardinal Friedrich Schwarzenberg; Joseph Othmar Rauscher and his opinions for the state chancellor; the bishops’ assembly at Vienna. VIII. Graf Leo Thun. Der Sieg der Bischöfe — Count Leo Thun; the union of the cults and instruction ministries; the attitude of Pius IX during the revolution; the opinions of Helfert and Ignaz Beidtel; the attitude of Schmerling and Bach; the emperor’s decision.
IX. Der Fall des Josephinismus — the fall of Josephinism; the imperial ordinances of 18 and 23 April 1850: the abrogation of the placetum regium, the restoration of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, the order of divine service, theological and religious instruction; the Concordat of 18 August 1855; the rule and freedom of the Church.
Rückblick — Retrospect
Friedjung’s closing retrospective on the period.
Anhang — Appendices
Anhang I — Letters of Prince Felix Schwarzenberg (Nos. 1–28). Anhang II — Acta 1850–1852 (Nos. 29–41), including No. 42 on the Vienna city expansion. Anhang III — A note on an alleged saying of Prince Felix Schwarzenberg, “Avilir puis démolir”.
