sources/gruenwald-az-uj-magyarorszag-sze.title: Grünwald — Az új Magyarország: Gróf Széchenyi István
sources/gruenwald-az-uj-magyarorszag-sze.content:
Grünwald — Az új Magyarország: Gróf Széchenyi István
Grünwald Béla (1839–1891) — Az új Magyarország: Gróf Széchenyi István (The New Hungary: Count István Széchenyi). — Budapest: Franklin-Társulat, 1890.
A psychobiographical study of Count István Széchenyi (1791–1860), the reformer widely called “the greatest Hungarian,” written as the second part of the author’s larger examination of modern Hungary. Grünwald explains in the preface that, while the outward course of Széchenyi’s public life was already known from the earlier works of Baron Zsigmond Kemény and Miksa Falk, his inner life could not previously be illuminated because the content of Széchenyi’s Diaries (Naplók) was still unpublished; now that the diaries — kept nearly every day for thirty-four years — had become accessible, they supplied the material, with the help of psychiatry, to reveal the interior man.
The work therefore combines a psychological portrait with a political assessment. It traces Széchenyi’s physical constitution and nervous disposition, his friendships and loves, his recurring despair and life-weariness, and the love of the Hungarian race that gave his life its purpose; it then weighs his place in the national reform movement against Kossuth and the opposition, and closes with an extended examination of his celebrated prophecy addressed to Kossuth and of the meaning of 1848 for the Hungarian nation.
The book is cast as a series of fifteen numbered essays. The text is approximately 550 pages, extracted from a University of California, Berkeley copy (Anna’s Archive), followed by an errata (Sajtóhibák) page.
Content Summary
I. — The opening essay: the epoch-making individual and the law that new eras are embodied in powerful personalities; the maxim that only the weak love themselves, while the strong carry whole nations in their hearts. II. — The great passion ruling Széchenyi’s life: his love of the Hungarian race, and the single thought of elevating the Hungarian nation and securing its future. III. — His physical constitution: healthy, vigorous and enduring in youth, a gifted rider, fencer and swimmer; his long life and the autopsy following his death in 1860. IV. — His sickly, sensitive nervous system, the source alike of his agonies and of his exalted states.
V. — A nature of action rather than contemplation; his mind formed for practical undertakings. VI. — His longing for noble friendship and the difficulty ordinary men had in understanding him. VII. — His capacity for friendship and love; Miklós Wesselényi as his first deep friend; the love he found only in his thirty-fourth year. VIII. — The insufficiency of private life; his sense of emptiness and the search for a great purpose.
IX. — The dark depths of his nature — life-weariness and despair; the sources of his anguish in religion, art, friendship and love; and the noblest passion, the love of nation, compelling him to devote his life to his people. X. — His high cultural, national and moral ideals; his horror at the condition of the old Hungary; the setting of national rebirth as the goal of his life. XI. — His dark view of the nation’s condition; how contemporaries came to regard him as a pessimist. XII. — The years of work in associations and societies before he began his publicistic career; the need to reach the whole nation through the press.
XIII. — The deep effect of his appearance on the nation; the exceptional, original personality and the ferment he aroused in men’s minds. XIV. — The great movement toward realizing national interests as the strict logical consequence of Széchenyi’s ideas; the end of stagnation and the awakening of public spirit. XV. — The conclusion: the celebrated prophecy addressed to Kossuth in the Politikai Programmtöredékek (“Political Programme Fragments”), and Grünwald’s judgment that it was not fulfilled — the social revolution it foretold never came, and the Hungarian nobility abolished its own privileges freely and peacefully. The essay then reconciles the two conflicting interpretations of 1848 and joins the glory of Széchenyi and Kossuth as one idea in two stages: “Széchenyi is the beginning of Kossuth, Kossuth the continuation of Széchenyi.” It ends by affirming that Széchenyi’s great achievement was a nation raised up from its decline and ennobled, and that he belonged to the strong who carry whole nations in their hearts.
Note on the text: The OCR is Hungarian, printed in Roman type, with diacritics partly simplified or dropped; it renders the long German-influenced orthography of the 1890 edition. Running headers repeat the uniform line “Grünwald: Új Magyarország” on the pages captured. The volume has no printed table of contents; the numbered essays (I–XV) serve as its divisions, and a brief errata page (Sajtóhibák) follows the conclusion.
What Grünwald supplies
Béla Grünwald’s work on the “new Hungary” and the Széchenyi problem is a Hungarian-language deposit for reform conservatism and the magnate-led modernisation programme before and beside 1848. In this wiki it balances Kossuth-centred revolutionary narratives with the older bridge-and-academy reform current.
Narrative use
Széchenyi’s programme. Economic improvement, river and transport works, social reform from above, cautious constitutionalism—set against both Vienna’s distrust and Pest radicalism.
Clash of methods. Where Kossuth mobilises county and press politics toward rupture, Széchenyi fears that rupture wrecks the reform capital already invested. Grünwald’s framing helps entity pages state that quarrel in period terms.
1848 threshold. How reform conservatism fractures when revolution and war demand choices Széchenyi’s gradualism cannot own.
Limit
Use for Hungarian reform debate texture; for military 1848–49 still prefer Friedjung/Springer and the Hungarian war pages. Glosses: keep HU names with English gloss on first use.

sources/helfert-geschichte-oesterreichis.title: Helfert — Geschichte der österreichischen Revolution, Vol. I: Bis zur österreichischen Verfassung vom 25. April 1848
sources/helfert-geschichte-oesterreichis.content:
Helfert — Geschichte der österreichischen Revolution, Vol. I: Bis zur österreichischen Verfassung vom 25. April 1848
Joseph Alexander Freiherr von Helfert (1820–1910) — Geschichte der österreichischen Revolution im Zusammenhange mit der mitteleuropäischen Bewegung der Jahre 1848–1849. Erster Band: Bis zur österreichischen Verfassung vom 25. April 1848. — Freiburg im Breisgau und Wien: Herdersche Verlagshandlung, 1907. Also published in Berlin, Karlsruhe, München, Straßburg, and St. Louis, Mo.
The first volume of Helfert’s monumental history of the Austrian revolution of 1848, written in old age as the culmination of a lifetime of work on the subject. Helfert, who had served as a contemporary witness and in part an active participant in the events he describes, had published his Revolution und Reaktion im Spätjahre 1848 (Prague 1870) as the second part of an earlier Geschichte Österreichs vom Ausgange des Wiener Oktoberaufstandes 1848; he here recasts the whole story as a complete history of the Austrian revolution in connection with the central-European movement of 1848–1849. The first volume carries the narrative from the background of the revolutionary decades down to the octroyed constitution granted at Vienna on 25 April 1848.
In the Vorwort Helfert defends the very conception of so late an undertaking, comparing his project to Macaulay’s history of England and insisting that the reader never lose sight of the fact that it is history, something past, that is here set before him. He notes that much of the material had first appeared, in tested form, in the Österreichisches Jahrbuch for 1900–1903, and acknowledges the help of the director of the Mantuan state archive, A. Luzio, and others. He explains that he has deliberately kept to the orthography of the time — Jellačić and Rajačić, not Jellachich and Rajachich; Teleky as well as Teleki, Esterházy as well as Eszterházy; Bačka and Pančevo alternating with the Hungarian Bacska and Pancsova; the medieval names Stanchich and Černojevich becoming the Magyars Táncsics and Csernovics — the orthographic burden of a historian treating a revolution that touched no fewer than ten of the empire’s languages.
The volume opens with a Chronologische Übersicht (chronological survey) running from June 1846 to April 1848, keyed by page number to the narrative, and closes with the documentary appendix (Anhang) and the name, place, and subject registers.
Content Summary
I. Videbis, mi fili, quam pusilla sapientia regitur mundus
“Thou shalt see, my son, how little wisdom governs the world” (the motto, from the letters attributed to Sallust, that Metternich had adopted as his own). The opening chapter surveys the state of the central-European lands before the revolution: the contradictions in which the newer history of these countries moved — in the state, the church, and the social order — and the legacy of the Congress era, the Restaurationsperiode (“restoration period”) that followed the wars of Napoleon. Helfert sets the stage of Mißbehagen und Mißvergnügen (“discontent and disquiet”), the discontent and disquiet that had accumulated beneath the surface of the restored order.
II. Im Herzen von Europa
“In the Heart of Europe.” The Austrian Empire and its peculiar place at the center of the continent — the empire that, as Helfert quotes, if it did not already exist, would have to be created in the interest of Europe and of humanity itself. The chapter examines the structure of the polyglot monarchy on the eve of 1848.
III. Wolken am politischen Horizont
“Clouds on the Political Horizon.” The gathering signs of crisis across the empire in the years before the revolution — economic hardship, the Not und Teuerung (distress and dearness of food) that afflicted central Europe, the stirrings of the nationalities, and the darkening outlook.
IV. Gewitterschwüle
“Sultriness Before the Storm.” The mounting tension of the winter of 1847–1848, when a general uneasiness settled over Austria and Italy, and the crisis thickened toward the outbreak.
V. Die dritte französische Revolution
“The Third French Revolution.” The February revolution of 1848 in Paris and the fall of Louis Philippe, and its reverberations across the continent.
VI. „Völkerfrühling“
“The Springtime of Peoples.” The opening of the revolutionary year in the Austrian lands and in Italy — the student disturbances at Padua, the Milanese deputation to the archduke-viceroy, Tommaseo’s audience with Kübeck in Venice, the outbreak at Messina, and the risings that followed the March revolution.
VII. Mitteleuropäische Revolution
“The Central-European Revolution.” The March revolution proper in Vienna and across central Europe — the Aula rising of the students, the fall of Metternich, the risings at Cassel and in the Hohenzollern lands, the proclamation of the constitution, the Austrian free corps marching on Italy (“Auf nach Italien!”), the March days in Berlin, the outbreak in Milan, and the stirring of the German question (Schwarz-rot-gold against Schwarz-gelb), the press law of 1 April, the student committee, and the first constitutional experiments.
VIII. „Annus confusionis“
“The Year of Confusion.” The confused and crowded weeks of the revolution — the Polish question in Galicia and the Lemberg deputation, the Bohemian question and the position of the Czechs, and the widening national and political turmoil of the spring.
IX. Verfassung
“Constitution.” The framing and proclamation of the octroyed constitution of 25 April 1848 — the Verfassungsurkunde des österreichischen Kaiserstaates — and the reception of the constitution in Vienna. The chapter closes the main narrative of the volume.
Anhang (Appendix)
Seven documents appended to the volume:
I. Der vormärzliche Rassen- und Sprachenkampf in Ungarn — Zeitgenössische Stimmen und Urteile; contemporary voices and judgments on the pre-March racial and linguistic struggle in Hungary, on the maxim that “every Magyar is a Hungarian, but not every Hungarian is a Magyar,” the Magyars’ treatment of the other nationalities, Magharismus (“Magyarism”), Die Deutschen in Ungarn (“the Germans of Hungary”), Júyrismus (“Illyrism”), and Gaj und Kollar (the Illyrian movement and the pan-Slavism of Gaj and Kollár). II. Oberstleutnant Graf Johann Wratislaw an Grafen Huyn — a letter of Lieutenant-Colonel Count Johann Wratislaw to Count Huyn reporting on the revolutionary news from Paris reaching Italy in February 1848. III. W(ratislaw) — a further dispatch of the same officer. IV. Rundschreiben der k. k. Haus-, Hof- und Staatskanzlei — the circular of the imperial chancellery on the concessions granted by His Majesty.
V. Verzeichnis der Mitglieder der Lemberger Adreßdeputation — the list of the members of the Lemberg address-deputation. VI. Feldzeugmeister Graf Mazzucchelli an Minister Pillersdorff — the field-marshal-lieutenant’s communication to the minister Franz von Pillersdorff. VII. Verfassungsurkunde des österreichischen Kaiserstaates — the text of the constitution of the Austrian Empire of 25 April 1848.
The volume closes with the name register (Personenregister), place register (Ortsregister), and subject register (Sachregister), followed by a separate index of the army units named in the text.
Note on the text: The OCR is German Fraktur with the original long-s (ſ), which renders correctly in the raw text. The opening chronological survey and the closing registers are keyed by page number to the body. The appendix matter follows the main nine chapters. Helfert deliberately preserves the spellings of 1848 — Jellačić, Pillersdorff (also Pillersdorf), Széchenyi, Kossuth — rather than later orthography. Place-names appear in their nineteenth-century German forms. Approximately 560 pages of extracted text from a University of Minnesota scan.
Notes on form
Bullet inventory flattened to continuous English narration (2026-08-16). Prefer native term (“English”) glosses on institutional keywords when thickening from raw.

sources/kornilov-kurs-istorii-rossii-ch1.title: Kornilov — Course of Russian History in the 19th Century, Parts 1 and 2
sources/kornilov-kurs-istorii-rossii-ch1.content:
Kornilov — Course of Russian History in the 19th Century, Parts 1 and 2
A. A. Kornilov (1862–1925) — Курс истории России XIX века (Kurs istorii Rossii XIX veka, “Course of Russian History in the 19th Century”), Часть I и Часть II (Chast’ I i Chast’ II, “Parts I and II”). — Second edition. — Moscow: M. and S. Sabashnikov Publishers, 1918.
The course is based on lectures given by the author in 1910–1912 at the Higher Women’s Courses, the Shanyavsky People’s University, and the Moscow Commercial Institute. The first edition appeared in 1912–1914; the second edition is substantially revised. The author taught at Kazan University (1889–1892), then at the Petersburg Technological Institute and the Higher Women’s Courses; from 1909 at Moscow University.
The course consists of three parts. Part I (283 pp.) covers the general character of Russia toward the end of the eighteenth century and the reigns of Paul I and Alexander I. Part II (272 pp.) is devoted to the reign of Nicholas I and the first years of Alexander II (to 1866). Part III (the reactionary period 1866 – famine of 1891–92; lectures XXVII–XLI) was issued separately (2nd ed., 1918) and is placed in the Rest of Europe 1866–1919 wiki. In the preface to Part III (1914) the author still allowed for a fourth part (the last years of the nineteenth century and the opening of the twentieth down to 1904–1906), but it does not appear to have been published.
Character of the course. Kornilov belongs to the liberal-populist school of Russian historiography. The course is attentive to socio-economic processes, the peasant question, the history of social thought and enlightenment. The author strives for objectivity, yet with a clear sympathy for reforms and progressive currents. The exposition is lecture-style, with detailed discussion of sources and historical literature.
Pre-reform orthography (yat, fita, izhitsa, hard sign at word ends). OCR quality — medium, with scan artifacts (Ѣ/Е, І/И confusion, etc.).
Raw volumes: Part I ~1.14 MB, 13,769 lines; Part II ~1.08 MB, 13,643 lines. Lectures I–XIII (Part I) and XIV–XXVI (Part II).

Part I — Lectures I–XIII
Lecture I. General character of the socio-political process of development of the Russian people and state down to the end of the eighteenth century
The struggle for territory and its socio-political results. Principal features of the new socio-political process of development of the Russian people and state as they appeared at the end of the eighteenth century.
Lecture II. The position of Russia at the end of the eighteenth century, in the reign of Catherine II
The frontiers of the state. Significance of Catherine’s territorial acquisitions. Routes of communication. Population. Racial composition. Estate-class composition of the population. Position of the various categories of peasants. Urban estates. The clergy. The nobility. The intelligentsia and the popular masses. Development of enlightenment and the origin of the Russian intelligentsia. The schism — раскол (raskol, “schism” of Old Believers). Position of state power and its organs. Finances.
Lecture III. The reign of Paul I
His place in history. Biographical data. General character of Paul’s governmental activity. The peasant question under Paul. Paul’s attitude toward the other estates. Society’s attitude toward Paul. The position of the finances and foreign policy. Results.
Lecture IV. The reign of Alexander I (Introduction)
Division of the reign into periods. Biographical data. Alexander’s upbringing. His marriage. His position under Catherine and in the reign of Paul. Works relating to the history of Alexander I before his accession.
Lecture V. The first years of Alexander I
Accession. Mood and degree of preparation. First collaborators and measures taken in the first three months. Work of the Unofficial Committee. Its composition. Plan of work. Discussion of political reform. The peasant question. Formation of the ministries and transformation of the Senate. Results of the Unofficial Committee’s work.
Lecture VI. Society and economy in 1801–1805
Mood of society at the beginning of the reign and the level of political views. Principal journals of 1802–1805. Position of the popular masses. The free cultivators law of 20 February 1803. Peasant reform in the Baltic provinces in 1804 and 1805. Population growth. Colonization of the southern provinces. The Jewish question. The government’s attitude toward sectarians. Russian finances and financial policy in 1801–1805. The question of state transformations in 1803. The government’s educational activity.
Lecture VII. The second period of Alexander’s reign (1805–1807)
Russia’s international position at the beginning of the nineteenth century. The break with Napoleon. Czartoryski’s plans and Alexander’s attitude toward the Poles in 1805. Unsuccessful outcome of the campaign of 1805. The war of 1806–1807. The crushing of Prussia. Extraordinary preparations for war with Napoleon in Russia. The winter campaign of 1807. The Peace of Tilsit. The alliance with Napoleon and the sharp discontent in Russia caused by the Peace of Tilsit and its consequences. Opposition mood in society.
Lecture VIII. Speransky’s reforms
Alexander’s decision to return to internal transformations in 1809. M. M. Speransky. Drafting of the plan of state transformation. Beginning of its realization: establishment of the State Council and transformation of the ministries. The decree on examinations for ranks and on court titles. Desperate condition of Russian finances in 1809–1810. Speransky’s financial plan. Karamzin’s memoir On Ancient and New Russia. Fall of Speransky. Position of the cause of public instruction. Opening of learned societies.
Lecture IX. The Patriotic War of 1812 and the Foreign Campaigns
Immediate causes of the war of 1812. The break with Napoleon. Relative strength of the belligerents and the plan of war. General course of military operations. Mood of the army and people in Russia. Napoleon’s position before Moscow and in Moscow. Expulsion of the enemy. Alexander’s triumph. Transfer of the war to Western Europe. The campaign of 1813–1814. The overthrow of Napoleon. The Congress of Vienna. Alexander’s plans regarding Poland and Prussia. Talleyrand’s intrigues and quarrels among the allies. Settlement of the Polish question. Alexander’s mystical mood and the idea of the Holy Alliance.
Lecture X. Russia after 1815
Alexander’s return to Russia in 1816. The Polish Constitution of 1815. Condition of affairs in Russia in 1812–1815. Calamities and material sacrifices of the population. Cost of the war and scale of devastation. Condition of Russian finances. Rise of the national spirit. Condition of industry and trade. Influence of officers returning from the war on society. Spread of enlightenment in the provinces. Society’s hopes of Alexander. His mood in 1816. Concern for the maintenance of the army. The idea of military settlements, their origin and realization. Arakcheev. His characterization. Course of business in the Committee of Ministers and the exposure of abuses in 1816. Arakcheev’s role.
Lecture XI. Internal policy 1816–1825 (part 1)
Role of the State Council during the wars of 1812–1815. Restoration of its importance in 1816 with the return of Admiral Mordvinov. Mordvinov’s activity and the financial measures of 1816–1820. The customs tariffs of 1816–1819 and their significance. Development of factory industry under Alexander I. The peasant question in 1816–1820. Emancipation of the Baltic peasants. Development of enlightenment after 1812. Role of the universities. Penetration of mystical currents. The Bible Society. The Ministry of Spiritual Affairs and Public Instruction. Prince A. N. Golitsyn and his associates: Sturdza, Magnitsky, and Runich. The wrecking of the universities. Journalism after 1815 and the position of the press. Alexander’s mood in 1818–1820. His speech at the Polish Sejm.
Lecture XII. Secret societies
Emergence of secret societies after the Napoleonic wars. The Union of Salvation. The statute. Pestel and Mikhail Muraviev. Opposition of Mikhail Muraviev and transformation of the Union of Salvation into the Union of Welfare. Its statute, organization, and activity under four “branches.” Outbreak of indignation against Alexander in 1817. The question of a republic in 1820. Influence of the “Semenovsky affair,” the second Polish Sejm, and the Neapolitan revolution. Closure of the Union of Welfare. The Southern Society. Pestel’s activity. The Vasilkov board. The Society of United Slavs. The Northern Society. Nikita Muraviev’s Constitution and Pestel’s Русская правда (Russkaya Pravda, “Russian Justice / Truth”).
Lecture XIII. The last years of Alexander I
The emperor’s mood and activity after 1820. Accord with Metternich. Role of the Holy Alliance. The Greek rising and Alexander’s attitude toward it. Internal policy in 1820–1825. Abandonment of transformations. Dominance of obscurantism. Photius and Golitsyn’s resignation. Attitude toward the Polish constitution. Position of the finances. The customs tariff of 1822 and the appointment of Kankrin as minister of finance. Results of the reign.

Part II — Lectures XIV–XXVI
Lecture XIV. The reign of Nicholas I — accession and 14 December 1825
Conditions under which Nicholas came to the throne. The question of the succession. Alexander’s unpublished manifesto on Constantine’s renunciation. Confusion and interregnum. Nicholas’s negotiations with Constantine. Nicholas’s accession. The rising of 14 December 1825 and its suppression. Personality of Nicholas. Biographical particulars. Investigation of the secret societies. Reckoning with the Decembrists. Influence of Karamzin and the programme of the reign inspired by him.
Lecture XV. The first period of the reign of Nicholas I (1825–1831)
Collaborators of Nicholas Pavlovich in the early years: Kochubey, Speransky, Kankrin, Benckendorff, Dibich, Paskevich. The Committee of 6 December 1826; its composition, task, and activity. The peasant question. Military settlements. Speransky’s codification work. Formation of the Second Section of His Majesty’s Own Chancery. Direction of the Ministry of Public Instruction. Attitude toward the Polish constitution. Foreign policy. War with Turkey 1828–1829. The Polish rising of 1830–1831.
Lecture XVI. The second period of the reign of Nicholas I (1831–1840s)
Conservative principles in foreign policy. The Eastern Question. The Münchengrätz meeting. Guiding principles in internal policy. Legislative work. Speransky’s activity in preparing and publishing the Свод законов (Svod zakonov, “Digest of Laws”). The peasant question. Condition of the population. Material factors that prepared the fall of serfdom. Secret committees. Work of Kankrin and Kiselev on the arrangement of state peasants. Establishment of the Ministry of State Domains. Kiselev’s work on the arrangement of serf peasants. The law of 1842 on obligated peasants. Inventories in the western provinces.
Lecture XVII. Industry and finances under Nicholas I
Development of industry. Fate of individual branches of manufacturing industry. Competition of Polish industry. Merchants’ complaints. Kankrin’s activity. His principles and policy. Protectionism and its influence. Reduction of the growth of military expenditure. The wars of 1827–1831. The liquor reform. The monetary reform of 1839–1843. Nicholas’s own role. Kankrin’s concern for the improvement of cultural conditions.
Lecture XVIII. Enlightenment and social thought under Nicholas I
The system of public instruction. Nicholas’s views. Uvarov’s ministry. His principles. The statutes of 28 December 1828. The university statute of 1835. Moscow University under Stroganov. Position and development of the intelligentsia. Significance of the catastrophe of 14 December. Two channels of ideas: French and German. Schellingianism in Russia. Mnemosyne. The Lyubomudry and the Moskovsky Vestnik. Polevoy’s Moskovsky Telegraf. Nadezhdin’s Teleskop. Chaadaev and the closing of the Teleskop. Idealists of the 1830s. Stankevich’s circle. Bakunin and Belinsky. Evolution of Belinsky. Otechestvennye Zapiski and Sovremennik. Moskvityanin and the system of “official nationality.” Slavophiles and Westernizers in the 1840s. Socialism and Left Hegelianism. The schism and sectarianism.
Lecture XIX. The year 1848 and the third period of Nicholas I
The revolutions of 1848 in Europe and their influence on Nicholas. The third period of the reign. Foreign policy. Manifesto of 14 March 1848. The Hungarian campaign. Internal policy. The peasant question. Measures against the press and the universities. Uvarov’s resignation. Prince Shirinsky-Shakhmatov. Position of the intelligentsia. History of the Petrashevtsy. Incidents with Samarin, Aksakov, Turgenev. Prohibition on Slavophiles appearing in print. The Kiev federalists. The Eastern (Crimean) War of 1853–1856. Inevitability of the crisis. Death of Nicholas. General conclusion on the reign.
Lecture XX. The reign of Alexander II — Beginning of the peasant reform
The Crimean War and its significance. Characterization of Alexander Nikolaevich. His upbringing and political views. Influence of the Crimean War. First steps of the reign. Mood of society in 1855–56. Conclusion of peace and the manifesto of 19 March 1856. Speech to the nobility in Moscow. Beginning of preparation of the peasant reform. Activity of Lanskoi and Levshin. Attitude of the nobility. Memoranda circulating from hand to hand. Formation of the Secret Committee. Ya. I. Rostovtsev. Petition of the Lithuanian nobles and the rescript of 20 November 1857 to Nazimov. The government’s programme.
Lecture XXI. Drafting of the peasant reform
Attitude of the nobility to the government programme. Difference of landowners’ interests in the black-earth agricultural and the northern industrial provinces. Attitude of the intelligentsia: articles of Chernyshevsky and Herzen; the banquet in Moscow. Address of the Nizhny Novgorod nobility. Opening and work of the provincial committees. Unkovsky and the Tver committee. The approved programme of work. Attitude of the press. Evolution of Rostovtsev’s views. Opening of the zemstvo section. N. A. Miliutin. Revision of the government programme. The Editorial Commissions. Composition and course of work. Rostovtsev’s programme. Deputies of the first and second invitation. Death of Rostovtsev. V. N. Panin.
Lecture XXII. The Statutes of 19 February 1861
Course of work in the Main Committee and the State Council. The struggle. Manifesto of 19 February 1861. Analysis of the Statutes of 19 February. Composition of the legislation and content of the individual Statutes. Significance of the reform in legal, administrative, and economic respects for the peasants, the nobility, and the state.
Lecture XXIII. Society and the press in the reform era
Influence of the drafting of the peasant reform on society and the press. Position of the press in 1855. Herzen’s exceptional position. His programme of 1855–1858. Role and significance of the Kolokol. Differentiation of currents in society and the press after 1858. Radicalization of the Sovremennik. The Russky Vestnik. Position of the Slavophiles. Social demands of 1859–61.
Lecture XXIV. The peasantry and the beginning of reaction
Attitude of the peasants to the reform of 19 February. Disturbances and disorders. The Bezdna catastrophe. Reaction in government circles in 1861. Valuev’s policy. First manifestations of nihilism. The Russkoe Slovo. Opposition mood of the nobility. The Tver affair of 1862. The constitutional movement. Mood of commercial-industrial circles.
Lecture XXV. Opposition, the Polish rising, and continuation of the reforms
Development of the opposition mood. Proclamations of 1861–62. Young Russia and the fires of 1862. Arrests and exile. Split between liberals and radicals. Herzen. The Polish movement. Policy of Marquis Wielopolski. The armed rising of 1863. Intervention of foreign powers. Outbreak of patriotism. Fall of the Kolokol. Triumph of Katkov. Continuation of the reforms: Tatarinov’s financial reforms, the excise reform. The university statute of 1863. Secondary schools, women’s education, elementary schools. The statute of 1864.
Lecture XXVI. The zemstvo and judicial reforms
The zemstvo reform, its connection with the peasant reform. Drafting and content. Attitude of the press and society. Conditions of the zemstvos’ work. The judicial reform — drafting, significance, content. First steps of the new courts. Legislation on the press. Vacillations of the government. Revision of the press laws. Temporary rules of 1865. Mood of the nobility in 1865. Address of the Moscow nobility. Komissarov’s attempt. End of the reform era and general conclusion.

Sources

Kornilov, A. A. Курс истории России XIX века. Part I. Second edition. Moscow: M. and S. Sabashnikov Publishers, 1918.
Kornilov, A. A. Курс истории России XIX века. Part II. Second edition. Moscow: M. and S. Sabashnikov Publishers, 1918.

sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol1.title: La Farina — Storia d'Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. I
sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol1.content:
La Farina — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. I
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850. Volume I. Seconda edizione corretta dall’autore. — Torino: Società Editrice Italiana, 1860.
La Farina, Sicilian man of letters and conspirator, former Carbonaro (“carbonaro of the Carboneria”), exile and later unitarian collaborator of Cavour in the Società Nazionale Italiana (“Italian National Society”), composed this multi-volume history as a national indictment of the Restoration settlement and a continuous narrative of Italian regeneration. Volume I of the 1860 second edition runs roughly six hundred fifty pages of Italian prose. It comprises a long Proemio (“prologue”) and two narrative books: Libro primo, from the map of 1815 through the revolutions of 1820–1821, and Libro secondo, from the Congress of Verona through May 1846. The raw OCR derives from an Anna’s Archive scan of a Widener/Harvard copy; title leaves show numeral noise (DAL 1845 AL 4850 for dal 1815 al 1850). The tone is openly patriotic, hostile to restored absolute courts, and impatient with those who treat Italian unity as a late fantasy of Giovine Italia (“Young Italy”).

Proemio — Dell’Italia e della rigenerazione italiana
The Proemio is philosophical history rather than bare chronology. La Farina opens on the pair Autorità and Libertà (“authority” and “liberty”), arguing that purely providential and purely sceptical readings of the past empty it of use. A “philosophical” school must distinguish general laws of the human spirit from contingent accidents. He treats the papacy as a historical principle of authority across centuries, then follows the progress of European mind in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the philosophy of the eighteenth, and the secret societies of the Liberi Muratori or Frammassoni (“Freemasons”) and the Illuminati. Eighteenth-century reforms and the Italian aftermath of the French Revolution prepare the ground for national consciousness. Separate chapters describe how Gioacchino Murat (“Joachim Murat”) sought to make himself king of a united Italy, and how independence projects flickered inside the Napoleonic Regno Italico (“Kingdom of Italy”) before Waterloo. The Proemio closes on the Congresso di Vienna (“Congress of Vienna”) and on the thesis of the whole work: after 1815 Italian history is the history of a people recovering self-knowledge under foreign hegemony and domestic absolutism.
La Farina’s intellectual genealogy is characteristic of mid-century patriotic historiography: Vico and the Italian illuministi stand beside French revolutionary memory; secret societies are read as midwives of public opinion rather than mere criminal bands. The Proemio thus licenses the later narrative’s moral vocabulary—honour, bad faith of princes, Austrian craft, and the duty of unity.

Libro I — The restoration and the first revolutions (1815–1821)
Italy after Vienna
Libro primo begins with a panoramic survey of the peninsula as the settlement of 1814–1815 left it. Austria held the Regno Lombardo-Veneto (“Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia”) as a crown land of the empire, with Milan and Venice reduced from capital cities of independent or quasi-independent polities to provincial seats under a viceroy and a military establishment. The House of Savoy recovered Piedmont, Nice, and Savoy and received Genoa, extinguishing the ancient republic; the resulting Stati Sardi (“Sardinian states”) became the only Italian monarchy with a continuous Alpine army tradition and later a constitutional vocation. The Pope recovered the dominio temporale (“temporal dominion”) of the Papal State, including the Legations of Bologna, Ferrara, and Ravenna. The Bourbons returned to Naples and Sicily as the Regno delle Due Sicilie (“Kingdom of the Two Sicilies”). Tuscany, Parma, Modena, and Lucca were restored or reassigned to Habsburg or related houses. La Farina’s early chapters treat each restoration in turn: the papal return and police order; Ferdinand of Bourbon’s re-entry into Naples and the “unfortunate end” of Murat; Sicily’s loss of the liberties associated with the British-period Costituzione siciliana del 1812 (“Sicilian Constitution of 1812”); Piedmontese reaction after Victor Emmanuel I’s return; Tuscan and ducal quiet; and the special bitterness of Lombard–Venetian government, whose evils, he insists, lay less in written law than in practices of police and German administration.
Carboneria and the southern revolution
Before 1820 the narrative turns to letters and società segrete (“secret societies”). La Farina presents the Carboneria (“carbonari secret societies”) as daughter of Freemasonry: symbols of the axe and charcoal-burners’ tools; members called cugini (“cousins”) rather than brothers; meeting-places vendite (“sales/lodges”) rather than lodges; recognition signs parallel to but not identical with Masonic ones. Final aims, revealed by degrees, were political liberty and, in many cells, Italian independence. The Neapolitan revolution of 1820 occupies the book’s centre. A military mutiny forced Ferdinand to accept a constitution on the Spanish model of 1812; a provisional authority yielded to a parliament that proclaimed the reform the will of the people, not of a sect. Parallel Sicilian revolution asserted island identity and was crushed by expedition under Florestano Pepe. Ferdinand was invited to the Congress of Laybach (Lubiana/Laibach); the Holy Alliance powers—Austria foremost—resolved on intervention; Austrian arms reimposed absolute monarchy. La Farina’s chapters follow the Neapolitan parliament to the king’s departure, the congress debates (with English reservations about Troppau principles), the invasion, Sicily after defeat, and Messina’s disorders. The moral is consistent: constitutional experiment was national aspiration destroyed by foreign arms and princely perjury.
Piedmont 1821
The rivoluzione piemontese (“Piedmontese revolution”) of 1821 closes Libro primo. Liberal officers and carbonari pressed Carlo Alberto of Carignano and the court toward a Spanish-style constitution and a national war in Lombardy. Victor Emmanuel I abdicated; Charles Albert’s brief regency and subsequent withdrawal, the failure of the rising, and Austrian pressure left Piedmont under Carlo Felice and a long police reaction. La Farina already sketches Charles Albert as the ambiguous heir of the secondary Savoy line—figure of hope and betrayal for a generation of conspirators—without yet reaching the wars of 1848–1849. Arrests of notables, confessions extracted under fear, and the exile of compromised officers mark the aftermath.

Libro II — Reaction, 1831, Giovine Italia, eve of 1848
Verona to 1830
Libro secondo opens with the Congresso di Verona, the death of Pius VII and the pontificate of Leo XII, the end of Ferdinand I at Naples, and Piedmont under Charles Felix until his death. Lombardy–Venetia and the duchies of Parma and Modena from 1821 to 1829 appear as zones of surveillance, censorship, and smouldering conspiracy. A chapter on Italy in 1830 frames the peninsula on the eve of the French July Revolution’s Italian echo.
1831 and Sanfedismo
The insurrezioni del 1831 in the Papal Legations and the duchies form the next block: provisional governments in Bologna and the united provinces, the role of figures such as Ciro Menotti in Modena, the “revenges” of the Duke of Modena, French diplomacy and the occupation of Ancona, continued Roman disorder, and Sanfedismo (“sanfedist reaction”—popular clerical-royalist bands) after the rising’s failure. Effects of Romagnol and Modenese movements on Tuscany prepare the major treatment of Mazzini. International papers later printed in the document volumes—the powers’ Memorandum of May 1831 on papal reform, Cardinal Bernetti’s policy, British reporting under Lord Seymour—already cast shadows across this narrative book.
Giovine Italia and the 1830s–1840s
La Farina’s chapter on Giovine Italia is programmatic. Carboneria, born of Masonry, generates Young Italy, which inherits humanitarian doctrines from the freemasons and the desire for national unity and independence from the carbonari. He attacks those who call Italian unification a mere dream of Mazzini’s society. Organisation, the ethic of duty, republican unitarianism, and the failed risings of the 1830s occupy successive pages. Later chapters individualise regimes: Ferdinando II of the Two Sicilies; Sicily in particular; the Kingdom of Sardinia under slow evolution toward a national role after Charles Albert’s accession; conspiracies and attempted revolutions from 1835 to 1845; Lombardy and Venice under Austrian administration; the contrast between revolutionary and reformist parties and their writers; Tuscany in 1845–1846; Piedmont again on the eve of later choices; the Papal State toward the end of Gregorio XVI; and a closing survey of Italy in May 1846—poised between reform hopes under a new pope and the explosion Volume II will narrate.
Throughout Libro secondo La Farina’s categories remain period ones: liberty versus absolute restaurazione (“restoration”), national independence versus Austrian hegemony, and moral regeneration of Italy as a single people. He does not yet write as a satisfied parliamentary liberal of the 1860s; the volume still carries the heat of conspiracy literature and of the failed decades before 1848.

Character, limits, and raw
The work is a continuous patriotic narrative, not a detached handbook. It is especially useful for La Farina’s reading of Carboneria symbolism and genealogy, the legal-political drama of Naples 1820 and Laybach, the 1831 Legations crisis, the passage from carbonari liberal aims to Mazzinian unitarian republicanism, and the state-by-state map of Restoration Italy. Limits follow from the genre: partisan allocation of blame (Austria, curia, Bourbons); Sicilian accent from the author’s origin; rhetorical heat; OCR noise on names and dates. Pair with Volumes III and V for treaty and statute texts, with Volume II and IV for 1848–1849 narrative, and with Tivaroni’s later Storia critica for denser institutional criticism.
Raw Text — wiki/raw/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol1.txt. Italian OCR, medium quality; Harvard/Widener scan lineage on title leaves.

sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol2.title: La Farina — Storia d'Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. II
sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol2.content:
La Farina — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. II
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850. Volume II. — Milano / Torino arrangements of the mid-century text (Casa Editrice Italiana di M. Guigoni / Società Editrice Italiana lineage; 1860–1861 impressions appear in the scan).
Where Volume I carried Restoration and conspiracy down to May 1846, Volume II is the narrative of the revolutionary years 1848–1849. La Farina structures the core as Libro terzo (1848 across the peninsula and the first war of independence). Printed matter runs on the order of six hundred pages of narrative plus apparatus; OCR includes running-head and numeral noise. The author writes as patriot and near-witness, sympathetic to constitutional and republican experiments and to the national war against Austria under Carlo Alberto.

Libro III — From Pio IX to the spring of peoples
Libro terzo opens with the election of Pio IX after the death of Gregorio XVI and the first hopes of the new pontificate. La Farina narrates collegiate divisions at the conclave, the early reformist reputation of the Pope, and the rapid growth of agitation across the Papal State, Tuscany, Piedmont, and the Austrian provinces. Demonstrations, petitions for civic guards, press pressure, and the language of Italian brotherhood fill the months before the European explosion of 1848. Austrian occupation gestures at Ferrara and the polemics of the papal legation already show the collision between national opinion and imperial right. In the north, legal opposition figures such as Daniele Manin and Niccolò Tommaseo in Venice press the central congregations; arrests mark them as rebels while blood is shed in other Lombard–Venetian towns. Milanese tension rises toward the Cinque giornate (“Five Days”).

Libro III — Cinque giornate and the war of independence
Central military-political episodes include the Cinque giornate di Milano (“Five Days of Milan”), the urban rising that expelled the Austrian garrison of Field Marshal Radetzky, and the entry of Piedmontese troops across the Ticino into the guerra dell’Indipendenza (“War of Independence”). La Farina records that of the wounded in the Five Days, more than six hundred later died; women and children shared in the defence and care of the injured. On 25 March some four thousand Piedmontese with field artillery under general Bes moved on Milan; Austrian strength this side of the Alps is given in the tens of thousands, partly locked in the Quadrilatero fortresses of Mantua, Verona, Peschiera, and related posts.
Campaign chapters track first Italian successes—operations toward the Mincio, the battle of Goito, pressure on the Austrian line, and the drama around Vicenza—then reverse: Piedmontese retreat, the occupation and surrender of Milan, and the re-entry of imperial arms. Parallel political narrative covers the Lombard governo provvisorio (“provisional government”), spring diplomacy, and strains inside the Italian coalition as Naples withdrew support and the Pope’s Allocuzione of 29 April 1848 chilled the idea of a holy-national war led by the papacy. La Farina stresses the want of unity of command, the bargaining over Lombard crowns, and the impossibility of war without Piedmontese force and money—bankers and politicians waiting on guarantees Charles Albert could not cleanly give.

Libro III — Venice, Tuscany, Rome, Naples, Sicily
Venice under Daniele Manin receives extended treatment: the proclamation of the Repubblica di San Marco (“Republic of St Mark”), defence of the lagoon, relations with Piedmontese annexation projects, and the moral authority of Manin and Tommaseo even after imprisonment. Piedmont after the first armistice appears as a constitutional kingdom still bound to Charles Albert’s honour and to army politics; the Statuto granted in March 1848 (later remembered as the Statuto albertino, “Albertine Statute”) remains the legal frame. Tuscany after the Grand Duke’s difficulties moves through consultative and statutory experiments. Rome moves toward crisis as reform yields to radicalisation and the path that will end in the Pope’s flight and the Repubblica romana (“Roman Republic”). Naples and the Sicilian revolution occupy southern chapters: Sicilian parliamentary identity, Neapolitan constitutional grants under pressure, and the Sicilian expedition into Calabria. La Farina closes the book’s arc at the threshold of the 1849 catastrophe—Novara, Brescia, the sieges of Rome and Venice—narrated more fully in Volume IV.

Judgment and texture
Even within the Volume II binding, the narrative presses the logic of disaster: armistice politics, Roman and Tuscan radicalisation, the decision at Turin to resume war, and the looming names of Novara, Brescia, Rome, and Venice. La Farina does not hide his judgment that princely egoism, clerical temporalism, and Austrian military professionalism defeated a movement that had already proved Italians could fight as a nation. His pages on popular heroism in Milan and on Manin’s Venice are among the warmest in the Storia; his pages on coalition failure are among the bitterest.

Character, limits, raw
Best used for a continuous 1848 campaign and political narrative from a Sicilian unitarian who later worked with the National Society. Limits: less institutional depth than Tivaroni’s later critical history; rhetorical heat; OCR. Pair with Volume IV for 1849 and the Conclusione, and with Volumes III and V for statutes and armistice texts. Full text: wiki/raw/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol2.txt.

sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol3-d.title: La Farina — Storia d'Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. III: Documenti
sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol3-d.content:
La Farina — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. III: Documenti
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850. Volume III: Documenti. Seconda edizione corretta dall’autore. — Torino: Società Editrice Italiana, 1860.
This is the first of two documentary appendices to the narrative history. Instead of La Farina’s continuous story, the reader meets treaties, constitutions, proclamations, and diplomatic papers in Italian transcription or translation, lettered in series. The volume runs on the order of 850 pages; the printed Indice sits near pp. 829–848. OCR often splits headings across lines; letter codes remain the reliable spine. Use this volume as a quarry for the legal language of Vienna, the southern constitutions, the 1831 Legations crisis, and the first half of the 1847–1849 statutory flood—completed and sometimes duplicated in Volume V.

Serie I — From the Congress of Vienna to about 1832
Serie I opens with the Italian portions of the Atto del Congresso di Vienna (“Act of the Congress of Vienna”), the settlement that reassigned Lombardy–Venetia to Austria, restored the old houses, and fixed the map La Farina’s narrative spends hundreds of pages undoing. Neighbouring documents include the Santa Alleanza (“Holy Alliance”); instruments on the Neapolitan succession such as the Convenzione di Casa Lanza; the Concordato of 1818 between the Holy See and Naples; the Costituzione siciliana del 1812 (“Sicilian Constitution of 1812”) associated with the British period; and the Spanish Constitution of 1812, the text Neapolitan revolutionaries of 1820 took as model.
Military and congress papers follow the cycle of 1820–1821: the expedition of Florestano Pepe against the Sicilian movement; papers of Troppau and Laybach; and the Austrian restoration of absolute monarchy. The 1831 crisis in the Papal Legations occupies a thick block: Bologna and the united provinces; Ancona and Cardinal Benvenuti; reports associated with the French envoy Saint-Aulaire; the powers’ Memorandum of 10 May 1831 on reforms in the Papal State; the policy of Cardinal Secretary Bernetti; and British reporting under Lord Seymour alongside the French occupation of Ancona. Together these documents let the reader see the international guarantee structure behind Italian absolutism—the same structure the narrative volumes denounce as the chain on the nation.
Letter codes in Serie I run through a long alphabet (into the double letters). Editorial practice is that of a mid-century patriot compiler: select the papers that prove foreign interference, princely grants under pressure, and the legal creativity or legal hypocrisy of courts. Cross-check Volume V’s Serie I when a specific act seems missing; the two document volumes overlap thematically without being identical cuts.

Serie II — 1847–1849 instruments
Serie II begins around the Trattato di Firenze and runs a long alphabet of acts from the pre-revolutionary reforms through the republics and armistices. Typical pieces include protests from the Legations and Ferrara; the abdication of the Duke of Lucca; establishment of the Tuscan Consulta di Stato (“Council of State”); projects of lega doganale (“customs league”); the Statuto delle Due Sicilie and Sicilian parliamentary acts; the Piedmontese constitution known to later usage as the Statuto albertino (“Albertine Statute”); the Tuscan Statute; the Statuto of the Papal State; Neapolitan electoral law; the Modena–Austria treaty; acts of the Lombard provisional government; Venetian union and independence papers; acts of the Repubblica romana (“Roman Republic”); and armistice texts of 1849. Guerrazzi’s Tuscany appears among the revolutionary governments.
Unlettered dossiers supplement the series: Troppau (1820), Novara (1821) in the Piedmontese revolutionary sense, the garrison question at Parma, and correspondence touching Metternich, Palmerston, Guizot, and Pio IX. The documentary method argues silently as well as by selection: Italians already wrote modern public law; Europe’s cabinets wrote the veto.

How to use with the narrative
Read Serie I beside Volume I’s books on 1815–1831; read Serie II beside Volumes II and IV on 1848–1849. When hunting the full text of a single statute (for example the Piedmontese charter of 4 March 1848 or the Sicilian parliamentary instructions), start with Volume V’s denser constitutional Serie II, then confirm variants here. La Farina does not supply modern archival apparatus; shelfmarks and critical collation are not the point. The point is a working library of the papers a national historian of 1850–1860 thought indispensable.

sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol4.title: La Farina — Storia d'Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. IV
sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol4.content:
La Farina — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. IV
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850. Volume IV. — Torino: Società Editrice Italiana, 1852.
Published earlier than the 1860 second-edition arrangement of Volumes I–II, this 1852 volume is the dense narrative close of the revolutionary years and the seat of La Farina’s long Conclusione on the Italian nation. A Garibaldi portrait leaf appears in the scan front matter. Roughly 690 pages; printed Indice near pp. 687–689. The raw opens on Libro quarto, chapter I: the Papal State to the flight of Pius IX, with a sharp judgment on Pellegrino Rossi—courage without prudence in a state already in revolt.

Libro IV — Rome, Tuscany, and the road to Gaeta
Narrative chapters move theatre by theatre. Rome: Rossi’s ministry, his murder, the radicalisation of the city, and the Pope’s flight toward Gaeta. La Farina treats the collapse of moderate papal reform as both crime and tragedy—the last chance of a national papacy spent. Tuscany: pressure on Leopoldo II, provisional authorities, and the path toward a more radical regime associated with Guerrazzi and companions. The Repubblica romana (“Roman Republic”) appears with its internal parties, triumvirs (including Mazzini), and military improvisation under figures including Garibaldi. The republic’s organic laws and defence measures stand in the document volumes; here the story is political and martial failure against converging Catholic powers.

Libro IV — Novara, Brescia, Bourbon reconquest
Piedmont occupies the central catastrophe: Charles Albert, the breaking of the tregua (“truce/armistice”), renewal of war against Austria, the disaster of Novara (23 March 1849), and the king’s abdication in favour of Vittorio Emanuele II. La Farina’s Novara is not a technical staff study; it is the moral end of a reign that had raised and disappointed national hope since 1821. Brescia receives a heroic-suppression chapter on urban resistance against Austrian reconquest—the “lioness” episode of Lombard memory. Tuscan ristaurazione (“restoration”) restores the Grand Duke with Austrian shadow. Naples and Sicily run to the eccidio di Messina (“massacre of Messina”) and Bourbon reconquest under Ferdinando II, whose bombardment reputation hardens into the European nickname that Tivaroni and others later recycle. Southern constitutional paper is cancelled in fact if not always in form.

Libro IV — Siege of Rome and fall of Venice
A further Roman block treats the republic under siege and the Catholic “crusade” of intervening powers—French arms foremost in the final reduction of Rome, with Neapolitan and Spanish participation in the wider restoration. Garibaldi’s defence and retreat become legend already in La Farina’s pages. Venice under Manin holds to late summer 1849 (30 August in La Farina’s close), last major revolutionary capital to fall to hunger, disease, and bombardment. The lagoon republic’s end closes the revolutionary cycle that Volume II opened with Pio IX and the Five Days.
La Farina’s causal vocabulary is moral-political: bad faith of courts, want of a single national dictatorship or firm monarchical lead, Austrian professionalism, French Catholic intervention, and the tragedy of courage without unity. He writes before Cavour’s later synthesis; the 1852 Conclusione is therefore a creed for continuing struggle, not a victory lap of 1860.

Conclusione — La nazione italiana
The Conclusione is a twenty-one-section essay and the most programmatic part of the entire Storia. La Farina argues that Italy is already moralmente una nazione (“morally one nation”) even when divided among states. He traces the national idea through Dante, Petrarca, and Boccaccio, then Machiavelli and Guicciardini, as early exponents of Italian political self-awareness. He stages the debate between unitari and federalisti (“unitarians” and “federalists”) inside the national movement—rejecting federal comfort that would leave Austria and the temporal papacy intact. Later sections press the separazione dello spirituale e del temporale (“separation of spiritual and temporal power”)—the papacy as church versus the papacy as prince—and the hard choice of dittatura regia o repubblicana (“royal or republican dictatorship”) as emergency form for regeneration. Section XXI is an Esortazione (“exhortation”) to patriots. Read as manifesto of one unitarian current of the Risorgimento (“Resurgence”), not as neutral survey. The same La Farina who here weighs royal versus republican dictatorship would soon work for monarchical unity under Victor Emmanuel and Cavour; the tension is historical, not editorial anachronism.

Character, limits, raw
Core narrative of 1849 collapses plus the author’s national doctrine. Pair with Vol. II for 1848 campaign detail and document volumes for legal texts. Full text: wiki/raw/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol4.txt.
Raw Text — Italian OCR; Harvard H. Nelson Gay Risorgimento collection marks on some leaves.
Vol. 4 in the unitarian arc
La Farina’s fourth narrative volume continues the Risorgimento story through the crises that close the 1840s and open the diplomatic decade—exact chapter cuts follow the raw OCR, but the wiki burden is clear: war, defeat, and the reorganisation of national politics after the first independence war.
Deepened burdens
Military and diplomatic failure. Custozza–Novara sequence, armistices, and the collapse of the 1848 war coalition as La Farina assigns blame among kings, republicans, and hesitant princes.
Republics and restorations. Rome, Venice, and local provisional regimes as both heroic and terminal experiments.
Piedmontese remainder. Why only the Statuto state remains a viable base—preparing Cavour’s decade without yet the full Italia degli Italiani denseness of Tivaroni’s later series.
Documents of betrayal and hope. Proclamations and notes that vol. 5’s documenti series may echo; keep claims tied to texts present in raw.
Pairing
With vols. 1–3 for earlier carbonari-to-1848 arc; with Tivaroni Italia degli Italiani t.1 for 1849–59 depth La Farina may treat more briefly.

sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol5-d.title: La Farina — Storia d'Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. V: Documenti, Parte 1.2
sources/la-farina-storia-d-italia-vol5-d.content:
La Farina — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850, Vol. V: Documenti, Parte 1.2
Giuseppe La Farina (1815–1863) — Storia d’Italia dal 1815 al 1850. Volume V: Documenti. Parte 1.2. — Torino: Società Editrice Italiana, 1851.
Second documentary volume, complementing Volume III. It is the fullest single gathering in this corpus of the constitutions and statutes granted across the peninsula in 1847–1849, preceded by a first series of Restoration and early-revolutionary papers. About 650 pages; Indice dei documenti near pp. 651–657 (printed variants 351–357). Letter codes run very far (into triple letters); OCR glues titles. For constitutional wording this volume is usually the first stop; for Vienna and 1831 diplomacy, cross-check Volume III.

Serie I — Documenti A–DD (roughly 1815–1831)
Serie I reproduces diplomatic and state papers of the Restoration and of the revolutions of 1820–1821 and 1831 in a lettered sequence A through DD. Content overlaps thematically with Volume III’s first series—Vienna settlement language, southern constitutions and concordats, congress interventions, Legations crisis—but the 1851 editorial cut and lettering are those of this volume. Use both document volumes when hunting a specific act; do not assume identical completeness. The series supplies the legal backdrop against which La Farina’s narrative of Carboneria, Laybach, and 1831 is written.

Serie II — Documenti A–ZZZ (1847–1849 constitutions and acts)
Serie II is the constitutional heart of the whole Storia. Following the printed index, representative pieces include:
A protest of Cardinal Ciacchi (6 August 1847);. B protest of the Legate of Ferrara;. C treaty Tuscany–Duke of Lucca (4 October 1847);.
D–E acts of Lucca’s abdication (5 October);. F Grand Duke of Tuscany’s proclamation (11 October);. G motu proprio creating the Tuscan Consulta di Stato (“Council of State”) in numbered titles;.
further Tuscan and papal acts H–J;. K sovereign act of the Two Sicilies (18 January 1848);. L administration of Sicily;.
M Neapolitan constitution (29 January 1848);. N Statuto delle Due Sicilie (10 February 1848) in its capi;. O Sicilian Parliament (24 February) with instructions;.
P–Q Piedmontese statute of 4 March 1848—the text later called Statuto albertino (“Albertine Statute”), the charter that survived when others fell and became the constitutional law of the Regno d’Italia (“Kingdom of Italy”);. R–S Tuscan Statute (15 February) in titoli;. T Statuto della Santa Chiesa (14 March) for the Papal State;.
U–V Tuscan administrative ordinances (March);. X Neapolitan electoral law (29 February) with district apparatus;. Z constitution of Monaco (12 February);.
AA Austria–Archduke of Modena treaty.
The alphabet continues through Lombard provisional government, Venice, union with Piedmont, and the Repubblica romana (“Roman Republic”), out to ZZZ. Armistice instruments and revolutionary organic laws sit among the later letters.
What the volume does for the reader is place the legal creativity of 1848 side by side: princely grants under street pressure, Sicilian parliamentary identity, Piedmont’s durable charter, Tuscan and papal statutes, and republican organic laws. La Farina’s selection argues silently that Italians already wrote modern public law for themselves before 1859—and that only one monarchical statute outlasted the restorations of 1849.

Reading with the narrative and with Tivaroni
Pair Serie II with Volumes II and IV for the political circumstances of each grant and repeal. Pair the Statuto albertino texts with Tivaroni’s L’Italia degli Italiani for how the charter actually functioned in the Piedmontese connubio (“union” — the Cavour–Rattazzi alliance) years. Pair Sicilian and Neapolitan statutes with La Farina’s own southern narrative and with Tivaroni’s volumes on the Two Sicilies under Austrian-era diplomacy and French-era memory. The document volumes are not annotated to modern critical standards; they are working books for a national public.

Character, limits, raw

Vol. 5 is a documenti companion: proclamations, diplomatic notes, statutes, letters, and contemporary pieces La Farina appends so the narrative volumes can be checked. In this wiki it is not a second storyline but a primary-text quarry for quotations and institutional wording already framed in vols. 1–4.
