sources/list-nationales-system.title: Friedrich List — Das nationale System der Politischen Ökonomie
sources/list-nationales-system.content:
Friedrich List — Das nationale System der Politischen Ökonomie
Friedrich List (1789–1846). The deposited text is the Waentig edition in the series Sammlung sozialwissenschaftlicher Meister (Jena: Gustav Fischer; second edition of that series text), OCR’d as Internet Archive item dasnationalesys00list. List’s own title-work is the 1841 Cotta statement: Das nationale System der politischen Oekonomie, first volume Der internationale Handel, die Handelspolitik und die deutsche Zollunion (Stuttgart und Tübingen). The OCR carries List’s continuous chapter numbering with original-edition page markers in parentheses and a modern editor’s front matter (Eheberg/Waentig-style introductory apparatus).
Raw status (2026-08-16): raw/list-nationales-system.txt restored (~1.2 MB OCR of the Waentig German text). Earlier deposit had been an HTML 500 error stub. Claims below are drawn from that restored file.

What the book is for
The Einleitung (“Introduction”) opens on the gap between theorists and practitioners over internationaler Handel (“international trade”) and Handelspolitik (“trade policy”). No other branch of political economy, List says, so directly touches nations’ prosperity, civilisation, independence, power, and duration. England’s contemporary Manufaktur- und Handelssuprematie (“manufacturing and commercial supremacy”) is described as a consistent system aiming to monopolise manufactures, great commerce, shipping, colonies, and the seas, and to reduce other nations to manufacture- and trade-dependence “wie die Hindus.” Russia’s turn to a Prohibitivsystem (“prohibitive system”) is cited as yielding national prosperity; North America’s wider opening to English goods after a protective rise is cited as yielding “Konvulsion und Ruin.” The science that cannot light the path of practice is useless; the fault of the theory–practice breach lies with both sides. Political economy for international trade must draw its lessons from experience and calculate measures for the needs of the present and the peculiar condition of each nation.

Book I — Die Geschichte (chs. 1–10)
Historical chapters treat, in order: the Italians; the Hansards; the Netherlanders; the English; Spaniards and Portuguese; the French; the Germans; the Russians; the North Americans; then Die Lehren der Geschichte (“The Lessons of History”).
The English path (Navigation, protective rise to industrial supremacy) and Colbert’s France recur as positive school examples of state commercial policy. Germany appears as a nation long bled by internal splintering and by neighbours’ commercial regimes. North America supplies the laboratory of protective reaction after free competition with England. The tenth chapter generalises those stories into maxims for policy: free trade with more advanced countries can lift a people quickly from barbarism through pastoral and early agricultural stages and into the first beginnings of manufactures and shipping; a complete Manufakturkraft (“manufacturing power”), large shipping, and great foreign trade are attained only with Einschreitung der Staatsgewalt (“intervention of state power”).

Book II — Die Theorie (chs. 11–27)
Political versus cosmopolitan economy (ch. 11)
Before Quesnay there was only administrative practice for one’s own nation. Quesnay first extended inquiry to the whole human race and titled his work as most advantageous au genre humain; he asks one to imagine the merchants of all nations as one Handelsrepublik (“commercial republic”). That is kosmopolitische Ökonomie — how the entire human race may prosper — as against politische Ökonomie, which teaches how a given nation, under given world conditions, reaches prosperity, civilisation, and power through agriculture, industry, and trade.
Adam Smith, List argues, likewise pursued the cosmopolitan idea of absolute world free trade. His title speaks of the wealth of nations as of all humanity; he treats systems of political economy mainly to show their nullity and to put world-economy in place of national economy. War appears only in passing; perpetual peace underlies the arguments. J. B. Say expressly requires imagining a Universalrepublik (“universal republic”) to make general free trade intelligible. List’s national system is the counter-science: the nation remains the unit of analysis.
Productive powers versus exchange values (ch. 12)
Title theme: Theorie der produktiven Kräfte and Theorie der Werte. Causes of wealth differ from wealth itself. An individual (or nation) rich in Tauschwerte but without power to create more value than it consumes grows poor; one poor in stock but strong in creating power grows rich. Die Kraft, Reichtümer zu schaffen, is infinitely more important than wealth itself — it secures possession, increase, and replacement of losses. Germany, repeatedly devastated, saved productive powers and recovered; Spain, with peace and rich soil and mines, lost productive power and sank. The American war of independence cost hundreds of millions yet strengthened productive power through national independence, after which wealth rose beyond prior levels. Smith saw labour and the productive power of labour in his introduction, but was so dominated by cosmopolitan free trade and by Teilung der Arbeit that he did not carry through the idea of productive power as List requires.
National division of operations and confederation of national productive forces (ch. 13)
Division of labour is incomplete if limited to operations inside a workshop. List extends it to the nationale Teilung der Geschäftsoperationen and to the Konföderation der Nationalproduktivkräfte — the joining of a nation’s forces across territory, sectors, and institutions. Political and commercial fragmentation taxes that confederation; national economic unity multiplies it.
Private economy and national economy; nationality (chs. 14–16)
What is rational for a private merchant is not always rational for the nation. Nationalität (“nationality”) is an economic fact: nations stand at unequal stages; policy that ignores nationality serves the already dominant manufacturing power. List distinguishes popular/state economy and political/Nationalökonomie (“national economy”) in successive chapters as he fences off Smith–Say individualism.
Manufakturkraft (chs. 17–25)
A run of chapters ties Manufakturkraft (“manufacturing power”) to personal, social, and political productive forces; to natural productive forces; to instrumental forces (material capitals); to the agricultural interest; to trade; to shipping, sea power, and colonisation; to instruments of circulation; to continuity and “work-continuation”; and to stimuli of production and consumption. Manufacturing is the lever that raises agriculture, skills, credit, and political power together. A pure Agrikulturstaat (“agricultural state”) remains dependent when it only exchanges raw produce for foreign manufactures.
Stages and the limited case for protection (esp. around nationality / ch. 15 material)
In economic development nations pass through: original wildness; pastoral condition; agricultural condition; agricultural-manufacturing condition; agricultural-manufacturing-commercial condition (Agrikulturmanufakturhandelsstand). Free trade with more advanced cities and lands best speeds the early climb. Restriction of trade to plant and protect one’s own manufacturing power is justified only for nations that already have the spiritual and material means to plant that power and reach the highest civilisation and power, yet are held back by a more advanced foreign manufacturing power — and only so long as domestic manufacturing is not yet strong enough to face foreign competition, thereafter only so far as needed to protect manufacturing “in its roots.” A protective system that shut out foreign competition entirely and at once would violate both cosmopolitan economy and the nation’s own well-understood interest. Early Schutzzölle must be moderate and rise only gradually with capital, skill, and enterprise; not every branch needs equal protection — the great branches (large fixed and circulating capital, machinery, technical knowledge, many workers, goods of general consumption) claim special care.
The customs house (chs. 26–27)
Die Douane als Hauptmittel zu Pflanzung und Beschützung der inneren Manufakturkraft — the tariff administration is the chief means to plant and protect internal manufacturing power. A following chapter confronts the Douane with the ruling school’s objections (monopoly, consumer loss, etc.). List treats the temporary sacrifice of exchange-value as the price of building productive power.

Book III — Die Systeme (chs. 28–32)
Italian national economists; the Industriesystem (which the school falsely calls the mercantile system); the physiocratic or agricultural system; the Tauschwertsystem (which the school falsely calls the industrial system) under Adam Smith; continuation on J. B. Say and his school. List rehabilitates the older industrial/statecraft system as misunderstood historical practice and attacks the dominant school as a theory of exchange-value that dissolves the nation.

Book IV — Die Politik (chs. 33–36)
Insular supremacy, continental powers, North America and France (ch. 33)
England’s island supremacy structures the options of continental states and of the United States; France and America appear as counterpart cases of policy under that pressure.
Insular supremacy and the German commercial union (ch. 34)
Germany’s last twenty years show what a great nation is without a capable commercial policy and what it can become with one. Germany was, in Franklin’s phrase on New Jersey, a barrel tapped by all its neighbours. England ruined much of German manufacturing, flooded Germany with woollens, cottons, and colonial goods, yet shut out German grain and timber (and at times wool). German sales to England once dwarfed England’s much-praised East Indian outlet, yet the German was not even allowed what the Hindu was allowed — to pay for manufactures with agricultural products. France sold wine, oil, silk, and fashion goods into Germany while cramping German outlets for cattle, grain, and linen. Against that double pressure List sets the deutsche Handelsunion — commercial union among Germans — as the instrument of national economic self-assertion.
Continental policy (ch. 35)
Wider continental alignment against exclusive insular manufacturing and trade supremacy; the German union sits inside a broader continental commercial problem.
Commercial policy of the German Zollverein (ch. 36)
If any nation is called to plant a national manufacturing power, it is the German — by rank in sciences and arts, literature and education, administration and useful institutions; by morality, religion, industry, thrift, persistence, inventive spirit; by size and quality of population; by extent and nature of territory; by advanced agriculture and physical, social, and spiritual resources. From a protective system suited to its condition Germany may expect fruits for internal manufactures, foreign trade and shipping, internal transport, agriculture, and the maintenance of independence. The chapter is the practical programme: Handelspolitik des deutschen Zollvereins — external protection and internal freer exchange as the school of national manufacturing power. Closing pages discuss extension of the union (coasts, neighbouring lands, relation to Austria) as commercial-political tasks continuous with the same national system.

Apparatus in the deposit
The OCR opens with series title, Waentig as editor, and a long German introduction on List’s life, the Handelsverein, agitation for the Zollverein, and the place of the 1841 system — editorial matter, not List’s 1841 chapters. List’s own Inhalts-Anzeige lists Einleitung + four books (History, Theory, Systems, Politics) through chapter 36 and a Nachtrag. Parenthetical numbers track pages of the “Ausgabe letzter Hand.”

Notes for the wiki

Core lemmas in List’s own vocabulary: nationale System, politische vs kosmopolitische Ökonomie, Produktivkräfte / produktive Kräfte, Tauschwerte, Manufakturkraft, Schutzzoll / Schutzsystem, Douane, Zollverein / deutsche Handelsunion, Agrikulturstaat vs manufacturing stages, Konföderation der Nationalproduktivkräfte.
“Infant industry” / Erziehungszoll is later shorthand; this deposit’s running terms are Schutzzoll, Schutzsystem, and planting/protection of Manufakturkraft for a limited historical phase.
Glosses: Produktivkräfte (“productive powers”); Manufakturkraft (“manufacturing power”); Schutzzoll (“protective tariff”); Zollverein (“customs union”); kosmopolitisch (“cosmopolitan”); Tauschwert (“exchange value”); Douane (“customs / tariff office”).

sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t5.title: Ollivier — L'Empire libéral, Tome V
sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t5.content:
Ollivier — L’Empire libéral, Tome V
Émile Ollivier (1825–1913) — L’Empire libéral; études, récits, souvenirs. — Tome cinquième. — Paris: Garnier frères, libraires-éditeurs, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1900.
The fifth volume of Ollivier’s eighteen-volume memoir-history of the Second Empire. Title-band: L’Inauguration de l’Empire libéral — Le Roi Guillaume. Participant-observer narrative (the Cinq, Corps législatif debates, private conversations with Morny, Billault, Persigny, La Valette) sits beside Mexican, Italian, American, and Prussian diplomatic history. Typ. Chamerot et Renouard, Paris.
Core narrative runs from the Corps législatif session of 1860 and the decree of 24 November 1860 through the 1861–62 sessions, the London Convention and early Mexican expedition (Soledad, Puebla), Italian affairs after Cavour’s death (Ricasoli, Rattazzi, Aspromonte), the Trent and religious conflict, Fould’s financial reform, and closes with Livre XI on Prussian army reform and Bismarck’s appointment (22 September 1862). Dominant years in the text: 1860–1862.
Approximately 640 pages (text through the Éclaircissements and table). From the Internet Archive item lempireliberal05olli (UCLA / University of California Library copy; OCR ABBYY FineReader 8.0).
Chapters
Livre X — L’Inauguration de l’Empire libéral — Le décret du 24 novembre 1860
French interior liberalism under the November decree; Italy after Cavour; Mexico from the London Convention through Puebla; religious and financial reform; Aspromonte and the fall of Thouvenel (1860–October 1862).
Chapitre I. La session de 1860 — Treaty of commerce and Italian policy shift majority feeling; Morny tries to conciliate the Cinq; Ollivier’s conversation with Thiers. Conservative opposition (La Terrière nullity, Dalmas election, Graissessac railway). Italian policy debate (Lemercier, Favre, Cassagnac, Baroche, 11–12 April 1860). Commercial-treaty discussion (Pouyer-Quertier, Baroche, Ollivier); annexation of Savoy; budget fight of the Cinq; Larrabure on finances and the China war; Paris municipal budget; journalists and auditors (Gambetta, Floquet, Clément Duvernois); Prévost-Paradol; death of King Jérôme (24 June 1860); imperial tour of Savoy, Corsica, Algeria; Empress to Scotland (November 1860). Chapitre II. État d’esprit de l’Empereur depuis la guerre d’Italie — Will to reorganise the army and create a trained reserve; Randon’s decentralisation project not adopted for cost; contrast with King William of Prussia, who accepts parliamentary conflict for army reform; work on the Vie de César (Mme Cornu, Maury); order to stage Wagner’s Tannhäuser at the Opéra. Chapitre III. Le décret du 24 novembre 1860 — Privy council and ministers (22 November); ministerial reshuffle; publication of the decree; why Haussmann is not made minister of Paris. Real scope and spontaneity of the decree; public reactions (Proudhon, Doudan, Prévost-Paradol, Mérimée, Troplong). How the decree gives Ollivier the conception of the Empire libéral — not restoring liberty but establishing it; critique of French parliamentary practice; place of the plebiscite; Persigny’s application as interior minister (press theory; refuses journals to Veuillot and Ollivier, authorises Nefftzer); clerical–anticlerical conflict; Saint-Vincent-de-Paul; Lacordaire reception (24 January 1861); Mgr Pie on Pilate. Chapitre IV. La session de 1861 — Opening (4 February): Emperor and Morny; arrest of Mirès (17 February). Senate Address and Prince Napoléon vs Billault. Corps législatif Address: Keller, Favre; the Cinq’s method of principle-amendments; Ollivier’s speech on the November decree (14 March) and whether it was a rally to the Empire. Devinck on exhaustible resources; Picard on Paris; Favre on Rome; clerical amendment reaches 90 votes. Arrest of Blanqui (11 March); first Tannhäuser (13 March). Roman agitation; Aumale letter; seizure of Broglie’s book. Senate on Syrian evacuation (5 June) and Lebanon organisation (9 June). Old-age pensions, contingent, end of the sliding scale. Budget: Keller vs Persigny; Ollivier meets Guizot; income-tax proposal; press law; Billault declares the November decree a fin, not a beginning (18 June).
Chapitre V. L’Italie après la mort de Cavour — Ministère Ricasoli — Ricasoli succeeds Cavour (12 June); French recognition of Italy on Thouvenel’s report (27 June); Emperor’s letter to Victor Emmanuel (12 July); Nigra ambassador at Paris. King wants Venice first, Ricasoli Rome; programme speech alludes to ceding Sardinia (1 July); severe words to Arese. Naples: d’Azeglio and Cialdini on conquest; Ricasoli’s Capitolato (10 September); English failure to get Prussian and Russian recognition; King of Prussia at Compiègne (6–9 October 1861). Chapitre VI. Le Mexique — La convention du 31 octobre 1861 — Mexican civil war as religion vs liberty; Constitution of 5 February 1857; Comonfort and Juárez; clerical revolt; Juárez president (19 January 1858). Portrait of Juárez; Vera Cruz government; Laguna Seca; entry into Mexico (11 January 1861); Pacheco and Dubois de Saligny. Expulsion of Spanish ambassador, nuncio, bishops; Church–State separation. Suspension of foreign conventions (17 July 1861); Anglo-French rupture of relations. Mexican émigrés at Paris (Almonte). Ollivier’s judgment: no grande pensée in the expedition; neither just nor politic. London Convention of 31 October — clear on its face. Plenipotentiaries: Saligny, Jurien de la Gravière; Prim. English instructions aim only at debt recovery; French and Spanish instructions ambiguous and hostile to Juárez, contrary to nationalities; Emperor’s Italian motives for the blunder. Chapitre VII. La guerre de la Sécession aux États-Unis — L’affaire du Trent — Slavery as true cause; France with England treats the South as belligerents (May 1861). Southern envoys seized on the British Trent (8 November); Emperor supports English claims; settlement (26 December). Chapitre VIII. Le conflit religieux — La Société de Saint-Vincent-de-Paul — Un refus d’institution canonique — Lay character of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul as work of liberty; Persigny dissolves the central committee; circular on the society and freemasonry (18 October 1861); society refuses a government-named director. Renan’s course opened (11 January 1862) then suspended; schoolmaster of Sel; refusal of canonical institution to the bishop named for Martinique; reciprocal rights of civil and ecclesiastical power in episcopal nominations.
Chapitre IX. La réforme financière — Le sénatus-consulte du 31 décembre 1861 — Economic and financial crisis; warning to the Revue des Deux Mondes; Emperor’s letter to Achille Fould; Fould’s memoir and nomination as finance minister; virements instead of supplementary credits. Principles of budgetary speciality; comparison of systems; advantages of virements. Text of the senatus-consulte of 31 December 1861; Fould neglects reforming the French budget-vote mechanism (English contrast). New budget divisions; budget of 1863; optional conversion of the 4½ per cent. Chapitre X. Le silence de l’Empereur — La Valette à Rome — Dotation Cousin-Montauban — L’Adresse de 1862 — Ricasoli refuses connubio with Rattazzi; uses Mazzinian and Garibaldian agitation to press the Emperor; Emperor remains silent. La Valette at Rome with Pius IX and Antonelli (18 January 1862); bishops summoned for Japanese martyrs’ canonisation. Session of 1862 opens (27 January); Morny against written speeches; Senate: La Rochejaquelein, Piétri, Prince Napoléon (À bas les prêtres); prince on Rome denies even the Leonine City; Billault disavows him; George Sand and Girardin. Conversion of the 4½ per cent voted; Corps législatif refuses a dotation to Cousin-Montauban; Emperor withdraws the bill. Amendments of the Cinq; Favre, Keller, Billault on Rome; Ollivier on revolution. Chapitre XII. Effet à Turin et à Rome de la discussion de l’Adresse — Chute de Ricasoli — Ministère Rattazzi — La Valette à Paris (body and table skip Chapitre XI) — At Turin Victor Emmanuel wants Venetia not Rome; Ricasoli’s advances to Garibaldi anger moderates; vote read as no-confidence; Ricasoli resigns; Rattazzi cabinet (1 March 1862); Benedetti not the author of the change. At Rome the Address grieves the Pope; La Valette sees an opening to treat; called to Paris (26 March); obtains recall of general de Goyon. Chapitre XIII. La réforme financière et le Mexique au Corps législatif — Devinck criticises Fould; Plichon and Picard ask military reductions; Granier de Cassagnac and Roques-Salvaza revive income tax; Magne replies; Ollivier’s income-tax speech. Favre against the Mexican expedition; Billault’s confident reply.
Chapitre XIV. Les débuts de l’expédition du Mexique — La convention de la Soledad — Puebla — Emperor’s conception vs first reality: Spaniards first (17 December 1861); English and French land (9 January 1862); quarrel over claims; Wyke and Prim refuse French demands; Wyke blocks Miramón at Vera Cruz (27 January). Juárez’s legal and actual replies; Soledad convention (19 February) — conforms to London, contradicts monarchical schemes. Paris reaction; Lorencez and Almonte sent; Almonte blames Soledad; Jurien’s volte-face; Prim’s letter to the Emperor (17 March); Jurien’s ultimatum project and protection of Almonte. European cabinets; Orizaba conference (9 April) and rupture. Notification to Mexico; war begins. Lorencez breaks his word on retiring beyond the Chiquihuite (19 April); crosses the Cumbres (28 April). Paris judgment; Jurien disavowed; Lorencez’s confidence and check before Puebla (5 May). Retreat; Orizaba siege; Détrie at Cerro Borrego; deliverance; officers’ disillusion; soldiers’ bearing. Rupture approved abroad on diverse grounds; Emperor’s letters to Lorencez; Randon’s letter; Forey named successor on condition of serving Saligny’s policy; Wyke treaty disavowed in London. Corps législatif: Favre and Billault. Chapitre XV. Les difficultés de Morny pendant la session de 1862 — Le prince Napoléon — Ollivier’s exterior-policy speech read by Hénon; Picard on Paris; Ollivier proposes Corps législatif vote and control of the city budget; reduction of Paris deputies; sociétés en commandite for stockbrokers’ offices. Morny’s session difficulties and body-to-body with Picard; last words; interview with Ollivier. Portrait and role of Prince Napoléon. Chapitre XVI. La magistrature — Les livres — Michelet — Proudhon — Victor Hugo — Mirès acquitted at Douai (21 April 1862). Augier’s Les Effrontés; Duvergier de Hauranne on the 1819 press laws; last volume of Thiers’s Consulat et Empire; Barante on Royer-Collard; Michelet’s Louis XIV. Proudhon on tax; La Guerre et la Paix — war glorified, force creates right. Hugo’s Les Misérables; Lamartine’s judgment. Chapitre XVII. Les États-Unis — L’Espagne — La Serbie — Emperor’s velleity to recognise the South; Thouvenel opposes. Incident of the Emperor’s reply to Coucha, Spanish minister. Thouvenel’s Eastern policy: Montenegro, Serbia; Belgrade fortress arrangement (8 September 1862).
Chapitre XVIII. Dernière tentative de conciliation entre l’Italie et Rome — Garibaldi’s official Lombard tour; Tyrol project; double-dealing. Emperor obtains Russian then Prussian recognition of Italy; orders La Valette to reopen with the Holy See — four points. Japanese martyrs’ canonisation; ex cathedra condemnation of modern errors; rejection of the four points (25 July 1862); Italian parliament protests. Emperor has Dupanloup congratulated on his Roman conduct. Chapitre XIX. Aspromonte — Garibaldi in Sicily; Palermo speech (8 July 1862); takes arms for Rome (1 August); royal manifesto (3 August); Moniteur note (25 August). Arrival in Calabria; defeat at Aspromonte (29 August). Chapitre XX. Fin des tentatives de conciliation entre Rome et l’Italie — Chute de Thouvenel — Effect at Rome of Garibaldi’s rising; La Valette and Montebello with Pius IX; Pius turns to England. Turin seeks to atone Aspromonte by gaining something on Rome; Thouvenel’s trouble; Gramont’s suggested term for occupation; Empress’s opposition; Proudhon; Emperor defers and leaves for Biarritz (4 September 1862). Durando dispatch claiming evacuation (10 September); Russell supports; Moniteur publishes La Valette negotiation papers (25 September); Arese’s illusion; Victor Emmanuel presses the Emperor. Emperor back in Paris (8 October); struggle of Italian friends and foes; Thouvenel replaced by Drouyn de Lhuys (15 October) — real meaning of the change. Effect at Rome and Turin; Ollivier visits Garibaldi at Spezia; amnesty; Drouyn circular answering Durando brings Rattazzi’s fall. Real cause of Rattazzi’s fall; Farini cabinet against Turin more than for Rome. Arrival of Bismarck in office (22 September 1862)..
Livre XI — La réforme de l’armée prussienne — Le roi Guillaume — Roon — Bismarck
Prussian military reorganisation, Landtag conflict, and Bismarck’s entry into power (to autumn 1862).
Chapitre I. Le roi Guillaume — Character of the King. Roon and Moltke. Roon’s importance: make universal service real and exclude the Landwehr from the active army; war minister (5 December 1859); projects to the Landtag (10 February 1860). Landtag opposition; bill withdrawn yet executed. Dissent between King and ministers (feudal homage, constitutional theory); Roon sides with the King and advises calling Bismarck. Bismarck has become a new man — no longer believes absolute government possible; constitutional monarchy the only monarchical form; his parliamentarism differs from Cavour’s. King brings him from Petersburg; agreement on interior policy, divergence on German policy; still dare not make him minister for fear of coup d’État imputation. German effervescence; opposition majority in new Landtag (6 December 1861); dissolution; Hohenlohe–Ingelheim; Hesse affair; Bismarck’s counsel; Landtag still hostile (6 May); Bismarck sent as ambassador to Paris (June 1862). Chapitre II. L’attente de Bismarck — Farewell to Russia (Nitchevo); conversations with the Emperor, who formally proposes an alliance. Visits to Thiers and Persigny. Judgment on the Emperor and his government; impatience; southern journey; Roon’s telegram summons him to Berlin (18 September). King’s discouragement and prepared act of abdication; interview with Bismarck; King tears the abdication and names Bismarck minister of state and president of the council (22 September). Chapitre III. Bismarck ministre (body running head OCR also labels this “Chapitre IV”) — Bismarck as minister: physique, character, maxims. Effect of the nomination; failed conciliation; Landtag adjourned; King’s trouble (14 October 1862). Collaborators: Robert von der Goltz ambassador at Paris. Conflict at the Diet between Prussia and the small states backed by Austria; Bismarck’s threatening language; seeks the Emperor’s support via Talleyrand at Berlin; categorical refusal from Drouyn de Lhuys; chagrined, Bismarck renounces provoking war for the moment.
Éclaircissements

Une lettre du Prince Napoléon (Rome, 8 January 1891)
Les relations d’Émile Ollivier avec Wagner
Discours d’Émile Ollivier contre l’impôt sur le revenu
Madame Cornu
Errata du IVe volume

Notes
Volume 5 of 18 in the Garnier series L’Empire libéral. Title-page band (L’Inauguration de l’Empire libéral / Le Roi Guillaume), interior Livre X–XI heads, and imprint year 1900 fix the volume identity; IA catalog date 1895 is the series start, not this tome’s imprint. IA identifier lempireliberal05olli trailing 05 matches the printed tome.
Historical span for cataloguing: 1860 – October 1862 (with short backstory into the late 1850s for Mexico and Prussian army reform from 1859). Placed in the 1800–1865 wiki with Tome VII; Tome XI (1868–69 Veillée des armes), Tome XIV (July 1870), and Tome XVI (August 1870 Le Suicide) sit in the 1866–1919 wiki.
Structural quirks of the printed book (not OCR invention): Livre X table and body jump from Chapitre X to Chapitre XII (no Chapitre XI); Livre XI’s closing chapter on Bismarck as minister is Chapitre III in the table and sometimes mislabelled IV in body running text.
Raw text from IA lempireliberal05olli_djvu.txt via /download/ (UTF-8). Light cleanup applied (collapsed OCR double-spacing). French OCR retains residual character errors and broken words at line ends; chapter digests follow narrative chronology and standard dates rather than every OCR slip (e.g. table “1881” for Saint-Vincent démarche = 1861).
Notes on form
Converted from chapter-bullet inventory to continuous English narration (2026-08-16). Institutional terms kept in the source language on first emphasis as Term — English restatement. Re-deepen from raw before heavy entity extraction.

sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t7.title: Ollivier — L'Empire libéral, Tome VII
sources/ollivier-empire-liberal-t7.content:
Ollivier — L’Empire libéral, Tome VII
Émile Ollivier (1825–1913) — L’Empire libéral; études, récits, souvenirs. — Tome septième. — Paris: Garnier frères, libraires-éditeurs, 6, rue des Saints-Pères, 1903.
The seventh volume of Ollivier’s eighteen-volume memoir-history of the Second Empire. Ollivier, lawyer, deputy of the Corps législatif, and later head of the ministry of 2 January 1870, writes as participant-observer: personal journal, private conversations (Morny, the Empress, Napoléon III, Rouher, La Valette), and parliamentary oratory sit beside diplomatic narrative. The title-band of this tome is Le démembrement du Danemark — Le Syllabus — La mort de Morny — L’entrevue de Biarritz.
Core narrative runs from the Danish crisis of late 1863 through the war and Treaty of Vienna (30 October 1864), the September Convention and Syllabus (1864–65), Morny’s death and the Empress’s second regency (1865), Gastein and the Biarritz interview with Bismarck (August–October 1865), the decision to abandon Maximilian (January–February 1866), and the formation of the tiers-parti (“Third Party”) around Ollivier’s address speech (February 1866). Backstory on the Elbe duchies and the Treaty of London reaches to 1848–1852.
Approximately 650 pages (text through p. 647 plus table). From the Internet Archive item lempireliberal07olli (UCLA copy; OCR ABBYY FineReader 8.0). Typ. Ph. Renouard, Paris.
Chapters
Livre XII — Le démembrement du Danemark
Schleswig-Holstein crisis, German-Danish War, London Conference, Treaty of Vienna (1863–1864), with 1848–1852 backstory.
Chapitre I. La situation des duchés de l’Elbe dans le Danemark — Le traité de Londres — Political geography of the Danish monarchy after 1814 (loss of Norway); Holstein, Schleswig, and the German Confederation; effects of 1848 in the duchies; Prussian intervention; Augustenburg renunciation (23 April 1852); Treaty of London (8 May 1852) and its tension with the principle of nationalities. Chapitre II. Le roi Frédéric — Commencement de son conflit avec l’Allemagne — Character of Frederik VII; morganatic union with Mme Rasmussen; Danish constitution of 2 October 1855; Diet protests; Russell against Denmark (24 September 1862); minister Hall; patent on Holstein administration (12 November 1862); marriage of the Prince of Wales to Alexandra of Denmark (10 March 1863); ordinance of 30 March 1863 and Austro-Prussian note (17 April); new constitution (13 November 1863); death of Frederik VII (15 November 1863). Chapitre III. Christian IX — Portrait of the new king; hesitation then sanction of the constitution; Napoléon III’s congress invitation (16 November 1863); Augustenburg candidacy for the duchies; German enthusiasm for that claim. Chapitre IV. La politique de Bismarck dans l’affaire des duchés — Bismarck’s aim of Prussian annexation against king, parliament, Diet, and Europe; rally of Austria; dual declaration to the Diet (7 December 1863); Fleury mission to Copenhagen; fall of Hall, Monrad ministry (29 December 1863); Napoléon’s telegram to Fleury not to speak of the Rhine; refusal of a restricted congress and of armed opposition to German national feeling.
Chapitre V. La guerre — Saxon and Hanoverian entry into Holstein (24 December 1863); Augustenburg at Kiel; Austro-Prussian occupation of Schleswig as pledge; Prussian Landtag refuses the loan; Napoléon refuses Russell’s proposal to block the invasion; invasion of Schleswig (1 February 1864); Wrangel against the Danewerk; Meza’s retreat (5 February) and Oversø; debate on invading Jutland; Russell’s naval demonstration proposal and Napoléon’s unanswered Rhine question; fall of Düppel (18 April 1864); Russell proposes the London Conference. Chapitre VI. La conférence de Londres — Portraits of the plenipotentiaries; prior understanding of Napoléon III and Bismarck; Clarendon’s Paris visit; Garibaldi in England (April–May 1864); armistice (May 1864); five solutions and Russell’s dismemberment line; Kappeln–Husum frontier and failed ultima; Danish refusal of compulsory arbitration; Bismarck’s manœuvre; rupture of the Conference (25 June 1864); English confidence motion saved by Cobden. Chapitre VII. La fin de la guerre — Application du principe de la conquête — Traité de Vienne du 30 octobre 1864 — Resumption of war (26 June); capture of Als (29 June); Christian IX dismisses Monrad and signs preliminaries; definitive peace at Vienna (30 October 1864); the king after the treaty. Chapitre VIII. Les effets du traité — Revival of conquest as principle; German protests; Palmerston’s judgment; Austria’s incomprehensible conduct; defence of Napoléon’s non-intervention; discord of Wilhelm and Franz Joseph over the spoils; fall of Rechberg, Belcredi–Mensdorff; European position of Napoléon III after the Danish affair.
Livre XIII — Projets d’évacuation de Rome et du Mexique
Roman question under Drouyn de Lhuys, September Convention, Syllabus, Maximilian in Mexico (1864–early 1865).
Chapitre I. La question romaine à Rome sous le ministère Drouyn de Lhuys — Lallemand’s reports; alleged Oddo Russell offer of Malta hospitality to the Pope; small difficulties and reform demands refused at Rome. Chapitre II. La question romaine à Turin sous Drouyn de Lhuys — Farini and Minghetti ministries; Visconti-Venosta; decision to “decapitate” Turin (move the capital). Chapitre III. La convention du 15 septembre 1864 — Preliminary negotiations; Garibaldi fears; approaches to La Marmora; Victor Emmanuel informed; text of the Convention (15 September 1864); execution measures; Turin riots (21–22 September) and La Marmora ministry (29 September); national programme, Mazzini’s rupture, Garibaldi’s insults; Drouyn’s seven points (30 October) and La Marmora’s reply (17 November); Italian parliamentary debate and d’Azeglio; capital-transfer decree (11 December 1864) and Turin hostility (January 1865); true meaning of the Convention — meant to save the temporal power, it made that power harder to keep; papal anger. Chapitre IV. Le Syllabus — Government changes: Vuitry president of the Conseil d’État (28 September 1864); Prince Napoléon vice-president of the Conseil privé (24 November); death of Mocquard (9 December); the Syllabus itself; thesis vs hypothesis; Montalembert at the Malines Congress and Syllabus condemnation of that reading; government ban on publication and episcopal protest; Malines speech held to have defeated the Syllabus; Vegezzi mission.
Chapitre V. Maximilien au Mexique — Maximilian courts popularity by dismissing clericals and leaning on the anti-French party; nuncio Meglia (“nonce-Syllabus,” 9 December 1864) and rupture with the Mexican government; Bazaine’s operations and fall of Oaxaca (February 1865); proposal to cut the expeditionary force to 25,000; Maximilian’s discontent; impossibility of his government; protest against the Miramar family arrangements (December 1864).
Livre XIV — La mort de Morny et la régence de l’Impératrice — L’entrevue de Biarritz — L’abandon du Mexique
Interior politics 1865, Gastein, Biarritz, abandonment of Maximilian, formation of the tiers-parti (1865–February 1866).
Chapitre I. Méditations personnelles — Death and portrait of Prosper Enfantin; Ollivier’s view of the September Convention; Persigny’s letter to Girardin on La Presse (November 1864). Chapitre II. Mort de Morny — Last conversations with Morny; reconciliation with Prince Napoléon; death of Morny (10 March 1865); portrait of Morny; death of Proudhon; Prince Napoléon’s liberal intentions; meeting with Duruy. Chapitre III. Le discours de l’Empereur à l’ouverture de la session de 1865 — Analysis of the throne speech (Baltic neutrality and nationalities; southern Europe); Piedmontese reaction to the “petit pays au pied des Alpes”; debates on free and compulsory primary instruction; Duruy’s report. Chapitre IV. La Vie de César — Judgment on Caesar’s assassination; judgment on Napoléon III’s work; George Sand’s testimony; publication of the first volume (9 March 1865).
Chapitre V. Les questions intérieures dans l’Adresse de 1865 — Schneider provisional president; Left excludes Ollivier and Darimon from its meetings; Ollivier’s speech that the moment has come for the Empire to grant liberty (27 March 1865); Thiers and Thuillier; La Valette interior minister (28 March); Picard on 2 December as a crime. Chapitre VI. Les questions extérieures dans la discussion de l’Adresse — September Convention in the Senate: Darboy (15 March), Rouher (17 March); Thiers against the Convention; Ollivier’s reply and Rouher; Jules Favre on failure to defend the Treaty of London and Ollivier’s answer; Mexican loan debate and Rouher’s optimism (11 April); Emperor’s reply to the Corps législatif. Chapitre VII. La seconde régence de l’Impératrice — Emperor’s departure for Algeria; testament; Empress instituted regent (26 April 1865); Ollivier’s first interview with the Empress (6 May 1865). Chapitre VIII. Le discours d’Ajaccio — Prince Napoléon’s Ajaccio speech at the Napoleon monument (15 May 1865); the Emperor’s letter to the prince.
Chapitre IX. La fin de la régence et de la session de 1865 — Regent’s activity (Buffet’s testimony); Emperor in Algeria and letter to Mac-Mahon (20 June); senatus-consulte on naturalization (14 July); Thiers on bankruptcy and income tax; close of the session (4 July 1865). Chapitre X. Première entrevue d’Émile Ollivier avec l’Empereur — Élections municipales — À Biarritz — La fille d’Émile de Girardin et l’Impératrice — Roquette juvenile-detainees commission and Ollivier’s first sight of the Emperor; commission sittings; opposition gains in municipal elections; Emperor at Biarritz (7 September 1865); the Empress and Girardin’s daughter. Chapitre XI. Les embarras d’une conquête faite en commun — Prussian conditions for organizing the duchies (22 February 1865) rejected by Austria; Prussian constitutional conflict, Roon and Bismarck; Landtag refuses Danish-war credits and is closed (17 June 1865); Schmerling’s difficulty, Mensdorff, soft Austrian diplomacy; Bismarck’s encroachments and Crown syndics’ opinion (5 August); king and Bismarck at Carlsbad (21 June); Bismarck–Gramont conversation and opening toward Italy; probes of Napoléon’s mind and Drouyn’s evasions; pressure on La Marmora. Chapitre XII. La convention de Gastein — Analysis of Gastein (14 August 1865); emotion in Paris and Drouyn circular (29 August); effects in England, Vienna, Germany; Berlin reaction to the circular; Napoléon’s calming and Drouyn telegram to Berlin (23 September 1865).
Chapitre XIII. L’entrevue de Biarritz — Bismarck with Lefebvre de Béhaine on French-speaking lands; Manteuffel in Schleswig and imprudent speeches; what actually passed between Bismarck and the Emperor at Biarritz; what the Emperor wanted — immobility not from military exhaustion (Mexico had neither emptied the arsenals nor the treasury); why Bismarck could not read the Emperor; beginnings of the Emperor’s illness. Chapitre XIV. La mort de Palmerston — La lettre de Pie IX à Mgr Darboy — Death of Palmerston (18 October 1865); Russell prime minister; Pius IX’s grievances against Darboy and censure letter (26 October 1865). Chapitre XV. Fera-t-on de nouvelles concessions libérales? — Bad effect of the Ajaccio speech on the Emperor; Rouher’s turn under La Valette; Persigny proposes restoring the imperial nobility; Fould obtains cadre reductions (15 November 1865); Ollivier’s impressions and La Valette’s propositions; Compiègne fêtes, Henriette Maréchal, Liège student congress; deaths of Léopold, Thuillier, and Dupin. Chapitre XVI. L’abandon de Maximilien — Bazaine’s indolence, double reports, and recriminations; Maximilian’s complaints and letters to Napoléon III (26 May, 27 July 1865); value of mutual recriminations; decree of 3 October 1865 under Bazaine’s pressure; Maximilian’s letter of 27 December 1865; United States diplomatic pressure; Drouyn proposals to the U.S. (recognition / non-overthrow) rejected; Napoléon decides abandonment — Drouyn to Dano (14 January 1866), letters to Bazaine (15 January), Saillard mission; state of the Mexican army and certainty of fall after French departure; Bazaine’s contrary hope (26 February 1866); how Maximilian received the news — letter to Napoléon III (18 February 1866).
Chapitre XVII. La formation du tiers-parti — Throne speech opening the 1866 session: constitution likened to that of the United States, intention not to modify it further; Ollivier’s discontent expressed to La Valette; conversation with the Empress (23 February 1866); amendment of the 44 and portrait of Chevandier de Valdrôme; Address debates in Senate and Corps législatif — Persigny, Emperor’s softened Senate reply (18 February), Thiers on dynastic rights, Berryer on the Arab letter, Chesnelong on Rome, German affairs; Left amendment on interior liberties; Buffet on the amendment of the 44; Rouher’s reply; Ollivier’s reply; the speech that constitutes him chief of the tiers-parti; continuation of the campaign in La Presse.
Éclaircissements
Anecdotes of Rouher on the coup d’État; ministers in the Assemblies; ministerial responsibility; letters of Émile Ollivier to various correspondents; letter of Drouyn de Lhuys to the duc de Gramont; the Société de Saint-Vincent de Paul.
Notes
Volume 7 of 18 in the Garnier series L’Empire libéral (tomes I–VI published 1895–1901; this tome 1903). Title-page band and interior Livre heads fix the volume identity independently of the IA identifier suffix 07. Tome V (1860–62; L’Inauguration de l’Empire libéral — Le Roi Guillaume) is also extracted in this wiki; Tome XI (1868–69; Livre XIX La Veillée des armes), Tome XIV (July 1870; Livre XXII La Guerre), and Tome XVI (August 1870; Livre XXIV Le Suicide) sit in the 1866–1919 wiki.
Historical span for cataloguing: late 1863 – February 1866 (Elbe-duchies backstory 1848–1852 only). Placed in the 1800–1865 wiki by content weight (Danish war, September Convention, Syllabus, Morny, Gastein, Biarritz); the closing chapters on Mexico abandonment and the tiers-parti cross into early 1866, analogous to Sybel Vol. IV’s straddle at the 1865/66 boundary.
Raw text from IA lempireliberal07olli_djvu.txt (UTF-8). Light cleanup applied (collapsed OCR double-spacing). French OCR retains residual character errors (e.g. numeral confusions in running heads and a TOC slip dating Morny’s death 1863 for 1865); chapter digests above follow narrative chronology and standard dates.
Notes on form

sources/springer-geschichte-oesterreichs.title: Springer — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809, Vol. I: Der Verfall des alten Reiches
sources/springer-geschichte-oesterreichs.content:
Springer — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809, Vol. I: Der Verfall des alten Reiches
Anton Springer (1825–1891) — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809. Erster Theil: Der Verfall des alten Reiches. — Leipzig: Verlag von S. Hirzel, 1863. The volume forms Band VI of the series Staatengeschichte der neuesten Zeit, edited by Karl Biedermann.
The first of two volumes of Springer’s history of Austria from the Treaty of Schönbrunn (1809) to the revolution of 1848. The present volume — Der Verfall des alten Reiches (The Decline of the Old Empire) — carries the monarchy from the condition it had reached at the end of the Napoleonic wars, through the long policy of standstill under Emperor Francis I and Prince Metternich, the financial crises and the Hungarian Diets, down to the disintegration of the governing powers and the collapse of the old Empire on the eve of the revolutionary year 1848. Its companion volume, Die österreichische Revolution (1865), continues the narrative through the revolution itself.
Springer, a historian of art and of the German national movement, writes in the German-Fraktur historical idiom of the era, treating Austria as a European great power whose internal structure — the estates, the crownlands, the Hungarian constitution, and the claims of the non-German nationalities — was dissolving even as its diplomatic standing held. The volume is notable for its extended treatment of the Hungarian Diets and of the constitutional friction between Vienna and Pesth (Budapest).
The text is approximately 580 pages, extracted from a New York Public Library scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Erstes Buch — Die gegebenen Zustände (The Existing Conditions)
An introductory book describing the state of the Austrian monarchy at the close of the Napoleonic era and the foundations on which its subsequent policy rested.
1. Einleitung — an introduction affirming Austria’s political necessity and its role in the European balance of power. 2. Die Reaction gegen Josephs II. Reformen — the reaction against the reforming spirit of Joseph II; the conservative restoration that followed the revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. 3. Die Kriegsjahre 1792 bis 1809 — the war years from 1792 to the Treaty of Schönbrunn (1809); Austria’s struggles against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France.
Zweites Buch — Die Begründung der Politik des Stillstandes und Gleichgewichtes (The Founding of the Policy of Standstill and Balance)
The establishment under Francis I and Metternich of a system of political stagnation and equilibrium.
1. Kaiser Franz und Metternich — the character and policy of Emperor Francis I and his minister Metternich; the principles of the system of standstill. 2. Das Finanzpatent — the Financial Patent (the great state bankruptcy of 1811) and the handling of the Austrian finances. 3. Der ungarische Reichstag 1811 — the Hungarian Diet of 1811 and the friction between the crown and the Hungarian estates. 4. Die Befreiungskriege — the Wars of Liberation (1813–1815); Austria’s part in the overthrow of Napoleon and the settlement of the Congress of Vienna.
Drittes Buch — Die Jubeljahre der Reaction (The Jubilee Years of Reaction)
The high point of the conservative restoration after 1815.
1. Die Wiederherstellung der österreichischen Macht — the restoration of Austrian power in the European system after the fall of Napoleon. 2. Der Sieg über den Liberalismus — the victory over liberalism; the suppression of liberal and national aspirations within the monarchy. 3. Die Regelung der Finanzen — the regulation of the finances after the disorders of the war years.
Viertes Buch — Schwankungen und Rückschritte (Vacillations and Setbacks)
The growing strain on the system of standstill in the later years of Francis I.
1. Der ungarische Reichstag 1825 — the Hungarian Diet of 1825; the renewed constitutional conflict with Hungary. 2. Die orientalische Frage — the Eastern Question; Austria’s involvement in the affairs of the Ottoman Empire. 3. Die letzten Lebensjahre des Kaiser Franz — the last years of Emperor Francis (d. 1835); the end of the old emperor’s reign.
Fünftes Buch — Die Zersetzung der Regierungsgewalten (The Disintegration of the Governing Powers)
The decline of the old Empire on the eve of 1848.
1. Die Vormundschaft der Staatsconferenz — the guardianship of the State Conference; the regency-like council that governed in the name of the feeble Emperor Ferdinand I (1835–1848). 2. Der Operatenreichstag — the long Hungarian Diet of 1832–1836, so called for the royal reform propositions (Operate) laid before it; the language and nationality questions, the railway and taxation debates, the closing of the Diet in 1836. 3. Die ständische Bewegung in den deutsch-slawischen Ländern — the estates movement in the German and Slavic crownlands (including Bohemia); the stirring of national sentiment among the subject peoples. 4. Der Verfall des alten Reiches — the decline and fall of the old Empire; the disintegration of the governing powers that opened the way to the revolution of 1848.
The volume closes with the running heading Der Verfall des alten Reiches carrying the narrative to the threshold of the revolutionary year.
Note on the text: The OCR is German Fraktur with the original long-s (ſ), which renders correctly in the raw text. Running headers repeat identically on facing pages and carry the book titles. The full table of contents (Inhalt) appears at the opening of the volume. The Operate in the chapter Der Operatenreichstag is the Hungarian administrative term for the royal reform propositions submitted to the Diet.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Springer vol. 1 is Austrian history baseline before or into the revolutionary break—Metternich-era structures and the empire’s peoples as Springer orders them.
Imperial structure
Court, bureaucracy, police, and the non-German crowns as administrative problems.
Toward 1848
Pre-March grievances Springer stacks so vol. 2’s revolution does not appear ex nihilo. Pair with Friedjung for denser 1848–60 political narrative.

sources/springer-geschichte-oesterreichs.title: Springer — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809, Vol. II: Die österreichische Revolution
sources/springer-geschichte-oesterreichs.content:
Springer — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809, Vol. II: Die österreichische Revolution
Anton Springer (1825–1891) — Geschichte Oesterreichs seit dem Wiener Frieden 1809. Zweiter Theil: Die österreichische Revolution. — Leipzig: Verlag von S. Hirzel, 1865. The volume forms the companion to Springer’s Erster Theil: Der Verfall des alten Reiches (1863); together they comprise Band VI of the series Staatengeschichte der neuesten Zeit, edited by Karl Biedermann.
The second of two volumes of Springer’s history of Austria from the Treaty of Schönbrunn (1809) to the revolution of 1848. Where the first volume carried the monarchy from the Napoleonic settlement through the long policy of standstill down to the disintegration of the old Empire, the present volume — Die österreichische Revolution (The Austrian Revolution) — takes up the revolutionary year itself and carries the narrative through the risings, the constitutional experiments, and the civil war in Hungary to the restoration of absolutism.
Springer structures the volume in five books, following the revolution from its genesis to its close. He treats the movement as above all a national one: the opening chapter insists that the political struggle turned essentially on the relation of the nationalities to one another and on the measure of their state rights and privileges, and advances the maxim that “the true constitutional charter of Austria is its language map.” The narrative then moves from the growth of national consciousness and the Hungarian parties, through the March days of 1848 in Vienna, the jubilee weeks of the revolution, the Slav Congress in Prague, the parliamentary period of the Austrian and Hungarian diets, the October revolution and the Winter Campaign in Hungary, to the octroyed constitution of 1849, the summer campaign in Hungary, and the closing Schlußwort.
The volume is approximately 770 pages of text, extracted from a University of Michigan scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Erstes Buch — Die Genesis der Revolution (The Genesis of the Revolution)
The origins of the revolutionary movement.
1. Die Entwickelung des nationalen Bewußtseins — the growth of national consciousness among the many peoples of Austria; the linguistic and ethnic map of the monarchy (the German element about 23 per cent of the population), the status of the Italian, Slavic, and Magyar nationalities, and the view that the whole political struggle turned on the relations of the nationalities to one another. 2. Die politischen Parteien in Ungarn seit 1840 — the political parties in Hungary since 1840; the reform movement, the Magyar opposition, and the growth of Hungarian political life under the old constitution. 3. Die Märztage 1848 — the March days of 1848; the outbreak of revolution in Vienna and the fall of Metternich.
Zweites Buch — Die Jubelwochen der Revolution (The Jubilee Weeks of the Revolution)
The brief triumph of the revolutionary movement in the spring of 1848.
1. Die Erbtheilung zwischen den Volksstämmen Oesterreichs — the division of the inheritance among the peoples of Austria; the competing claims of Germans, Magyars, Slavs, and Italians to a share in the new order. 2. Gründung und Sturz der Verfassung vom 25. April — the framing and overthrow of the constitution of 25 April 1848; the constitution granted by the court and its rejection in Vienna. 3. Der Slawencongreß in Prag — the Slav Congress in Prague (June 1848); the pan-Slav congress and the rising in Prague.
Drittes Buch — Die parlamentarische Periode (The Parliamentary Period)
The summer and autumn of 1848, when representative assemblies sat across the monarchy.
1. Die Landtage in den kleinen Provinzen — the diets of the smaller provinces; the provincial assemblies in the German and Slavic crownlands. 2. Der Wiener Reichstag — the Reichstag (constituent assembly) at Vienna. 3. Der Agramer Landtag — the Diet of Agram (Zagreb); the Croatian Diet and the conflict between Croatia and the Hungarian government. 4. Der ungarische Reichstag — the Hungarian Diet; the Hungarian revolutionary government under Kossuth and the quarrel with the court over Hungary’s separate constitution and the Croatian question.
Viertes Buch — Die Krisis der Revolution (The Crisis of the Revolution)
The turning of the revolution toward civil war and reaction.
1. Die Octoberrevolution — the October revolution in Vienna (October 1848); the rising of the Viennese against the government, the flight of the court, and the reconquest of the city by Windischgrätz. 2. Der Reichstag in Kremsier — the Reichstag removed to Kremsier (Kroměříž); the constituent assembly’s sittings in Moravia and its constitutional labors. 3. Der Winterfeldzug in Ungarn — the Winter Campaign in Hungary (1848–1849); the imperial military operations against the Hungarian revolutionary government.
Fünftes Buch — Die Rückkehr zum Absolutismus (The Return to Absolutism)
The restoration of imperial authority and the suppression of the revolution.
1. Die octroyirte Verfassung — the octroyed (imposed) constitution of March 1849; the dissolution of the Kremsier Reichstag and the imposition of a constitution by decree. 2. Der Sommerfeldzug in Ungarn — the Summer Campaign in Hungary (1849); the Russian intervention and the crushing of the Hungarian revolution. 3. Schlußwort — the conclusion; the final victory of reaction and the restoration of absolutism under Francis Joseph.
The volume closes with the running heading Die österreichische Revolution carrying the narrative to the re-establishment of absolutism in 1849.
Note on the text: The OCR is German Fraktur with the original long-s (ſ), which renders correctly in the raw text. Running headers repeat identically on facing pages and carry the book titles. The full table of contents (Inhalt) appears at the opening of the volume. Place-names appear in their nineteenth-century German forms (Kremsier for Kroměříž, Agram for Zagreb), consistent with the era and source.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Springer vol. 2 carries Austria through revolution and reaction—the companion to Friedjung with different chapter cuts.
1848 theatres
Vienna, Prague, Hungary, Italy as Springer distributes attention; military restorers and failed diets.
Neo-absolutist landing
Bach-era administration in Springer’s terms (Absolutismus — “absolutism” — of officials). Cross-link bach-system and nationality pages.
