sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 1
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 1
Heinrich von Sybel (1817–1895) — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I. Erster Band. — 2. unveränderte Auflage. München und Leipzig: Verlag von R. Oldenbourg, 1889.
The opening volume of Sybel’s multi-volume history of the foundation of the German Empire under Wilhelm I. (“William I”). In the Vorrede (“preface”) Sybel explains that after his Geschichte der Revolutionszeit 1789–1800 had traced the collapse of the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation, the events of 1866 and 1870 made him wish to recount the rebirth of the German Reich from authentic sources. Political obstacles delayed the plan until Fürst Bismarck (“Prince Bismarck”) allowed publication of his Frankfurt reports and letters and, on 19 March 1881, authorized use of the Prussian state archives and the Foreign Office registry for Prussian history 1850–1870. Sybel inventories the material he was permitted to see: ministerial decrees and ambassadors’ reports, conference protocols, telegrams and correspondence of every kind, notes and despatches of foreign powers, chamber proceedings and newspaper cuttings, all ordered in long series of hundreds of file bundles. Desired supplements came from the records of the State Ministry and of the Great General Staff, from oral communications of persons who took part in or stood near the events, and, for the opposing policy, from the older archives of Hanover, Electoral Hesse, and Nassau. He claims that after countless incomplete, half-true, or untrue accounts, the possibility now existed to write the history of those decades from the documents that grew out of Prussian action or determined it, following every turn of policy day by day and in decisive crises hour by hour.
This first volume runs from the revolutionary crisis of 1848–49 through the Prussian Union project and the Olmützer Punktation (“Punctation of Olmütz”) of late 1850. Sybel’s interpretive line is already firm: German unity under a hereditary empire offered by a popular assembly failed because Prussia’s king would not accept a crown from revolution and because Austria and the secondary states would not accept Prussian hegemony without coercion; the dualist contest ends, for this volume, in Austria’s temporary restoration of the old Bund (“Confederation”). The books that follow inside the volume—National Assembly, imperial question, Union policy, renunciation of the Union—form a single dramatic arc from parliamentary hope to cabinet defeat.
Erstes Buch — Die Nationalversammlung (The National Assembly)
Sybel opens with the Frankfurt Nationalversammlung (“National Assembly”) as the institutional expression of the 1848 national movement. He presents it not as a free creation of the German people alone but as the product of a Europe-wide revolutionary shock that toppled Metternich’s system and forced princes and cabinets into provisional cooperation with liberal and national committees. The book follows the Assembly’s struggle to define the territorial scope of the future Germany—großdeutsch versus kleindeutsch (“greater-German” including Austria’s German lands versus “lesser-German” under Prussia without the Habsburg monarchy)—the catalogue of fundamental rights of the German people, and the executive power that might give a constitution force. Sybel stresses the Assembly’s lack of an army and treasury of its own: its authority depended on the goodwill of the larger states, above all Prussia and Austria, and on the residual prestige of the old federal institutions. Debates over the Reichsverweser (“Imperial Regent”) Erzherzog Johann (“Archduke John”), over the provisional central power, and over relations with the dynastic governments occupy the early chapters; Sybel portrays a body rich in legal and historical learning yet weak in the instruments of state.
The narrative then turns to the military and diplomatic environment in which the Assembly worked. Wars and interventions on the periphery—Italy, Hungary, Schleswig-Holstein—drew off Austrian and Prussian attention and periodically raised hopes that one or the other great power might lend the national constitution a sword. Sybel follows the Schleswig-Holstein entanglement as a test case: popular German sympathy for the duchies collided with European treaty law and with Prussian cabinet caution, producing armistices and protests that damaged the Assembly’s credit among nationalists without securing durable gains. Inside Germany, the failure of radical risings and the recovery of monarchical armies narrowed the space for a purely parliamentary solution. Party groups inside the Paulskirche (“St. Paul’s Church”)—moderate liberals, democrats, Catholics, particularists—receive attention as they form and reform majorities on rights, central power, and the Austrian question. By the time the Assembly approached the imperial constitution and the question of the hereditary emperor, Sybel argues, the decisive fact was already clear: only Prussia could furnish the power to make a German constitution real, and Prussia’s crown would not take that power on revolutionary title. Austrian recovery after the Italian campaigns and the suppression of the Hungarian rising stiffened Vienna’s refusal to be reduced to a non-German great power outside a Prussian-led empire.
Zweites Buch — Die Kaiserfrage (The Imperial Question)
The second book is devoted to the Kaiserfrage (“imperial question”)—whether and on what terms a German emperor should be created. Sybel reconstructs the constitutional draft that vested hereditary imperial dignity in the King of Prussia, the negotiations and party alignments inside the Assembly, and the famous deputation that offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV. (“Frederick William IV”) in Berlin. He treats the king’s refusal not as a mere personal quirk but as the consistent expression of a legitimist and federalist conscience: the crown of Charlemagne’s heirs, in the king’s view, could not be accepted from a popular assembly without the free consent of the princes and without a settlement that preserved the monarchical principle. Sybel recounts the king’s public answers and private language, the pressure of Prussian conservatives and of the court camarilla, and the disappointment of moderate liberals who had hoped Berlin would accept leadership even with reservations. Austrian statesmen, recovering authority, made clear that a kleindeutsch hereditary empire meant the political expulsion of the Habsburg monarchy from Germany—an outcome Vienna would fight by diplomacy and, if need be, by arms in alliance with particularist courts.
Around the refusal cluster the secondary states’ calculations. Bavaria, Württemberg, Saxony, and Hanover weighed particular interests, dynastic dignity, and fear of both Prussian centralization and democratic excess. Sybel details the crumbling of the Assembly’s majority, the withdrawal of Austrian and then other deputies, the rump’s move toward Stuttgart, and the extinction of the parliamentary experiment amid military restoration. The book closes the revolutionary chapter of national unity: the constitution of the Paulskirche remains a monument of German liberal statecraft, but without force behind it the imperial project collapses, leaving the field to cabinets. Sybel’s judgment is that the Assembly educated the nation in constitutional forms and national goals even as it failed as a governing body—an education later cabinets would inherit and redirect under different titles and with different instruments.
Drittes Buch — Die preußische Unionspolitik (The Prussian Union Policy)
With the Assembly gone, Sybel turns to Prussia’s attempt to organize Germany from above through the Unionspolitik (“Union policy”). The Dreikönigsbündnis (“Three Kings’ Alliance”) of Prussia, Saxony, and Hanover becomes the core of a projected Erfurter Union (“Erfurt Union”)—a narrower federation under Prussian leadership, with a constitution more conservative than Frankfurt’s yet still national in ambition. Sybel follows the drafting of the Union constitution, the invitation to other German governments, the elections and meeting of the Erfurt parliament, and the simultaneous Austrian effort to revive the old Bundestag (“Federal Diet”) at Frankfurt as the sole legitimate federal organ. He gives weight to Joseph Maria von Radowitz as the intellectual and diplomatic driver of the Union idea at the Prussian court, and to the tension between Radowitz’s national programme and the king’s reluctance to risk war with Austria and Russia.
The narrative emphasizes dualism. Fürst Schwarzenberg (“Prince Schwarzenberg”) in Vienna works to restore Austria’s federal primacy and to isolate Prussia; Berlin under Friedrich Wilhelm IV and his ministers oscillates between national leadership and fear of European war. Sybel uses diplomatic correspondence to show how the middle states hedged, how Russian influence weighed against a Prussian-led reorganization that might upset the post-1815 balance, and how public opinion in northern Germany remained more favorable to Union ideas than many cabinets. Military demonstrations, mobilization measures, and the Hessian constitutional crisis tighten the confrontation: the question is no longer only constitutional form but which great power will dominate the Confederation’s executive and army. Sybel tracks the Zollverein (“Customs Union”) as a quiet Prussian asset—economic cohesion in the north and centre that outlasted the political Union—without yet making commerce the sole key to unity. Erfurt’s parliamentary episode is treated with respect for its moderating constitutional work and with clear-eyed recognition that without Bavaria, Württemberg, and Austria, and without a king ready to fight, the Union remained a torso.
Viertes Buch — Der Verzicht auf die Union (Renunciation of the Union)
The fourth book carries the Union crisis to its end. Sybel narrates the progressive defection of allies, the legal and military pressure Austria and the restored Diet can bring to bear, and the Prussian court’s decision to avoid a general German war. The climax is the Olmützer Punktation of November 1850: Prussia agrees to demobilize and to abandon the Union experiment in favor of conferences that will discuss federal reform under conditions favorable to Austria. Sybel does not hide the contemporary sense of humiliation in Prussian national circles; he presents Olmütz as a necessary retreat given Prussia’s unpreparedness and isolation, yet also as the nadir from which a later, better-armed Prussia under different leadership would reverse the verdict. He follows the road to Olmütz through the autumn mobilizations, the role of Tsarist mediation, and the internal Prussian debate between those who preferred a “glorious war” and those who preferred survival of the monarchical state without a premature trial of strength. The Hessian affair and the competing claims to execute federal law supply the immediate fuse; the deeper cause is Prussia’s inability to convert Union paper into recognized hegemony.
The volume thus ends with the old Confederation temporarily restored, Austrian influence reasserted at Frankfurt, and the national question postponed—setting the stage for the long dualist contest that subsequent volumes will follow through the Crimean years, the New Era, Bismarck’s appointment, and the wars of unification. For Sybel, 1848–50 is not a closed failure but the first act of a foundation story whose decisive instruments will be army reform, diplomatic isolation of Austria, and wars whose outcomes the documents of the 1860s will illuminate as carefully as this volume illuminates the documents of the revolutionary biennium.
Significance for this wiki
Volume 1 is the documentary foundation for Sybel’s Prussian-national reading of 1848–50: Frankfurt’s failure, the Union’s promise and collapse, and Olmütz as the reverse of 1866. Use it for actors (Schwarzenberg, Friedrich Wilhelm IV, Radowitz, the Erfurt circle), for the institutional sequence National Assembly → Union → restored Bund, and for archive-based detail on Prussian cabinet policy. Pair with Treitschke’s earlier narrative volumes for Vormärz background and with later Sybel volumes for Schleswig-Holstein and 1866.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 2
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 2
Heinrich von Sybel (1817–1895) — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I. Zweiter Band. — 2. unveränderte Auflage. München und Leipzig: Verlag von R. Oldenbourg, 1889.
The second volume of Sybel’s foundation history runs from the aftermath of the Olmützer Punktation (“Punctation of Olmütz,” 1850) into the first phase of Bismarck’s ministry (1862). Where volume 1 closed on Prussia’s renunciation of the Erfurt Union and Austria’s recovery of federal primacy, volume 2 asks how that primacy was institutionalized, how the Crimean War shook the conservative concert that had enforced Olmütz, how the Neue Ära (“New Era”) under the regency and reign of Wilhelm I. (“William I”) reopened national and constitutional hopes, and how the conflict over army reform brought Otto von Bismarck to the head of the Prussian government. Sybel continues to work from Prussian state papers, Diet records, and diplomatic correspondence; the tone is that of a national-liberal archive historian who treats the 1850s not as empty reaction but as the incubation of the power instruments used in the 1860s. Approximately five hundred pages of narrative bind four major books: restoration of the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”), the Crimean War, the New Era, and Bismarck with the constitutional conflict.
Fünftes Buch — Herstellung des Bundestags (Restoration of the Bundestag)
Sybel’s fifth book reconstructs the Herstellung des Bundestags (“restoration of the Federal Diet”) at Frankfurt as Austria’s constitutional prize after Olmütz. The old Deutscher Bund (“German Confederation”) returns as the sole recognized federal frame; Prussia must resume its seat under a presidency Vienna means to exercise in substance as well as ceremony. The Dresdener Konferenzen (“Dresden Conferences”) of 1850–51 are presented as the promised forum for federal reform that might have softened the humiliation of demobilization. Sybel follows the agendas item by item—army contingent and federal fortress obligations, forms of representation, executive competence in crises, the thorny place of Austria’s non-German lands inside any tighter union—and shows why results remained meagre. Fürst Schwarzenberg (“Prince Schwarzenberg”) pushed toward a stronger central authority in which the entire Habsburg monarchy would weigh as a unit; Berlin refused to be permanently outvoted inside a client-majority Diet; the middle states sought guarantees for particular rights without paying the military and fiscal price of a real federal executive. Reform talk yields restoration more than transformation: the Bund of 1815 is patched, not replaced.
Alongside the federal story Sybel places the internal settlement of the German courts after 1849–50: press and association laws, disciplined chambers, surviving constitutions narrowed in practice by emergency statutes and loyal ministries. He is not writing a social history of the reaction; he is writing how restored cabinets used the Bund to coordinate conservative order while commercial ties—especially Prussian leadership of the Zollverein (“Customs Union”)—continued to integrate the north and centre under Berlin’s tariff. That double track, political subordination in the Diet and economic primacy in the customs league, structures his 1850s. He notes personnel at the Prussian mission in Frankfurt, including Bismarck’s apprenticeship as envoy learning Austrian methods from across the table, the tone of protocols, and the gradual Prussian conclusion that open challenge must await better military and diplomatic conditions. Schwarzenberg’s death and the uneven quality of his successors already hint that Austrian leadership will be harder to sustain than the ceremonial revival of 1851 suggested. Sybel also records how smaller states used the restored Diet to seek protection against both Prussian commercial pressure and democratic agitation, making Frankfurt once again a marketplace of particularist bargains.
Sechstes Buch — Der Krimkrieg (The Crimean War)
The sixth book treats the Crimean War as the European stress test of the post-Olmütz order. Sybel narrates the Eastern crisis from the Russian occupation of the Danubian Principalities through the formation of the Western alliance and the fighting in the Crimea to the Congress of Paris. For German history his interest is alignment rather than Black Sea topography. Austria’s armed diplomacy against Russia along the Danube breaks the old conservative solidarity of the Holy Alliance years; Prussia under Friedrich Wilhelm IV. (“Frederick William IV”) seeks a path between Western solicitation and dynastic gratitude to the Tsar who had helped police Germany in 1850. Cabinet debates in Berlin, instructions to envoys at London, Paris, Vienna, and St Petersburg, and discussions at the Diet over neutrality and possible federal measures fill Sybel’s chapters. He presents the future minister Bismarck—still primarily Prussian representative at Frankfurt—as already arguing that Prussia’s interest is freedom of action, not automatic solidarity with Austria’s Balkan and Italian exposures or with a crusade defined in London and Paris.
Sybel shows the war years weakening Austria financially and diplomatically without yet handing Prussia a German mandate. The Paris settlement rearranges the Black Sea regime and the Principalities; in Germany the practical residue is a clearer sense that Austrian federal leadership no longer rests on a solid monarchical concert. Public opinion and chambers discuss the East, but cabinets decide; the king’s personal scruples brake any bold exploitation of Austria’s embarrassment. Sybel links Crimean habits of independent Prussian calculation to the Italian crisis of 1859 and to the German crises of the 1860s: the school of dualist diplomacy continues even when the German question is not formally on the agenda. He also registers the limited military reform pressure that the war’s lessons exert on Prussian professionals watching rifled weapons, siege work, and logistics at a distance—pressure that will mature in the army bills of the New Era. The Bund’s inability to speak with one voice on a European war becomes, in Sybel’s telling, further proof that dualism without Prussian leadership means German impotence.
Siebentes Buch — Die Neue Ära (The New Era)
With the king’s incapacity and the regency of the Prince of Prussia, Sybel opens the Neue Ära. Liberal ministries and a conciliatory language raise hopes that Prussia will reconcile crown and chamber, cleanse administration of the worst reactionary habits, and resume a national German policy by legal means. Sybel recounts ministerial combinations, programmes of internal reform, and the firm limits of the experiment: the regent, soon king Wilhelm I., remains a soldier whose first care is the army’s readiness and the crown’s undivided command. The book connects modest domestic liberalization to German policy—firmer leadership in the Zollverein, a less apologetic tone at Frankfurt, cautious room for national associations—without claiming that the New Era solved dualism. Austria’s defeat in 1859 in Italy damages Habsburg prestige and finances; Sybel treats that shock as reopening German possibilities once Prussia possesses a reliable military instrument and a ministry willing to use it.
Detailed passages address army reorganization projects associated with Roon and the general staff tradition, the influence of the military cabinet, and friction between a liberal chamber majority and a crown that will not surrender the officer corps, three-year service, and regimental structure to parliamentary bargaining. Sybel presents the New Era as a bridge that educates parties in constitutional struggle and educates the king in the difficulty of governing a great-power Prussia against both his generals and a hostile house of deputies unless he finds a minister prepared to fight on both fronts. Economic chapters note railway expansion, banking growth, and customs politics as quiet accumulations of Prussian weight inside Germany even while the Diet remains ceremonially Austrian. The book’s closing mood is unstable hope: national liberals believe time works for Prussia; the crown believes time works only if the army is ready.
Achtes Buch — Bismarck und der Verfassungskonflikt (Bismarck and the Constitutional Conflict)
The eighth book brings the constitutional conflict and Bismarck’s appointment to the centre of the foundation story. Sybel narrates the army bills, the chamber’s refusal to approve the reorganized forces on the crown’s terms, the breakdown of New Era ministries, and the decision to call Bismarck from the diplomatic service—Frankfurt, St Petersburg, Paris—to the premiership. The new minister appears as the man who will govern if necessary without a budget law, defend monarchical military prerogative with a theory of constitutional gap, and reopen the German question by cabinet diplomacy and force rather than by liberal Diet majorities. Sybel insists on the link between domestic and foreign policy: a Prussia paralyzed by internal strife cannot lead Germany; a Prussia that restores executive force may. Early measures of the ministry—press conflicts, skirmishes at the Diet, defense of Zollverein prerogatives against Austrian commercial counter-schemes—close the volume on the eve of the Danish crisis that volume 3 will treat at length.
Sybel’s portrait is the national-liberal reading in which Bismarck’s conflict ministry is the necessary harsh prelude to wars that the documents of later volumes will justify by success. He does not deny the bitterness of the parliamentary struggle or the novelty of prolonged budgetless government; he embeds both in a longer story whose criterion is the foundation of a German national state under the Prussian crown. The reader leaves volume 2 with Olmütz’s political order still standing on paper, but with its European props weakened, Prussia’s commercial and military tools sharpened, and a chief minister in office who treats German dualism as a power problem.
Significance for this wiki
Use volume 2 for Dresden and Bund restoration, Prussian neutrality in the Crimean War, the New Era, Zollverein politics, the constitutional conflict, and Bismarck’s appointment. It bridges revolutionary dualism (vol. 1) and Schleswig-Holstein (vol. 3).

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 3
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 3
Heinrich von Sybel (1817–1895) — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I. Dritter Band. — 3. Auflage. München und Leipzig: Verlag von R. Oldenbourg, 1890.
The third volume is wholly given to the Schleswig-Holstein question and the German-Danish War of 1864. Sybel moves from the constitutional and dynastic history of the duchies and the succession crisis under Christian VIII. and Friedrich VII. through the Londoner Protokoll (“London Protocol”) of 1852 and the Bundesexekution (“federal execution”) of 1863–64 to the campaign over the Danewerk (“Danevirke” — the Danish earthwork fortification), Düppel (“Dybbøl”), and Alsen, and the peace that strips Denmark of the Elbe duchies. In the architecture of the Begründung, this is the first of the three wars of unification: it rehabilitates Prussian arms after the long shadow of Olmütz, teaches joint action and joint quarrel with Austria, and shows Bismarck steering national passion without surrendering policy to the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”) or to a pure Augustenburg solution. Roughly five hundred pages bind legal prehistory, federal politics, operational narrative, and peace diplomacy into one continuous argument that 1864 opens the road to a German settlement by cabinet power.
Neuntes Buch — Die Herzogtümer (The Duchies)
Sybel opens with the legal labyrinth of Schleswig and Holstein: personal union with the Danish crown, Holstein’s membership in the German Confederation, Schleswig’s intermediate position between kingdom and German world, and the clash between the Danish Gesamtstaat (“unitary state”) programme and German ducal and national claims. He recounts the open letter of 1846, the risings and war of 1848–50, and the European packing of the result in the London Protocol, which sought to preserve the Danish monarchy’s integrity under great-power guarantee while promising the duchies protections that German opinion never trusted. For Sybel the Protocol did not reconcile federal law and nationality with Danish integration; it froze a contradiction that any vigorous Copenhagen constitution would reopen.
The narrative of the 1850s follows administrative incorporation efforts, language ordinances, petitions from the estates, debates at the Diet, and the growth of a German public committed to the duchies’ separation from Danish unitary constitutionalism. Professors, journalists, and the Nationalverein (“National Association” — the 1859 German national-liberal pressure group) keep the question warm while cabinets prefer quiet. When Friedrich VII dies and Christian IX. ascends under the Protocol order, the November constitution of 1863—binding Schleswig more tightly to the kingdom—becomes the immediate casus. Sybel presents princes and press as convinced that law and nationality condemn Copenhagen, while Bismarck calculates how Prussia can lead the response without delivering the duchies to the Diet’s majority methods or to an Augustenburg middle state that would complicate later Prussian expansion and create another client for Austria. The book thus joins antiquarian succession law to cabinet interest and explains why a “federal” cause becomes a great-power war.
Zehntes Buch — Die Bundesexekution (The Federal Execution)
The tenth book narrates federal execution against Denmark for Holstein and Lauenburg, the occupation measures, and the enlargement of a federal police action into a Prussian-Austrian war for Schleswig. Sybel stresses the dualist bargain at every step: Austria enters to keep hold of the German national cause and to prevent unilateral Prussian aggrandizement; Bismarck accepts Austrian partnership as European cover and as a means of outflanking pure großdeutsch (“greater-German”) and Augustenburg politics at Frankfurt. Diplomatic chapters cover proposals for a London conference, British and Russian caution, French observation under Napoleon III., and the collapse of compromise once operations widen beyond Holstein. Sybel details legal notes justifying the crossing of the Eider, the management of smaller German states that cheer the national war yet fear a great-power condominium, and Bismarck’s use of national enthusiasm without yielding the helm to the Nationalverein or to the princes’ college. The execution becomes a school of Austro-Prussian military cooperation whose political afterbill—joint ownership of the spoils—will come due in volume 4.
Elftes Buch — Der Feldzug von 1864 (The Campaign of 1864)
Military narrative fills the campaign book: Danish reliance on the Danewerk (“Danevirke”) line, the decision to withdraw, the siege and storm of the Düppel fortifications, operations against Alsen and into Jutland, and the constant interplay of headquarters with political aims in Berlin and Vienna. Sybel writes as a historian proud of Prussian performance yet attentive to logistics, allied friction, naval limits, and modern firepower. He notes how rifled artillery and infantry tactics shorten a war that older observers expected to resemble 1848–50. Each success has a double meaning—it raises German prestige and tightens the quarrel over who will dispose of the conquered land. Austrian units share the field; Sybel records cooperation and jealousy alike, preparing the reader for the administrative deadlock after peace. The impression on public opinion and on the Prussian chamber opposition is carefully marked: quick victory advertises the reformed army whose budget the conflict ministry had forced through, weakening the moral position of those who had called the reorganization a threat to liberty rather than a tool of national policy.
Zwölftes Buch — Der Friede (The Peace)
The twelfth book treats armistice, preliminaries, and the Friede von Wien (“Peace of Vienna”), by which Denmark renounces the duchies. Sybel follows the diplomatic packing carefully: the result is not a simple gift to Augustenburg or to the Bund as such, but a cession that leaves Prussia and Austria as joint disposers of the territory. Language of the treaty, protocols on administration, and the first disputes over garrisons and civil authority already mark the next conflict—which the following volume develops through the Gasteiner Konvention (“Convention of Gastein”) and the rupture of 1866. Domestic politics re-enter in the closing pages: military glory weakens the constitutional opposition; crown and Bismarck stand higher than in 1862; national liberals begin to divide between those who will support success and those who hold to constitutional purity. For Sybel, 1864 liberates German soil from Danish rule and simultaneously opens the second act of Prussian-led unification, whose antagonist will no longer be Copenhagen but Vienna.
Documentary texture and Sybel’s judgments
Across the four books Sybel repeatedly returns to the interplay between legal title and power. Succession tables, protocol articles, and Diet resolutions matter because cabinets use them as weapons; they do not decide outcomes by themselves. He gives space to Danish arguments for the integrity of the monarchy and to the German counter-claim that Holstein’s federal status and Schleswig’s pledges barred unilateral incorporation. The London conference diplomacy of 1864 is treated as a serious European attempt that failed when military facts outran protocol drafting. Sybel’s Bismarck appears neither as pure realist indifferent to the duchies’ German character nor as a mere agent of the Nationalverein: he wants Prussian strategic ports and a precedent for solving German questions with Austria only so long as Austria can be managed, then against Austria when dualism blocks annexation and reform. For researchers, volume 3 supplies a continuous cabinet-level story from 1846 open-letter politics through Vienna 1864, usable for timeline construction, actor maps, and the institutional path Diet execution → great-power war → condominium.
Significance for this wiki
Volume 3 is the principal Sybel narrative for the Second Schleswig War, London Protocol background, federal execution, Düppel/Alsen, and the Peace of Vienna. Pair with volume 4 for the Austro-Prussian quarrel over the spoils and with Treitschke for earlier national agitation over the duchies.

sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.title: Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 4
sources/sybel-begrundung-des-deutschen-r.content:
Sybel — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I., Vol. 4
Heinrich von Sybel (1817–1895) — Die Begründung des Deutschen Reiches durch Wilhelm I. Vierter Band. — 3. unveränderte Auflage. München und Leipzig: Verlag von R. Oldenbourg, 1890.
The fourth volume covers the decisive approach to the Austro-Prussian War: rising tension after the Danish settlement, the Gasteiner Konvention (“Convention of Gastein”), failed mediation and congress projects, arming on all sides, the break between the German great powers, and the Prussian-Italian alliance. Sybel’s contents structure (recovered from the volume’s Inhalt des vierten Bandes) organizes the story in books on tension, rupture, the Italian alliance, and the Gastein interlude—treated as a temporary partition of the Elbe duchies that postpones rather than prevents collision. The documentary base remains Prussian and related archives; the interpretive line is that dual control of Schleswig-Holstein made conflict structural once Bismarck had secured Italian diversion and French uncertainty.
Dreizehntes Buch — Spannung zwischen Österreich und Preußen (Tension between Austria and Prussia)
After 1864 the condominium over the duchies becomes Sybel’s engine of crisis. He follows disputes over civil administration, garrisons, the Augustenburg candidacy, press wars, and appeals to the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”). Austria seeks to recover popularity among the middle states by leaning toward federal and Augustenburg solutions; Prussia under Bismarck treats the duchies as leverage for a reordering of Germany, not as a gift to another princely house. Sybel details notes and conferences in which each power accuses the other of violating joint possession. Public opinion in Germany splits between national liberals who still hope for a reform of the Bund and particularists who fear Prussian annexation. The book establishes that Gastein will be attempted precisely because tension has become dangerous, yet the underlying dualism is unresolved.
Vierzehntes Buch — Bruch zwischen Österreich und Preußen (Break between Austria and Prussia)
Erstes Capitel — Allseitige Rüstung (Arming on all sides)
Sybel’s first chapter of the rupture book catalogues mobilization. Both empires protest peaceable intent while expanding armaments; alarming news from Italy interacts with Austrian measures; Prussian mobilization steps follow; middle states arm in uncertainty. He records the mood of the Vienna public, the hesitation and then completion of Prussian mobilization, and the state of German opinion as war becomes probable. The chapter is deliberately parallel: neither side is presented as wholly surprised; each reads the other’s preparations as proof of bad faith.
Zweites Capitel — Letzter Einigungsversuch (Last attempt at agreement)
Napoleon III’s congress proposal and the mission of Anton von Gablenz occupy the second chapter. Sybel follows French suggestions for a European congress, shifts in French policy, Thiers’s speech against German unity, French approaches to Italy and Italian refusal, Bismarck’s conciliatory despatch of 7 May, Gablenz’s peace programme, conversations between the generals Gablenz and Manteuffel, audiences in Vienna, and the final rejection of the Gablenz proposal. The narrative stresses how close paper compromise came and how incompatible the minimum terms remained once prestige and the duchies’ future were engaged.
Drittes Capitel — Österreich und Frankreich (Austria and France)
Secret exchanges between Vienna and Paris fill the third chapter: Napoleon’s plans, openings to the Prussian ambassador Goltz, Prussian refusal of French compensation schemes at German expense, Napoleon’s irritation with Italy, congress proposals, Austrian rejection of the congress and appeal to the Diet, the threat Sybel sees to the national future of Germany and Italy, and the Wiener Vertrag (“Treaty of Vienna”) of 12 June between Austria and France. Prussia’s refusal of German territorial cessions to France and Napoleon’s public manifesto of 11 June close the diplomatic tangle out of which open war follows.
Viertes Capitel — Die Kriegserklärung (The declaration of war)
Sybel narrates the final legal-political break: Prussia’s treatment of the Gastein arrangement as ended, motions at the Diet, the federal majority against Prussia, Prussian declaration that the Bund is broken, and the invasion paths that open the German war. The chapter links Italian moves to the German timetable so that Austria faces two fronts.
Fünfzehntes Buch — Preußisch-italienisches Bündnis (Prussian-Italian Alliance)
A dedicated book covers the April 1866 alliance between Prussia and the Kingdom of Italy: negotiation, terms, Bismarck’s strategic aim of diverting Austrian forces, and Italy’s stake in Venetia. Sybel shows how the treaty transforms a German dualist quarrel into a European war of redistribution, and how French policy oscillates between fear of a united Italy-Germany bloc and hope of holding the balance. Military coordination remains imperfect; the political fact of the alliance is what matters for the opening of hostilities.
Sechzehntes Buch — Übereinkunft und Gastein (Agreement and Gastein)
Although Gastein chronologically precedes the final rupture, Sybel’s architecture gives the convention its own book as the failed stabilizer. The August 1865 agreement partitions administration—Schleswig toward Prussia, Holstein toward Austria—while preserving joint sovereignty on paper. Sybel recounts terms, European reception, German press reaction, and the rapid return of friction over ports, customs, and political meetings in Holstein. Gastein appears as a truce that allowed both powers to prepare rather than as a durable settlement. Together with the tension and rupture books, it completes Sybel’s prehistory of 1866: the Danish spoils, unshared, become the proximate cause of the war that decides German dualism.
Significance for this wiki
Volume 4 is the core Sybel narrative for Gastein, the May–June 1866 diplomacy (Gablenz, Napoleon’s congress, Austro-French bargain), Italian alliance, and mobilizations. Use it for the immediate origins of the Austro-Prussian War; battle narrative belongs to later volumes of the set.
Narrative continuity and reading notes
Sybel intends volume 4 to be read as the hinge between the Danish success and the Bohemian decision. Tension over the duchies is not a sideshow; it is the German question in local form. Gastein’s administrative split—Prussia leaning on Schleswig, Austria on Holstein—creates daily friction over the Kiel harbour, customs lines, and political meetings that Austria allows and Prussia denounces as revolutionary or anti-Prussian. Sybel’s chapters on French policy stress Napoleon III’s hope to be arbiter and paymaster of any map change, and Prussia’s refusal to buy French neutrality with Rhenish or Belgian bargains that would poison national legitimacy. The Gablenz episode receives sympathetic detail as a soldierly attempt at compromise that cabinets could not ratify without losing face.
Italian alliance chapters connect Venetian ambitions to Moltke’s two-front planning. Sybel does not narrate Custoza here at length; he establishes why Austria must divide armies. Mobilization tables and Diet votes (including the federal reform motions and the seizure of the Holstein question at Frankfurt) supply the public-law death of the Bund as Sybel sees it: once a Diet majority authorizes action against Prussia, Berlin treats the Confederation treaty as broken and marches. The volume ends at the threshold of campaign history, having documented that war came from failed dual ownership, failed congress diplomacy, and successful Prussian timing with Italy amid French hesitation.
Researchers should use volume 4 for diplomatic chronology of 1865–June 1866, for Gastein terms and breakdown, and for the legal-political sequence by which dualism passed from condominium to open war. Pair with volume 3 for the origin of the condominium and with military histories for Königgrätz and the Nikolsburg/Prague settlement.

sources/tivaroni-italia-degli-italiani-t.title: Tivaroni — L'Italia degli Italiani, Tomo I (1849–1859)
sources/tivaroni-italia-degli-italiani-t.content:
Tivaroni — L’Italia degli Italiani, Tomo I (1849–1859)
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. L’Italia degli Italiani. Tomo I (1849–1859). — Torino: Roux Frassati e Co., 1895.
The first volume of the third series-within-the-work of Tivaroni’s critical history, bearing the new title L’Italia degli Italiani. After the survey of the eighteenth century and of the French domination, and then of the Austrian Restoration through 1849, this volume carries the story forward through the decade of reaction after Novara into the prelude of the war of 1859. It treats both halves of the peninsula — the Austrian-occupied lands and the restored absolutist states in the centre and south — together with the constitutional Kingdom of Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II, where the national revival was being prepared.
Tivaroni frames the period in two Parti: the first surveys the “Italian Austria” of the reaction years, state by state; the second follows the consolidation of the constitutional monarchy in Piedmont under the ministries that led toward the Crimean War, the Congress of Paris, and the Anglo-French alliance that opened the way to the war against Austria. The volume closes with the attentato of Felice Orsini (1858), on the eve of the war of 1859.
The volume is approximately 500 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte I — L’Italia austriaca
The restored and occupied states of the peninsula after the defeats of 1849.
Capitolo I — Il Lombardo-Veneto — the military reaction in Austrian Lombardy and Venetia: the rigours of the martial courts, the political trials and the processi di Mantova (1851–1852), the rising of 6 February 1853 in Milan, Pietro Fortunato Calvi and Felice Orsini, Austria’s gradual relaxation of the reins, the passive resistance of the Veneto, and the last attempt of the Archduke Maximilian. Capitolo II — Modena — the restored Duchy of Modena under Duke Francis V and the survival of absolutism. Capitolo III — Parma — the Duchy of Parma under Duke Charles III and the regent Maria Luisa di Borbone. Capitolo IV — Toscana — the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and the Austrian influence after the restoration.
Capitolo V — Lo Stato Pontificio — the Papal States under the restored Pius IX: the reaction after 1849, the Austrian and French occupation zones, and the Pope’s journey into Romagna (1857). Capitolo VI — Il Reame di Napoli — the last decade of the Bourbons: the restored absolutism of Ferdinand II, the special courts and the galleys, the expedition of Carlo Pisacane (1857), and the unvarying character of Bourbon rule. Capitolo VII — La Sicilia — the Bourbon reaction in Sicily, the attempted rising of Francesco Bentivegna, and the closing years of Bourbon government on the island.
Parte II — Vittorio Emanuele in Piemonte
The constitutional Kingdom of Piedmont and the preparation of the national war.
From Novara to the proclamation of Moncalieri and the ministry of De Launay. The ministry of Massimo d’Azeglio. The connubio — the parliamentary union of the Centre-Right and Centre-Left (Cavour and Rattazzi). The great ministry of Camillo Benso di Cavour.
The alliance with France and England. The ministry of Cavour in danger. The Crimean War and the sending of the Piedmontese expedition. The Congress of Paris (1856).
The work of preparation — army, railways, finances, the national cause. The attentato of Felice Orsini (1858).
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, and in this volume the perspective is squarely that of the Risorgimento: the restored absolutisms of central and southern Italy are treated as the foil to the constitutional Piedmont of Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour, whose policy is presented as the channel through which the national cause moved toward the war of 1859.
Expanded part-by-part reading
Parte I in depth — L’Italia austriaca
Lombardo-Veneto. Martial courts after Novara; the Mantua trials (Belfiore martyrs in national memory); Milan’s 6 February 1853 rising; Calvi and Orsini as revolutionary types under white coats; Archduke Maximilian’s later conciliatory experiment as too-late soft power. Passive resistance in Venetia—taxes, society, and silence—matters as much as failed plots.
Duchies. Modena under Francis V as stubborn absolutism; Parma under Charles III and the Bourbon-Parma regency weather after assassination politics; Tuscany under restored Leopoldine rule with Austrian shadow. These chapters are the foil to Piedmont’s Statuto world.
Papal States. French and Austrian occupation zones after the Roman Republic; restored Pius IX’s rejection of neo-Guelph hopes; the 1857 Romagna journey as pastoral-political tour through disaffected legations.
Naples and Sicily. Ferdinand II’s special courts and galleys; Pisacane’s 1857 expedition as both tragedy and indictment; Bentivegna in Sicily; Tivaroni’s moral contrast between Bourbon immobility and Piedmontese parliamentary life.
Parte II in depth — Vittorio Emanuele in Piemonte
From Novara to stable majority. Moncalieri, d’Azeglio’s cleaning of the ultra-clerical right, then the connubio that pairs Cavour with Rattazzi and creates a workable centre. Great ministry reforms: finance, church legislation (Siccardi-era lineage), railways, army.
Crimea and Paris. Sending the expeditionary force; Cavour at the Congress of Paris placing the Italian question in a European minute even without immediate territory. The diplomacy is Tivaroni’s proof that the national cause has left pure conspiracy for cabinet politics.
Preparation and Orsini. Military and financial readiness; national society networks; Orsini’s 1858 bombs in Paris as the shock that accelerates Napoleon III’s Italian choice—closing the tome on the eve of war.
Method note
Tivaroni writes storia critica from a national-liberal Piedmontese telos. Read Bourbon and papal chapters as hostile witnesses with rich administrative detail, not as neutral ethnography. For documentary dumps on earlier decades, La Farina’s volumes remain complementary.

sources/tivaroni-litalia-degli-italiani-.content:
Tivaroni — L’Italia degli Italiani, Tomo II (1859–1866)
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. L’Italia degli Italiani. Tomo II (1859–1866). — Torino: Roux Frassati e Co., 1896.
The second volume of the series-within-the-work bearing the title L’Italia degli Italiani. It carries the national story from the war of 1859 through the making of the Kingdom of Italy in 1860–1861 and the first five years of the constitutional monarchy, closing on the eve of the war of 1866. Where the first volume had surveyed the restored absolutisms and the constitutional Piedmont, this volume is taken up almost entirely with the armed unification of the peninsula and with the ministries that governed the new Kingdom after the death of Cavour.
Tivaroni divides the volume into eight Parti (Parte III through Parte X, the numbering continuing from the two Parti of the first volume). The opening Parti treat the war against Austria and the annexations of central Italy; the middle of the volume follows the expedition of the Thousand and the fall of the Bourbons; the closing Parti follow the successive ministries of the new Kingdom — Ricasoli, Rattazzi, Farini-Minghetti and Lamarmora — down to 1866.
The volume is approximately 500 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive). It is the 506-page digitization.
Content Summary
Parte III — La guerra del 1859
The war of Italian independence against Austria.
The secret meeting of Plombières between Cavour and Napoleon III (1858). The excitements and the plan for a European congress. The battle of Magenta (4 June 1859). The battle of Solferino and San Martino (24 June 1859).
Villafranca and the peace.
Parte IV — L’Italia Centrale
The revolutions and annexations of central Italy in 1859–1860.
Capitolo I — Le quattro rivoluzioni — the risings in Florence (27 April 1859), Modena, Parma and Bologna. Capitolo II — Bettino Ricasoli e Luigi Carlo Farini — the Tuscan and Emilian provisional governments. Capitolo III — Le Assemblee Costituenti — the constituent assemblies of the central states. Capitolo IV — L’imbarazzo del Governo di Torino — the embarrassment of the Piedmontese government.
Capitolo V — La cessione di Savoia e di Nizza — the cession of Savoy and Nice for the annexation of central Italy.
Parte V — L’anno decisivo
The decisive year of 1860: the expedition of the Thousand and the conquest of the south.
La spedizione dei Mille — the Sicilian precursors; the decision; the landing at Marsala; Calatafimi (15 May 1860) and the astonishing capture of Palermo (27 May 1860); Milazzo (20 July 1860); the crossing of the Straits of Messina; Naples in 1859 and 1860; the invasion of the Marches; the battle of the Volturno (1–2 October 1860); the Plebiscite (21 October 1860); the capture of Gaeta; the conclusion. La morte del conte di Cavour (6 June 1861) — the financial recklessness; Naples within the Kingdom of Italy and the brigantaggio; the negotiations of Cavour with the Holy See. Il primo Parlamento d’Italia — the opening of the first Italian Parliament.
Parte VI
This Parte (its title is partly illegible in the OCR’d Indice) carries the early consolidation of the Kingdom through the first Parliament: the finances of the new state, the southern brigandage, and the negotiations with the Holy See over Rome.
Parte VII — Il Ministero Ricasoli
The ministry of Bettino Ricasoli (12 June 1861 – 2 March 1862).
The financial question. The solicitations of Ricasoli to Napoleon and to the Pope. The Comitati di provvedimento.
Parte VIII — Il Ministero Rattazzi
The ministry of Urbano Rattazzi (3 March – 1 December 1862).
Sarnico — the Garibaldian rising in the north. Aspromonte — the wounding and capture of Garibaldi.
Parte IX — Il Ministero Farini-Minghetti
The ministry of Luigi Carlo Farini and Marco Minghetti (9 December 1862 – 23 September 1864).
The enquiry into the southern railways. The September Convention (15 September 1864) with France over the Roman question.
Parte X — Il Ministero Lamarmora
The ministry of Alfonso Lamarmora (23 September 1864 – 20 July 1866).
The armed bands in the Veneto. The ratification of the Convention.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume and is partly garbled, so the structure above also draws on the running part-headers within the text. Tivaroni writes throughout from the perspective of the Risorgimento: the unification of the peninsula is treated as the culmination of the national movement, and the ministries after Cavour’s death are judged by how far they advanced the remaining national goals of Venice and Rome. The volume ends on the eve of the war of 1866, which the third volume takes up.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Tomo 2 carries Tivaroni from the war of 1859 through the Thousand, annexations, Gaeta, and the Kingdom’s first years toward 1866.
War of 1859 and central annexations
Plombières’ fruits in the field: Magenta, Solferino, Villafranca’s shock to unitarians, then the central Italian revolutions and plebiscites that Cavour’s party folds into the monarchy.
South and the Thousand
Garibaldi’s expedition, Bourbon collapse, Piedmontese intervention, and the awkward merger of revolutionary legitimacy with Statuto annexation law.
First parliament and open files
Parliament of the new kingdom, administrative fusion problems, brigandage in the south as Tivaroni frames it, and the still-open Roman and Venetian questions through the mid-1860s.

sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo I: L'Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L'Italia settentrionale
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo I: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia settentrionale
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Tomo I: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia settentrionale. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1892.
The first volume of the second series-within-the-work of Tivaroni’s critical history, opening a new era: after the survey of the eighteenth century and the French domination, this volume treats the Austrian Restoration in northern Italy, from the settlement of 1815 to the crisis of 1848–1849. It carries the story of the northern states — Piedmont, Lombardy, the Veneto, Parma, and Modena — through the years of restored autocracy, the abortive revolutions, and the climactic upheaval of 1848, ending with the defeats of Novara and Brescia and the return of Austria.
Tivaroni treats the north in five Parti, following the Restoration reaction, the revolutionary conspiracies of the 1820s and 1830s, and the events of 1848–1849 state by state. The volume is a study of how the Austrian Restoration and the national reaction against it together forged the modern Italian movement in the north of the peninsula.
The volume is approximately 688 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte I — Il Piemonte
The Kingdom of Sardinia under the Restoration and the House of Savoy.
La ristorazione — the Restoration of 1815: the return of Victor Emmanuel I and the reactionary order, the suppression of the French institutions, the court and the religious restoration, the edicts and the restored laws, and the early discontent. Il 1821 — the revolution of 1821: the rising of the army and the carbonari, the granting of the constitution, the abdication of Victor Emmanuel I, the regency and the intervention of Austria, and the reaction that followed. Carlo Alberto — Lo Statuto — the reign of Charles Albert: his ambiguous path between reform and reaction, the Conciliatore and literary agitation, and the eventual granting of the Statuto (constitution). Carlo Alberto — La guerra dell’Indipendenza — the war of independence of 1848: the decision for war against Austria, the opening campaign, the collapse before the Austrian recovery, and the defeat of Novara (1849) with the king’s abdication.
Parte II — La Lombardia
Austrian Lombardy from the Restoration to the Five Days.
L’Austria in Lombardia — the Austrian organism in Lombardy: the emperor Francis and Prince Metternich, the classicists and the Romantics, the Biblioteca italiana and the Conciliatore, the political trials of 1822 and Federico Confalonieri, the tranquil period (1822–1831), the trials of 1833, the reign of Emperor Ferdinand (1835–1846), and the condition of Lombardy. La rivoluzione lombarda — the Lombard revolution of 1848: the prodromes, the Five Days of Milan (18–22 March), the insurrection in Lombardy, the fusion with Piedmont, the Lombard army, the return of Milan to the Austrians, and the Ten Days of Brescia.
Parte III — Il Veneto
The fate of the Venetian lands under restored Austrian rule.
Il Veneto sotto l’Austria — the Veneto under Austria: the first years, and the carbonari of Fratta. La rivoluzione di Venezia — the revolution of Venice: the prodromes, the revolution of 22 March 1848, the republic of Daniele Manin, 11 August, Venice blockaded, the sortie of Mestre (27 October 1848), resistance at all costs, Marghera, and the end of the republic.
Parte IV — Parma
The Duchy of Parma under its Habsburg duchess and in revolt.
Maria Luigia d’Austria — the reign of Marie Louise of Austria, Napoleon’s widow and Napoleon III’s mother, over the Duchy of Parma. Parma in rivolta — Parma in revolt during the upheavals of 1848.
Parte V — Il Ducato di Modena
The Duchy of Modena under its reactionary duke and in conspiracy.
Francesco IV — the reign of Francis IV: the reaction, the trial of Rubiera and Don Giuseppe Andreoli, the continuing reaction, the revolution of 1831 and Ciro Menotti, and the fury of the reaction. Modena col Piemonte — Modena with Piedmont: the adhesion of Modena to the national cause and the events of 1848–1849.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, presenting the Austrian Restoration as the repressive foil against which the Risorgimento was forged in the north; his treatment of the revolutionaries — the carbonari, Confalonieri, Manin, and Menotti — is correspondingly sympathetic in tone.
Northern Italy under Austrian dominion
Tomo 1 of the Austrian-dominion series is Lombardy–Venetia and the northern hinge of the Restoration: from the Congress settlement through the carbonari seasons and into the pre-1848 order. Tivaroni’s “critical” stance means administrative and police detail in the service of a national indictment.
Expanded map
Settlement and institutions. How Austrian sovereignty is organised in the Lombardo-Veneto—viceregal apparatus, censorship, conscription, and fiscal extraction—after the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy’s fall.
Conspiracy and 1820s–31 echoes. Carbonari and moderate networks; failed military plots; exile pipelines toward Piedmont and France.
Economic and municipal life. Not only police: property, trade, and municipal elites under white-yellow administration, including the tensions that later feed the 1848 five days.
Toward 1848. The accumulation of grievances that La Farina and Tivaroni both treat as making Milan and Venice revolutionary capitals in March 1848. Cross-link milan-five-days-1848, manin, radetzky.
Pairing
Read with tomo 2 (centre) and tomo 3 (south) for full Austrian-system geography; with Italia degli Italiani t.1 for the post-1849 sequel in the same north.

sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo II: L'Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L'Italia centrale
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo II: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia centrale
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Tomo II: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia centrale. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1893.
The second volume of the Austrian-domination series of Tivaroni’s critical history, carrying the same chronological span (1815–1849) into central Italy. It treats the Tuscan Grand Duchy and the Papal State through the years of the Restoration, the moderate liberal movement, the revolutions of 1831 and 1848, and the collapse of the Roman Republic in 1849. Where the first volume covered the north, the present volume follows the fortunes of the two great central states whose fate shaped the national question in the peninsula’s middle.
Tivaroni treats the centre in two Parti — Tuscany and the Papal State — and carries each through the full arc from the Restoration to 1849. The volume is a study of the moderate reformism of Tuscany against the clerical absolutism of Rome, and of how both were overtaken by the revolutionary crisis of 1848–1849.
The volume is approximately 472 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte VI — La Toscana
The Grand Duchy of Tuscany from the Restoration to the revolution.
La Ristorazione — the Restoration of 1815: Ferdinand III and Vittorio Fossombroni. Leopoldo II — Venti anni di governo paterno — twenty years of paternal government under Leopold II: the Antologia and the moderate liberal intellectual life, the reforms, and the quiet reformism of the Tuscan grand dukes. La Rivoluzione — the revolution of 1848 in Tuscany: the first steps, the ministry of Ridolfi, the ministry of Capponi, the baraonda (turmoll) of Montanelli and Guerrazzi, and the restoration of the constitution (12 April). Lucca — the Duchy of Lucca and its annexation to Tuscany.
Parte VII — Lo Stato Pontificio
The Papal State from the Restoration of Pius VII to the fall of the Roman Republic.
La ristorazione di Pio VII — the Restoration of Pius VII: the ecclesiastical government, the tendencies of Cardinal Consalvi, the attempted rising of Macerata, and the unquiet period. Leone XII — the papacy of Leo XII: the victory of the zelanti (zealots), the trials of Cardinal Rivarola, and the last years. Pio VIII — the brief pontificate of Pius VIII. Gregorio XVI — the pontificate of Gregory XVI: his election, the revolution of 1831, the occupation of 1832, the centurioni and the sects, the bands of 1843 and the rising of Rimini of 1845, and the reign of Gregory XVI.
Pio IX — the early pontificate of Pius IX: the amnesty, the slow steps, the reforms granted, the concessions wrested, the encyclical of 29 April, the ministry of Mamiani, the ministry of Fabbri, and the ministry of Pellegrino Rossi. La Repubblica Romana — the Roman Republic of 1849: the Constituent Assembly, the proclamation of the Republic, the government of Mazzini, the French intervention, 30 April, Velletri, the mission of Lesseps, San Pancrazio, the last defence, and the retreat of Garibaldi.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, counterposing the moderate reformism of Tuscany to the clerical absolutism of the Papal State; his treatment of the Roman Republic and its defenders is correspondingly sympathetic in tone.
Scope of the tome
Central Italy under the Austrian-restored order after 1815 and through the crises that lead into 1848–49: Tuscany, Parma, Modena, and the Papal States as Tivaroni’s “critical history” frames them—not as picturesque duchies but as police, concordat, and legation regimes inside the wider Austrian system.
Chapter spine (expanded narration)
Capitoli on the dynastic restorations. Return of Habsburg-related or Austrian-protected princes; the vacuum after Napoleonic kingdoms; how French administrative wreckage and Italian notable society meet restored courts. Tivaroni keeps a critical distance: restoration is not mere nostalgia but a security architecture backed by Austrian arms.
Police, index, and public debt. Recurring machinery—censorship, Congregazione dell’Indice, passport regimes, and the gran libro of public debt—shows how central Italian states finance themselves and discipline reading publics. These administrative chapters matter for entity pages on ministers and for concepts of restoration governance.
1848 approaches. Liberal conspiracies, moderate petitioning, and the unequal readiness of each state for statute constitutions when the revolutionary year arrives. Cross-links: Leopold II in Tuscany, Francis V of Modena, papal legations’ special harshness.
Military and diplomatic overlay. Austrian garrisons and intervention rights after earlier carbonari seasons; the sense that central Italian “independence” is conditional. Prepares the later Italia degli Italiani volumes where the same states reappear under reaction after 1849.
Wiki use
Primary deposit for central Italian restoration entities and events before and around 1848. Pair with dominio austriaco tomo 1 (north) and tomo 3 (south) for full peninsular coverage; with La Farina for a more unitarian narrative voice on the same geography.

sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo III: L'Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L'Italia meridionale: Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo III: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia meridionale: Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Tomo III: L’Italia durante il dominio austriaco (1815–1849). L’Italia meridionale: Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1894.
The final volume of the second series-within-the-work of Tivaroni’s critical history, treating the Austrian Restoration in southern Italy. Where the first two dominio austriaco volumes covered the north and the centre, this third completes the series by turning to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and then to the intellectual elaboration of the national idea. It carries the story from the Restoration of 1815 through the Neapolitan revolution of 1820–21, the reaction and the revolutions of 1848–49, to the defeat of the Bourbon Monarchy in the Sicilian upheaval of 1849.
Tivaroni treats the south in two historical Parti — the Kingdom of Naples and Sicily — and closes with a third, the synthetic survey of the development of national thought that gives the volume its subtitle. The treatment of the south follows the fortunes of the Bourbon dynasty from Ferdinand I through the reactionary reign of Ferdinand II, while the final Parte gathers the writers and statesmen of the movement into a single intellectual portrait of the age.
The volume is approximately 704 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive). It is the sequel to the two northern and central volumes of the dominio austriaco series, which cover the same span (1815–1849).
Content Summary
Parte VIII — Il Regno di Napoli
The Kingdom of Naples under the restored Bourbons, from the Restoration to the revolution of 1848.
Capitolo I — La ristorazione — the Restoration: the promises and the treaties, the machinery of the restored state, the brigands, and the Concordat. Capitolo II — Il 1820 — the revolution of 1820: the carbonari, the pronunciamento, the Murattians in government, the Spanish constitution, the parliament, and the rout at Rieti. Capitolo III — Napoli borbonizzata (1821–1844) — Naples under the pure Bourbon regime: the vengeance of King Ferdinand, King Francis and the rising of the Cilento, Ferdinand II and the hopes he raised, Ferdinand II and the pure Bourbon regime, and the Cosenza conspiracies and the expedition of the Bandiera brothers. Capitolo IV — Il 1848 — the revolution of 1848: from 1845 to 1847, the granting of the constitution, 15 May, and the revolt and the reaction.
Parte IX — La Sicilia
The fate of Sicily as a province of the Two Sicilies, in revolt against Bourbon rule.
Capitolo I — La Sicilia provincia — Sicily as a province: the King of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and from 1816 to 1820. Capitolo II — La rivoluzione del 1820 — the revolution of 1820 and the Murattians in government. Capitolo III — Dal 1821 al 1846 — from 1821 to 1846: the Marchese Pietro Ugo delle Favare, the repression of General Del Carretto, and the condition of Sicily. Capitolo IV — La rivoluzione del 1848 — the revolution of 1848: the outbreak at Messina and Palermo, the parliament that demanded independence, the struggle between the Bourbons and Sicily, and the conclusion.
Parte X — Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale
A synthetic survey of the development of the national idea across Italy, the intellectual dimension that completes the narrative of the Austrian domination.
Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale — the development of national thought: the necessity of conspiracy, Austria in control, the growth of the sects, the Congress of Verona, exiles and combatants, the year 1831, Young Italy and the work of Giuseppe Mazzini, the elaboration of the idea, reformers and revolutionaries, the condition of Italy, 1848, unity and federation, the culture of the century, errors and virtues, the terrible year, and the portraits of the leading figures of the movement — Carlo Botta, Pietro Colletta, Silvio Pellico, Alessandro Manzoni, Giacomo Leopardi, Giuseppe Giusti, Giovanni Battista Niccolini, Giuseppe Montanelli, Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi, Carlo Cattaneo, Guglielmo Pepe, Nicolò Tommaseo, Daniele Manin, Terenzio Mamiani, Pellegrino Rossi, Gino Capponi, Cesare Balbo, Vincenzo Gioberti, Pio IX, Carlo Alberto, and Mazzini himself.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. This final Parte is less narrative than the two that precede it; it moves from the story of the southern revolution to the intellectual history of the whole national movement. Tivaroni’s treatment of the southern revolutionaries — the carbonari, the Bandiera brothers, and the Sicilian insurgents — is, as throughout the work, sympathetic to the national cause.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Tomo 3 is the southern panel of Austrian-age dominion history: Naples and Sicily under Bourbons inside the post-1815 security system Tivaroni criticises.
Bourbon restoration machinery
Police, special courts, and fiscal spine of the Two Sicilies after 1815; carbonari seasons and 1820 constitutional episode as treated in the tome’s chapter order.
1848 in the south
Sicilian and Neapolitan revolutionary calendars, grants and revocations of constitutions, and the military reconquest that makes 1849–60 reaction intelligible.
Toward collapse (horizon)
How the tome’s portrait of immobility feeds later Italia degli Italiani chapters on Pisacane, Bentivegna, and 1860—without replacing those later volumes.

sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo I: L'Italia durante il dominio francese. L'Italia settentrionale
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo I: L’Italia durante il dominio francese. L’Italia settentrionale
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Tomo I: L’Italia durante il dominio francese. L’Italia settentrionale. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1889.
The second published volume of Tivaroni’s critical history, covering the era of the French domination in northern Italy from the opening of the revolutionary wars in 1789–1796 to the fall of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy in 1814–1815. Where the first volume surveyed the eighteenth-century ancien régime, the present volume follows the transformation of the Italian states under French arms and French institutions — the establishment of the satellite republics, the Cisalpine, Ligurian, and Italian Republics, the Kingdom of Italy under Napoleon and his viceroy Eugène de Beauharnais, and the extension of French administration and the Code over the north of the peninsula.
Tivaroni treats the north in five Parti, covering the Kingdom of Sardinia, Lombardy, the Cispadane lands (Bologna, Modena, and Parma), the Veneto, and Genoa. The volume is a study of the revolutionary and Napoleonic impact on northern Italy as the crucible in which the institutions of the future Risorgimento were forged.
The volume is approximately 542 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte I — Il Regno di Sardegna
The Kingdom of Sardinia during the revolutionary wars.
Il Regno di Sardegna combattente — the kingdom under the pressure of war: the malcontents and the league against France. Carlo Emanuele IV, la reazione, gli accordi con la Francia, i nuovi torbidi del 1798, l’abdicazione — the reactionary reign of Charles Emmanuel IV, the agreements with France, the renewed disturbances of 1798, and the king’s abdication. I Francesi in Piemonte; la Repubblica provvisoria — the French entry into Piedmont and the establishment of the provisional republic. Gli Austro-Russi in Piemonte — the Austro-Russian occupation of Piedmont (1799).
Il Piemonte di nuovo francese; ancora repubblica; dipartimento francese; fusione colla Francia — Piedmont again French: the re-established republic, its organization as a French department, and its annexation to France. L’isola di Sardegna — the island of Sardinia: its defence against the French in 1793, the revolt of Cagliari in 1794, the conflict of Sassari against Cagliari, and the hospitality offered to the exiled royal House of Savoy.
Parte II — La Lombardia
The heart of Tivaroni’s volume, tracing the transformation of Lombardy from Austrian province to capital of the Napoleonic state.
Gli ultimi tempi dell’Austria — the last times of Austrian rule: the reforms of Leopold II, the secret Milanese societies, and the reign of Francis II. Bonaparte a Milano — Bonaparte at Milan (1796): the first days, the popular agitation, the campaign against Beaulieu, the military agency, the operations of Wurmser, the Central Administration, the campaign of Alvintzy, the provisional government, and the battle of Rivoli. La Cisalpina (il triennio) — the Cisalpine Republic in its triennium: the constitution, the festival of the federation, and the role of Bonaparte. Il ritorno dell’Austria (i tredici mesi) — the return of Austria: the thirteen months of the Austro-Russian restoration (1799–1800).
La seconda Cisalpina — the second Cisalpine Republic after Marengo (1800) and its resurrection. La Repubblica italiana — the Italian Republic: the Comizi of Lyon (1802) and the establishment of the republic under Napoleon’s presidency. Il Regno d’Italia — the Kingdom of Italy (1805): Napoleon’s coronation at Milan, the viceroyalty of Eugène de Beauharnais, the personnel of the court, Napoleon’s dissatisfaction, the campaign of 1805, the annexation of the Veneto, the affair of the priest Passerini, the quiet years of the kingdom, the campaign of 1809, the descending arc, growing Italian discontent, the catastrophe of the Russian campaign, the campaign of 1813, the condition of the kingdom, the last campaign of Eugène, the negotiations with Murat, the events of 20 April 1814 at Milan, the regency, Eugène’s departure from the kingdom, and the military conspiracy.
Parte III — La Cispadana (Bologna e Modena; Parma)
Bologna e Modena — the Cispadane lands: the rising of Luigi Zamboni and De Rolandis, the occupation of Bologna, the insurrection of Reggio, the Assembly of Modena, the Constitution of Bologna, the Assembly of Reggio, the fusion of the Cispadane Republic with the Cisalpine, the reaction at Bologna, and the annexation to the Kingdom. Parma — Parma: the fall of the Republic (the refusal of the Italian league by Venice), its neutrality, the refusal of alliance, the first exigencies, and the Prussian alliance.
Parte IV — Il Veneto
The fate of Venice from the collapse of the Republic to its incorporation into the Napoleonic state.
I — the closing crisis of the Venetian Republic. Campoformio — the Treaty of Campo Formio (1797), by which Bonaparte ceded Venice to Austria. Venezia si arrende — the surrender of Venice: the attempted bribery at Paris, the summons of Junot, the forces of April, the parties, the three last assemblies of the Maggior Consiglio, the last tumult, and the conclusion of the republic. Il Governo Democratico — the democratic government: the municipality of Venice.
Venezia sotto l’Austria — Venice under Austrian rule. Venezia nel Regno d’Italia — Venice in the Kingdom of Italy.
Parte V — Genova (Genova ballottata)
Tra Francia ed Inghilterra; Giacobini e Conservatori; la Repubblica Ligure — Genoa between France and England, the Jacobins and Conservatives, and the establishment of the Ligurian Republic. Massena difende Genova; il passaggio degli Austriaci (1800) — Masséna’s defence of Genoa and the passage of the Austrians (1800). Genova francese; la Repubblica democratica; l’annessione alla Francia — Genoa French: the democratic republic and its annexation to France. Genova — Genoa under the French Empire.
L’annessione al Piemonte — the annexation of Genoa to Piedmont (1814–15). La Corsica definitivamente francese — the definitive annexation of Corsica to France.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, presenting the French domination as the institutionally generative phase from which the modern Italian state and the Risorgimento would emerge; his treatment of the Cisalpine and Italian Republics and the Kingdom of Italy is correspondingly positive in tone.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
French dominion tomo 1: northern Italy—Cisalpine/Italian Republic and Kingdom, Eugene’s viceroyalty, material and legal change.
State-building under France
Departments, codes, elites, and the army as school of later officers of 1848–59.
Memory
How Napoleonic northern Italy becomes both a model and a warning in Risorgimento argument.
