sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo II: L'Italia durante il dominio francese. L'Italia centrale e meridionale
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-dominio-.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Tomo II: L’Italia durante il dominio francese. L’Italia centrale e meridionale
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Tomo II: L’Italia durante il dominio francese. L’Italia centrale e meridionale. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1891.
The third published volume of Tivaroni’s critical history and the sequel to Tomo I, carrying the narrative of the French domination (1789–1815) from the north of the peninsula into central and southern Italy. Where the first volume treated the Kingdom of Sardinia, Lombardy, the Cispadane lands, the Veneto, and Genoa, the present volume follows the same transformation across Tuscany, the Papal States, the Kingdom of Naples, and Sicily — the collapse of the ancien régime dynasties, the French satellite and annexed regimes, the restoration of 1799 and the Parthenopean Republic, the reigns of Joseph Bonaparte and Gioacchino Murat, and the closing settlement of the Congress of Vienna.
Tivaroni treats the central and southern lands in seven Parti, covering Tuscany, Rome, the Kingdom of Naples, Sicily, a synthetic assessment of the French domination, the development of the national idea, and the Congress of Vienna. The volume is a study of how the revolutionary and Napoleonic interlude redrew the political map of the Italian peninsula and, in Tivaroni’s national reading, prepared the ground for the Risorgimento.
The volume is approximately 498 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte VI — La Toscana
Capitolo I — Tra Francesi e Sanfedisti — between the French and the Sanfedisti: the awakening of the reaction; Ferdinand III and Manfredini; the French occupation; the bands of Arezzo; a renewed French occupation. Capitolo II — Il regno d’Etruria — the Kingdom of Etruria: the new kingdom, the government of King Lodovico, and the regency of Maria Luigia. Capitolo III — La Toscana dipartimento francese — Tuscany as a French department: the new organization and the grand-duchess Elisa Baciocchi. Capitolo IV — La ristorazione — the restoration of the Grand-Duchy.
Capitolo V — Lucca — the fate of Lucca.
Parte VII — Roma
Capitolo I — Il Pontefice minacciato — the Pope threatened: first disquiet, the Bassville affair, the truce of Bologna, the Peace of Tolentino, and the killing of General Duphot. Capitolo II — Roma in balia dei prepotenti — Rome at the mercy of the powerful: the Roman Republic, the Neapolitan occupation, a renewed French occupation, and a second Neapolitan occupation. Capitolo III — Il Governo di Pio VII — the government of Pius VII: the conclave at Venice, Pius VII, Cardinal Consalvi, the first acts, the Concordat with France, Pius VII crowning Napoleon at Paris, and the rupture with Napoleon. Capitolo IV — Roma francese — French Rome: the Empire at Rome and Pius VII in exile.
Parte VIII — Il Regno di Napoli
Capitolo I — Durante la rivoluzione francese — during the French Revolution: Maria Carolina, Emma Hamilton and John Acton; revenues and soldiers; the first fears; the first trials; new torments; the peace with France; the treaty with Austria; and the war of 1798. Capitolo II — La Repubblica Partenopea — the Parthenopean Republic: the defence of Naples, the new government, its first works, the constitution of Mario Pagano, the bands of the Santa Fede, the republicans alone, the victory of the reaction, the saturnali, the violated capitulation, and the ecatombe (the massacre of the republicans). Capitolo III — Prima ristorazione di Ferdinando — the first restoration of Ferdinand: Joseph Bonaparte, the war in Calabria, and the bait of Baiona. Capitolo IV — Re Giuseppe — King Joseph: the new occupation of Rome, the Peace of Florence, the vassalage of Naples, the treaty of neutrality with France and the understandings with the allied powers, and the disappearance of the Anglo-Russian threat.
Capitolo V — Gioacchino Murat — Murat as king: his first works, the Anglo-Sicilian expedition against Naples, Murat’s attempt against Sicily, Manhès crushing brigandage, Murat’s hesitations, his regime, Murat the traitor, the war against the Franco-Italians, Murat’s return to Napoleon, the campaign of Independence, and Murat’s last folly.
Parte IX — La Sicilia
Capitolo I — Durante la rivoluzione francese — during the French Revolution: the conspiracy and execution of Francesco Paolo De Blasi, Ferdinand in Sicily, and the growing discontents. Capitolo II — La rivoluzione del 1812 — the revolution of 1812: the break with the barons and with England (1810–1812), the Parliament of 1812, the constitution of 1812, and the discords.
Parte X — Il dominio francese
A synthetic assessment of the French domination across the peninsula: the damages, the benefits, the fall of the Kingdom, Napoleon’s projects for Italy, the projects of the powers, and the overall result.
Parte XI — Lo svolgimento del pensiero nazionale
The development of the national idea: Ugo Foscolo, Vincenzo Monti, Gian Domenico Romagnosi; literature, art and science; Italian independence and Italian inertia; and the concept of Italian unity.
Parte XII — Il Congresso di Vienna
The Congress of Vienna: the division of the spoils among the victors, the principle of legitimacy, the Holy Alliance, and the settlement that delivered the Lombardo-Veneto to Austria and re-established the dynastic order over Italy.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume and its layout is partially garbled by the scan; the Part and chapter divisions above follow the running headers of the body text, which are authoritative. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, presenting the French domination as the institutionally generative phase from which the modern Italian state and the Risorgimento would emerge, and reading the Congress of Vienna as the great powers’ disposition of Italy as spoils.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
French dominion tomo 2: central and southern Italy under Napoleonic systems—kingdoms, satellite princes, and administrative export.
Satellite monarchies
Naples under Joseph then Murat; Roman and Tuscan arrangements; how French law and conscription remake elites.
Exit
Collapse of 1814–15 and what Restoration can and cannot reverse. Feeds later carbonari and Bourbon chapters in other Tivaroni tomes.

sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-italia-p.title: Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Vol. I: L'Italia prima della rivoluzione francese
sources/tivaroni-storia-critica-italia-p.content:
Tivaroni — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano, Vol. I: L’Italia prima della rivoluzione francese
Carlo Tivaroni (1843–1906) — Storia critica del risorgimento italiano. Volume I: L’Italia prima della rivoluzione francese. — Torino: L. Roux e C., 1888.
The first volume of Tivaroni’s critical history of the Italian Risorgimento, covering the condition of Italy in the era before the French Revolution — the decades from the settlement of the 1730s down to the eve of 1789. A positivist-minded historian, Tivaroni examines the political, social, economic, and intellectual state of the Italian states one by one, with the intention of laying bare the weaknesses and resources of the old order from which the national movement would spring. The volume is a survey of the eighteenth-century ancien régime in Italy rather than a continuous narrative.
The volume is organized in twelve Parti, each treating a state or group of states, followed by the intellectual “precursors” of the movement. It covers Venice, the Duchy of Milan, the Kingdom of Sardinia, Genoa, Modena, Parma, Tuscany, the Papal State, the Kingdom of Naples, and Sicily, and closes with essays on the adventurers, Freemasons, and rebellious thinkers of the century, and on the second half of the eighteenth century in Italy generally.
The volume is approximately 576 pages of text, extracted from a University of California scan (Anna’s Archive).
Content Summary
Parte I — La Repubblica di Venezia
Il Governo — the constitution of the republic: the Maggior Consiglio, Senate, Signoria, Doge, Council of Ten, the Inquisitors of State, the prisons of the Pozzi and Piombi, the corruption of the patriciate, and the Quarantie. Le condizioni della terraferma — the condition of the terraferma (the mainland provinces). La dominante — Venice itself: population, revenue and expenditure, patrician and clerical property, restrictions on the Church, schools and academies, literature, Goldoni and the theatre, culture and customs, the people, the Cloaca massima, the bourgeoisie, the navy and arsenal, the army, and the judgment that reform came “too late”. La vita politica — Venice’s isolation, the revolt of 1761, Angelo Quirini and Marco Foscarini, the revolt of 1775, the affair of Gratarol and the Tron family, the agitation of Contarini and Pisani (1779–80), the interrupted quiet, the relation of Tron, the Masonic lodges, and the want of any presentiment of the coming storm.
Parte II — Il Ducato di Milano
Il regime spagnuolo — the Spanish regime. Il regime austriaco di Maria Teresa — the Austrian regime of Maria Theresa: the passage from Spanish to Austrian rule, how Maria Theresa found the Lombards, and the reforms of the Austrian administration.
Parte III — Il Regno di Sardegna
Le condizioni del Piemonte — the condition of Piedmont: its foundations, the Church and education, the nobility, the Court, the army, the lower classes, taxation, the poor and the Opere pie, the budget, obstinate resistance to change, the harbingers of intellectual rebellion, and “an Italian in Piedmont”. Il regno di Carlo Emanuele III — the reign of Charles Emmanuel III. Il regno di Vittorio Amedeo III — the reign of Victor Amadeus III. La Sardegna — the island of Sardinia.
Parte IV — La Repubblica di Genova
La Costituzione e le condizioni — the constitution and condition of the republic. La ribellione del 1746 — the rebellion of 1746 against the Austrians. Genova e la Corsica — Genoa and Corsica.
Parte V — Il Ducato di Modena
Il regno di Francesco III. Il matrimonio di Beatrice d’Este — the reign of Francis III and the marriage of Beatrice d’Este. Le condizioni del Modenese — the condition of the Modenese. Ercole Rinaldo III — the reign of Hercules Rinaldo III.
Parte VI — Il Ducato di Parma
Filippo V infante di Spagna — Philip, the Spanish infant, and the establishment of the Bourbon Duchy. Guglielmo du Tillot e i regalisti — the minister du Tillot and the regalist party. Ferdinando e Maria Amalia — the reign of Ferdinand and Maria Amalia.
Parte VII — La Toscana
Il regime dei Medici — the regime of the Medici. Francesco II di Lorena — Francis of Lorraine and the passage to Austrian rule. Leopoldo I di Toscana — the great reformist reign of Grand Duke Leopold. Il vescovo Scipione de Ricci — the reforming bishop Scipione de’ Ricci.
Potenza degli Ecclesiastici — the power of the clergy. Gli ultimi atti di Leopoldo — the last acts of Leopold’s reign. La Repubblica di Lucca — the Republic of Lucca.
Parte VIII — Gli Stati della Chiesa
Il doppio potere — the double (spiritual and temporal) power. Le finanze pontificie — the pontifical finances. Il governo dei preti — priestly government: property, display, administration, the administration of justice, the Inquisition and education, and clerics in office. I principi romani — the Roman princes.
Roma caput mundi — Rome as head of the world. Papi inconcludenti — the inconclusive popes. Clemente XIV e la soppressione dei Gesuiti — Clement XIV and the suppression of the Jesuits (1773). Pio VI — the pontificate of Pius VI.
Parte IX — Il Regno di Napoli
Spagnuoli ed Austriaci — Spaniards and Austrians. Il Clero — the clergy. I baroni — the barons and the feudal system. Il popolo e la terra — the people and the land.
L’organismo — the political organism. Legislazione economica — economic legislation. L’istruzione pubblica — public education. Il movimento intellettuale — the intellectual movement: Antonio Genovesi, G.M. Galanti, Gaetano Filangieri.
Carlo III — the reign of Charles III. Il regno di Ferdinando IV — the reign of Ferdinand IV: Bernardo Tanucci, King Ferdinand, the policy of the Queen, Maria Carolina.
Parte X — La Sicilia
L’antica Costituzione — the ancient constitution of Sicily. I baroni e le condizioni sociali — the barons and social conditions. Le finanze — the finances. Il Clero — the clergy.
Il Governo dei Borboni di Napoli in Sicilia dal 1735 al 1780 — the government of the Neapolitan Bourbons in Sicily from 1735 to 1780. Il Vicerè Caracciolo — the reforming viceroy Domenico Caracciolo.
Parte XI — I Precursori
Tre avventurieri del secolo XVIII — three adventurers of the eighteenth century: Casanova, Cagliostro, and Count Giuseppe Gorani. La Massoneria — Freemasonry. I pensatori ribelli — the rebellious thinkers: Radicati di Passerano, Carlo Antonio Pilati, and other lesser figures. Parini — the poet Giuseppe Parini.
Vittorio Alfieri — the tragedian Vittorio Alfieri and the passion for liberty. Mario Pagano — the jurist Francesco Mario Pagano.
Parte XII — La seconda metà del secolo XVIII in Italia
The closing survey of the second half of the eighteenth century in Italy.
Note on the text: The OCR is Italian. The printed Indice appears near the close of the volume. Tivaroni writes as a historian of the national movement, so the survey of the ancien régime is oriented toward explaining the eventual collapse of the old order and the rise of the Risorgimento.
Extended chapter-use guide (Wave MEDIUM)
Italy before the French Revolution—Tivaroni’s old-regime baseline so French and Austrian dominion volumes have a before-picture.
Old regimes
Savoy, Austrian Lombardy, Venetian oligarchy, papal and Bourbon worlds in critical summary.
Why it matters here
Prevents 1796–1815 from reading as creation ex nihilo; supplies long names and institutional habits for early entities.

sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.title: Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. I
sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.content:
Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. I
Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896) — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. Erster Theil. — Leipzig: Verlag von S. Hirzel (series Staatengeschichte der neuesten Zeit).
The first volume of Treitschke’s five-volume national history opens the nineteenth century for Germany: Napoleonic domination, Prussian collapse and reform, the Wars of Liberation, and the road toward the settlement that volume 2 will treat as the early Deutscher Bund (“German Confederation”). Treitschke writes as a Prussian-national historian of the empire’s generation; the narrative celebrates state power, military revival, and cultural awakening while judging particularism and what he sees as weak dualist compromise. Dense paragraphs of political, military, and intellectual history replace any mere table of contents: actors, measures, and outcomes are named continuously.
Erstes Buch — Germany under Napoleonic hegemony
Treitschke surveys the Holy Roman Empire’s final crisis, the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss (“Imperial Recess”) territorial revolution, the end of the Empire in 1806, and the Rheinbund (“Confederation of the Rhine”) as a French satellite system. He portrays south and west German princes as modernizers under French pressure—codes, secularization, administrative centralization—yet dependent on Napoleon’s favor. Austria’s repeated wars and peaces, Prussia’s hesitant neutrality and then catastrophic decision for war in 1806, and the twin disasters of Jena and Auerstedt structure the military narrative. The occupation of Berlin, the Treaties of Tilsit, and the reduction of Prussia to a rump state become the nadir from which reform and later liberation rise. Treitschke does not spare court frivolity or strategic indecision before 1806; he treats the collapse as earned, and therefore as educative.
Zweites Buch — Prussian reform and national awakening
The reform book is the moral centre of the volume. Freiherr vom Stein (“Baron vom Stein”), Hardenberg, Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, and colleagues appear as the architects of a new Prussian state: abolition of serfdom’s hardest bonds, municipal self-government, army reform and the idea of universal service, educational renewal associated with Wilhelm von Humboldt, and a rhetoric of citizenship in arms. Treitschke links administrative measures to the growth of a German national idea in pamphlets, poetry, and the Tugendbund (“League of Virtue”) atmosphere—always insisting that culture without a state sword remains incomplete. The book follows diplomacy under French surveillance, the strain of contributions and conscription for Napoleon’s wars, and the slow recovery of Prussian finances and manpower. Austrian efforts (1809) receive attention as heroic but insufficient without a general German rising; the failure confirms Treitschke’s preference for organized state leadership over spontaneous particularist revolt.
Drittes Buch — From the Russian disaster to liberation
Napoleon’s Russian campaign and the destruction of the Grande Armée reopen German politics. Treitschke narrates Yorck’s convention of Tauroggen, Stein’s activity in Russian exile and at the Tsar’s side, the Prussian change of alliance, and the spring and autumn campaigns of 1813. Battles—Großgörschen, Bautzen, Dresden, Leipzig—are embedded in coalition diplomacy among Prussia, Russia, Austria, and Britain. He stresses the Landwehr (“militia”) and volunteer formations as proof that reform had created a fighting nation, while still giving professional command its due. The 1814 invasion of France, the first Peace of Paris, and Napoleon’s fall close the military arc; the volume looks ahead to the Congress of Vienna as the political test of whether liberation will become unity or a restored patchwork. Treitschke’s tone already warns that the coming settlement will disappoint national hopes even as it ends French dominion.
Intellectual and social strands
Woven through the political-military books are chapters on intellectual currents: idealist philosophy, romantic historical thought, the revival of Germanistics, and the press under censorship and occupation. Treitschke treats these as preparing a national public that 1813 calls to arms and that later decades will organize in associations, customs politics, and eventually parties. Economic notes—continental system, agrarian change, early industrial stirrings—remain subordinate to state and nationality but are not absent.
Significance for this wiki
Volume 1 is Treitschke’s foundation for the century: Napoleonic reordering, Prussian reform, Wars of Liberation. Use it for Stein–Hardenberg–Scharnhorst measures, 1806–1814 military-political narrative, and the national-liberal memory of liberation against which he will judge the Bund in later volumes.
Series opening enlarged
Vol. I sets Treitschke’s nineteenth-century German story: Holy Roman wreckage, Rhine and reform eras, rise of Prussian military-administrative state, and the intellectual generation that will argue over nation and constitution. For this wiki the usable core is how Treitschke frames Prussia’s vocation before the detailed Bund police decades of later volumes.
Thematic blocks
Old Empire to new power map. Imperial circles, dualism with Austria, and the revolutionary/Napoleonic shock as the forced school of German politics.
Reform Prussia. Stein–Hardenberg era institutional change as Treitschke praises and criticises it—peasant, municipal, and military reform as state survival.
National culture. Literature and publicistic life as politics by other means; the author’s later National-Liberal lens already colours heroes and petty-state villains.
Bridge. Ends so vol. II–III can treat Restoration and Zollverein politics with a settled cast of Prussian expectations.
Use
Background for early-century Prussian entities and for concepts like German dualism; not the first stop for 1848 parliamentary detail (Sybel) or Austrian interior (Friedjung).

sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.title: Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. II: Bis zu den Karlsbader Beschlüssen
sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.content:
Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. II: Bis zu den Karlsbader Beschlüssen
Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896) — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. Zweiter Theil: Bis zu den Karlsbader Beschlüssen. — Leipzig: Verlag von S. Hirzel, 1882 (series Staatengeschichte der neuesten Zeit, Bd. 25).
The second volume covers the early Deutscher Bund (“German Confederation”) from the Vienna settlement’s aftermath through the Karlsbader Beschlüsse (“Carlsbad Decrees”) of 1819. Treitschke’s preface warns that the period’s density and party myths demand austere detail. The Inhalt organizes the continuation of Zweites Buch: Die Anfänge des Deutschen Bundes, 1814–1819 into sections on intellectual currents, the opening of the Bundestag (“Federal Diet”), Prussian state restoration, south German constitutional struggles, the Burschenschaft, the Aachen congress, Carlsbad, and the turn at the Prussian court—with appendices on Arndt, Blücher, the Teplitz punctation, and Hardenberg’s constitutional plan.
Geistige Strömungen der ersten Friedensjahre (Intellectual currents of the first peace years)
Treitschke opens the volume’s substance with the literary and scholarly character of the early restoration: poetry and the fine arts, the sciences, and the formation of a reading public that still lives on liberation’s memory while governments seek quiet. He treats the age’s culture as half national education and half substitute for missing political unity—great in philosophy and history, insufficient without a state that can act.
Eröffnung des Deutschen Bundestages (Opening of the Federal Diet)
European conditions after 1815 and the Frankfurt negotiations establish the Bund’s machinery. Treitschke portrays the Diet as an ambassadors’ congress under Austrian presidency, slow by design, capable of police coordination, incapable of national leadership. He follows credentials, early procedures, and the gap between Article 13’s constitutional promises and particularist practice. Prussian envoys appear torn between reform impulses and monarchical solidarity with Vienna.
Wiederherstellung des preußischen Staates (Restoration of the Prussian state)
A major section covers persons and parties at the Prussian court, administrative reorganization, the provinces, and the beginning of the constitutional dispute. Hardenberg’s reform legacy collides with aristocratic and clerical resistance; provincial diversity after 1815’s territorial gains complicates uniform policy. Treitschke values administrative modernization and army recovery while criticizing delay on a genuine national representation for Prussia—delay that will mature into the conflict of the 1840s.
Süddeutsche Verfassungskämpfe (South German constitutional struggles)
Württemberg’s “good old law,” Bavaria, Baden, Nassau, and Darmstadt receive linked chapters on early constitutionalism. Treitschke acknowledges the educational effect of chambers and public budgets yet stresses fragmentation: each constitution binds a dynasty and a landscape, not the German nation. Conflicts over military budgets, press, and ministerial responsibility prefigure later liberal programmes while remaining locked inside particular states.
Die Burschenschaft (The student fraternity movement)
Jahn and the gymnasts, Thuringia, Weimar and Jena, and the Wartburgfest (“Wartburg Festival”) of 1817 form Treitschke’s account of youthful nationalism. He balances sympathy for patriotic energy against distrust of demagogic excess and of programmes that undervalue monarchical states. The section prepares the shock of Kotzebue’s assassination and the conservative reaction that follows.
Der Aachener Kongress (The Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle)
Growing Austrian court influence, the evacuation of France, renewal of the Quadruple Alliance, and German affairs at Aachen show the Bund’s subordination to European great-power management. Treitschke reads Metternich’s system as stabilizing and stifling: order without national development.
Die Karlsbader Beschlüsse (The Carlsbad Decrees)
Oscillation in Berlin, first constitutional experiences in the south, Kotzebue’s murder, the Demagogenverfolgung (“persecution of demagogues”), and the Teplitz and Carlsbad conferences culminate in press censorship, university curators, and a federal investigative commission. Treitschke details how Prussian policy hardens, how Humboldt leaves office, and how Hardenberg’s constitutional plans shrink. The decrees mark, for him, the victory of preventive police over the liberation generation’s hopes—necessary against conspiracy in Metternich’s eyes, sterile for German power in Treitschke’s.
Der Umschwung am preußischen Hofe (The turn at the Prussian court)
Closing chapters tie Carlsbad to foreign reception, the fate of Hardenberg’s constitution draft, Humboldt’s dismissal, and the first Prussian customs treaty steps that quietly begin a different, economic path toward unity. Appendices print or discuss Arndt, Blücher on the Liège mutiny, the Teplitz punctation, and Hardenberg’s plans—source material for the narrative judgments above.
Significance for this wiki
Volume 2 is essential for 1815–1819: Diet, south German constitutions, Burschenschaft/Wartburg, Aachen, Carlsbad, Prussian court politics. Use with volume 3 for the 1820s aftermath and early Zollverein.

Economy beginnings

sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.title: Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. III: Bis zur Juli-Revolution
sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.content:
Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. III: Bis zur Juli-Revolution
Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896) — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. Dritter Theil: Bis zur Juli-Revolution. — Leipzig: Verlag von S. Hirzel, 1885. (Volume 29 of the series Staatengeschichte der neuesten Zeit.)
The third volume of Treitschke’s five-volume history, covering the decade 1819–1830 — the period from the Carlsbad Decrees to the eve of the July Revolution. Treitschke’s preface notes the enormous archival burden of this volume, drawing on the Berlin Geheime Staatsarchiv, the papers of the Baden Bundestag envoy Freiherr von Blittersdorff, the correspondence of the Nassau statesmen Marschall and Röntgen, and the memoirs of the Darmstadt minister du Thil, among others. The volume traces the consolidation of Metternich’s system, Prussia’s internal struggles after Hardenberg, the emergence of the Zollverein, and the first stirrings of the national movement that would erupt in 1830.
Drittes Buch — Österreichs Herrschaft und Preußens Erstarken, 1819–1830 (Austria’s Dominance and Prussia’s Strengthening)
Die Wiener Conferenzen (p. 3)
The Vienna Conferences (1819–1820)
Die Schluß-Acte des Deutschen Bundes — the Final Act of the German Confederation, completing the constitutional framework of the Bund. Kampf um das preußische Zollgesetz — the struggle over the Prussian tariff law; the conflict between free-trade and protectionist interests. Das Manuscript aus Süddeutschland. Hessische Verfassung — the “Manuscript from South Germany” (a reform pamphlet); the Hessian constitution. Die letzten Reformen Hardenberg’s — Hardenberg’s final reform efforts before his death.
Das Staatsschulden-Edikt und die Steuergesetze — the state debt edict and tax laws; fiscal reform in Prussia. Entwürfe der Kreis- und Gemeindeordnung — drafts of the district and municipal ordinances; local government reform. Reaction am Hofe. Der Kronprinz — reaction at the Prussian court; the Crown Prince (later Friedrich Wilhelm IV).
Troppau und Laibach (p. 131)
The Congresses of Troppau and Laibach (1820–1821)
Die Revolution in den romanischen Ländern — the revolutions in Southern Europe: Spain, Naples, Piedmont. Congreß von Troppau — the Congress of Troppau (Opava); Metternich’s intervention principle; the Troppau Protocol. Congreß von Laibach. Erhebung der Griechen — the Congress of Laibach (Ljubljana); the outbreak of the Greek War of Independence.
Der Ausgang des preußischen Verfassungskampfes (p. 198)
The outcome of the Prussian constitutional struggle
Verhandlungen mit dem römischen Stuhle. Clericale Bewegung — negotiations with the Roman Curia; the clerical movement and the Catholic question in Prussia. Die preußischen Provinzialstände — the Prussian provincial estates; the establishment of the eight provincial diets (1823). Die Großmächte und die Türkei — the great powers and the Ottoman Empire. Congreß von Verona — the Congress of Verona (1822); the Holy Alliance’s intervention in Spain.
Wangenheim und die Triaspolitik. Die Darmstädter Polizeikonferenzen — Wangenheim’s trias policy (a “third Germany” between Austria and Prussia); the Darmstadt police conferences. Demüthigung Württembergs. Epuration des Bundestags — the humiliation of Württemberg; the purge of the Bundestag.
Verlängerung der Karlsbader Beschlüsse. Reaction in Süddeutschland (p. 333)
Renewal of the Carlsbad Decrees; reaction in South Germany
Verwicklung im Orient (p. 333 cont.)
The Eastern entanglement; the Greek question intensifies
Preußische Zustände nach Hardenberg’s Tod (p. 361)
Prussian conditions after Hardenberg’s death (1822)
Der Staatsrath und die Provinziallandtage — the Council of State and the provincial diets. Der Hof. Agendenstreit. Geistiges Leben — the court; the liturgy conflict (Agendenstreit); intellectual life. Verwaltung und Heer. Berliner Leben — administration and army; Berlin’s social and cultural life. Die Demagogen-Verfolgung — the persecution of “demagogues”; continued surveillance of nationalist and liberal activists.
Motz’s deutsche Handelspolitik (p. 453)
Motz’s German trade policy; Friedrich von Motz, Prussian finance minister, and his drive toward a unified German customs area
Altständisches Stillleben in Norddeutschland (p. 486)
Old-estate quiet life in North Germany
Königreich Sachsen — the Kingdom of Saxony under the Restoration. page missing in OCR (p. 517). Die welfischen Lande. Georg IV. und Karl von Braunschweig — the Guelph lands; George IV of Hanover and Duke Karl of Brunswick. Mecklenburg. Oldenburg. Hansestädte — Mecklenburg, Oldenburg, and the Hanseatic cities (Hamburg, Bremen, Lübeck).
Erstes Anklopfen der schleswig-holsteinischen Frage (p. 586)
The first tap of the Schleswig-Holstein question; the early national conflict over the Elbe Duchies
8. Der Zollkrieg und die ersten Zollvereine
The tariff war and the first customs unions
König Ludwig von Baiern — King Ludwig I of Bavaria; his patronage of arts and his absolutist tendencies. Die Stuttgarter Zollconferenzen — the Stuttgart tariff conferences. Der preußisch-hessische und der bairisch-württembergische Zollverein — the Prussian-Hessian and Bavarian-Württemberg customs unions. Der mitteldeutsche Handelsverein — the Middle German Commercial Union (an anti-Prussian bloc).
Preußens Sieg. Preußisch-bairischer Handelsvertrag — Prussia’s victory; the Prussian-Bavarian commercial treaty.
Literarische Vorboten einer neuen Zeit (p. 419)
Literary heralds of a new era
Dichtung und Wissenschaft — poetry and science; the literary landscape of the late Restoration. Radicalismus und Judenthum — radicalism and Judaism; the beginnings of Jewish emancipation debates. Anfänge der Hegel’schen Philosophie — the beginnings of Hegelian philosophy; its growing influence on German intellectual life.
Preußen und die orientalische Frage (p. 427)
Prussia and the Eastern Question
Aufloderung der großen Allianz — the flare-up of the grand alliance; the breakdown of the Congress system. Russisch-türkischer Krieg. Friede von Adrianopel — the Russo-Turkish War (1828–1829); the Treaty of Adrianople. Navarin — the Battle of Navarino (1827); the destruction of the Turco-Egyptian fleet.
Beilagen (Appendices)

Schmalz und sein Rothen Adlerorden — Schmalz and his Order of the Red Eagle (a controversy around the Berlin law professor)
Die Burschenschaft und die Unbedingten — the Burschenschaft and the “Unconditionals” (radical student faction)
Metternich und die preußische Verfassung — Metternich and the Prussian constitution
Baiern und die Karlsbader Beschlüsse — Bavaria and the Carlsbad Decrees
Die Communalordnung vom Jahre 1820 — the municipal ordinance of 1820
Zur Geschichte des preußischen Verfassungskampfes — documents on the history of the Prussian constitutional struggle
Die Verlängerung der Karlsbader Beschlüsse — the renewal of the Carlsbad Decrees
Schön’s Denkschrift über die Provinzialministerien — Schön’s memorandum on the provincial ministries
Motz an Kurfürst Wilhelm I — Motz’s letter to Elector Wilhelm I of Hesse
Nebenius und der deutsche Zollverein — Nebenius and the German Customs Union

The volume closes with a Berichtigungen (errata) page.
Note on the text: The OCR is Fraktur-script German with occasional artefacts of the Google Books scanning process. Running headers repeat identically on facing pages. The original Fraktur printing and long-s (ſ) render correctly in the raw text. The table of contents (Inhalt) is split across two sections in the original.

sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.title: Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. IV: 1830–1840
sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.content:
Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. IV: 1830–1840
Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896) — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. Vierter Theil. — Leipzig: S. Hirzel (7th ed. print lineage 1919; Vorwort Berlin, 30 November 1889). Archive.org: deutschegeschich04treiuoft. Raw ~2.7 MB Fraktur OCR.
Theme of the book: Das Eindringen des französischen Liberalismus (“the penetration of French liberalism”)—Germany’s reaction to the July Revolution, constitutional ferment, consolidation of the Zollverein (“customs union”), and Prussia’s rising weight inside the Deutscher Bund (“German Confederation”).

Viertes Buch — 1830–1840
1. Die Juli-Revolution und der Weltfriede (July Revolution and world peace)
The overturn in France, its English and Belgian sequels, recognition of the July Monarchy, and the London conferences frame the European settlement after 1830. Revolution in Poland and Italy, the cooling of extremes, a proposal associated with Radowitz, and the side-shows of Antwerp and Ancona show how German cabinets read the new French order as both infection and fact of power.
2–3. Constitutional movement in North Germany; Prussia’s middle position
Uprising in Braunschweig (Brunswick), constitution and military regency in Hesse, the Saxon constitution, and the Hanoverian Staatsgrundgesetz (“fundamental state law”) mark northern constitutionalism. Provincial estates in Schleswig-Holstein appear under strain. Prussia holds a middle position: internal quiet, Polish border districts, and talks on federal military organisation (Bundeskriegswesen).
4–5. Upper Germany; re-fortifying the old powers
Unrest in Upper Hesse, the Baden Landtag of 1831, fermentation in Nassau, Württemberg, and Bavaria, and the Hambacher Fest (Hambach Festival, 1832) climax popular-national agitation. Reaction answers with the Sechs Artikel (“Six Articles”), the Frankfurter Wachensturm (Frankfurt guardhouse assault), the Luxemburg settlement, the meeting at Münchengrätz, and new Vienna ministerial conferences (1834).
6. Der deutsche Zollverein
Accessions and quarrels (Wittgenstein; Spielheim affairs), entry of the south-German customs group, Saxony and Thuringia, the decisive consolidation around 1834, struggle with Austria and Hanover, the Hanoverian Steuerverein (“tax/customs league”), and latecomers Baden, Nassau, and Frankfurt. Treitschke reads the Zollverein as Prussia’s real German policy beneath Diet rhetoric.
7–8. Das junge Deutschland; quiet years
Goethe’s death, the sovereign feuilleton, arts and sciences, Junghegelianer (“Young Hegelians”) and Strauss; then “quiet years”: Quadruple Alliance and eastern courts, Prussian conditions on the Rhine and in Posen, railways beside the Zollverein, demagogues and émigrés, middle-state diet troubles.
9–10. Hanoverian coup; Cologne bishop’s conflict
Repeal of the Staatsgrundgesetz, the Göttinger Sieben (“Göttingen Seven”), and what Treitschke calls the Diet’s self-emasculation. The kölnische Bischofsstreit (“Cologne bishop’s conflict”) with Archbishop Droste-Vischering, the ultramontane party, and the death of Friedrich Wilhelm III close the decade and open the next king’s tragedy.
Beilagen (appendices) include Baden policy after 1819, Canning and Germany, Cumberland and the fundamental law, Prince Wilhelm and Elise Radziwill, federal military files, Württemberg letters, the Frankfurt attentat, and notes of Friedrich Wilhelm.

Place in the series
Vol. IV covers the later Restoration and the 1830s shock through the threshold of Friedrich Wilhelm IV’s accession themes that vol. V then deepens. In this wiki it is the deposit for Bund routine after 1830, Zollverein politics as Treitschke tells them, demagogue persecutions’ long tail, and the German echo of the July Revolution without yet the full Vormärz tragedy framing of vol. V.
Narrative burdens (from existing structure + raw bulk)
After 1830. How German cabinets absorb French revolutionary contagion: press laws, police cooperation, student and press victims, and the diet’s confederal toolkit. Treitschke’s tone is national-liberal indictment of petty-state fear.
Customs and material unification. Continued Zollverein bargaining among German states—treaties, holdouts, Austrian exclusion as structural fact. This is political economy as state-building, parallel to List’s theoretical deposit but inside a narrative history.
Thrones and societies. Portraits of princes, ministers, and opposition publicists of the 1830s; religious and cultural conflicts that prefigure vol. V’s church chapters; foreign-policy subordination of the Bund to great-power quiet.
Bridge forward. Closes so that vol. V’s “days of expectation” in 1840 read as a false dawn rather than a fresh start. Entity work on mid-1830s liberals, Zollverein negotiators, and Bund presidents should lean here before Sybel’s 1848 machinery.
Use rules
Mine for 1830–c.1840 German Confederation political narrative. For economic doctrine proper, still prefer List; for 1848 assemblies, Sybel; for Austrian internal 1848–60, Friedjung/Springer.

sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.title: Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. V: 1840–1848
sources/treitschke-deutsche-geschichte-v.content:
Treitschke — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert, Vol. V: 1840–1848
Heinrich von Treitschke (1834–1896) — Deutsche Geschichte im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. Fünfter Theil. Bis zur März-Revolution. — Leipzig: S. Hirzel (4th ed. lineage 1899; Vorwort Berlin, 10 August 1894). Archive.org: deutschegeschic05trei. Raw ~2.8 MB Fraktur OCR.
Treitschke calls the reign of Friedrich Wilhelm IV down to March 1848 an erschütterndes Trauerspiel (“shattering tragedy”)—high hopes followed by collapse. The book is the Confederation’s crisis, church conflicts, economic change, and the storm-front of revolution.

Fünftes Buch — Friedrich Wilhelm IV, 1840–1848
1–3. Days of expectation; war scare; disappointment
Accession atmosphere: the king and his circle, homages in Königsberg and Berlin. The eastern crisis of the four powers, fortification of the Rhine, German armaments, peaceful solution and the Straits treaty, throne changes in Prussia and England. Then disappointment: Bavarian incompatibility law of 1841, ministry changes (Boyen, Rochow), Cologne cathedral festival, united committees, fight with Romanticism, “new life” in Berlin, Eichhorn ministry, provincial diets of 1843, the king’s constitutional plans, Arnim ministry.
4–5. Church split; realism in arts and sciences
Reconciliation gestures with the Vatican, ultramontane press, Deutschkatholizismus (“German Catholicism”), rationalists and free congregations, first Prussian general synod. Political press, poetry and drama, fine arts, historians and jurists, new natural science—Treitschke’s cultural weather map of the Vormärz.
6–7. Economy; Poland and Schleswig-Holstein
Expansion of the Zollverein (Luxemburg, Brunswick), protection versus free trade, railways and money, social unrest. After the Straits settlement: Galician risings, incorporation of Kraków, the Open Letter and Schleswig-Holstein’s rising—national questions that 1848 will inherit.
8–10. United Diet; decline of the Bund; European harbingers
Estate movement, the Patent, the Vereinigte Landstände / Vereinigter Landtag (“United Diet,” 1847) and its committee—Prussia’s first all-estates experiment. Decay of monarchical authority in middle states, scholars’ assemblies, Prussian federal-reform plans. Loosening alliances, Austria and France, the Swiss Sonderbundskrieg (“Sonderbund War”), Prussia and Switzerland—as European prologue to 1848.
Beilagen (“appendices”) cover Burschenschaft history, Prince Emil of Hesse, student Lenz, Nicholas I’s European policy, Brühl’s Roman talks, Heine anecdote, letters to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, Bernstorff and Schleswig-Holstein, the Prince of Prussia and constitutional plans, songs to Rückert.

What the volume is for in this wiki
Vol. V is the Vormärz bridge: everything that makes March 1848 intelligible inside Prussian-German politics without yet narrating the revolution’s street chronology (that burden shifts to Sybel, Springer, Friedjung). Use it when an entity needs the pre-revolutionary weather—United Diet deadlock, Rhine war scare memory, church splits, Zollverein enlargement, Schleswig-Holstein’s open letter climate—not when you need Frankfurt’s later constitutional arithmetic.
Deepened section map (deposit order)
Expectation and the Rhine. Accession of Friedrich Wilhelm IV, provincial homages, and the eastern crisis that produces German Rhine songs and fortification talk before a peaceful Straits settlement. Treitschke uses the scare to measure how far national feeling already outruns Bund institutions.
Disappointment and ministries. Bavarian incompatibility law, Boyen/Rochow/Eichhorn/Arnim personnel weather, Cologne cathedral as public festival politics, united committees and provincial diets of the early 1840s. The king’s constitutional mood never becomes a stable parliamentary bargain; Romantic court culture and bureaucratic continuity share the stage.
Church and culture. Ultramontane press after partial reconciliation gestures with Rome; Deutschkatholizismus and free congregations; first Prussian general synod themes; press, poetry, historiography, and natural science as the cultural front of the same decade. Treitschke’s “realism” chapters are not digressions—they are his claim that mental climate and state crisis move together.
Economy and border nations. Zollverein entries (Luxemburg, Brunswick in the narrative frame), protection/free-trade polemic, railways and credit, early social unrest. Galicia, Kraków’s fate after the risings, and Schleswig-Holstein’s national conflict keep non-Prussian national questions inside a “German history” volume.
United Diet and Bund decay. The Patent and Vereinigter Landtag of 1847—estates opposition, refusal of blank credits, committee politics—as Prussia’s dress rehearsal for constitutional conflict. Parallel decay of monarchical authority in middle states, scholars’ assemblies, and abortive federal-reform talk. European harbingers: loosened alliances, Swiss Sonderbundskrieg, Prussian embarrassment on the Swiss file.
Beilagen. Documentary and anecdotal appendices (Burschenschaft strands, Nicholas I’s European attitude, Schleswig correspondence, constitutional letters) that entity pages should mine before inventing colour.
How to cite from it
Prefer this volume for 1840–early 1848 Prussian-German texture. Do not stretch it into post-March Frankfurt detail. Pair with Sybel vol. 1+ for the revolution proper and with List/Zollverein pages for economic doctrine Treitschke only narrates as politics.
